docs.title: Home
docs.text: Know which services a change breaks before it ships.

docs.title: What is Pacto?
docs.text:
Pacto tells you which services a change breaks before it ships, and checks what is actually running. You describe each service once, in a contract: one YAML file that says who owns the service, what it offers, which services it calls and which of their versions it accepts. It lives in the OCI registry you already run. pacto diff says whether a change is breaking and pacto impact says which consumers it breaks once Pacto can see your fleet. The runtime checks compare a running service with its contract.

When you are ready, Pacto's opt-in delivery component (alpha, Kubernetes) ships the changes the contract graph clears. Flux or Argo CD still apply every version. GitlessOps means signed artifacts in your registry and evidence decide which version runs where, while your code and manifests stay in git. Delivery starts by watching and climbs the autonomy ladder, from observe (watch only) to autonomous, set per Stage. A person confirms every step up. A change that breaks a consumer waits for that consumer's owners, and when Pacto cannot see enough it says Unknown and waits for a person.

A contract looks like this:

pacto.yaml
pactoVersion: "2.0"

service:
  name: checkout
  version: 4.2.0
  owner: { team: commerce, dri: alice }

interfaces:
  - name: rest-api
    type: openapi
    ref: interfaces/openapi.yaml       # the OpenAPI document you already maintain
    visibility: public

dependencies:
  - name: auth
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/auth-pacto
    required: true
    compatibility: "^2.0.0"            # the range this revision accepts

docs.title: Who breaks when a dependency ships a new version
docs.text:
The compatibility range above records which versions of auth this revision accepts. Each consumer's range lets Pacto answer per consumer when auth is about to ship 3.0:

$ pacto impact ./auth-2.1.0 ./auth-3.0.0 --local .
Impact: auth 2.1.0 -> 3.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 1
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Affected consumers (2):
  checkout                     direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=commerce
  reporting                    direct     confidence=contractual  compat=compatible   owner=analytics
    note: compatible only means the range >=2.0.0 <4.0.0 accepts 3.0.0; this change is BREAKING, so check that reporting does not use what it removes or changes
Release gate: unverified
unverified: the change is BREAKING and 2 consumers depend on auth, but none is shown to be both incompatible and running. Review each consumer, and add a source that knows where services run (for example --target-state) to tell deployed impact apart

pacto diff lists the breaking change itself. checkout accepts ^2.0.0 and 3.0.0 falls outside it. reporting accepts >=2.0.0 <4.0.0 and 3.0.0 is inside, though a range match does not prove reporting avoids what changed. direct means each one declares auth itself. contractual means the answer comes from the declared ranges alone, without a runtime observation of the call. The folder says nothing about where the consumers run, so the release gate is unverified and the command exits 2.

See who breaks in CI for the sources pacto impact needs.

You check one file when you write it, compare it with the previous revision and then compare it with what is running.

docs.title: What each command answers
docs.text:
Command Question it answers pacto validate Is this contract legal? pacto diff Is my change breaking for anyone who uses it? pacto impact Which consumers, and where do they run? The operator, a controller you install in the cluster Does reality still match what was declared?

validate and diff pay off at one service; impact and the graph of who calls whom pay off at the second consumer.

docs.title: Check what is actually running
docs.text:
Pacto checks what a running service does on the network against what its contract says, on Linux, and reports only what it can confirm:

What it catches Finding A process reports healthy but nothing listens on the declared port INTERFACE_ABSENT A declared dependency the service keeps failing to reach DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE A call to another Pacto service no dependency declares (seen by the node agent or pacto agent; a warning, so the contract reads Warning rather than NonCompliant) DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED 
pacto run --contract ./payments --bind api=8080 --fail-on noncompliant -- ./payments-server

Pacto watches TCP connections in the Linux kernel with eBPF (small, safe programs the kernel runs on events). The kernel watcher reads connection metadata, never payloads or secrets. The optional probes read only the response they need. When it cannot see something, it says so. Run it three ways: pacto run wraps one command (a laptop, a CI job), pacto agent watches a Docker host or a server and the Kubernetes operator can deploy the same agent on every node (opt-in). See Runtime conformance for the kernel and privilege requirements.

docs.title: What delivery needs
docs.text:
Contracts work anywhere, and the checks above work on Linux. Delivery, the part that moves versions, is alpha: its settings and commands may still change. It needs:

  • Kubernetes 1.30 or later, with Flux (Argo CD works too, as an experimental option).
  • Your container registry, to hold contracts and versions.
  • For signed records, and so for the two automatic levels, a registry that serves the OCI Referrers API: the feature that lets a registry list the files attached to an image, here the signed records. zot, an open source registry, serves it. GitHub's registry does not serve it today, so a Stage that uses it stays on observe or advise. For any other registry, check its documentation for "referrers API".
  • For checks on error rates after a release, traces in Mira, an OpenTelemetry trace store, or a check you call over HTTP. Without them Pacto still checks the contract.
  • For a person to approve anything, a cluster that can tell how recently that person signed in to your company login. That works where you set the Kubernetes API server's flags yourself (tested on kind). EKS, GKE and AKS are not verified yet. Where it does not work, nobody can approve, so no Stage can move up the ladder. See where approving works.

To try it, start a new service on observe, where Pacto moves nothing, or open the live demo in your browser.

docs.title: Agents take the same path
docs.text: An AI agent asks for a delivery change over MCP the way a person or a CI job does: it creates an Operation, and the promoter plans and checks it. Agents get no approve tool, and the admission policies the chart installs with delivery refuse an approval from an agent. Kubernetes RBAC still governs what the agent's identity may do outside Pacto. Agents take the same path says what the policies close and what your platform closes itself. The delivery security model gives the detail.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
You want to Read Know what Pacto is and whether it fits Why Pacto, Who breaks when a dependency ships, How Pacto relates to other tools and the live demo Give many existing services a contract Generate contracts from what you already have Pactify your first service (give it a contract and connect it to delivery) Quickstart, then Pactify a service Approve or unblock a change Decide, unfreeze and roll back Verify a record Check a record without Pacto Drive Pacto from an AI agent AI assistants (MCP) Write and check contracts For developers and the contract reference

New words are explained in the glossary.

Pacto delivery builds on Flux's Gitless GitOps, ConfigHub's configuration as data and Anthropic's Scion; the manifesto says what it takes from each. The contract graph is ours, and all of Pacto is open source under the MIT licence.

docs.title: Ladder reference
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

This page lists the rules behind the autonomy ladder: its fields, blockers and commands.

docs.title: Levels and what each one changes
docs.text:
Level (status.level) Automatic promotes Promote not raised by a person observe none Rejected: GitOps owns the version field advise none Held for a person (approve) auto-nonbreaking NON_BREAKING changes only Held for a person unless the change is NON_BREAKING autonomous any plan that proceeds Same floors as any promote

On every level the holds in Why you were asked stay, and an automatic rollback that cannot run freezes the Stage. The level never rejects rollbacks or break-glass overrides.

docs.title: Stage fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning spec.startLevel Level a new Stage starts on, read once while status.level is empty. Default observe. Any level is accepted, because creating a Stage is an admin action. A Stage whose status is lost seeds back to this level, so an automatic start level comes back automatic. pacto init --delivery always writes observe spec.autonomy.proposeAfter How many qualifying changes earn a proposal. Default 10, from 1 to 20 status.level Current level. After the start, only delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy operations change it status.observedRevision On observe: the digest the GitOps source reports and since when Pacto saw it status.shadow On observe: the newest 20 "would have" plans, with when the source reported each and its shadow verification status.proposal The next level Pacto proposes with its evidence, or the blockers that stop it

kubectl get stages shows a Level column.

docs.title: When Pacto proposes the next level
docs.text:
N is proposeAfter. Evidence comes from the Stage's own status windows, which hold at most 20 entries.

From → to Needs observe → advise The newest N shadow entries the source reported all verified, none failed; the applyRef labelled; an observed digest advise → auto-nonbreaking The newest N concluded promotes all Succeeded and verified; no automatic rollback or failed digest in the window; not frozen; RecordStoreReady=True auto-nonbreaking → autonomous The same, plus at least one cleared breaking promote in the window; the newest plan had a complete graph and no uncontracted callers

A cleared breaking promote is a promote whose change was not NON_BREAKING, whose impact check passed and that then verified.

docs.title: Blockers
docs.text: Kind Meaning Fix missing-contract A caller seen at runtime has no contract pacto init for it undeclared-range A consumer declares no usable version range Add compatibility to its dependency unlabelled-apply-ref The applyRef lacks delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref See Leaving observe no-observed-digest The GitOps source reports no digest Point the source at a digest-addressed artifact no-record-store The recorder is not ready Turn on the recorder needs-verified Not enough verified changes yet Wait needs-cleared-breaking No cleared breaking promote in the window Approve one breaking change on auto-nonbreaking incident A failure or rollback in the window Wait for N clean changes partial-graph The newest plan could not see the whole graph Fix the missing sources

docs.title: Changing the level
docs.text:
A level change is an operation of type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy:

pacto delivery propose --type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy --stage payments-prod --to advise
pacto delivery approve <operation>
  • One level at a time. A jump of two levels is Rejected.
  • From must equal the current level, or the request is Rejected as stale.
  • Raising needs an Approval from a person other than the raiser, from the team the running contract declares. If Pacto cannot read that contract, the verdict is Unknown.
  • A raise passes only when status.proposal names exactly the next level and the Stage's status still earns it when the raise is planned. Anything else is Unknown and needs accept-unknown.
  • Raising to auto-nonbreaking or autonomous without RecordStoreReady=True is Rejected.
  • Lowering needs no approval. An agent may not lower to observe. The promoter never raises, and lowers only one level from an automatic level (the step-down below); admission enforces both.
  • Lowering to observe clears status.pointer: GitOps owns the version again, and leaving observe adopts what the source then reports.
  • The approval is checked again just before the level moves. A proposal that lapsed in between sends the request back to a person.

docs.title: Step-down
docs.text: The step-down is a delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy operation the controller raises when a promote with no approval (raised by the promoter or an agent) has a confirmed Fail on an automatic level. It lowers the Stage one level, never below advise, needs no approval and restarts the proposal window.

docs.title: Leaving observe
docs.text:
The raise from observe to advise also sets status.pointer to the observed digest, so Pacto owns exactly what was running. It needs two things in place first, as Ship the next version does step by step:

Applier Version field git must stop setting Flux OCIRepository spec.ref, removed from the git manifest Argo CD Application /spec/source/targetRevision, under ignoreDifferences with RespectIgnoreDifferences=true

The applyRef carries the label delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref=<stage name>. From then on, admission lets only the promoter and break-glass change the version.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy operation is signed like any other when the recorder is on. The record carries the Stage policy, the approver, the pacto.autonomy verdict with the evidence it cited, and outcome.level ({from, to}). Check one record without Pacto gives the commands; read .predicate.outcome.level from the payload.

Shadow entries are status, not records.

docs.title: The autonomy ladder
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Pacto starts by watching your changes. It earns more freedom one step at a time, and a person confirms each step up. This page explains those steps, called levels. Words in links are defined in the glossary.

docs.title: The four levels
docs.text:
Each Stage sits on one level.

Level What Pacto does Who moves a version observe Works out what it would do for every change and moves nothing Your GitOps tool, as today advise Shows each new version and what it would do with it A person asks, or approves what an AI agent asked for auto for non-breaking (auto-nonbreaking) Ships non-breaking changes on its own Pacto, for non-breaking changes; a person for the rest autonomous Ships every change the contracts clear on its own Pacto, unless a consumer would break or a check is Unknown

Once Pacto moves versions, the same safety rules hold on every level: a change that could break a consumer, or that a check could not judge, waits for the teams Why you were asked names. The level only decides how often a person is asked when the contracts say a change is safe.

docs.title: Manifests and the levels
docs.text: The levels judge only the contract. The manifests that ship with it play no part. A version with the same contract and new manifests (a new ClusterRoleBinding, say) is non-breaking, so an automatic level ships it with no person. What those manifests can do is what the account Flux applies them as may do. Give the Kustomization a namespaced serviceAccountName, as pacto init --delivery does, and keep the key that signs pacto publish as safe as the cluster: it is the root of trust. The Stage's Mediated condition is False with the reason ApplierUnscoped while the Kustomization runs as Flux itself.

docs.title: Cold start: begin by watching
docs.text:
A new Stage starts on observe. Connecting a service to delivery with pacto init --delivery (part of pactifying it) always puts it there. Flux or Argo CD keep doing what they do today, and Pacto changes nothing.

For each version your GitOps tool runs, Pacto writes down what it would have done: ship it, or hold it and ask a team. Then it runs the checks it would run after a real release. The Pacto dashboard, a web page, shows "what Pacto would have done" next to what really happened. These notes are advice only.

Watching also shows what is missing. If Pacto sees a service call yours and that caller has no contract, Pacto cannot know which versions it accepts. A breaking change then waits for a person, and Pacto names the caller so you can give it a contract.

docs.title: Earned autonomy: Pacto proposes, a person decides
docs.text:
Pacto proposes the next level when the evidence supports it. By default the evidence is the last 10 versions on that Stage, and Pacto waits until there are 10. For a service that rarely releases, the platform team can lower that number, down to 1:

  • observe to advise: the versions GitOps ran all passed Pacto's checks.
  • advise to auto for non-breaking: the versions Pacto moved all passed their checks, with no rollback and no failure.
  • auto for non-breaking to autonomous: the same, plus at least one breaking change that the contracts cleared, a person approved and that then passed its checks, and no caller seen at runtime without a contract.

When something blocks a proposal, Pacto says what and how to fix it, for example "this caller has no contract".

A proposal changes nothing by itself. To act on it, someone asks for the raise in the dashboard or with pacto delivery propose, and a different person of the service's owner team approves it. Someone can also ask for a raise Pacto has not proposed; then the approver must accept the unknown. A level goes up one step at a time. Raising a Stage to either automatic level also needs the recorder, so every grant of autonomy leaves a signed record that anyone can check without Pacto.

Lowering a level needs no approval. A person can do it at any time. An AI agent can too, except down to observe: once git stops setting the version (see Leaving observe), a Stage on observe has nothing moving it at all, and only a person may stop a service that way.

An agent previews these changes with the MCP tool pacto_delivery_operation_plan and asks for them with pacto_delivery_operation_propose (see Publish and delivery servers). Its Operation goes through the same plan and admission policies as a person's, as Agents take the same path explains.

docs.title: Step-down: one failure costs one level
docs.text:
On every level where Pacto moves versions, a promote that fails its checks after release is rolled back once or the Stage freezes, as What happens to a change explains.

If the failed version is one Pacto shipped with no person, the Stage also drops one level, whether it was rolled back or froze. Autonomous goes back to auto for non-breaking, and auto for non-breaking goes back to advise. The drop is recorded like any other change and needs no approval. The count of good versions starts again from zero, so Pacto has to earn the level back.

A version that shipped with no person and that an AI agent rolls back before its checks judge it counts as failed too: it is never promoted on that Stage again and the Stage drops a level. The failure stays on the Stage's record.

An Unknown never causes a step-down, because Unknown means Pacto could not see enough to judge the version.

docs.title: Leaving observe
docs.text: On observe, your GitOps tool still writes which version runs. To leave it, a person removes the version from the GitOps manifest in git and labels the object Pacto then writes, once enough versions passed their checks. Someone asks for the raise to advise and a second person approves it. Between those two steps nothing moves the version, so do them promptly. Ship the next version gives the commands, and the ladder reference names the field and the label for Flux and Argo CD.

docs.text:

  • Decide, unfreeze and roll back: answer the questions Pacto asks
  • Ladder reference: the exact rules, fields and commands

docs.title: Generate contracts from what you already have
docs.text:
pacto init reads the files a service folder already holds and writes a contract for it. It takes many folders in one run. This guide takes a folder of existing services, such as services/* in a monorepo, to one checked contract per service.

Every command here runs on your machine. It writes plan.json, files in the service folders and, with --cluster, drafts in the --out folder. It publishes nothing.

docs.title: 1. Take an inventory
docs.text:
Plan every folder at once. --plan changes nothing:

pacto init --plan --output-format json services/* > plan.json
jq -r '.results[] | [.service, .mode, (.unknown | length)] | @tsv' plan.json

checkout  pactify  2
ledger    blank    1
notifier  blank    0
payments  pactify  2

Each entry in results has a mode. pactify means init found a Dockerfile or Kubernetes manifests and read the contract from them. blank means it found neither and plans a starter template with placeholder values. The found, dependencies, unknown and next lists say what init read, which services the workload calls, what it could not tell and what a person still has to do. List every open question across the fleet:

jq -r '.results[] | .service as $s | .unknown[] | "\($s): \(.)"' plan.json

docs.title: What init reads
docs.text:
Input Contract fields Dockerfile (or Dockerfile.*, *.Dockerfile) an image artifact under publish.artifacts, built from the Dockerfile Kubernetes YAML with a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job or CronJob service.name from the workload, service.version from the image tag, the registry from the image, workload and a manifests artifact that copies the YAML files The team label on the workload service.owner.team The workload's environment, with the ConfigMaps in the folder that it reads a configuration schema at configuration/schema.json, each value as its default An environment value that names another in-cluster service dependencies, with the range from that service's contract in --fleet, or the placeholder ^1.0.0 A readiness, liveness or startup probe a health capability A file named exactly openapi or swagger, with a .yaml, .yml or .json extension one openapi interface kustomization.yaml the manifests artifact keeps the folder layout, and init asks you to set the Kustomization's spec.path

Init reads only these. A file such as api/openapi.v1.yaml is missed, and state stays for you to write. A placeholder range is named in a comment above the dependency and under unknown.

Init skips the files and folders that the service's .pactoignore lists. It also skips every folder that holds a Chart.yaml, and documents in the backstage.io and skaffold API groups, such as catalog-info.yaml and skaffold.yaml.

docs.title: 2. Prepare the folders init cannot read
docs.text:
Init keeps a pacto.yaml that is already there, so prepare these folders before step 3.

Helm charts. Init does not render charts. It skips each chart's templates, subcharts and CRDs and names every chart under unknown, so a chart-only folder plans as blank. Render the chart into the folder, then init reads the result:

mkdir -p services/ledger/k8s
helm template --include-crds ledger services/ledger/chart \
  > services/ledger/k8s/rendered.yaml

The contract then publishes the rendered file, so render again when the chart changes. The unknown line that names the chart stays after you render it. To publish the chart itself, add it under publish.artifacts as a chart (Publish).

Compose files. Init does not read compose.yaml. A Compose-only folder gets the blank template. The blank template writes pactoVersion: "2.0" and no publish section, so pacto publish refuses it until you set pactoVersion: "2.1" and add publish (Publish).

docs.title: 3. Write the contracts
docs.text:
pacto init services/*

Init prints what it found per folder and ends with a summary table. It only adds files and missing .pactoignore lines, so you can run it again after you fix a folder.

Check the build command before you publish

Init treats any other YAML file with an apiVersion and a kind as a Kubernetes manifest, such as a kind cluster configuration, and lists it in the manifests artifact's build.command. List such a file in the folder's .pactoignore before you run init. In a pacto.yaml that init already wrote, read the cp list and remove any file that is not a manifest your cluster applies.

docs.title: 4. Fill in what init could not tell
docs.text:
Work through the unknown list of each service.

  • Owner. Write service.owner.team, or pass --owner when one team owns every folder in the run.

  • Interfaces. The openapi-infer plugin writes interfaces/openapi.yaml from FastAPI or Huma code and needs the pacto.yaml from step 3. Run it from the service folder with the project's dependencies installed:

    cd services/payments
pacto generate openapi-infer . -o .

    Then add the interface to pacto.yaml:

    interfaces:
  - name: api
    type: openapi
    ref: interfaces/openapi.yaml

  • Configuration. Init's schema lists the environment only. schema-infer writes a JSON Schema from a config file (For developers).

  • Dependencies. Replace each placeholder compatibility with the versions the service accepts.

Then check every contract and see who declares each service:

for d in services/*/; do pacto validate "$d"; done
pacto init --plan services/payments --fleet services

--fleet reads the other contracts and lists the services that declare this one under Used by.

docs.title: Draft from a running cluster
docs.text:
pacto init --cluster --namespace <ns> --out <dir> drafts a contract for each workload in the namespace that no Pacto resource describes, in <dir>/<ns>/<name>, from your current kubeconfig context. Without --namespace it reads every namespace, kube-system included. It lists Services, EndpointSlices, Pactos and node runtime observations in every namespace even with --namespace, so your identity needs cluster-wide list on them. It needs that permission even when the Pacto CRDs are not installed.

Each draft holds a manifests.yaml with the workload and its Services as the cluster returns them, without namespace, uid or status. It also holds a pacto.yaml and a .pactoignore. --plan writes nothing. A workload that a Pacto targets is skipped.

Without the node agent, dependencies come only from environment values, as in a folder. The draft holds no ConfigMaps, so each one the workload reads is named under unknown and its keys stay out of the configuration schema. A value such as host:6443 matches whether or not host is a Service, so a control-plane endpoint can become a dependency. Check each one.

docs.title: From an agent
docs.text: The MCP tool pacto_create with pactify: true and paths plans the same contracts for an agent. It plans only, unless the agent sets dry_run to false (AI assistants).

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Goal Page Publish a contract and connect it to delivery Pactify a service Check every change in CI Put it in your repository Write the fields init leaves out Contract sections

docs.title: Put it in your repository
docs.text: Add Pacto to your build pipeline (CI) so a pull request that would break the services using yours fails its checks, and every merge publishes a version. This page assumes you have a contract, pacto.yaml, from Pactify a service. The examples use the names from that page: the contract is published to oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/my-service, the publish.bundle field of pacto.yaml.

docs.title: What to commit
docs.text:
Commit what pacto init wrote (pacto.yaml, .pactoignore, .gitignore, delivery/ and any files the contract points to, such as an OpenAPI document).

If your contract lists dependencies, also run pacto lock . and commit the pacto.lock it writes. It records the exact published build of every contract yours depends on, so every build checks against the same ones. It is optional: without it, Pacto looks dependencies up fresh each time. See Lockfile.

docs.title: Declare your API first
docs.text:
pacto diff sees API changes only in the interfaces the contract declares. If pacto init did not find your OpenAPI document, add it to pacto.yaml yourself, with the path from the repository root:

interfaces:
  - name: rest-api
    type: openapi
    ref: api/openapi.yaml
    visibility: public          # other teams may call it

Other interface types and fields are in Contract sections.

docs.title: On every pull request
docs.text:
The snippets below are steps of a GitHub Actions job, after actions/checkout. Install Pacto first; the token avoids GitHub's limit on anonymous API calls, which shared CI runners hit:

- name: Install Pacto
  run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh | bash
  env:
    GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

Add two checks. The second reads your registry, so give the job a login. These variables work for any registry; on GitHub's, the built-in token will do:

env:
  PACTO_REGISTRY_USERNAME: ${{ github.actor }}
  PACTO_REGISTRY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

- name: Validate the contract
  run: pacto validate .

- name: Check for breaking changes
  run: pacto diff oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/my-service .

pacto validate catches missing or malformed fields, fields that contradict each other and failed policies, the rules your platform team may set for every contract.

pacto diff compares the contract in the pull request (the second argument) with the last one you published (the first). With no version after the name, it picks the highest published version. It exits 1 only when the change is BREAKING (POTENTIAL_BREAKING and NON_BREAKING pass), a breaking change, so the check fails. Your branch protection rules decide whether a failed check blocks the merge.

Until the first version is published there is nothing to compare with and pacto diff fails, so add this step after your first pacto publish. To compare two folders with no registry, run pacto diff ./main ./feature-branch.

docs.title: On every pull request: who breaks
docs.text:
pacto diff says whether a change is breaking. pacto impact says which consumers it breaks, from the consumer contracts it can see. Your repository holds only your contract, so name each consumer's published contract with --root, one per consumer, and keep that list current. The step needs jq, which GitHub-hosted runners include, and the same login variables:

- name: Check who the change breaks
  run: |
    pacto impact oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/my-service . \
      --root oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/checkout \
      --root oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/reporting \
      --output-format json > impact.json || [ $? -eq 2 ]
    jq -r '.consumers[] | select(.compatibilityVerdict == "incompatible") | "\(.service) (owner \(.owner // "unknown")) accepts \(.compatibility)"' impact.json
    jq -e '.classification != "BREAKING" or all(.consumers[]; .compatibilityVerdict != "incompatible")' impact.json

The first jq lists each consumer whose compatibility range rejects the new version, with its owner. The second fails the step when the change is BREAKING and at least one consumer is incompatible. A consumer whose range Pacto cannot evaluate, such as one with an invalid contract, reads unknown and does not fail the step.

pacto impact ends in a release gate and exits on it: 0 clear, 1 blocked and 2 unverified. Contracts from --root carry no targets, so a BREAKING change with consumers exits 2, and GitHub Actions fails a step on any non-zero exit. || [ $? -eq 2 ] lets the step go on to the jq checks after a 2. A 1, for a blocked change or a command that could not run, still fails the step.

To gate on what is deployed, keep the --root flags and add a source of targets: --k8s reads the Pacto resources in the current cluster and --evidence-url reads an Evidence Server. Exit 1 then fails the step when an incompatible consumer runs somewhere. --target-state reads targets from a fixture file, for demos and tests.

docs.title: After a merge: publish
docs.text:
With the same login variables:

- name: Set up a Docker builder
  run: docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container

- name: Publish a version
  run: |
    echo "$COSIGN_KEY" > cosign.key      # publish.sign reads it from the repository root
    pacto publish
  env:
    COSIGN_KEY: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY }}
    COSIGN_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_PASSWORD }}

pacto publish builds the image, pushes it to your registry with your Kubernetes files and the contract, and signs them; delivery only rolls out versions published this way. Store the contents of cosign.key and its password as CI secrets. On GitHub, the job also needs permissions: packages: write to push.

It never overwrites a published version, and a merge that does not raise service.version in pacto.yaml, such as a docs change, fails here. Raise the version with each change you want to ship, or run this step only when pacto.yaml changed. See Publish a version.

If you use contracts without delivery, pacto push oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/my-service -p . uploads only the contract.

docs.title: A breaking change you need to ship
docs.text:
Sometimes a breaking change is the right call. Give it a new major version (1.4.2 becomes 2.0.0): pacto publish refuses a breaking change with a smaller version. With delivery, the change then waits for the teams whose services it would break. Do not remove fields or change pactoVersion to get past the check.

pacto diff still fails with the new major version, because the change is still breaking, so that pull request's check stays red. Merge it the way your repository lets a reviewer override a failed check, such as an admin bypass. Or make the diff step informational (continue-on-error: true on GitHub) and let pacto publish be the gate, since it refuses a breaking change without a new major version.

docs.title: GitHub Actions and other CI systems
docs.text: The GitHub Actions integration wraps these steps in a ready-made action that also installs Pacto and comments on the pull request. For GitLab CI, Jenkins or CircleCI, install Pacto with the installer script and run the same commands.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text:
Every command accepts -v / --verbose for debug-level logging and --help for detailed usage. --output-format is a global flag taking text (the default), json or markdown.

What --output-format guarantees

Read this before you parse Pacto's output in a script.

  • json describes a successful result. When a command fails to produce its result, for example because a reference is unreachable or pacto.lock is missing, the error goes to stderr as plain text and stdout stays empty, whatever --output-format says. A negative verdict is still a result: pacto validate on an invalid contract and pacto diff on a breaking change both print their whole JSON document to stdout and exit 1. An empty stdout tells you there is nothing to parse. Read stdout when it is non-empty, and read the exit code for the verdict.
  • Only pacto diff implements markdown, for posting a diff as a CI comment. Every other command renders text.
  • Keys are camelCase in every command ("path", "valid", "errors", "upToDate"). Before v4, init, validate, pack, pull and push emitted capitalised keys ("Path", "Valid").
  • An unrecognised value is rejected. --output-format yaml exits 1 with unsupported output format "yaml" before the command runs.

The interactive and side-effecting commands (login, logout, update, mcp, dashboard) inherit the flag from the root command and always emit text.

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text:
--config string          config file path
  -h, --help                   help for pacto
      --no-anim                disable animations
      --no-cache               disable OCI bundle cache
      --output-format string   output format (text, json, markdown) (default "text")
  -v, --verbose                enable verbose output

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Pacto exits 0, 1 or 2, apart from pacto run (below). 0 means the command produced its result and the result was acceptable. 1 means the check failed or the command could not run, so the exit status alone cannot distinguish "the check failed" from "the command could not run". 2 means pacto impact could not show that a breaking change is safe, and no other command exits 2 for its own result. pacto run exits with the exit code of the command it wraps, whatever it is, or 1 when that command exits 0 and the final verdict fails --fail-on.

Exits 1 Exits 0 pacto diff where the overall classification is BREAKING a POTENTIAL_BREAKING or NON_BREAKING diff pacto validate reporting at least one error validation that reported only warnings pacto lock --check on a stale lockfile, or with none at all (LOCK_MISSING) a lockfile that is up to date pacto impact where the gate is blocked: a BREAKING change reaches a consumer that does not accept the new version and runs on a known target pacto impact where the gate is clear: the change is not BREAKING, or the snapshot is complete and no service depends on the changed one any command that could not run, for example on an unresolvable reference, an unreadable bundle or an unknown flag Exits 2 pacto impact where the gate is unverified: a BREAKING change that nothing is shown to block, on a partial answer or with consumers none of which is shown to be safe

Two cases affect CI gates:

  • A pacto diff against a missing reference exits 1, the same as a breaking change.
  • pacto impact exits 1 only when the change is breaking and a source that knows where services run shows an incompatible consumer on a target. Sources that know no targets, such as --local alone, cannot show that, so a breaking change with consumers exits 2. A job that gates on deployed impact alone can treat 2 as a pass; any other job fails on it.

Use stdout to tell a verdict from a failure. A command that produced a verdict writes it to stdout and puts a one-line summary on stderr. A command that could not run leaves stdout empty:

Invocation Exit stdout stderr pacto diff --output-format json OLD NEW (breaking) 1 the full JSON result breaking changes detected pacto diff --output-format json oci://…/absent:1.0.0 NEW 1 empty old contract: artifact not found: …

In a script, branch on stdout when it is non-empty, and treat an empty stdout with exit 1 as a tool failure.

docs.title: OCI version resolution
docs.text:
All commands that accept oci:// references support automatic version resolution. When a reference omits the tag (for example oci://ghcr.io/acme/svc-pacto with no :1.0.0), pacto queries the registry for available tags and selects the highest semver version.

For dependency references declared with a compatibility constraint, only tags satisfying the constraint are considered. For example, a dependency with compatibility: "^2.0.0" and available tags 1.0.0, 2.0.0, 2.3.0, 3.0.0 resolves to 2.3.0.

Resolution ignores non-semver tags such as latest and main. Digest-pinned references (@sha256:...) and explicitly tagged references are used as-is.

Constraints apply to the CLI's dependency graph

The CLI applies compatibility constraints when it resolves a contract's declared dependencies, for example in pacto graph. The dashboard's version discovery selects the highest semver tag and ignores per-dependency compatibility constraints. Root-contract pulls (a tagless top-level oci:// ref) also select the highest semver tag with no constraint.

docs.title: pacto agent
docs.text:
Runs until interrupted. Watches TCP listeners and outbound connection outcomes with an eBPF program, attributes each socket to the workload that created it (a Kubernetes pod, a container, a systemd unit or a pacto run session, from its cgroup, or from its network namespace when the cgroup names none) and publishes a snapshot every --publish-interval. --sink kubernetes writes the node's NodeRuntimeObservation status (pods only; what the Pacto operator's node agent DaemonSet runs); --sink stdout prints one JSON snapshot per line.

--sink local and --sink evidence check workloads against their contracts on this host. The workloads come from --bindings (a YAML list of {match: {unit|container|cgroup|session|pid}, contract, host, interfaces: {name: port}, dependencies: {name: host:port}}) and with --docker from running containers labelled dev.pacto.contract=, dev.pacto.bind.<interface>=<port> and dev.pacto.dep.<dependency>=. Interfaces and dependencies are judged from the kernel's view, health and metrics capabilities by probing the bound port; a negative is reported once it persists for --stabilization-window. --sink local prints every target's compliance and findings each interval in --output-format; --sink evidence signs each target's evidence and sends it to an Evidence Server, which needs contracts pinned as oci://...@sha256:<digest>. Envelope sequences start at the wall clock in nanoseconds and count up, so they keep increasing across restarts as long as the clock does.

Needs Linux 5.11 or later with BTF, or 5.8 or later with BTF and root or CAP_SYS_RESOURCE; root (or BPF, PERFMON and SYS_PTRACE); and the host's /proc and cgroupfs.

pacto agent [flags]

Examples:

  pacto agent --sink stdout --publish-interval 5s
  pacto agent --sink kubernetes --cgroup-root /host/sys/fs/cgroup
  pacto agent --sink local --docker --cgroup-root /host/sys/fs/cgroup
  pacto agent --sink evidence --bindings bindings.yaml --evidence-url https://evidence.example.com \
    --evidence-key agent.key --evidence-key-id k1 --evidence-producer host-1

Flags:

      --bindings string                   with --sink local or evidence: YAML file binding workloads to contracts
      --cgroup-root string                where the host cgroup v2 hierarchy is mounted; empty attributes by network namespace only (default "/sys/fs/cgroup")
      --docker                            with --sink local or evidence: check running containers labelled dev.pacto.contract (Docker Engine API on /var/run/docker.sock)
      --docker-label-filter stringArray   with --docker: only check containers that also carry this label (key=value or key; repeatable, all must match), e.g. com.docker.compose.project=demo
      --enable-probing                    also probe the wire protocol of every interface found listening
      --evidence-key string               with --sink evidence: private key file envelopes are signed with
      --evidence-key-id string            with --sink evidence: key id (must match the server's trust entry)
      --evidence-producer string          with --sink evidence: producer id
      --evidence-url string               with --sink evidence: Evidence Server base URL
  -h, --help                              help for agent
      --namespace string                  namespace the NodeRuntimeObservation is written to with --sink kubernetes (default $POD_NAMESPACE)
      --node-name string                  name of this host; with --sink kubernetes also the NodeRuntimeObservation name (default $NODE_NAME)
      --proc-root string                  where the host /proc is mounted (a pod needs hostPID, a container --pid=host) (default "/proc")
      --publish-interval duration         how often a snapshot is published (whole seconds) (default 30s)
      --resync-interval duration          how often workloads, network namespaces and listeners are re-read from /proc (default 1m0s)
      --ringbuf-size uint32               kernel ring buffer size in bytes; a power of two and a multiple of the page size (default 262144)
      --sink string                       where snapshots go: one of [kubernetes stdout local evidence] (default "stdout")
      --stabilization-window duration     how long a negative must persist before it is reported (default 2m0s)

docs.title: pacto dashboard
docs.text:
Launches an operational dashboard over the fleet snapshot: the same operational graph the CLI's pacto fleet commands query, served as a web UI.

The dashboard is the exploration and observability layer of the Pacto system. It visualizes the same contracts the CLI manages and the operator verifies, organised around four workflows: an operational Overview, the Services inventory, the Operational Graph and Change analysis.

Each positional argument is a contract source reference: - oci://registry/repo → OCI registry source (can be repeated) - ./path/to/dir → local filesystem source (at most one)

When no arguments are given, sources are auto-detected: - local: enabled if pacto.yaml is found in the working directory - cache: enabled if the OCI bundle cache (~/.cache/pacto/oci) holds bundles - k8s: enabled if a kubeconfig or in-cluster config resolves - oci: from the positional arguments, the PACTO_DASHBOARD_REPO env var, or the status.contract.resolvedRef of the cluster's Pacto resources

When running alongside the Kubernetes operator, OCI repositories are automatically discovered from the status.contract.resolvedRef fields of Pacto CRD resources on every refresh. The result combines runtime state from the operator with contract content from OCI.

Every source contributes to one snapshot, rebuilt in the background, and each answer carries the as-of time and the completeness of the sources behind it.

pacto dashboard [sources...] [flags]

Examples:

  # Start dashboard with auto-detected sources
  pacto dashboard

  # Start from a specific directory
  pacto dashboard ./services

  # Include OCI repositories
  pacto dashboard oci://ghcr.io/org/order-service oci://ghcr.io/org/payment-service

  # Mix local and OCI sources
  pacto dashboard ./services oci://ghcr.io/org/payment-service

  # Custom port
  pacto dashboard --port 9090

  # Specify Kubernetes namespace (default: all namespaces)
  pacto dashboard --namespace production

Flags:

      --cors-origin string                explicit cross-origin allowed to call the API (default: same-origin only)
      --delivery-namespace string         namespace Pacto delivery runs in, whose published identity policy (agent, break-glass and human groups, team prefix) says who is an agent and who may answer (default "pacto-delivery")
      --delivery-trust string             the trust config delivery records are verified with, so History reads signed records (the recorder's PEM public key or a YAML trust config; default $PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST)
  -h, --help                              help for dashboard
      --host string                       bind address for the dashboard server (default "127.0.0.1")
      --mira-url string                   Mira's address, to link the health-check citations of delivery verdicts
      --namespace string                  Kubernetes namespace (empty = all namespaces)
      --oidc-ca-file string               PEM bundle of the CAs that sign the issuer's certificate, trusted on top of the system roots (also PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CA_FILE)
      --oidc-client-id string             OpenID Connect client id of the dashboard
      --oidc-display-name string          the identity provider's name on the sign-in button, as in Sign in with Keycloak (default OIDC; also PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_DISPLAY_NAME)
      --oidc-extra-scopes strings         scopes to ask for beyond openid, profile and groups
      --oidc-groups-claim string          ID token claim the API server takes the groups from; must match its claim mapping (default groups)
      --oidc-groups-prefix string         prefix the API server puts before every group; must match its claim mapping
      --oidc-internal-issuer-url string   address the dashboard reaches the issuer at when it differs from the public issuer URL browsers use, such as an in-cluster Service; ID tokens must still name the public issuer (also PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_INTERNAL_ISSUER_URL)
      --oidc-issuer-url string            OpenID Connect issuer people sign in with before the dashboard shows anything; every view then shows what the signed-in person's Kubernetes RBAC lets them read, and every action runs as them (also PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_ISSUER_URL; the client secret comes from PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET)
      --oidc-redirect-url string          the dashboard's /auth/callback as browsers reach it (https)
      --oidc-username-claim string        ID token claim the API server takes the username from; must match its claim mapping (default sub)
      --oidc-username-prefix string       prefix the API server puts before the username; must match its claim mapping (default the issuer URL and #, none for the email claim; - for none)
      --port int                          port for the dashboard server (default 3000)
      --session-idle-timeout duration     a session without a request for this long ends (default 1h)
      --session-max-age duration          a session ends this long after sign-in, renewed or not (default 12h)
      --token-login                       let people sign in by pasting a Kubernetes bearer token, for a cluster whose API server trusts no identity provider; a token session never decides on a held change (also PACTO_DASHBOARD_TOKEN_LOGIN)
      --trace-source stringArray          named offline OTLP/JSON trace source as NAME=PATH, where NAME is its stable data-source identity (repeatable; also PACTO_DASHBOARD_TRACE_SOURCES)
      --traces stringArray                OTLP/JSON trace file to fold observed dependencies from (repeatable; also PACTO_DASHBOARD_TRACES)

It auto-detects sources: pass OCI repositories as arguments, or run it next to the operator (with a kubeconfig) and it discovers OCI repositories from each Pacto resource's status.contract.resolvedRef. Use --no-cache for a cold start (it skips scanning pre-existing cached bundles; bundles fetched during the session are still cached).

For a tour of what the dashboard surfaces, see For platform engineers; to run it as a container, see Dashboard container.

docs.title: pacto delivery
docs.text:
Pacto delivery decides which version each environment (a Stage) runs. Every change is an Operation: plan it to see what the promoter will do and who must agree, propose it, and a person approves only when the contracts say a consumer would break, Pacto cannot see enough or the Stage asks for approval on every promote.

There is no approve tool for agents. approve is for people.

pacto delivery [flags]

Flags:

      --delivery-namespace string   namespace Pacto delivery runs in, whose published identity policy (agent, break-glass and human groups, team prefix) says who is an agent and who may answer (default "pacto-delivery")
  -h, --help                        help for delivery
  -n, --namespace string            namespace of the Stage and its Operations (default "default")
      --trust string                the trust config delivery records are verified with: the recorder's PEM public key, or a YAML file of keys and the streams each may sign (default $PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST)

docs.title: pacto delivery approve
docs.text:
Record your decision on a held operation, as the person your kubeconfig signs you in as. When the promoter asks for a fresh login (delivery.promoter.authFreshness), the command instead makes you log in again in your browser (prompt=login, max_age=0) with its own OpenID Connect client and sends the Approval with that login's token, never your kubeconfig's: an agent running in your shell cannot approve as you without you typing your password at that moment. The token is not stored.

pacto delivery approve <operation> [flags]

Flags:

      --decision string             approve, reject or accept-unknown (default "approve")
  -h, --help                        help for approve
      --note string                 why, for the record
      --oidc-ca-file string         PEM bundle of the CAs that sign the issuer's certificate, trusted on top of the system roots (also PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_CA_FILE)
      --oidc-client-id string       OpenID Connect client used only for approvals, never by a kubeconfig (a confidential client's secret comes from PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET) (default "pacto-approve")
      --oidc-extra-scopes strings   scopes to ask for beyond openid, profile and groups
      --oidc-issuer-url string      OpenID Connect issuer the cluster trusts, to log in again with (also PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL)
      --oidc-redirect-port int      loopback port the identity provider sends the browser back to (default: a free port)

docs.title: pacto diff
docs.text:
Compares two contracts (local paths or oci:// references) and produces a classified change set (BREAKING, POTENTIAL_BREAKING, NON_BREAKING).

pacto diff <old> <new> [flags]

Examples:

  # Compare a remote contract with a local one
  pacto diff oci://ghcr.io/acme/svc-pacto:1.0.0 my-service

  # Markdown output for CI comments
  pacto diff --output-format markdown oci://ghcr.io/acme/svc-pacto:1.0.0 my-service

Flags:

  -h, --help                     help for diff
      --new-set stringArray      set a value on the new contract (e.g. --new-set service.version=2.0.0)
      --new-values stringArray   values file to merge into the new contract (can be repeated)
      --old-set stringArray      set a value on the old contract (e.g. --old-set service.version=1.0.0)
      --old-values stringArray   values file to merge into the old contract (can be repeated)

Exit code: 1 when the overall classification is BREAKING, and also when the diff could not be produced. A non-zero exit alone is therefore no contract verdict. See Exit codes for how to tell the two apart. A POTENTIAL_BREAKING result exits 0, so a CI gate that stops on it must read the classification.

The diff engine performs deep comparison of referenced OpenAPI specs, detecting changes at the path, method, parameter, request body and response level. The optional docs/ directory is ignored: documentation changes produce no diff entries and leave the compatibility classification unchanged.

When both bundles include an sbom/ directory with recognized SBOM files (.spdx.json or .cdx.json), pacto diff reports package-level changes: added, removed or modified packages (version and license). SBOM changes are informational and leave the overall classification and exit code unchanged.

When dependencies change between the old and new contracts (version upgrades, additions or removals), a dependency graph diff section is displayed showing the tree of affected nodes.

See Change Classification for the full rules.

docs.title: pacto doc
docs.text:
Reads a pacto.yaml in the given directory (or oci:// reference) and generates structured Markdown documentation.

pacto doc [dir | oci://ref] [flags]

Examples:

  # Print documentation to stdout
  pacto doc my-service

  # Write documentation to a file
  pacto doc my-service -o docs/

  # Serve documentation in the browser
  pacto doc my-service --serve

  # Serve on a custom port
  pacto doc my-service --serve --port 9090

  # Launch an interactive API explorer (Swagger UI)
  pacto doc my-service --ui swagger

  # Select a specific interface
  pacto doc my-service --ui swagger --interface public-api

  # Point try-it-out requests to a running backend
  pacto doc my-service --ui swagger --target http://localhost:3000

  # Per-interface target mapping
  pacto doc my-service --ui swagger --target public-api=http://localhost:3000 --target admin-api=http://localhost:3001

Flags:

  -h, --help                 help for doc
      --interface string     interface name to display (used with --ui)
  -o, --output string        output directory for generated Markdown; a NAME.html value writes a static documentation site to a NAME/ directory instead
      --port int             port for the documentation server (used with --serve or --ui) (default 8484)
      --serve                serve the offline dashboard-grade documentation site over a local HTTP server
      --set stringArray      set a contract value (e.g. --set service.version=2.0.0)
      --target stringArray   target server URL for try-it-out requests; supports interface=url mapping (used with --ui)
      --ui string            UI type for the interactive API explorer (one of: swagger)
  -f, --values stringArray   values file to merge into the contract (can be repeated; last wins)

The header line reports the contract's own state. pacto doc reads a bundle and observes no cluster. A contract that has never been runtime-evaluated therefore reads status NotEvaluated, and one that declares no workload reads compliance REFERENCE. Both are the expected result for a freshly scaffolded contract. See Compliance states.

Markdown prints to stdout by default. -o DIR writes DIR/<service>.md. -o NAME.html writes a self-contained static documentation site (a directory) that reuses the dashboard UI offline.

--serve serves that static site locally. --ui swagger launches an interactive API explorer.

--serve, --ui and -o are mutually exclusive. Use --interface to pick one OpenAPI interface with --ui. --target and --target iface=url point try-it-out at a backend.

Sibling dependencies are resolved in parallel. OCI bundles cache under ~/.cache/pacto/oci/. --no-cache bypasses the cache.

docs.title: pacto evidence
docs.text:
Produce and verify the signed, versioned envelopes that carry a Pacto EvidenceSet from a remote or disconnected environment to a platform that ingests it. Keys are Ed25519; the wire format is defined by pkg/evidenceenvelope.

pacto evidence [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help   help for evidence

docs.title: pacto evidence keygen
docs.text:
Writes the private seed to <keyId>.key (base64, 0600) and the public key into --out. With --producer, the public key is written as <producer>__<keyId>.pub, which binds the key to that producer in the trust store. Hand that file to the platform. Sign with the SAME --producer and --key-id. With no --producer, a bare <keyId>.pub binds the key to a producer named after the key id (the single-producer default).

pacto evidence keygen [flags]

Flags:

      --force             overwrite existing key files instead of failing
  -h, --help              help for keygen
      --key-id string     key id (defaults to a fingerprint of the public key)
      --out string        directory to write the keypair into (default ".")
      --producer string   producer id to bind the key to (writes <producer>__<keyId>.pub)

docs.title: pacto evidence send
docs.text:
Reads a signed envelope JSON file and POSTs it to an ingestion host's --url. Prints the host's JSON response and exits non-zero on a non-2xx status.

pacto evidence send <envelope.json> [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help         help for send
      --url string   ingestion host envelope endpoint URL

docs.title: pacto evidence serve
docs.text:
Starts an HTTP host that accepts signed evidence envelopes at POST /api/evidence/v1/envelopes, verifies them against --trust, evaluates the carried evidence against its resolved contract and publishes accepted records to the contract registry as OCI 1.1 referrers of the exact contract revision each report is about. Every --subject is an immutable oci://<repo>@sha256:<digest> reference; the registry is the only durable store, so the host keeps no local state and survives restarts. GET .../health is an always-200 liveness probe; .../ready reports 503 while a subject cannot be resolved or its referrers enumerated; .../producers advertises trusted producer ids; .../targets exposes the latest accepted targets. Registry credentials come from the same sources as pacto pull. Exactly one server may write to a subject set. Serves until interrupted.

pacto evidence serve [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help                    help for serve
      --listen-address string   host:port to listen on (supersedes --port)
      --port int                port to listen on (127.0.0.1); superseded by --listen-address (default 8686)
      --producer stringArray    advertised trusted producer id (repeatable)
      --subject stringArray     exact contract revision evidence is stored on: oci://<repo>@sha256:<digest> (repeatable, required)
      --trust string            trust store: a public-key file or a directory of <keyId>.pub files

docs.title: pacto evidence sign
docs.text:
Reads an EvidenceSet JSON file, wraps it in an Ed25519-signed envelope and prints the envelope JSON. Only --issued-at is non-deterministic (it defaults to now), so pinning it is enough to make re-signing the same evidence produce a byte-identical envelope.

pacto evidence sign <evidence.json> [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help                      help for sign
      --id string                 envelope id (defaults to a hash over the API version, producer id, sequence and evidence, so two producers reporting identical evidence never collide)
      --issued-at string          issued-at timestamp (RFC3339; defaults to now)
      --key string                path to the private key file
      --key-id string             producer key id (must match the trust-store entry)
      --producer string           producer id
      --producer-version string   producer version (optional)
      --sequence uint             producer-scoped monotonic sequence; each report must be strictly greater than the producer's last
      --ttl duration              validity window; 0 disables expiry (default 24h0m0s)

docs.title: pacto evidence verify
docs.text:
Decodes an envelope and verifies its signature, freshness and trust against a --trust public-key file or directory of <keyId>.pub files. Exits non-zero when verification fails.

pacto evidence verify <envelope.json> [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help           help for verify
      --trust string   trust store: a public-key file or a directory of <keyId>.pub files

docs.title: pacto explain
docs.text:
Parses a pacto.yaml in the given directory (or oci:// reference) and produces a human-readable summary of the service contract.

pacto explain [dir | oci://ref] [flags]

Examples:

  pacto explain my-service

Flags:

  -h, --help                 help for explain
      --set stringArray      set a contract value (e.g. --set service.version=2.0.0)
  -f, --values stringArray   values file to merge into the contract (can be repeated; last wins)

What it covers. The text output summarises identity, workload, state, capabilities, interfaces, dependencies and readiness. To read configurations and policies, use pacto doc or open pacto.yaml. metadata is carried by --output-format json only; the text output omits it.

Readiness output. When the contract declares a readiness section (a pactoVersion: "2.0" feature), explain adds a Readiness block: the derived Score, the Gate result (PASS/FAIL with score / minScore), Earned and Total Weight, the partial credit multiplier, the assessment expires date with countdown (or an Expired state) and a per-check table showing each check's declared status (done/partial/not-done/deferred), category, weight, earned weight and evidence. The Readiness block also includes a revision-history table when history[] is present. --output-format json includes the same data plus doneCount, partialCount, notDoneCount, deferredCount and expired (boolean). Readiness status is time-dependent: the score is 0 when the current date is past the assessment-level expires.

docs.title: pacto fleet
docs.text:
Compose contracts, contract revisions and operational targets from local bundles and ingested evidence into a versioned, navigable graph, then search, inspect, traverse and explain it. Every answer reports its as-of time and completeness.

pacto fleet [flags]

Flags:

      --cache                      include every bundle in the local OCI cache as an offline baseline revision
      --evidence-url stringArray   base URL of an Evidence Server to consume its read-only operational-graph contribution over HTTP (repeatable)
      --freshness duration         mark target evidence older than this as stale (0 disables)
  -h, --help                       help for fleet
      --k8s                        include live Pacto CRs from the current Kubernetes cluster as targets
      --local stringArray          local bundle root(s) to scan (repeatable) (default [.])
      --namespace string           namespace to read Pacto CRs from with --k8s (empty = all namespaces)
      --oci stringArray            registry reference to include as a published-baseline revision (repeatable)
      --root stringArray           contract root whose whole dependency closure joins the snapshot: a local bundle path or an oci:// reference (repeatable)
      --target-state stringArray   offline target-state fixture file(s) supplying targets, for demos and tests; production targets arrive as signed EvidenceSets (repeatable)
      --traces stringArray         OTLP/JSON trace file supplying runtime-observed dependency edges, folded into the snapshot as observed relationships (repeatable)

docs.title: pacto fleet explain
docs.text:
Explain the deterministic reasons for a service or target state

pacto fleet explain <subject> [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help   help for explain

docs.title: pacto fleet get
docs.text:
Inspect a logical service or an operational target

pacto fleet get [service] [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help            help for get
      --target string   inspect an operational target by key or name

docs.title: pacto fleet graph
docs.text:
Traverse the operational graph from an explicit root. Give a service name to aggregate across its revisions, or --revision/--target to root an exact revision (never 'latest').

pacto fleet graph <service> [flags]

Flags:

      --direction string   traversal direction (dependencies, dependents) (default "dependencies")
  -h, --help               help for graph
      --max-depth int      maximum transitive depth (0 = unlimited)
      --revision string    root an exact contract revision key
      --target string      root the revision linked to this target key or name
      --transitive         traverse transitively (cycle-safe)

docs.title: pacto fleet reconcile
docs.text:
Reconciles what the fleet's contracts declare against what runtime traces prove. Reports matched dependencies, declared-but-not-observed (dormant or unseen in the trace window, so possibly still in use) and observed-but-not-declared (shadow dependencies).

pacto fleet reconcile [flags]

Examples:

  pacto fleet reconcile --traces traces.json --local .

Flags:

  -h, --help            help for reconcile
      --traces string   OTLP/JSON trace file supplying observed dependencies (required)

docs.title: pacto fleet search
docs.text:
Search logical services in the fleet

pacto fleet search [text] [flags]

Flags:

      --compliance string   filter to services with a target of this compliance
      --has-capability      only services declaring a capability
      --has-dependency      only services declaring a dependency
  -h, --help                help for search
      --label stringArray   filter by label key=value (repeatable)
      --limit int           maximum results (0 = 100, capped at 500)
      --not-ready           only services whose readiness gate does not pass (below minScore, expired or undeclared)
      --offset int          result offset for paging
      --owner string        filter by owner (team, DRI or contact)
      --ready               only services whose readiness gate passes (score >= minScore, not expired)
      --scope string        correlate to a target with this scope
      --source string       filter by observing source
      --status string       filter by aggregate status (Compliant, Invalid, NonCompliant, NotEvaluated, Reference, Unknown, Warning)
      --workload string     filter by workload (service, job, scheduled)

docs.title: pacto fleet snapshot
docs.text:
Emit the whole fleet snapshot

pacto fleet snapshot [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help   help for snapshot

docs.title: pacto fleet status
docs.text:
Reports what needs attention: non-compliant, unknown, invalid and stale targets, revisions without readiness, unresolved dependencies and dependencies whose provider version is outside the declared range. With no category flag it reports every category.

pacto fleet status [flags]

Flags:

  -h, --help                 help for status
      --invalid              report structurally invalid contracts
      --limit int            maximum results (0 = 200)
      --missing-readiness    report revisions without a readiness assessment
      --needs-attention      report every attention category
      --non-compliant        report non-compliant targets
      --stale                report targets with stale evidence
      --unknown              report targets with unknown compliance
      --unresolved-deps      report unresolved declared dependencies
      --unsatisfied-ranges   report dependencies whose provider version is outside the declared range (DEPENDENCY_RANGE_UNSATISFIED)

docs.title: pacto generate
docs.text:
Invokes a pacto-plugin-<name> binary to generate deployment manifests, documentation or other artifacts from a contract directory or oci:// reference.

pacto generate <plugin> [dir | oci://ref] [flags]

Examples:

  pacto generate schema-infer my-service --option file=config.yaml -o out/

Flags:

  -h, --help                 help for generate
      --option stringArray   plugin option as key=value (can be repeated)
  -o, --output string        output directory (default: <plugin>-output/)
      --set stringArray      set a contract value (e.g. --set service.version=2.0.0)
  -f, --values stringArray   values file to merge into the contract (can be repeated; last wins)

pacto generate <plugin> invokes the pacto-plugin-<plugin> binary. See Plugins for plugin discovery, the plugin registry and the official plugins bundled with Pacto.

docs.title: pacto graph
docs.text:
Resolves the dependency tree from a pacto.yaml in the given directory (or oci:// reference) and displays the graph, cycles and version conflicts.

pacto graph [dir | oci://ref] [flags]

Examples:

  pacto graph my-service
  pacto graph --with-references
  pacto graph --only-references

Flags:

  -h, --help                 help for graph
      --only-references      Show only config/policy reference edges (no dependencies)
      --set stringArray      set a contract value (e.g. --set service.version=2.0.0)
  -f, --values stringArray   values file to merge into the contract (can be repeated; last wins)
      --with-references      Include config/policy reference edges alongside dependencies

Dependencies resolved from local paths are annotated with [local]. Shared dependencies (referenced by multiple parents) are annotated with (shared).

Reports cycles, version conflicts and unreachable dependencies.

Sibling dependencies are resolved in parallel. OCI bundles are cached locally in ~/.cache/pacto/oci/ for faster subsequent operations. Use --no-cache to bypass the cache.

docs.title: pacto impact
docs.text:
Composes a semantic contract diff (old→new) with the operational graph to answer which consumers a change really affects, how strong the evidence is and whether their declared compatibility still holds.

When no fleet source holds the changed service, the new revision is added to the snapshot so the services that depend on it are found.

The answer ends in a release gate, and the exit status follows it: 0 clear: the change is not BREAKING, or the snapshot is complete and no service depends on the changed one. 1 blocked: the change is BREAKING and a consumer that does not accept the new version runs on a known target. 2 unverified: the change is BREAKING and nothing is shown to block it, but the answer cannot clear it: the answer is partial, or consumers depend on the service and none is shown to be safe. A run over --local bundles alone knows no targets, so a BREAKING change with consumers exits 2. A command that could not run also exits 1, with nothing on stdout. Add --target-state (or a live source) so the gate can tell deployed impact apart.

Pacto finds consumers only in the sources you pass, such as --local, --root, --oci, --cache, --k8s, --evidence-url and --traces. With --local alone Pacto sees only the contracts in those folders, so "No affected consumers" is not evidence of safety.

pacto impact <old> <new> [flags]

Examples:

  # Impact of upgrading a local service against the local fleet
  pacto impact ./svc-v1 ./svc-v2 --local .

  # Include observed (runtime) evidence and emit JSON
  pacto impact oci://ghcr.io/acme/svc:1.0.0 ./svc --include-observed --output-format json

Flags:

      --cache                      include every bundle in the local OCI cache as an offline baseline revision
      --evidence-url stringArray   base URL of an Evidence Server to consume its read-only operational-graph contribution over HTTP (repeatable)
      --freshness duration         mark target evidence older than this as stale (0 disables)
  -h, --help                       help for impact
      --include-observed           let observed (runtime) relationships raise consumer confidence
      --k8s                        include live Pacto CRs from the current Kubernetes cluster as targets
      --local stringArray          local bundle root(s) to scan (repeatable) (default [.])
      --namespace string           namespace to read Pacto CRs from with --k8s (empty = all namespaces)
      --new-set stringArray        set a value on the new contract (e.g. --new-set service.version=2.0.0)
      --new-values stringArray     values file to merge into the new contract (can be repeated)
      --oci stringArray            registry reference to include as a published-baseline revision (repeatable)
      --old-set stringArray        set a value on the old contract (e.g. --old-set service.version=1.0.0)
      --old-values stringArray     values file to merge into the old contract (can be repeated)
      --root stringArray           contract root whose whole dependency closure joins the snapshot: a local bundle path or an oci:// reference (repeatable)
      --target-state stringArray   offline target-state fixture file(s) supplying targets, for demos and tests; production targets arrive as signed EvidenceSets (repeatable)
      --traces string              OTLP/JSON trace file; its observed edges corroborate and surface consumers (implies --include-observed)

docs.title: pacto init
docs.text:
Writes the contract for the service in dir (default: the current folder).

An empty or new folder gets a blank contract with the bundle structure (interfaces/, configuration/). A folder that already holds a service gets a contract read from its Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests, and a list of what Pacto found and what it could not tell (Unknown). The workload's environment, including the ConfigMaps it reads, becomes a configuration schema with each value as its default. A URL in it that names another service in the cluster becomes a dependency: with that service's contract in --fleet, its bundle and a range from its version; without it, a placeholder range that the comment above it and Unknown name. A readiness, liveness or startup probe becomes a health check.

The contract also gets a publish section, for pacto publish. To describe the service and leave delivery out, pass --describe-only: the contract then has no publish section and needs no signing key. --delivery also writes the cluster pieces: the Pacto resource that checks the running service, and per environment a Stage with the Flux OCIRepository and Kustomization it applies through. Each Stage starts at observe: it plans every new version and moves nothing, and the OCIRepository stays pinned to the tag you deploy, so GitOps keeps applying what it did. The last environment's Stage also asks a person to approve every promote.

--owner is the team's bare name, such as billing: usually the team label on the workload. An AI agent is a service too: its tools are an mcp interface, the model it calls is a dependency and its eval suite is a checks entry; see https://pacto.run/latest/contract-reference/checks/#an-agent-is-a-service.

Several folders are each pactified, with a summary at the end. --cluster drafts a contract for every workload in the namespaces that no Pacto describes yet, in <out>/<namespace>/<name>: its manifests are read from the cluster, and the services its pods were seen calling become dependencies pinned to the version seen running, for you to widen. Drafts are only written, never published, and a draft that is not valid fails the command.

It only adds files and missing .pactoignore lines; any other file already there is yours and is left as it is, so running it twice is safe. --plan shows exactly what would be added and changes nothing.

pacto init [dir...] [flags]

Examples:

  pacto init my-service
  pacto init --plan
  pacto init --describe-only --owner billing
  pacto init --delivery --owner payments --fleet ../contracts
  pacto init --delivery --no-transparency-log --insecure-registry
  pacto init --delivery --registry-secret registry-creds
  pacto init services/checkout services/payments --plan
  pacto init --cluster --namespace shop --out drafts

Flags:

      --cluster                  draft a contract for every workload in the cluster that no Pacto describes, reading the current kubeconfig context
      --delivery                 also write the cluster pieces: the Pacto resource, a Stage per environment and its Flux OCIRepository and Kustomization
      --describe-only            write a contract that only describes the service: no publish section, so no signing key
      --env strings              environments for --delivery, in promotion order (default [test,prod])
      --fleet strings            folders of other services' contracts to find the services that use this one
  -h, --help                     help for init
      --insecure-registry        with --delivery: the Flux OCIRepositories read the registry over plain HTTP (a local registry only)
      --name string              service name (default: the workload's name, then the folder's)
      --namespace strings        with --cluster: a namespace to read; repeat it for more (default: every namespace)
      --no-transparency-log      write transparencyLog: false under publish.sign, so signatures stay out of the public transparency log (offline signing, a throwaway key)
      --out string               with --cluster: the folder the drafts go in, one <namespace>/<name> folder each
      --owner string             the team that owns the service, as a bare name such as billing (default: the workload's team label)
      --plan                     show what would be added and change nothing
      --registry string          where to publish, as host/path (default: read from the workload's image)
      --registry-secret string   with --delivery: the docker-registry Secret, in each environment's namespace, that Flux and the Pacto resource log in to a private registry with

Scaffolds three files: a valid pacto.yaml, a placeholder OpenAPI spec at interfaces/openapi.yaml and a configuration JSON Schema at configuration/schema.json.

<name> is the service name: it becomes the directory and service.name, which must match ^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9])?$. pacto init fleet/checkout-web therefore scaffolds a bundle that fails validation: service.name gets the whole path and fails SCHEMA_VIOLATION. To scaffold inside a directory, cd there first and pass the bare name.

All three are required by the scaffolded contract, because its interfaces: and configurations: sections point at the other two files. If you delete a directory, also delete the section that references it, or validation fails with FILE_NOT_FOUND. A contract that declares neither section needs only pacto.yaml, so drop the section and the directory together.

The scaffold fails validate --readiness on purpose

Its two placeholder readiness claims are not-done, which scores 0 against the scaffolded minScore: 80 and fails with READINESS_GATE_UNMET. Plain pacto validate passes, because the gate is opt-in.
