See Bundle structure — Change One requested move of a Stage to another version, from request to outcome. In Kubernetes it is an object of kind Operation. See What happens to a change Change Check A test Pacto runs on a version before or after it moves: was it published and signed, does it break a consumer, does the running service do what its contract says. Each answers Pass, Fail or Unknown. See What happens to a change Checks Check suite A test or eval file a version ships in its checks list. A Stage runs it, and only a verdict about that exact file counts. See Checks — Clear The contracts clear a change when every consumer accepts the new version. See Who is asked and why — Cold start A new Stage begins on observe and earns more freedom from there. See Cold start — Collector What gathers evidence, such as the Kubernetes observer or the eBPF node agent. See Collectors — Compliant The compliance state of a contract whose evidence covers it and raises no error or warning. Compliant Consumer A service that calls another one. Checkout is a consumer of payments. See Impact analysis Consumers Consumer range Which versions of another service a contract accepts, such as ^2.0.0 (any 2.x), set in compatibility. Pacto judges each change per consumer by these ranges, never per field or endpoint. Also called version range. See Who is asked and why — Contract One file, pacto.yaml, that says what a service offers, who owns it and which other services it calls. See the contract reference Contract Contract graph All your contracts together: who calls whom and which versions each accepts. See Operational graph Graph cosign The Sigstore command-line tool that signs artifacts in a registry and verifies their signatures. pacto publish signs in the same format, so cosign verify checks a version, and cosign verify-blob-attestation checks a record. See Verify a record — Delivery The opt-in part of Pacto, also called the delivery component, that decides which version of each service runs in each environment. It is a separate install. See How delivery works Delivery Digest The fingerprint of one exact published artifact (sha256:...) — DRI Directly responsible individual: the one person a contract names as accountable for the service (service.owner.dri). When a contract names no team, the DRI is its owner. See OwnerInfo — Earned autonomy Raising a Stage's level after enough good changes, confirmed by a person. See Earned autonomy — Environment A place a service runs, such as test or prod. In Kubernetes it is a namespace of the same name Environment Evidence What was observed about a running service, such as which ports listen or which services it called. See Evidence Evidence Evidence Server The service that receives evidence and stores it in your registry next to the contract it is about. See Evidence Server — External dependency A dependency outside this Pacto system, such as a managed database or a model. It has a contract and a range, or only a version, and then anything relying on it is Unknown. See External dependencies — Finding One result of comparing a contract with the evidence: a contradiction such as INTERFACE_ABSENT, or a reason Pacto could not tell, such as EVIDENCE_STALE. See Compliance model Findings Fleet All your services together, as Pacto sees them from contracts, clusters and registries. See Fleet views Fleet Flux The GitOps tool that applies each version in the cluster. Pacto moves a version by writing its digest onto a Flux OCIRepository. See How a change moves — Follower A Stage in another cluster that takes the versions an upstream Stage verified, by reading that Stage's stream. See Follow a Stage in another cluster — Freeze Stop automation moving a Stage until a person unfreezes it. See When a Stage is frozen Frozen GitlessOps Signed artifacts in your registry and evidence decide which version runs where, while your code and manifests stay in git. See What GitlessOps means — GitOps Keeping a cluster in line with files in git, with a tool such as Flux or Argo CD. Pacto works with it — Held change A change waiting for a person to decide. See Why you were asked Inbox in-toto A standard format for signed statements about software. Every record is an in-toto statement. See What a record says — Invalid The compliance state of a contract that fails validation. It ranks worse than NonCompliant. Invalid Interface One way a service is called, such as an HTTP API described by an OpenAPI file. See interfaces Interfaces Kustomization The Flux object that applies a set of Kubernetes files, such as the files a version ships, as the ServiceAccount it names. See Manifests and the levels — Level How much a Stage lets Pacto do on its own: observe, advise, auto for non-breaking (auto-nonbreaking) or autonomous. Also called autonomy level. See The four levels Level MCP Model Context Protocol, the standard way an AI agent finds and calls tools. pacto mcp is an MCP server. See Drive Pacto from an agent — Mediated A Stage condition that says whether only the pointer decides what runs. See What the pointer guarantees — Node agent The Pacto collector that runs on every Kubernetes node and watches with eBPF which ports each service listens on and which services it calls. It is a program in the cluster, separate from an AI agent. See Runtime conformance — NonCompliant The compliance state of a valid contract when the evidence contradicts it, for example a declared interface that is absent. Non-Compliant OCIRepository The Flux object that points at one artifact in a registry, whose files a Kustomization applies. Pacto moves a version by writing its digest onto it. See How a change moves — Operator The Pacto controller you install in a cluster. It checks that each running service matches its contract. See Kubernetes overview — oras A command-line tool that lists and fetches artifacts and referrers in a registry. See Check one record without Pacto — Owner team The team a contract names under service.owner. Pacto asks its members about that service. See OwnerInfo Owner Pactify Give a service a contract and connect it to delivery. See Pactify a service — pactoVersion The contract format version in each pacto.yaml, "2.0", "2.1", "2.2" or "2.3". It is separate from the Pacto core and operator release versions. See Versions — Plan What Pacto would do with a change, and who must agree, before anyone asks. See Plan, propose and approve Plan Pointer The digest a Stage moved its environment to (status.pointer). See What the pointer guarantees — Policy A rule a contract must follow, such as "every service names an owner", checked with the contract. See policies Policy Promote Move a Stage to a newer version Promote Promoter The part of delivery that plans each change, runs its checks and moves the pointer. It holds no signing key. See How a change moves — Proposal The next level Pacto suggests for a Stage, with its evidence or what blocks it. See Earned autonomy — Readiness assessment A dated statement in a contract of which readiness claims are done, with evidence. It counts for nothing once it expires. See Readiness Readiness Recent sign-in An opt-in rule: deciding on a held change needs a login newer than delivery.promoter.authFreshness. Off by default, so a person decides with the sign-in they have. See A recent sign-in to decide Sign in again to decide Record A signed account of one finished change, stored in your registry and checkable without Pacto. See Verify a record Record Recorder The part of delivery that signs records. It is the only part that holds the signing key, and it is off until you turn it on. See Signed records and history — Referrer A file a registry stores attached to an artifact, listed by the OCI Referrers API. Evidence and records are stored this way, so they need a registry that serves that API. See What delivery needs — Registry The place your container images are stored. Pacto stores contracts, versions and records there too — Rollback Put back the version that ran before. See What happens to a change and Roll back by hand Roll back Service Something you run and other things call, such as payments Service Session What a shared dashboard keeps after a person signs in: their token, held on the server behind a cookie until dashboard.auth.session.idleTimeout or maxAge ends it. See Sessions Sign out Shadow consumer A service seen calling another at runtime that no contract declares. See Observed dependencies — Sign-in How a person proves who they are to a shared dashboard, with your identity provider or a pasted Kubernetes token. Every view and action then runs with their Kubernetes RBAC, and the delivery views need it. See Dashboard authentication Sign in Stage One service in one environment, such as payments in prod, and the version it runs there. See Stages and records Stages Step-down Dropping one level after a version Pacto shipped with no person fails. See Step-down — Stream The numbered history of one Stage's records, each naming the one before it, hung on the Stage's anchor. See Streams, stand-ins and gaps — Target One running deployment of a service, such as payments in one cluster. See Three identities Targets Transitive closure A service's dependencies, their dependencies and so on to the last one. pacto.lock pins all of them by digest. See Lockfile — Transparency log Sigstore's public, append-only log of signatures, which anyone can read. pacto publish writes each signature there unless told otherwise, so a private or throwaway key can stay out of it. See Signing — Unknown The answer when Pacto could not see enough to decide. A check answers Unknown instead of Pass or Fail, and a contract's compliance state is Unknown when its evidence is missing or inconclusive. Unknown never counts as a pass. See What Unknown means Unknown Version One published copy of a contract, such as payments 2.4.0. It never changes once published. See Publish a version Version Would have On observe, what Pacto would have done with a change. It is advice only. See Cold start —

docs.title: Impact analysis (pacto impact)
docs.text:
Impact analysis answers the question a reviewer asks before merging: if this revision ships, who is affected? Give it the old and new contract and it lists the services that depend on this one, whether each still works with the new version, where they run and who owns them.

pacto impact ./payments-api@1.4.0 ./payments-api@2.0.0 --local ./services

It joins two things Pacto already has. The semantic diff says how the contract changed (change classification). The operational graph says who depends on the service and where it runs. The CLI command, the MCP tool and the dashboard's Change analysis workspace run the same analysis and, given the same snapshot, return the same answer.

docs.title: Diff × graph → impact
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    OLD["Old revision<br/>contract + files"] --> DIFF["Semantic diff"]
    NEW["New revision<br/>contract + files"] --> DIFF
    DIFF --> CLASS["Classification<br/>NON_BREAKING · POTENTIAL_BREAKING · BREAKING<br/>breaking and potentially-breaking, kept separate"]

    SNAP["Operational graph<br/>immutable read model"] --> GRAPH["Dependents traversal<br/>direct + transitive"]

    CLASS --> IMPACT["Impact result"]
    GRAPH --> IMPACT
    IMPACT --> CONS["Affected consumers<br/>compatibility verdict · confidence"]
    IMPACT --> TARGETS["Active targets<br/>where the change lands"]
    IMPACT --> OWNERS["Owners to notify"]

A change can break consumers while every spec stays identical, such as an amount switching from cents to euros. Raise the interface's compatibilityEpoch and the diff classifies the revision BREAKING, so its consumers are listed.

The diff is computed once over the old→new revision. The changed service is then looked up in the graph and traversed in the dependents direction, direct and transitive. Each dependent becomes an affected consumer, annotated with the evidence Pacto has for that edge, and the result rolls up the active targets the change would land in and the owners to notify.

Every answer inherits the snapshot's asOf time, completeness and limitations, so a partial fleet always reads as partial. When no fleet source holds the changed service, pacto impact adds the new revision to the snapshot so the services that depend on it are found, and the answer carries newRevisionAdded: true. A snapshot it cannot add to, such as the dashboard's published snapshot, answers with a SERVICE_NOT_IN_FLEET limitation, no consumer list and an unverified gate.

docs.title: What an affected consumer carries
docs.text:
For each dependent the analysis records:

Field Meaning service / domain / owner Who is affected and who owns them. depth / direct / path depth is the shortest distance from the consumer to the changed service: 1 is a direct dependent and >1 is transitive. A consumer that depends on the changed service directly is direct even when it also reaches it through another dependent. path is a shortest dependency chain from the consumer to the changed service. required Whether the consumer declared this dependency as required. compatibility The consumer's declared compatibility range against the changed service. compatibilityVerdict Whether the new version satisfies that range. compatible and incompatible both need a declared range and a range and version semver can parse; without all three the verdict is unknown, because an unreadable or absent range is uncertainty. provenance Where the edge came from: declared, observed, declared+observed or inferred. confidence How strongly the evidence supports the claim (see below). status / targets The consumer's aggregate status and the operational targets it runs in. unmet Each guarantee the consumer requires that the new version does not meet, with both values. note A plain-words qualifier. On a BREAKING change a compatible verdict only means the range accepts the new version, so the note says to check that the consumer does not use what the change removes. An open range such as >=1.0.0 accepts every new major version, and the note says so.

docs.title: Confidence model
docs.text:
Confidence grades how strongly the available evidence supports each affected-consumer claim.

Confidence Exact meaning contractual A declared dependency with a usable compatibility range. The consumer's own contract says it depends on this service and pins the versions it accepts. declared A declared dependency without a usable compatibility range. The dependency is stated, but no version constraint was pinned, so Pacto cannot compute a compatibility verdict. observed Runtime use of the dependency was observed in a window. Requires --include-observed. corroborated The declared dependency and an observed one agree. This is the strongest grade: contract and runtime say the same thing. inferred A transitive effect reached through another affected service (depth > 1). It follows from the graph. unknown A direct edge with no declaration and no observation. The effect is possible but unverified.

An inferred path is a lead to verify. Pacto reaches a transitive consumer through the graph. It tells you where to look; confirm whether the consumer breaks before you act on it.

Observed evidence only raises confidence when you opt in. Without --include-observed the analysis is declared-only. Runtime observations then let a direct edge become observed or corroborated.

A partial snapshot is incomplete knowledge, an unknown verdict is uncertainty and an inferred consumer is a lead to verify.

Observed edges come from OpenTelemetry traces via --traces <file>. Beyond corroborating declared consumers, traces surface observed-only (shadow) consumers: services seen calling the changed service without declaring the dependency. With traces they appear as direct consumers at observed confidence.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
pacto impact <old> <new> --local .

<old> and <new> are the two revisions to compare: bundle paths or refs. They are separate from the fleet snapshot and may be oci:// references either way.

pacto impact reads the fleet through the same source flags pacto fleet does, --local included, which defaults to .. Point it only at offline sources and the whole analysis stays offline.

Turn on runtime corroboration with --include-observed, or supply an OTLP/JSON trace export with --traces, which implies it:

pacto impact ./payments-api@1.4.0 ./payments-api@2.0.0 \
  --local ./services \
  --traces ./traces.json

The output reports the classification, then the breaking and potentially-breaking changes in separate lists, so a potential break never counts as a confirmed one. It then lists each affected consumer with its owner, verdict and confidence, the active targets and a warning when the snapshot is partial. The JSON output also carries owners and completeness as fields.

Pacto finds consumers only in the sources you pass. With --local alone it sees only the contracts in those folders. A BREAKING change that none of them depends on ends clear and exits 0, so No affected consumers. covers only those folders.

docs.title: Release gate and exit status
docs.text:
Every answer ends in a release gate, gate, with the reason in gateReason. The CLI exits on it, and the MCP tool returns it:

gate Exit When blocked 1 The change is BREAKING and reaches a consumer that does not accept the new version, or has an unmet guarantee, and is active. unverified 2 The change is BREAKING and nothing is shown to block it, but the answer cannot clear it: the answer is partial, or consumers depend on the service and none is shown to be safe. clear 0 The change is not BREAKING, or the snapshot is complete and no service depends on the changed one.

A command that could not run also exits 1, with nothing on stdout.

Active means the snapshot knows of somewhere that consumer is deployed: at least one operational target. Compatibility is a statement about contracts; active is a statement about the world.

unverified exists because a breaking change with consumers is never safe by default. A consumer can be incompatible on paper with no known target, declare no range, or match only by range. --local bundles declare no targets, so a declared-only run of a breaking change with consumers exits 2:

$ pacto impact ./api-v1 ./api-v2 --local ./fleet
Impact: api 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 2
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Affected consumers (1):
  web                          direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=frontend
Release gate: unverified
unverified: the change is BREAKING and 1 consumer depends on api, but none is shown to be both incompatible and running. Review each consumer, and add a source that knows where services run (for example --target-state) to tell deployed impact apart
$ echo $?
2

Give the snapshot a source that knows where things run and the same command blocks:

$ pacto impact ./api-v1 ./api-v2 --local ./fleet --target-state ./targets.yaml
Impact: api 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 2
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Affected consumers (1):
  web                          direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=frontend
Active targets (1): [production/kubernetes-workload/shop%2Fweb]
Release gate: blocked
breaking changes affect active consumers, which run on known targets and do not accept api 2.0.0: web
$ echo $?
1

docs.title: Gating in CI
docs.text: In CI that is one of two deliberate choices. Fail on any non-zero exit and an unverified breaking change stops the job as a blocked one does. A promotion pipeline that gates on deployed impact alone can treat 2 as a pass, as long as the job supplies targets. Gate on the JSON instead (--output-format json, then classification == "BREAKING") and you gate on the contract alone, which is what you want before anything is deployed. That JSON carries schemaVersion: pacto.dev/impact/v1, the compatibility contract to branch on before reading any other field. Put it in your repository has a pull-request step that gates on the JSON. The file --target-state expects is documented under target-state fixtures.

docs.title: The MCP tool and the dashboard
docs.text:
Agents get the same analysis as the read-only pacto_impact MCP tool. It belongs to the fleet query family and shares that family's boundaries: it projects the operational graph. It is read-only and grants no permission. It is the one fleet tool that rebuilds the graph on every call; the others serve a frozen snapshot. Its asOf therefore advances, while the pacto_fleet_* tools' stays at the value they were started with. When the two disagree they describe the same system at two moments.

In the dashboard the analysis is one half of the Change analysis workspace, served by /api/fleet/impact. It is entered from the service or revision you are already looking at, and the analyzed pair is in the URL so the answer is shareable. It opens on a one-line answer: what kind of change it is and who it reaches. What changed, the affected consumers, owners and targets and the evidence gaps are folded below it, each with its count. It reads the currently published snapshot, the same one the Operational Graph shows, so its snapshotId matches the graph. The include-observed control is enabled only when the host declares an observation source, because observed evidence needs a real source.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• The Pacto Operational Graph: the read model impact projects onto, and the knowledge vocabulary every answer carries
  • Change classification rules: the semantic diff impact composes with the graph
  • MCP integration: the fleet query tool family pacto_impact belongs to

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the pacto command-line tool (CLI). Use the installer script: it installs pacto and the plugins with one command. The other two ways need Go and suit contributors.

Method Installs pacto version reports Installer script pacto plus both official plugins the release you installed go install pacto only dev, with commit and date unknown From source pacto only version, commit and date from your checkout

To look first, open the live dashboard demo. It runs Pacto in your browser.

docs.title: Via installer script
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh | bash

This puts three programs in /usr/local/bin: pacto, pacto-plugin-schema-infer and pacto-plugin-openapi-infer. The script checks each download's SHA-256 checksum first. If a plugin fails to install, the script warns and still installs pacto.

Pass --version for a specific release: bash -s -- --version v4.0.0. The CLI, the charts and the images each have their own version numbers. See Versions.

If the script cannot find a version (GitHub API rate limit)

The script asks the GitHub API for the latest version. Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests per hour per IP address, so on a shared network it can fail with Failed to fetch latest version. Set GH_TOKEN to any GitHub token and run it again:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh \
  | GH_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)" bash

docs.title: Installing without sudo
docs.text:
The installer calls sudo to write to /usr/local/bin. To install into your home directory with no sudo at all:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh \
  | PACTO_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin" bash -s -- --no-sudo

$HOME/.local/bin must be on your PATH, and the directory must already exist.

docs.title: Via Go
docs.text:
go install github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@latest

Requires Go 1.26.10 or later. The binary is placed in $GOBIN (typically ~/go/bin).

go install builds report as dev

pacto version prints Pacto: dev and pacto update refuses to run. Use the installer script if you need version metadata.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
Requires Go 1.26.10 or later, make and git.

git clone https://github.com/TrianaLab/pacto.git
cd pacto
make build

make build installs into $GOBIN (typically ~/go/bin) and stamps the version, commit and build date.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Pacto uses three version numbers:

Version What it versions Current major pactoVersion The contract format, set in each pacto.yaml "2.0", "2.1", "2.2" and "2.3" Pacto core The pacto CLI and the Go library github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4 4.x Kubernetes integration The operator, its Helm chart and delivery 6.x

The version selector at the top of these docs follows Pacto core.

A contract with pactoVersion: "2.1" needs Pacto core 4.1.0 or later and operator 6.1.0 or later. A contract with pactoVersion: "2.2" needs Pacto core 4.3.0 or later and operator 6.3.0 or later. A contract with pactoVersion: "2.3" needs Pacto core 4.4.0 or later and operator 6.4.0 or later. Older releases reject it. The integration's version compatibility table lists the current releases.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
pacto version

The first line should match the release you installed, or say dev if you used go install. If it names an older release, an earlier copy is ahead on your PATH: which pacto shows which one won.

docs.title: Installing the official plugins
docs.text:
The two official plugins (pacto-plugin-schema-infer and pacto-plugin-openapi-infer) are separate binaries from the pacto-plugins repository.

Install method Plugins Installer script Installed (best-effort) go install Not installed From source Not installed

Without them, pacto generate schema-infer fails with plugin "schema-infer" not found. To install by hand, download from pacto-plugins releases and put them on your PATH. See Plugins.

docs.title: Update the CLI
docs.text:
pacto update              # latest release
pacto update v4.0.0       # a specific version

This verifies the new binary's SHA-256 before replacing the current one. A go install build cannot use it; re-run go install github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@latest instead.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Pacto has no uninstaller. Remove the binaries, then the state they wrote:

# 1. The binaries (adjust the directory if you set PACTO_INSTALL_DIR, or use
#    ~/go/bin if you installed with `go install` or `make build`).
sudo rm -f /usr/local/bin/pacto \
           /usr/local/bin/pacto-plugin-schema-infer \
           /usr/local/bin/pacto-plugin-openapi-infer

# 2. Registry credentials and the update-check timestamp.
rm -rf ~/.config/pacto

# 3. The pulled-bundle cache.
rm -rf ~/.cache/pacto

The last two follow XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME where you set them. Removing ~/.config/pacto deletes stored registry credentials; run pacto logout <registry> first if you would rather drop them one registry at a time.

docs.title: Supply chain: signatures and checksums
docs.text:
Check what ships with each release artifact before you rely on a signature:

Artifact What ships with it ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/operator Cosign signature (keyless) ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator Cosign signature (keyless) ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/delivery Cosign signature (keyless) ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard Cosign signature (keyless) CLI binaries on the GitHub release checksums.txt (SHA-256) and an SPDX SBOM. No signature, no provenance attestation. ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard-contract Nothing. Unsigned. The demo contract bundles (ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/<service>) Nothing. Unsigned.

The release workflow signs the three images and the chart with Cosign "keyless" signing: the signature is tied to the GitHub workflow that built the image, so you store no key. Verifying it proves who built it:

cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/TrianaLab/pacto/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/operator:<version>

A successful run prints the certificate subject and the workflow ref it was issued to. Any other output, including no signatures found, means do not deploy it.

For the CLI binaries the check available to you is the checksum:

shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing

pacto update performs this check before replacing the binary. checksums.txt proves the download matches what the release published; it does not prove who published it. If your policy requires signed CLI binaries, build from source at the tag instead.

Next: Quickstart.

docs.title: Lockfile
docs.text:
pacto.lock pins the exact version of every contract yours depends on, so every build and every teammate resolves the same thing. Run pacto lock, commit the file and Pacto refuses to continue if a dependency later changes under you. It plays the same role as other lockfiles:

Tool Lockfile What it pins Go go.sum Module hashes Helm Chart.lock Chart versions and repository URLs npm package-lock.json Exact package versions and integrity hashes Pacto pacto.lock OCI digests for dependencies and references

It records a digest (a content hash) for every dependency and every configuration or policy reference, including the ones your dependencies pull in. When the lock is present, Pacto checks each one against its pinned digest. Any mismatch is an error: you cannot validate, graph, diff or push a bundle whose lock no longer matches.

The lock is optional. Without a pacto.lock next to pacto.yaml, Pacto resolves dependencies fresh each time. With one, pacto pack and pacto push include it in the bundle, so the dashboard can show pinned digests and drift for services read from a registry or a cluster too. To keep the lock out of a pushed bundle, list it in .pactoignore.

docs.title: What the lockfile pins
docs.text:
A pacto.lock file records:

  • Every dependency, all the way down: every dependency declared in dependencies[], recursively resolved through the dependency tree, pinned by OCI digest.
  • Every reference, all the way down: every config/policy reference declared in configurations[].ref and policies[].ref, followed through each referenced bundle, pinned by OCI digest. One entry per declared reference occurrence, tagged with the contract that declared it, so a root contract's settings reference and a referenced bundle's own settings reference stay distinct pins.
  • Local dependencies and references: file-based deps and refs pinned by their content hash (sha256:...) so local changes invalidate the lock.

The lock does not capture configuration values (configurations[].values), runtime metadata or scaling parameters. It only pins the structural dependencies and references that form the contract's external boundary.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: See the CLI reference for the full flag list; this section explains what each mode does.

docs.title: pacto lock
docs.text:
Creates or refreshes pacto.lock in the current directory. Resolves the full dependency and reference closures and writes the result to disk. Existing pins are preserved on rewrite when the dependency's constraint is unchanged; a consistent lock is left untouched.

# Create or refresh the lockfile
pacto lock

# Operate on a specific directory
pacto lock ./my-service

The lock command respects --values and --set overrides like validate and graph, so the lock you generate matches the contract as it would be evaluated at command time.

docs.title: pacto lock --update
docs.text:
Re-resolves the entire closure from scratch, ignoring existing pins. Use this when you want to bump all dependencies and references to their latest compatible versions.

# Re-resolve everything
pacto lock --update

The --update-name flag re-resolves only the named dependency (repeatable) to the newest version its constraint allows, leaving every other dependency pin untouched.

docs.title: pacto lock --check
docs.text:
Checks that the lockfile is up to date without changing it, and exits non-zero if it is stale or has conflicts. Run it in CI: the step fails until someone runs pacto lock after editing dependencies or references.

If a dependency points at a tag (not a digest) and that tag is republished, its digest changes and lock --check fails. Fix it with pacto lock --update or --update-name <dep>. Plain pacto lock keeps pins whose constraint did not change, so it does not clear this drift.

pacto lock --check

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
When a pacto.lock file exists in a contract directory, the following commands verify the lock before proceeding:

  • pacto validate
  • pacto graph
  • pacto diff
  • pacto push
  • pacto publish

If any resolved dependency or reference produces a digest that does not match the pin in the lock, the command fails with one of these error codes:

Code Description LOCK_DIGEST_MISMATCH A resolved OCI ref's digest does not match the lockfile LOCK_LOCAL_DRIFT A local file's content hash changed since the lock was written LOCK_STALE The lockfile is missing a newly added dependency or reference LOCK_CONFLICT The dependency closure requires the same service at two incompatible versions LOCK_UNRESOLVED A ref in the lockfile could not be resolved (network error, registry unreachable, bundle deleted) LOCK_MISSING pacto lock --check was run but no pacto.lock file exists. It is the only command that treats a missing lock as an error; the commands listed above skip verification entirely when there is no lock to verify LOCK_AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE One declared reference would have to be pinned to two different destinations, so the lock cannot record it LOCK_DUPLICATE_DECLARATION A contract in the closure declares the same configuration or policy name twice, so it holds two declarations the lock cannot tell apart LOCK_ERROR Fallback for a lock failure that carries no more specific LOCK_* code, for example a lockVersion outside the supported range

A lock below lockVersion 3 is reported as LOCK_STALE: re-run pacto lock to rewrite it. Rewriting is the whole migration: Pacto re-resolves the closure from the contract and ignores the old lock's content.

docs.title: Example pacto.lock
docs.text:
lockVersion: 3
pacto:
  version: v3.2.1
root:
  name: payments-api
  version: 2.1.0
dependencies:
  - name: auth-service
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/auth-service-pacto
    constraint: ^2.0.0
    version: 2.5.1
    digest: sha256:abc123...
    dependsOn:
      - crypto-lib
  - name: crypto-lib
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/crypto-pacto
    constraint: ~1.2.0
    version: 1.2.0
    digest: sha256:def456...
  - name: shared-lib
    source: local
    path: ../shared-lib
    constraint: ^1.0.0
    version: 1.5.0
    contentHash: sha256:789abc...
references:
  - kind: policy
    name: org-security
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/org-security-policy
    version: 1.3.0
    digest: sha256:fff111...
  - kind: config
    name: shared-config
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/shared-config
    version: 2.0.0
    digest: sha256:222eee...
  - from: oci:sha256:222eee...
    kind: config
    name: limits
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform-limits
    version: 4.0.0
    digest: sha256:333ddd...

The lockfile starts with lockVersion (schema version), pacto.version (the CLI version that wrote the lock) and root (the contract's name and version).

Each dependencies[] entry records the source (oci or local), the full ref or path as written in the contract, the constraint and resolved version and the digest (for OCI) or contentHash (for local). The lockfile's constraint is the dependency's compatibility range copied from pacto.yaml. The dependsOn field captures the dependency chain so Pacto can rebuild the full graph structure from the lock without re-resolving upstream refs.

The references[] section records config and policy refs with their kind, source and digest. Only dependencies carry a constraint. Local file-based refs appear here with a contentHash instead of an OCI digest. A contract that declares no config or policy refs produces a lock with no references key at all.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text: • The operator does not gate on the lock. The lockfile is a CLI-side reproducibility guarantee. The Kubernetes operator resolves contracts independently from CRD specs and does not consult the lockfile.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Moving a new version into an environment is still a pull request: someone bumps a tag in git, someone else approves it and a GitOps tool applies it. That made sense while a person wrote every change. Agents now produce changes faster than people can review them. The approval also rarely answers the real question: whether this version breaks the services that depend on it.

Answering that question needs a description of each service as an operating thing, and the pipeline has none. A reviewer approves a one-line diff, and the safety of the change rests on whoever remembers who calls whom.

Pacto moves that one line out of git and decides it from evidence. The contract graph says who depends on a service and which versions each accepts, checks say whether the new version behaves and a person is asked only when the evidence runs out.

docs.title: What GitlessOps means
docs.text:
GitlessOps means signed artifacts in your registry and evidence decide which version runs where, while your code and manifests stay in git. GitlessOps is three principles, and each one holds only under its stated condition:

  1. Desired versions are immutable artifacts in a registry. Every version Pacto promotes is an OCI digest that pacto publish signed. Which digest runs where is a pointer Pacto writes onto a Flux OCIRepository or an OCI-sourced Argo CD Application. Source code and manifests stay in git, and Flux or Argo CD still apply them.

  2. Evidence moves a change on a Stage set to an automatic level. A person is asked only when the evidence runs out, and only the team concerned; Why you were asked lists every case.

  3. Every decision can be verified without Pacto. With the recorder on, each finished operation leaves a signed in-toto record as an OCI referrer, checkable with oras and cosign; see Verify a record.

docs.title: Contracts are the foundation
docs.text:
A service's operational knowledge is real, but it has no home.

The API surface has an OpenAPI spec. The container has a registry. The deployment has a Helm chart. The service as an operating thing has no document: what it is, what it exposes, how it is configured, what it depends on, what compatibility it guarantees and whether reality still matches. Those facts are spread across artifacts built for other jobs, with no links between them:

  • OpenAPI describes one HTTP interface.
  • Helm charts encode how one orchestrator deploys the service.
  • Kubernetes manifests carry health checks and wiring with no link back to a service definition.
  • Configuration lives in .env.example files, wikis or nowhere.
  • Dependencies live in Slack threads and in the heads of the people who wired them.
  • READMEs go stale the day they are written.

Every consumer that needs to understand a service reassembles that picture from those fragments and fills the gaps with assumptions. The consumers: a platform, a CI pipeline, a controller, an on-call engineer, increasingly a program acting on someone's behalf. The picture is expensive to rebuild, different every time it is rebuilt and wrong the moment any fragment drifts.

docs.title: Contracts record version ranges
docs.text:
A Pacto dependency records which versions of another service a revision accepts, for example auth ^2.0.0. pacto.lock pins the rest of the transitive closure by digest. A catalog entry such as dependsOn: auth records only that the edge exists.

The range lives in a versioned artifact, so you can compare it with the previous revision, with the rules your platform sets for every contract (policies) and with what is deployed. A CI job, a controller or an agent needs that comparison before it concludes anything.

docs.title: Tenets
docs.text:
Pacto tells you which services a change breaks before it ships, and checks what is actually running. These tenets decide its design questions. They are in priority order: when two conflict, the earlier one wins.

  1. Every feature answers who a change breaks. A feature belongs in Pacto when it makes that answer more accurate, available earlier or easier to act on.
  2. A confirmed contradiction is an error. A missing observation is Unknown. Pacto reports a pass only for what it checked, and says so when it cannot see.
  3. The contract describes the service you already run. Pacto works with existing services in any language, and adopting it never requires a change to service code.
  4. Declaration stays separate from observation. The contract records author intent. Collectors gather runtime state, and Pacto evaluates that state against the contract, so one contract is validated at authoring time, compared in CI and checked against a running system.
  5. Every dependency states what it relies on. A dependency names the provider, the versions it accepts and the behavior it needs from it. CI can evaluate a range, and a bare edge gives it nothing to evaluate.
  6. Compatibility is computed from the contract. The diff rules, the version ranges and the lock decide whether a change is compatible. A version number is a claim that Pacto checks.
  7. Contracts travel through existing infrastructure. Each revision is an immutable OCI artifact, carried by the registries and the auth that already move container images. A contract references the schemas its interfaces already have, so it stays correct when they change.
  8. The core observes. Acting is opt-in. The core never changes what runs. The opt-in delivery component moves a version only when this change's compatibility, its impact on the consumers and its checks back it. A Stage earns the right to move on its own one level at a time, and a person confirms each level. When Pacto cannot see enough, it holds the change and asks a person on the teams concerned.
  9. People, CI and agents take the same path. They get the same checks, the same answer and the same next step.

docs.title: Agents take the same path
docs.text:
An agent, like any automation, reaches its goal by whatever path is open to it. A golden path it can skip protects little. Pacto gives agents building blocks that it checks and, with the recorder on, records. Those blocks are the only way Pacto makes a change.

Every change Pacto makes goes through the same checks for its type and the same admission policies, whether a person, a CI job or an agent over MCP asks for it. Agents get no approve tool, and the policies refuse an approval from an agent.

docs.title: What stays outside the path
docs.text: The admission policies decide who may write an Operation, an Approval and a pointer's digest. They do not cover workloads, objects without the pointer label or anyone allowed to delete the policies. RBAC alone limits kubectl apply on a workload. Your platform closes the rest with RBAC and its own admission. The delivery security model gives the detail.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: Pacto builds on ideas from others. The Flux team pioneered Gitless GitOps in 2022: container registries hold desired state as OCI artifacts and controllers read it from there. On Flux, Pacto moves a version by writing its digest onto an OCIRepository. ConfigHub treats configuration as data in a database behind an API. Pacto stores only "which version runs where" that way. Anthropic's Scion addresses stored content by what it holds, moves a pointer with one compare-and-swap and tests after a change merges and before it deploys. The contract graph is ours, and all of it is open source under the MIT licence.

docs.title: Drive Pacto from an agent
docs.text:
This page is for an engineer who wants an AI agent, such as Claude, Cursor or Copilot, to use Pacto. It covers how to connect the agent, what it can do and the limits that keep it safe. Every tool and input is listed in the MCP reference.

Words in links are defined in the glossary: MCP, contract, bundle, fleet, delivery and change.

docs.title: Connect your agent
docs.text:
Install the pacto command first (Installation) and check that pacto version works. Every agent then starts pacto mcp and talks to it over its standard input and output. Pick yours:

Claude CodeClaude DesktopCursorGitHub Copilot

Add to your project's .mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

Add to claude_desktop_config.json (~/Library/Application Support/Claude/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\Claude\ on Windows):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

Add to .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

Add to .vscode/mcp.json (requires VS Code 1.99+ and the Copilot Chat extension):

{
  "servers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

That starts the default server. To pick another, add its flag to args, for example ["mcp", "--delivery"].

docs.title: Pick what the agent may do
docs.text:
How you start the server decides what the agent can reach. Pick one mode: --root, --fleet, a bundle, --publish and --delivery cannot be combined with each other.

Start it with The agent can It can change pacto mcp Write and check contracts in local folders Contract files on disk pacto mcp --root oci://... Read published contracts and what they depend on Nothing pacto mcp --fleet Everything the default does, plus answer questions about your fleet Contract files on disk pacto mcp ./my-service --base-url https://... Everything the default does, plus call the service's own API, one tool per operation. The bundle is a folder or an oci:// reference; --base-url is where the running service answers Contract files; the live service only with --allow-writes pacto mcp --publish Everything the default does, plus publish a version to your registry Contract files and your registry pacto mcp --delivery Everything the default does, plus read delivery state and, if the cluster counts it as an agent, ask for or cancel a change Contract files and its own requests; it can never approve

If the agent must change nothing at all, use --root.

Files. The contract tools write to the folder the agent names in each call, relative to the folder the server was started in. Pacto does not limit which folder, so start the server in the project the agent should work on, as a user that can write only there. Claude Code and Cursor start it in your project; for Claude Desktop, have the agent pass full paths.

Fleet. --fleet reads the sources you name with more flags, such as --local ./contracts for folders, --oci <ref> for published contracts and --k8s for your kubeconfig's cluster. See pacto mcp.

Credentials. --publish, --root and --fleet use the registry logins of pacto login. A bundle's API calls use --auth name=value for the service's own sign-in, as its OpenAPI document declares it.

docs.title: Delivery: who counts as an agent
docs.text: --delivery acts on the cluster your kubeconfig points at, as the identity in it. Every service account counts as an agent, and so does anyone the platform team's groups name as one; see Who counts as a person, an agent or a team. Only an agent gets the tools to ask for and cancel a change; a person gets only the read tools. So give the agent a kubeconfig for its own service account, never yours: an agent holding your credentials is you to the cluster. Have the agent fill on_behalf_of on pacto_delivery_operation_propose with the person it works for: then that person cannot also approve the change, which keeps two people on every change.

docs.title: What keeps it safe
docs.text:
• An agent never approves. In delivery mode it can ask for a change, and Pacto's checks and the owning team decide (Who may approve). There is no approve tool.
  • Calls to your service are read-only by default. Only GET and HEAD operations become tools unless you pass --allow-writes. Each call stops after 30 seconds and follows no redirect.
  • Tools carry no safety labels. Pacto does not mark its tools as read-only or destructive in MCP, so build allow-lists by name from the table below.
  • Partial answers say so. Fleet answers carry asOf, the time they describe, and completeness, complete or partial. When a source was unreachable the answer says partial, and "not found" then means "not known".
  • Answers are frozen at start. --root, --fleet and a bundle (the ./my-service argument) are read once when the server starts. Restart it to see newer services or versions.
  • Over the network, callers must sign in. By default the server talks over standard input and output. With -t http it serves HTTP on this machine only. Serving other machines needs --auth-issuer and --resource, so every request carries a token from your company sign-in, and the server then refuses --auth and --allow-writes, which would lend one credential to every caller. See agents over the network.

docs.title: Which tools exist
docs.text:
Tools Mode Read or write pacto_create, pacto_edit every mode but --root Write contract files. pacto_create with pactify: true does what pacto init does for a folder or a cluster (see Pactify a service) pacto_check, pacto_schema every mode but --root Read pacto_fleet_search, pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_status, pacto_fleet_explain, pacto_impact --fleet Read pacto_catalog_revision, plus two MCP resources (documents the agent reads): pacto://catalog and pacto://catalog/closure, the contracts you named plus everything they depend on --root Read One tool per API operation, named by its operationId (or <method>_<path>) a bundle Calls your service: read-only, or its write operations too with --allow-writes pacto_skill a bundle Read: returns the notes a bundle ships for agents in skills/*.md pacto_publish_plan --publish Read pacto_publish --publish Writes to your registry pacto_delivery_operation_types, pacto_delivery_candidates, pacto_delivery_operation_plan, pacto_delivery_get, pacto_delivery_explain, pacto_delivery_history, pacto_delivery_blame, pacto_delivery_undo_plan, pacto_delivery_record_verify --delivery Read pacto_delivery_operation_propose, pacto_delivery_cancel --delivery, agents only Ask for or cancel a change

Pacto skips any API operation named pacto_*, so the prefix always means a Pacto tool. Inputs and outputs are in the MCP reference.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
You:    Create a contract for a stateful Go HTTP API called user-service
        that stores data in PostgreSQL
Claude: [writes pacto.yaml with an HTTP interface and marks the service as
         keeping data that survives a restart]

You:    Add a dependency on payments-api
Claude: [calls pacto_edit with add_dependencies]

You:    Check the contract in ./user-service
Claude: user-service is valid.

Pacto adds a dependency only from calls it observed, which pactify does when the node agent runs in the cluster. The node agent is a Pacto program on each Kubernetes node, separate from the AI agent that calls these tools. Add any other dependency yourself, as in the second prompt.

docs.title: If the tools do not show up
docs.text:
1. Run pacto version to check Pacto is installed and on your PATH.
  2. Check your MCP configuration file for JSON syntax errors.
  3. Ask your agent to list its tools (in Claude Code, /mcp).
  4. Add -v to args to see what the server does while it starts, such as reading a bundle from a registry. It logs nothing per tool call.

docs.title: MCP reference
docs.text: This page lists the tools, inputs and limits of pacto mcp. For a walkthrough, start with Drive Pacto from an agent.

docs.title: Three tool families and their boundaries
docs.text:
Family Tools What they do Safety boundary Authoring pacto_create, pacto_edit, pacto_check, pacto_schema Create, edit and validate Pacto contracts. Operate on contract files only. pacto_edit writes only after validation. Generated service Derived per operation from a bundle's OpenAPI interfaces (getUser, createRefund, …) Invoke the live service the contract describes. Read-only (GET/HEAD) unless you pass --allow-writes; every call has a 30-second timeout and follows no redirect, so a 3xx comes back to the agent as the result. Fleet query pacto_fleet_search, pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_status, pacto_fleet_explain, pacto_impact Read-only queries over the operational system: services, revisions, targets, relationships and status. pacto_impact projects a contract diff onto that system to report which consumers a change affects. Always read-only: they write nothing. They still make network calls, and the server that hosts them may also register write tools; see Fleet query safety. Catalog mode is the only server with no write tool.

Outside these families: pacto_skill (a bundle's skill files) and pacto_catalog_revision (one revision from the catalog, see Catalog mode). The publish and delivery tools are listed below.

These tasks are CLI-only: inspecting a registry contract, resolving a dependency graph, diffing revisions, generating docs and the two non-query pacto fleet operations, reconcile (declared dependencies against observed traffic) and snapshot (the whole read model as one document). Only pacto_publish pushes, and no tool deploys. In delivery mode an agent can ask for a change, and Pacto's checks and people decide it. Server modes lists which tools each invocation registers.

Tools carry no safety annotations

Pacto ships no MCP tool annotations. A tools/list response carries no annotations member (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint or idempotentHint) on any tool, including pacto_create, pacto_edit and a generated tool such as createRefund, which moves money. Build allow-lists by hand from the tool name. pacto_check, pacto_schema, pacto_skill, pacto_fleet_*, pacto_impact and pacto_catalog_revision are read-only; pacto_create and pacto_edit write contract files. Generated service tools carry no pacto_ prefix and reach a live service. They are read-only only when the server was started without --allow-writes; otherwise treat every unprefixed tool as able to change the live service. A bundle cannot claim a pacto_ name.

docs.title: Fleet query safety
docs.text:
• They are read-only. They project the Pacto Operational Graph and write nothing. The pacto_fleet_* tools answer from the snapshot built at startup. pacto_impact re-resolves both refs and rebuilds the snapshot on every call, so each invocation reaches your registry, and your cluster if --k8s is on, with the server's credentials.
  • They expose knowledge only. They never grant, scope or revoke a permission.
  • Partial or stale results are incomplete knowledge. Every answer carries an asOf time, a completeness value and structured limitations. Branch on those before trusting an answer.
  • Under partial coverage, a missing result means unknown. If a source was unavailable, "not found" means "not known here".
  • The snapshot is frozen for the session. A service deployed after the server started appears in pacto_fleet_* answers only after you restart the server.
  • The server keeps no state. The Kubernetes operator acts on contracts in a cluster, and durable evidence lives in an Evidence Server. The MCP server's state ends with its process.

--fleet names its sources the same way pacto fleet does:

pacto mcp --fleet --k8s --oci ghcr.io/acme/payments-api-pacto:2.1.0

See pacto mcp reference for source flags and The Pacto Operational Graph for the read model.

docs.title: The authoring tools
docs.text:
Every mode except --root carries these four.

Tool Description pacto_create Create a new contract from intent-level inputs. Supports dry run. pacto_edit Edit an existing contract. Supports dry run. pacto_check Validate a contract and return errors, warnings and suggestions. pacto_schema Return the full JSON Schema reference.

Structured inputs are JSON-encoded strings. Every input that carries structure has the MCP wire type string, and the value is JSON serialised into a string:

{
  "name": "orders",
  "interfaces": "[{\"name\":\"api\",\"type\":\"openapi\"}]"
}

Warning

Passing a real JSON array or object where the JSON-encoded string is expected is a silent no-op. The argument is discarded, the call still succeeds, changes comes back null and nothing is written. Check the result's changes and summary. pacto_check's own "add an interface" suggestion carries add_interfaces as a real array, so an agent that forwards that tool call verbatim hits this case.

pacto_check is pacto validate. It runs the same validation path, including pacto.lock verification and recursive policies[].ref resolution, so a contract it calls valid is one CI accepts. Its result carries the same stages and next as pacto validate --output-format json, and each error carries line and column when Pacto can locate it.

add_config_properties writes the schema. pacto_edit merges the properties into the first configuration's local schema file (configuration/schema.json when it has to declare one). A property already in the schema is replaced and required names are unioned.

docs.title: How pacto_create reads a description
docs.text:
description is matched against fixed keyword lists, case-insensitively and on whole words. A match only fills in what the call left unsaid: explicit interfaces or workload always win, and every inference is listed in the result's derived.

Keywords Inferred REST, HTTP, API, web a public openapi interface named http-api gRPC an internal grpc interface named grpc-api event, kafka, nats, pubsub, queue, message, rabbit an asyncapi interface named events worker, consumer, processor a job workload cron, scheduled, periodic, batch a scheduled workload (wins over job)

Interfaces are inferred only when the call passes none. The match is a keyword heuristic: "no HTTP" still matches HTTP.

State is never inferred: without the state flags the contract is stateless. Naming postgres declares a database dependency and leaves the service stateless.

docs.title: Bundle capabilities
docs.text:
Pass a bundle reference and Pacto turns that bundle's OpenAPI operations into executable agent tools:

pacto mcp ./my-service --base-url https://api.example.com

Each operation becomes an MCP tool named by its operationId (or derived as <method>_<path>).

The pacto_ names are reserved. A contract declaring operationId: pacto_check would take over the authoring tool. Pacto skips such operations.

Read-only by default. Only GET/HEAD operations are exposed unless you pass --allow-writes. The live host comes from --base-url, falling back to the spec's servers[0] URL. When you supply credentials, --base-url is required.

Service authentication (--auth). Credentials are supplied per OpenAPI security scheme with --auth name=value:

Scheme type How the credential is applied apiKey Sent as the declared header or query parameter http bearer (and oauth2 / openIdConnect) Authorization: Bearer <value> http basic Authorization: Basic <value> (supply pre-encoded user:pass)

pacto_skill. Bundles may ship domain knowledge as skills/*.md. The pacto_skill tool lists them and returns their content.

What a session freezes. Bundle mode, --fleet and --root resolve their inputs once at startup. To pick up changes, restart the server. Two exceptions: pacto_skill reads from disk on every call, and the authoring tools act on whatever is on disk.

docs.title: Catalog mode
docs.text:
pacto mcp --root <ref> starts a read-only contract catalog: the roots you name, plus their dependency closure, resolved once at startup and then frozen for the life of the process.

# One published platform, one contract you are still working on
pacto mcp \
  --root oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform:1.4.0 \
  --root ./experimental-platform

--root is repeatable and takes either a local bundle directory or an oci:// reference. Pacto discovers only what you name, plus its dependency closure. It never crawls a registry, guesses repository names or reads a catalog file.

The surface is two MCP resources (pacto://catalog and pacto://catalog/closure) plus one tool (pacto_catalog_revision). The catalog resource answers: schema version (pacto.dev/catalog/v1), catalog id, generation time, bounds, completeness and every requested root, including roots that did not resolve and why. The closure resource answers: every deduplicated revision with its content identity, rank and retained paths; every resolved dependency edge; every dependency that did not resolve; and every conflict and cycle, reported as found.

Catalog mode registers nothing else, so a server started for read-only discovery cannot modify a contract. A root or a dependency that could not be resolved stays visible with a category such as NOT_FOUND, AUTH_FAILED or UNAVAILABLE in place of the raw registry error, and the whole answer is marked partial. Under partial, a revision missing from the answer is unknown.

docs.title: Create a service's files with pactify
docs.text:
pacto_create with pactify: true does what pacto init does for a folder holding a service: it reads the Dockerfile and Kubernetes files and writes the contract. describe_only: true leaves out the publish section, for a request to describe or document a service. With delivery: true it also writes the cluster files. registry, environments, fleet_roots, no_transparency_log, insecure_registry and registry_secret match the CLI flags, and dry_run plans without writing. See Pactify a service.

pacto_create and pacto_edit return warnings for a value that validates but is likely wrong, such as an owner written as team/billing. pacto_schema returns the JSON Schema and, under agents, how to describe an AI agent as a service.

docs.title: Publish and delivery servers
docs.text:
--publish adds pacto_publish_plan (what publishing would write and which checks refuse it, without writing) and pacto_publish (publishes the version the same way pacto publish does, with this process's registry credentials, always to a new tag) beside the authoring tools. It runs over stdio only.

--delivery serves the delivery tools over the cluster your kubeconfig points at: pacto_delivery_operation_types, pacto_delivery_candidates, pacto_delivery_operation_plan, pacto_delivery_get, pacto_delivery_explain, pacto_delivery_history, pacto_delivery_blame, pacto_delivery_undo_plan and pacto_delivery_record_verify for everyone, plus pacto_delivery_operation_propose and pacto_delivery_cancel only when the cluster says the caller is an agent. Delivery mode has no approve tool.

pacto_delivery_candidates lists the versions a Stage may take, with their digests. The to input of plan and propose takes a version (3.0.0), a tag or a digest; a version or a tag must name exactly one of those candidates, or the tool refuses it and says why. A plan's next says what proposing it leads to: which teams must sign, that an agent cannot answer and the operation is then Held, and what happens at the approval deadline. pacto_delivery_get adds next with the deadline while an operation is held. Propose with the plan's intent digest and the same reason and on_behalf_of: the digest binds them, and PlanStale names the one that differs when it can tell. Over HTTP it needs token exchange; see agents over the network.

docs.title: The Pacto model
docs.text:
How Pacto decides whether a running service matches its contract. Three words carry the whole page:

  • A contract is what the service's authors say it is (pacto.yaml).
  • Evidence is what a tool saw in the running system, such as "a pod listens on port 8080".
  • A collector is the tool that gathers that evidence.

The engine compares the two and reports findings: one line per problem, each with a code such as INTERFACE_ABSENT. One rule governs it: a confirmed contradiction is an error, and a check Pacto could not make is Unknown. Most of what follows keeps those two apart.

docs.title: Declaration versus observation
docs.text:
The contract records intent: what a service is, whatever platform runs it. What it looks like at runtime is an observation, and it lives outside the contract. A contract carries only intent. Ports, scaling, images and other runtime settings belong to delivery and the integrations own them. Runtime facts travel separately, as an EvidenceSet produced by a collector, and the engine reasons over the two together.

flowchart TB
    A["Author intent<br/>pacto.yaml"] --> C["Contract"]
    R["Running environment"] --> COL["Collector"]
    COL --> E["EvidenceSet"]
    C --> EV["Evaluate"]
    E --> EV
    EV --> OUT["Findings + Coverage"]

docs.title: The engine: Evaluate(contract, evidence)
docs.text:
The heart of the system is a pure function, Evaluate:

Evaluate(contract.Contract, evidence.EvidenceSet) -> ([]finding.Finding, Coverage)

It keeps no state. Each observation carries an Outcome the collector set (Observed, Failed, Stale and so on), and the engine applies no timing, network or Kubernetes logic of its own. An assertion is one thing the contract claims, such as "the interface public-api is served". For each required assertion (an interface's availability, a capability, a dependency, a configuration, the workload or persistence), the engine looks for a matching observation and produces exactly one of three results:

Result When Finding Confirmed violation A matching observation has Outcome=Observed and its payload contradicts the contract. error, category RuntimeDrift, for example CONFIGURATION_ABSENT, CONFIGURATION_MISMATCH, INTERFACE_ABSENT, DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE. Uncertainty No usable observation exists: missing, Unsupported, Failed, Stale or Insufficient. unknown, category Inconclusive, for example EVIDENCE_MISSING, COLLECTION_FAILED. Satisfied A matching Observed observation is consistent with the contract. None.

A required assertion Pacto cannot observe never counts as a pass. Coverage is the count of what the engine could check: it reports how many required assertions were evaluated versus declared. Coverage leaves the aggregate compliance state unchanged, because a check Pacto could not make is uncertainty.

docs.title: Compliance model
docs.text:
The compliance model consumers derive from these findings has four substantive states, Compliant, NonCompliant, Unknown and Invalid, plus three informational ones:

State Meaning Warning A non-blocking finding. Reference The contract declares no workload, so there is nothing to run and nothing to observe. NotEvaluated The contract declares a workload but was never runtime-evaluated at all. This is what an offline OCI, cache or local source looks like, and what pacto doc, pacto fleet and the dashboard report for a bundle read off disk or out of a registry.

A workload that is being evaluated but has no usable evidence yet resolves to Unknown. The two answer different questions: Unknown means "we looked and could not tell" and NotEvaluated means "nothing has looked". The Kubernetes operator reports only Unknown. NotEvaluated is in the CRD enum for parity with the engine (see Kubernetes limitations).

docs.title: Collectors and the evidence boundary
docs.text:
A collector is any component that observes a real system and produces a valid EvidenceSet. That EvidenceSet is the stable extension boundary. A collector and a plugin extend Pacto in opposite directions: a plugin consumes a contract to generate an artifact, and a collector observes a system to produce evidence. You integrate a collector by producing an EvidenceSet. A collector is never installed as a plugin.

Pacto ships one general runtime collector and plugs it into each platform. The watcher observes TCP listeners and connection outcomes with eBPF and names the workload behind each socket: a pod, a container, a systemd unit, a pacto run session or a plain process. Its facts are platform neutral, and so are its health, metrics and protocol probes. It runs on Linux hosts that meet its requirements. Three front ends put it to work (see runtime conformance):

  • pacto run wraps one command and evaluates it locally.
  • pacto agent watches a host, binds workloads to contracts from Docker labels or a bindings file and evaluates them locally or sends signed evidence.
  • The Kubernetes operator (integrations/kubernetes) can deploy pacto agent on every node (opt-in: nodeAgent.enabled) and merges what it publishes with its own Kubernetes collector, which reads the API server, into one EvidenceSet.

Every path ends in the same Evaluate. The "custom collector" box below is a design extension point.

flowchart LR
    C["Pacto contract<br/>declared intent"]
    subgraph Collectors["Collectors: environment-specific"]
        W["Runtime watcher: eBPF + probes<br/><i>first-party, Linux</i>"]
        K["Kubernetes collector<br/><i>first-party, operator</i>"]
        X["Custom collector<br/><i>external integration</i>"]
    end
    W -- "pacto run / pacto agent" --> E["EvidenceSet<br/>observed facts"]
    W -- "node agent, merged by the operator" --> K
    K --> E
    X -.-> E
    C --> V["Evaluate"]
    E --> V
    V --> F["Findings + Coverage"]

In-process, a custom Go collector builds an EvidenceSet (pkg/evidence) and calls Evaluate (pkg/validation) directly. This is the compiled, run ExampleEvaluate in pkg/validation/collector_example_test.go:

// 1. The contract declares intent (loaded from a bundle in real use).
c := contract.Contract{
    Service:    contract.Service{Name: "orders", Version: "1.0.0"},
    Interfaces: []contract.Interface{{Name: "public-api", Type: "openapi", Ref: "interfaces/openapi.yaml"}},
}

// 2. A collector observes the environment and produces an EvidenceSet.
prov := evidence.Provenance{Collector: "example", DetectedAt: time.Unix(0, 0)}
ev := evidence.EvidenceSet{
    Subject:     evidence.SubjectRef{Kind: "service", Name: "orders"},
    ContractRef: "oci://example/orders:1.0.0",
    Source:      "example",
    ObservedAt:  time.Unix(0, 0),
    Observations: []evidence.Observation{
        evidence.NewInterfaceObserved(evidence.SubjectRef{Kind: "interface", Name: "public-api"}, "openapi", true, prov),
    },
}

// 3. The pure engine evaluates Contract x Evidence.
findings, coverage := validation.Evaluate(c, ev)

Across a trust boundary a remote environment reports a signed EvidenceSet over the evidence protocol instead.

docs.title: Distinctions the model keeps
docs.text:
The model keeps each of these pairs apart. Merging a pair turns an uncertain answer into a wrong one.

  • A requested reference and a resolved identity. payments-api:latest is a question; payments-api@sha256:… is an answer. A tag is mutable, so resolve the reference before you treat it as exact content.
  • The same name in two domains. Identity is domain-qualified, so two organizations that both run a payments-api stay two services. A repository basename or a path leaf is a label.
  • An exact revision match and retrievable content. A target can pin a digest that names a revision unambiguously while that content sits in a registry Pacto cannot read. A feature that needs the content reports it as missing; a feature that needs only the identity works as usual.
  • Declared ownership and a canonical owner identity. An owner identity carries both its kind and its value, so a team and a person who share a string stay separate. An email address is a contact for an owner.
  • Readiness and compliance. Readiness is a team's own scored self-assessment of a revision. Compliance comes from evidence. A revision that passes every readiness check can run on a target that is non-compliant.
  • No evidence and evidence of absence. Pacto records each observation as observed, unsupported, failed, stale or insufficient. "We could not look" and "we looked and it was missing" are different records.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Pacto records what a service revision guarantees, so that people and tools can compute against it. These limits hold for the contract engine and the operator. The opt-in delivery component changes two of them, as noted.

  • Pacto complements your developer portal and service catalog. A portal decides what people see and a catalog lists services to browse. Pacto has no onboarding, scaffolding templates or golden paths.
  • Pacto publishes to the OCI registries you already run.
  • Pacto models one service's operational intent. Your databases, queues and networks stay in the tools that manage them.
  • Permissions stay with your runtime controls. Pacto validates a contract against policy schemas. OPA, Kyverno, admission and IAM decide whether an action is permitted. Delivery adds its own admission policies, which decide who may move or approve a change to a Stage.
  • The engine reasons; collectors observe; actors act. The engine reads only Contract and EvidenceSet. Delivery is one such actor: it picks the version a Stage runs, rolls back and freezes, and Flux or Argo CD applies it.
  • Reading a contract grants no permission. Finding and reading a contract changes nothing and performs no action.

docs.title: The operational control loop
docs.text:
These roles compose into a loop a platform or an agent can drive. Steps 1, 2, 5 and 6 are implemented here: the CLI, the dashboard, the collector and Evaluate. Steps 3 and 4 belong to systems you already run.

  1. Declare. A contract states the service's identity, interfaces, capabilities, configuration, dependencies and policies.
  2. Read. A platform, a controller or an agent inspects the contract (pacto explain, the dashboard API or generated tools over MCP).
  3. Constrain. (External.) Policies, permissions, admission and IAM decide which actions are allowed.
  4. Act. (External.) Controllers, deploy systems, plugins or agents act through existing infrastructure.
  5. Observe. Collectors obtain runtime evidence from the real system and produce an EvidenceSet.
  6. Evaluate. Evaluate(contract, evidence) reports whether observed reality is consistent with the declared contract.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• The Pacto Operational Graph: the read model over many such evaluations, and the vocabulary for how much of the world an answer saw
  • Validation layers: whether a contract is valid, a separate question from whether it matches reality
  • Evidence protocol: reporting a signed EvidenceSet across a trust boundary
  • Impact analysis: the confidence model over a change

docs.title: Operational graph reference
docs.text: This page describes the sources of the operational graph, the target-state file format, what each query returns and how owners are keyed.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The graph is assembled from sources, each contributing the revisions and targets it can observe right now. The dashboard lists them as Data sources. A source is where the graph reads records from. A collector produces the compliance evidence that a source carries.

  • Local bundles (--local): the revision a developer is editing. The scan defaults to the working directory, descends 8 levels and skips hidden directories, node_modules and vendor. A directory the operating system refuses is reported as a gap and stepped over.
  • A contract root and its closure (--root <path|oci://ref>): the root you name plus every revision it declares, followed transitively. It is the same discovery pacto mcp --root freezes into a catalog, through the same resolver. Roots and dependencies that fail to resolve stay visible as limitations.
  • Contracts in OCI (--oci <ref>): the published revision catalogue, resolved cache-first so a pulled ref works offline.
  • Local OCI cache (--cache): every bundle already pulled to disk. Opt-in, because on a machine that has pulled contracts for months the cache holds everything anyone ever fetched. That is a useful offline baseline but a poor picture of the running fleet.
  • Live Kubernetes (--k8s [--namespace]): Pacto CRs read from a running cluster: which revision runs in which target, and its operator-computed compliance, findings, coverage and observed runtime.
  • Ingested external evidence (--evidence-url <url>): a running Evidence Server's read-only contribution over HTTP, exposing a remote environment's signed EvidenceSet reports as operational targets.
  • Offline target-state fixtures (--target-state): an unsigned demo and test adapter for supplying targets without a cluster.
  • Offline trace exports (--traces, or --trace-source NAME=PATH on pacto dashboard only): observed dependency edges. Pacto reads trace files only and ships no live OTLP receiver on ports 4317 or 4318. Run a Collector you own and point a source at the file it exports.

pacto fleet and pacto impact read every source flag above. pacto mcp --fleet reads all but --root, which on pacto mcp selects a frozen catalog and cannot be combined with --fleet. Two are narrower: impact takes a single --traces file, and --trace-source is pacto dashboard only.

docs.title: What a target-state fixture looks like
docs.text:
--target-state is the only source you author yourself: a single YAML or JSON document with schemaVersion: pacto.dev/fleet-targets/v1. Pacto rejects a second --- document, an unknown field or any other schemaVersion.

schemaVersion: pacto.dev/fleet-targets/v1
targets:
  - service: orders-service          # required: the service this target runs
    name: commerce/orders-service    # required: unique within the scope
    scope: production-eu             # the environment, for example a cluster
    kind: kubernetes-workload        # what sort of target it is
    labels: { env: production, region: eu }
    requestedRef: oci://ghcr.io/acme/orders-service:1.2.0
    resolvedRef: oci://ghcr.io/acme/orders-service:1.2.0
    digest: sha256:…
    compliance: NonCompliant
    coverage: { evaluated: 5, required: 5 }
    evidenceAt: 2026-07-29T09:40:00Z     # when the evidence was gathered
    reconciledAt: 2026-07-29T09:41:00Z   # when the target was last reconciled
    observedRuntime: { replicas: 3 }     # free-form; surfaced as a bounded preview
    findings:
      - code: STATELESS_PERSISTENT_CONFLICT   # required within a finding
        severity: error
        category: RuntimeDrift
        subjectKind: state
        subjectName: orders-db
        message: declared stateless but the observed workload mounts a volume
state:                               # optional: the source's own health
  status: available
  message: ""

Only service and name are required. Omit evidenceAt to model a target the collector could not observe. A file may declare at most 5000 targets. An entry that fails validation is skipped with a SOURCE_RECORD_INVALID limitation and the rest is kept. A failure of the file drops the whole source with SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE and marks the snapshot partial. Three fields are closed sets:

  • compliance: Compliant, NonCompliant, Unknown, Invalid, Reference, NotEvaluated, Warning or empty
  • findings[].severity: error, warning, info, unknown or empty
  • state.status: available, stale, partial or unavailable. A value outside this set is silently coerced to available, so a typo here reads as a healthy source

A malformed fixture is reported the same way as a missing one

Both produce exactly SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, and the output omits the parse error, even with -v. If the source drops and the path is right, suspect the file: check schemaVersion first, then field spelling and the closed sets above.

examples/demo/fleet-targets.yaml is a complete worked fixture, and it is the file the live demo runs on.

docs.title: Query semantics
docs.text:
The read model answers five kinds of question, each a pure operation with no I/O. A single snapshot serves concurrent queries.

Query Answers search Which logical services match this filter (owner, label, status, compliance, capability, dependency, readiness).
