Bounded and deterministically ordered. get Everything about one service (its owner, revisions, targets, declared dependencies, dependents, tools and skills) or one target. graph Traverse dependencies or dependents from a service, direct or transitive, cycle-safe, with unresolved edges surfaced. status What needs attention: non-compliant or unknown targets, invalid contracts, stale evidence, missing readiness, unresolved dependencies and dependencies outside their accepted range. With no category selected it reports every category. explain Deterministic, structured reasons for a subject's state. An agent can turn them into prose; Pacto itself embeds no model.

Two more operations sit beside the queries: snapshot emits the whole read model and reconcile compares declared dependencies with observed ones. Every answer carries a meta envelope, here from pacto fleet search --output-format json with an unreachable OCI source:

{
  "meta": {
    "schemaVersion": "pacto.dev/fleet/v1",
    "snapshotId": "sha256:c81df8fd572ecaa7c884968e728daff5b47c40b8e8c5cbcf1926c19740db95a9",
    "asOf": "2026-07-29T10:00:00Z",
    "completeness": "partial",
    "limitations": [
      { "code": "SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE", "source": "oci",
        "message": "source oci is unavailable; its records are missing from this snapshot" }
    ],
    "sources": [
      { "id": "local", "kind": "local", "status": "available",
        "lastSuccessfulSync": "2026-07-29T10:00:00Z",
        "revisionCount": 25, "targetCount": 0 },
      { "id": "oci", "kind": "oci", "status": "unavailable",
        "error": { "code": "UNAVAILABLE", "message": "the source is unavailable" },
        "revisionCount": 0, "targetCount": 0 }
    ]
  },
  "total": 1,
  "count": 1,
  "services": [
    { "key": "payments-service", "name": "payments-service",
      "owner": { "team": "payments" }, "status": "NotEvaluated",
      "revisionCount": 6, "targetCount": 0, "sources": ["local"] }
  ]
}

schemaVersion is the compatibility contract to branch on and snapshotId the content digest that proves two answers came from the same system view. On this envelope count is how many rows the page carries and total the whole matched population. Match on key, the canonical identity, because name can repeat across domains. A bounded preview nested in a get answer is the exception: it omits total when the walk was itself bounded, so an absent total means "we stopped counting".

Beside the rows, the dashboard's entity list and the TUI carry an aggregate over the complete matched population, computed before paging:

Tally Partitions Buckets serviceCompliance matched services compliance states, rolled up from each service's targets targetCompliance matched operational targets compliance states as observed per target ownership matched services consistent · conflicting · unowned readiness matched contract revisions passing · belowThreshold · expired · notDeclared

notDeclared is its own readiness bucket so that a missing assessment stays separate from a failing one.

get, graph and explain name a single subject and carry no envelope: a missing subject is a failure. pacto fleet get ghost exits 1 with service "ghost" not found in the fleet snapshot on stderr. These answers have no meta and so no completeness. Read completeness from search before you treat a subject miss as an absence.

docs.title: Resolved dependencies and accepted ranges
docs.text:
A declared dependency has two separate answers. resolved: true means a service with that name exists in the fleet. rangeStatus says whether the version the fleet holds satisfies the consumer's compatibility range:

rangeStatus Meaning satisfied Every revision of the provider in the fleet (or the one pacto.lock pins) is inside the range. unsatisfied None is. status reports it as DEPENDENCY_RANGE_UNSATISFIED in the out-of-range category. unknown The range or a version cannot be read as semver, the provider has no revision in the fleet, or its revisions disagree. absent The dependency declares no range or is unresolved.

A consumer that asks for ledger ^2.0.0 while the fleet holds ledger 1.6.2 is resolved and unsatisfied.

A dependency that declares requires also carries guaranteeStatus, checked against every provider revision it can reach: the one pacto.lock pins, or else every revision inside its range.

guaranteeStatus Meaning met Every revision it can reach offers what it requires. unmet None does. unmet lists what the newest one refuses. unknown The provider is not in the fleet, no revision is in range, its revisions disagree or the caller cannot see it. guaranteeReason says which. absent The dependency requires nothing.

deprecatedInterfaces lists each deprecated interface of the newest provider revision the dependency reaches, with its deprecated, sunset and successor. The dashboard shows both on the dependency, on the consumer's page and on the provider's.

docs.title: Ownership and the canonical owner key
docs.text:
The graph aggregates and navigates by a canonical owner key namespaced by which field named the owner, written kind:name:

  1. If owner has team → team:<team>
  2. If owner has dri (no team) → dri:<dri>
  3. If owner has only contacts → no canonical key. The service still counts as owned, but has no owner to rank or link to.

The namespace is part of the identity, so team:payments and dri:payments are different owners, and only the name is shown on screen, with a Team / DRI badge where two owners would otherwise be indistinguishable. The separate free-text owner filter is a human search over team, DRI and contacts. It can match several owners at once.

search and get return owner in one shape, the contract's own {team, dri, contacts}, and leave it out when no contract declares one. The owner comes from the newest revision that declares one. A service known only from Kubernetes has no revisions, so its owner comes from the owner the operator read from the running contract (status.contract.owner).

docs.title: The Pacto Operational Graph
docs.text:
The operational graph answers questions that span many services: what depends on payments-api, which revision runs in production-eu, is any of it failing its contract and how sure are we? It joins contracts, their published revisions and the places they run into one view that people, CLIs, platforms and agents can query.

pacto fleet search                                     # services found under .
pacto fleet graph payments-api --direction dependents  # who depends on it
pacto fleet status                                     # what needs attention

The graph is read-only. It collects results that other parts of Pacto produce.

docs.title: Three identities
docs.text:
The graph models three distinct things and keeps them separate: a name, a revision and a running instance answer different questions.

Identity What it is Example Logical service A stable name and owner. It has revisions and runs in targets. payments-api (owner: payments) Contract revision An immutable resolved revision. Identity is the service plus a content digest: the source's immutable digest, or one derived from the whole bundle when the source has none. A ref or a version is never an identity. Pacto omits a revision that it can neither pin nor hash. payments-api@sha256:… Operational target A concrete place a revision runs, generic as scope/kind/name. production-eu/customer-a → kubernetes-workload payments/payments-api

docs.title: How certainly a target is matched to a revision
docs.text:
A target can exist before Pacto knows which revision it runs, so every target records how the link was made.

Match What Pacto knows exact The target's content digest matches a revision's. Authoritative: this is the revision running there. inferred A unique correlation by mutable tag or version suffix. Probably right, but unproven. ambiguous Several revisions match that mutable reference. Pacto makes no link, and the target carries a REVISION_LINK_AMBIGUOUS limitation. unresolved Nothing matched, or the target's identity contradicts itself. No link, and a limitation on the target saying so.

The bottom two sit on the target itself, so a consumer can classify a link without parsing snapshot-level messages. The two read surfaces spell it differently, and the CLI's spelling has a trap:

  • Snapshot and pacto fleet get --target JSON carry revisionMatch, which is omitempty and only ever exact or inferred. An absent revisionMatch is the finding: it means ambiguous or unresolved. Read the target's limitations to learn which.
  • The entity-detail API (GET /api/fleet/entities/target?key=…, what the dashboard reads) carries linkState, always present, with all four values.

This inferred differs from the inferred relationship provenance below: one is how a target was matched to a revision, the other how an edge was derived.

docs.title: Relationships: declared, observed, inferred
docs.text:
Each edge carries a provenance discriminator that records where the fact came from:

  • declared: from a contract (dependencies[], and config/policy refs).
  • observed: seen in running traffic. Pacto keeps observed edges in their own adjacency index, so declared and observed answers stay separate.
  • inferred: deduced heuristically. Reserved for future use; Pacto produces none yet.
  • declared+observed: one edge backed by both. The neighborhood projection merges the two indexes for display and emits this combined value, so a consumer branching on provenance must handle all four.

docs.title: Sources and queries
docs.text: The graph is assembled from sources, each contributing what it can see right now: contracts in your registry, local folders, live Kubernetes, the Evidence Server and target-state files. It answers five kinds of question (search, get, graph, status and explain). The operational graph reference lists every source, the target-state file format, the query semantics and the canonical owner key.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
Every Pacto answer records how much of the world it saw. Each word below is a separate claim.

Word Claim complete Every source answered. Nothing is missing. empty Every source answered and there is genuinely nothing. This is complete knowledge of an empty result. partial At least one source was unavailable, stale or itself partial. What you see is a floor. stale Every source answered, but one of them last saw the world a while ago. Its records are real and may have moved on since. unavailable A source did not answer at all. Whatever it knows is missing from this answer entirely. unknown No completeness value arrived. This differs from empty.

Three of these travel on the wire, in every answer's meta.completeness: complete, partial and empty. The other three are a consumer's reading of the same envelope: stale and unavailable come from the per-source health reported alongside it, and unknown is what is left when no envelope arrived at all. The dashboard takes the worst of the six and gates every all-clear on that, so a source that is down shows even when the snapshot calls itself complete.

An unavailable source means missing data. A partial answer with zero rows is a set Pacto could not finish building.

docs.title: Who consumes it
docs.text:
A human portal and an agent consume the same graph.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources["Sources"]
        OCI["Contracts in OCI<br/>published revisions"]
        LOCAL["Local bundles<br/>revision being edited"]
        K8S["Live Kubernetes<br/>Pacto CRs: which revision runs where"]
        EVI["Evidence Server<br/>signed EvidenceSet reports"]
    end
    OTEL["OTel trace file<br/>offline analysis"]
    OCI --> OG
    LOCAL --> OG
    K8S --> OG
    EVI --> OG
    OTEL -->|--traces| OG
    OG["Operational Graph<br/><i>immutable read model</i>"]
    OTEL --> RECON["reconcile · impact<br/>declared vs observed"]
    OG --> RECON
    OG --> Q["Queries<br/>search · get · graph · status · explain"]
    Q --> DASH["Dashboard"]
    Q --> CLI["CLI<br/>pacto fleet …"]
    Q --> MCP["MCP fleet tools"]
    Q --> PLAT["Platforms"]
    Q --> AGENT["Agents"]
  • Dashboard: the visual front door. It builds one snapshot from every source it detects and serves the graph and change analysis through /api/fleet/*. The endpoints the UI reads (overview, entities, neighborhood and attention) carry their own schemaVersion, pacto.dev/fleet-product/v1, so a UI versions independently of the pacto.dev/fleet/v1 snapshot export above. The Operational Graph view offers three perspectives (Services, Revisions and Operational targets) and a Knowledge control (Expected · Observed · Differences). An operational target links to the dependency service it depends on. It draws no target-to-target mesh, because the snapshot has not observed that runtime routing.
  • CLI (pacto fleet …): the five queries on the command line, plus reconcile and snapshot. Scriptable, deterministic output.
  • MCP fleet tools: pacto_fleet_search, pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_status and pacto_fleet_explain, plus pacto_impact, give an agent read-only understanding of the operational system. See MCP integration for how they differ from authoring tools and generated service tools.

docs.title: A read model around many evaluations
docs.text:
Compliance is the pure Evaluate(Contract, EvidenceSet) function producing findings for one service in one environment (see the Pacto model). The graph is the read model around many such evaluations. It references each target's findings and coverage as the engine produced them.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Eval["Per-target evaluation (the engine, one at a time)"]
        C["Contract"] --> EV["Evaluate"]
        E["EvidenceSet"] --> EV
        EV --> F["Findings + Coverage"]
    end
    C -.-> OG
    F -.-> OG
    OG["Operational Graph<br/>composes many revisions + many targets"]
    OG --> ANS["Query answers<br/>with asOf · completeness · limitations"]

The graph also maintains a reverse-dependency index, which is what impact analysis traverses to answer "if this revision ships, which consumers are affected, directly and transitively".

docs.title: Observed dependencies and reconciliation
docs.text:
Declared intent is half the picture; the other half is what traffic does. The OTel observer (pacto otel observe <traces.json>) is an offline analyzer: it reads an exported OTLP/JSON trace file and derives the caller-to-callee edges its outbound spans prove. A missing span is no proof that a dependency is absent, so the observer reports only edges it saw. It can also emit signable EvidenceSets (pacto otel observe --evidence) so observed dependencies travel the same evidence protocol as any other report.

Those observed edges meet the declared graph in three places:

  • The snapshot itself: pacto fleet --traces <file> and pacto dashboard --traces resolve each raw observed endpoint name to a unique domain-qualified service and fold resolved edges in as observed relationships. A name that matches zero or more than one service stays unresolved and becomes an OBSERVED_IDENTITY_UNRESOLVED limitation, so observed traffic is always attributed to the right domain or to none.
  • Reconciliation: pacto fleet reconcile --traces <file> labels each dependency matched, declared-not-observed (dormant or unseen in the window) or observed-not-declared (a shadow dependency the contract never mentions). Anything unresolvable goes into a separate unresolved category.
  • Impact: pacto impact --traces <file> feeds the same observed edges into the affected-consumer list; the confidence model has what they change there.

The backend computes reconciliation: every declared edge carries a state computed against the snapshot's observed edges. A snapshot with no observation data returns insufficient, so an empty Observed view never reads as "there is no traffic".

docs.title: The fleet is a view
docs.text: Pacto discovers the graph from the sources you already have. A contract has no kind: Fleet and no fleet: section, because a hand-maintained fleet list drifts the moment a team adds a service. The fleet is a view, computed on demand and versioned by its as-of time.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Operational graph reference: sources, the target-state file, query semantics and owner keys
  • The Pacto model: the engine, the compliance states and the boundaries the graph inherits
  • Impact analysis: the consumers a change affects, projected onto this graph
  • Fleet tools: the dashboard, pacto fleet and the terminal UI
  • MCP integration: the three MCP tool families

docs.title: Decide, unfreeze and roll back
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

This page is for the person Pacto asks to decide on a change. It covers everything you need to do it. If you set up Pacto for your team, read Pactify a service first.

Words in links are defined in the glossary. Commands below name a Stage by its service and its environment's namespace, so -n prod means "in prod". A change is a Kubernetes object of kind Operation.

docs.title: Why you were asked
docs.text:
Pacto holds a change and asks a person in these cases:

  • It would break a consumer. For example, payments 3.0.0 removes a field and the checkout contract accepts only payments 2.x. Pacto asks the team that owns checkout, because theirs is the service it would break. The same holds when checkout requires a guarantee from payments that the new version does not meet, wherever checkout runs and also when Pacto cannot see where it runs.
  • Its contract does not back the Stage's environment. The contract lists environments, but none named like the Stage's spec.environment, or that environment's values fail their configuration schemas. The service's team approves it, alongside any consumer team the change also waits for.
  • It could not check something. Monitoring had too little data, or no contract depends on the part that changed, so a service without a contract might call it. That check says Unknown.
  • The Stage is set to ask for every promote. This is approval.always, which pactify turns on. A person approves every promote, whatever the level.
  • The Stage is on advise. A person approves every promote that a person did not ask for; see the autonomy ladder.
  • The Stage is on auto for non-breaking and the change is breaking, possibly breaking or unclassified. Every consumer's contract accepts it, but this level ships only non-breaking changes on its own, so a person approves it.
  • The Stage requires records and the recorder cannot write them now. A person approves the promote or rollback to go ahead before its signed record exists. The change itself runs as usual.
  • Someone asked to raise the Stage's level. A raise lets Pacto do more on its own and keeps the running version. A person of the team that owns the service, other than the one who asked, approves it.
  • The version changes who owns the service (the team, or the DRI when no team is named). The team that owns the service now approves it, so the author of a version never picks who approves it. A version that only edits the owner's contacts does not wait. When the running contract cannot be read, no team is asked, and only break-glass can answer if the promoter, the part of delivery that runs each change, requires an owner team.
  • The version number is too small for the change. A breaking change published as a minor (1.9.0 after 1.8.0) would pass every ^1 range, so a person approves it. So does a version whose contract moved to another registry domain, because consumers declared against the old domain would not be counted.
  • A person or agent asked to roll back to a version a consumer has moved past. That consumer's team approves it first; see Cancel and roll back.

Pacto asks members of the owner team of each affected service, or the changed service's own team when none of them names one, and skips the person who asked. If an AI agent asked for you without naming you, leave that change to a teammate; the rule is in Who may approve.

docs.title: Look, then decide
docs.text:
Find the held change and read what Pacto asks:

kubectl get operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod   # PHASE shows Held
pacto delivery explain -n prod <change>                       # what is asked and why

The question: line explain prints ends with what it asks for, for example Approve shipping it anyway? or Accept the unknown?. Give that answer, or reject.

Then give one answer:

Answer Use it when What happens approve The question says "Approve" and you accept it. Pacto asks that in every case in Why you were asked except a check that said Unknown Once every team asked has approved, the version goes ahead, or for a raise, the Stage moves up one level accept-unknown The question says "Accept the unknown": a check said Unknown and you accept the risk The version goes ahead and the record says "accepted". If the version already shipped and a later check said Unknown, only this or reject answers reject You do not want this version here If it has not shipped, the change ends and the Stage keeps the version it runs. If it already shipped, Pacto rolls it back to the version before. Someone can ask again later 
pacto delivery approve -n prod <change> --decision approve   # or accept-unknown, or reject

<change> is the name in the NAME column of the first command. All three answers go through approve; the --decision flag says which one.

A held change that nobody answers ends on its own after 24 hours. If it had not shipped, it ends as Expired and the Stage keeps the version it runs. If it had shipped and the question was about a later Unknown check, the Stage freezes instead, so a person looks at it. The person who asked can withdraw it at any time with pacto delivery cancel -n prod <change>.

In the dashboard (pacto dashboard), the Delivery tab's Inbox lists the changes Waiting for your decision. Changes another team may answer too sit behind a Shared with other teams count, and frozen Stages and changes that could not finish behind their own counts. Open a change: the page leads with the question and two cards, If you approve and If you reject, each saying what happens and each with its own button. Write your note, then press Approve shipping (or Accept the unknown) or Reject. The checks, the affected services and the timeline are folded below, one click away.

docs.title: What you need to be allowed
docs.text:
Three things, all set up once by your cluster admin:

  1. A role. Your Kubernetes user or group needs the approver role, and your group must be the owner team written in the contract of the service you are asked about: for a breaking change, the consumer that would break; otherwise, the service whose version or level is moving. Ask your admin for a binding like this one, for the team payments:
kubectl create clusterrolebinding payments-approvers \
  --clusterrole=pacto-operator-delivery-approver --group=payments
  1. The people group. If your admin named the groups people are in when turning delivery on (humanGroups), your login must be in one. Anyone outside them is treated like an AI agent and can never approve.
  2. A recent company login, if your admin asks for one. By default you decide with the sign-in you have. If your admin sets delivery.promoter.authFreshness (a recent sign-in to decide), the cluster must trust your company sign-in and you must have signed in within that time. Then pacto delivery approve prints an address, you sign in again in your browser and it sends your answer with that login, and the dashboard asks you to sign in again in the same way. Before the first time, set your company's sign-in address, which your admin gives you, in your shell: export PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL=https://login.example.com.

Where a recent sign-in is required but the cluster cannot check it (where approving works), nobody can give any of the three answers, reject included. A held change then has three ways out: the person who asked cancels it and publishes a version that asks nothing, it ends after 24 hours, or someone in the break-glass group forces it (below).

docs.title: When a Stage is frozen
docs.text:
A frozen Stage shows true under FROZEN in kubectl get stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod, and its reason says why: What happens to a change lists when a failed version freezes a Stage instead of rolling back. A forced version (below) also freezes it. Fix the cause first, then let automation move it again:

pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type unfreeze --reason "fixed the config"

An unfreeze takes effect at once and needs nobody else, even though the command is propose. It also clears HOLD, so run it on a Stage that is on hold even when FROZEN shows false. It needs the approver role but no fresh login, and only the team that owns the service (the owner team in the contract running on the Stage) or break-glass may unfreeze it: a person of another team is refused with NotYourTeam, even with a cluster-wide approver binding. In the dashboard, the Stages view has an Unfreeze button on each frozen Stage, shown only to the people the same rule lets unfreeze it.

docs.title: Roll back by hand
docs.text:
Pacto rolls a failed version back on its own. To remove a version that passed its checks, find the change that put it there and undo it:

pacto delivery blame -n prod --stage payments   # the "change:" line is the change to undo
pacto delivery undo -n prod <change>            # prints the exact rollback command; changes nothing

Run the command undo prints. If the Stage has moved on since, undo prints a normal change to the earlier version instead, and every check runs again. After a manual rollback, automation stops moving that Stage (the HOLD column shows true) until a person unfreezes it or asks for a new version, so your choice stays in place. In the dashboard, the History view has an Undo button on each change.

docs.title: Force a version (break-glass)
docs.text:
Someone in the break-glass group can force a version past every check. It shows in the history and freezes the Stage until a person unfreezes it. Use it only when nothing else works. <change> is the held change whose version you force:

to=$(kubectl -n prod get operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io <change> -o jsonpath='{.spec.params.to}')
pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type override --to "$to" --reason "why"

docs.title: Pactify a service
docs.text:
To pactify a service is to give it a Pacto contract, pacto.yaml kept next to your code, and let Pacto check every new version before it runs. This guide takes a plain service to a contract, signed published versions and environments Pacto only watches, and shows how an environment moves past watching once it has earned it. Every command is on this page except the one-time cluster setup for approvals. To preview the result, press Play the delivery story in the live dashboard demo, which runs in your browser.

In the cluster, Flux does the deploying and Pacto tells it which version. Each environment starts on observe, the first level of the autonomy ladder: Pacto watches and moves nothing until a person raises it.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the pacto command, from Installation;
  • a service in a git repository, with a Dockerfile and the Kubernetes files that run it (a Deployment and a Service). Those files are what lands in the cluster. Leave the namespace out of them: each environment gets its own;
  • Docker with a builder that can write an image to a folder, as Pacto builds the image there and pushes it itself: docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container;
  • a container registry, and a login to it: pacto login registry.example -u <user> (or docker login). Any registry works for this page. The optional signed record of each change is stored next to what you publish, in a registry that serves OCI Referrers. Without records a Stage stops at advise; see What delivery needs;
  • cosign, once, to make a signing key: brew install cosign, or go install github.com/sigstore/cosign/v2/cmd/cosign@latest;
  • for step 4, a Kubernetes cluster (1.30 or later), kubectl and helm. People approve with a fresh company login, which needs a one-time cluster setup, maybe by you: the cluster trusts your identity provider. Until it works, nobody can approve; see where approving works.

Pacto writes the contract from your service.

If you only want the contract and its CI checks, run pacto init --describe-only: the contract has no publish section and needs no signing key. Then go on to Put it in your repository: pacto push uploads the contract alone.

docs.title: 1. See what Pacto would add
docs.text:
From the root of your repository:

pacto init --delivery --plan

pacto init reads what is already there, such as the Dockerfile and the Kubernetes files, and fills in a contract from it. It reads your registry from the image name in your Deployment; pass --registry registry.example/acme if it cannot, or if the image is a bare name such as checkout: a Docker Hub official image only Docker can push to. --delivery adds the cluster files of step 4, so the first version you publish already carries them. With --plan it shows exactly what it would add and changes nothing. For a private registry, add --registry-secret registry-creds (step 4 creates that Secret). For a local registry that speaks plain HTTP, add --insecure-registry; to keep a throwaway key's signatures out of the public transparency log, add --no-transparency-log.

The plan lists the services yours depends on, what Pacto could not work out, marked Unknown, and a Next list of what to do after. Unknown marks a question that Pacto leaves for you to answer.

docs.title: 2. Write the contract
docs.text:
Add any flags you needed in step 1, such as --registry-secret:

pacto init --delivery --owner payments
pacto validate
echo cosign.key >> .gitignore

--owner names the team that owns the service: the name of its group in your company login, whose members Pacto asks about this service (Decide, unfreeze and roll back). init writes pacto.yaml, the delivery/ folder and a .pactoignore that keeps the signing key out of what is published, and never overwrites your edits. For an image registry.example/acme/my-service:1.0.0 and the files k8s/deployment.yaml and k8s/service.yaml, the contract is:

pactoVersion: "2.1"
service:
  name: my-service
  version: 1.0.0            # from the image tag (0.1.0 and an Unknown if none)
  owner:
    team: payments
workload: service           # from the Kubernetes workload kind
capabilities:               # from a readiness, liveness or startup probe
  - type: health
dependencies:               # one per service a URL in the environment names
  - name: billing
    ref: oci://registry.example/acme/contracts/billing   # its publish.bundle
    required: true                              # yours cannot run without it
    compatibility: "^1.0.0"                     # a placeholder: the versions yours accepts
configurations:             # the environment, ConfigMaps included, values as defaults
  - name: env
    schema: configuration/schema.json
    required: true
publish:
  bundle: oci://registry.example/acme/contracts/my-service   # where the contract goes
  deploy: manifests                                 # what Flux applies
  artifacts:
    - name: api
      type: image
      ref: oci://registry.example/acme/my-service
      build: {dockerfile: {context: .}}
    - name: manifests
      type: manifests
      ref: oci://registry.example/acme/deploy/my-service
      build:                # your Kubernetes files, the image just built, delivery/pacto.yaml
        command: [sh, -c, 'cp k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml "$PACTO_OUT"/ && sed -E "s,(^|[{,[:space:]])(image:[[:space:]]*[\"'']?)registry\.example/acme/my-service:1\.0\.0([\"'']?[[:space:]]*([,}#]|$)),\1\2$PACTO_REF_API@$PACTO_DIGEST_API\3,g" k8s/deployment.yaml > "$PACTO_OUT"/deployment.yaml && { grep -qF "$PACTO_DIGEST_API" "$PACTO_OUT"/deployment.yaml || { echo "pacto: no image: registry.example/acme/my-service:1.0.0 line to pin" >&2; exit 1; }; } && sed "s/@PACTO_VERSION@/$PACTO_VERSION/" delivery/pacto.yaml > "$PACTO_OUT"/pacto-resource.yaml']
  sign: {key: cosign.key}

Leave the long command line as it is. It copies your Kubernetes files with the image pinned to the digest this version built, in every manifest that runs it, and names any file it cannot rewrite. k8s/deployment.yaml stays as it is.

Fill in what the plan marked Unknown, above all the dependencies: set each placeholder compatibility to the versions yours accepts, such as ^2.0.0 for any 2.x. With that service's contract in --fleet, init reads its bundle and version instead. This version range lets Pacto ask the right team about a change. Declare an OpenAPI document under interfaces (how): Pacto sees API changes only there. Every field is in Publish and Dependencies. For private images, add imagePullSecrets: [{name: registry-creds}] under spec.template.spec in your Deployment. With dependencies, run pacto lock . (Lockfile), and commit what init wrote, as What to commit lists.

docs.title: 3. Publish a version
docs.text:
cosign generate-key-pair      # once: cosign.key (private) and cosign.pub
export COSIGN_PASSWORD=...    # the password you chose
pacto publish --plan
pacto publish

--plan changes nothing. pacto publish builds the image, pushes it with your Kubernetes files and the contract to your registry, signs them so anyone can check they came from you and labels them with the version in the contract. It reads cosign.key from the root of the repository, as publish.sign says. In your build pipeline, give the key and its password as secrets and run pacto publish after your tests.

Versions have three numbers, major.minor.patch, such as 2.4.1. Publishing refuses a version too small for the change (a change that breaks the services using yours needs 3.0.0) and never overwrites a published one; see Publish a version.

docs.title: 4. Connect the service to your cluster
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Install, once per cluster, Flux, the Pacto operator (it checks that each running service matches its contract) and delivery (it decides which version runs in each environment). One Helm chart installs both. Delivery reads your contracts: with a private registry, give it a login in the operator's namespace and add --set delivery.promoter.registryCredentials.secretName=registry-creds to the command that turns delivery on below:

kubectl create namespace pacto-operator-system
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system create secret docker-registry registry-creds \
  --docker-server=registry.example --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token>

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/releases/latest/download/install.yaml

helm install pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --version 6.4.0 \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace

helm upgrade pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --version 6.4.0 \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system \
  --reset-then-reuse-values --set delivery.enabled=true \
  --set delivery.identities.humanGroups={staff}

Replace staff with your people's group; Install says why.

Delivery is opt-in: without it, Pacto never changes what runs. Each environment is a namespace of the same name. Create them, give Flux your public key, so it takes only versions you signed, and apply the files init wrote:

for env in test prod; do
  kubectl create namespace $env
  kubectl -n $env create secret generic cosign-pub --from-file=cosign.pub
  # a private registry only:
  kubectl -n $env create secret docker-registry registry-creds \
    --docker-server=registry.example --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token>
done
kubectl apply -f delivery/test.yaml -f delivery/prod.yaml

registry-creds is the pull Secret your Deployment names and, with --registry-secret, the login Flux and the operator use. A read-only token is enough (on GitHub, read:packages); see Private registries.

Each delivery/<env>.yaml holds a Stage and the Flux pieces that watch your registry and apply what the Stage picks. delivery/pacto.yaml tells the operator to check the service; it ships inside every version, so you never apply it.

Each Stage starts at observe: it plans every new version and moves nothing, and the OCIRepository stays pinned to the tag you deploy (spec.ref.tag), so Flux applies what it did. With no version tag on the image, init writes no environment file.

kubectl get stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -A    # POINTER: the digest of the version each one runs
pacto delivery history -n test --stage my-service     # what happened in test
kubectl -n test describe stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io my-service  # if nothing moves: why, under Ready

docs.title: 5. Ship the next version
docs.text:
Make a change, raise service.version in pacto.yaml, then run pacto publish. While the Stages observe, you deploy the new tag as before: set spec.ref.tag in delivery/<env>.yaml and apply it. Each Stage records what it would have done.

To leave observe, in this order:

  1. Keep deploying this way until 10 versions passed their checks (autonomy.proposeAfter lowers that, see the ladder). The Stage's status.proposal lists what is still missing.

  2. Remove spec.ref from the OCIRepository in delivery/test.yaml and apply it, so Flux stops setting the version, and label it so only Pacto may write its digest. Pacto then proposes advise:

    kubectl -n test label ocirepository my-service delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref=my-service

  3. Ask for the raise; another person of the owner team approves it (see Why you were asked). Be quick: until the raise, nothing moves the version.

    pacto delivery propose --type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy --stage my-service -n test --to advise

Each level above that is one more approved operation. In prod, init also writes approval: always: true, so every promote there waits for a person: the contract check cannot see a consumer with no contract, or tell whether the version is healthy. Delete it from delivery/prod.yaml once a health check judges each version there (gates.verify.checks, see Delivery reference: health checks). A version that fails its checks after release is rolled back or freezes its Stage, as What happens to a change explains.

Each move is a change; one that waits for a person shows Held. To approve one, as a member of the owner team (Decide, unfreeze and roll back has the details):

kubectl get operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod   # PHASE shows Held
pacto delivery approve -n prod <name> --decision approve

docs.title: Many services at once
docs.text:
pacto init takes several folders and ends with a summary table. --cluster drafts a contract for every workload no Pacto describes yet, from your current kubeconfig context, in <out>/<namespace>/<name>. Pass --namespace: without it, --cluster reads every namespace, system ones included:

pacto init --plan services/checkout services/payments
pacto init --cluster --namespace shop --out drafts --plan

With the Pacto node agent running, the services a workload was seen calling become dependencies, pinned to exactly the version seen running (compatibility: "=2.3.0") for you to widen. Until you do, every new version of that service asks your team. Without the agent, environment URLs name dependencies, and one with no contract gets a placeholder range. Drafts are never published, and an invalid one fails the command. The MCP tool pacto_create with pactify: true takes paths, cluster and namespaces, and only plans unless dry_run is false. Generate contracts from what you already have lists the permissions --cluster needs and walks through a whole folder of services.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: Goal Page Decide on a waiting change or roll one back Decide, unfreeze and roll back Understand what happens to a change Delivery Fail a commit that would break a consumer Put it in your repository Check errors and response times after release Health checks Keep a signed record of every change Signed records Set up Stages by hand Setup and gates

docs.title: Packaging ignore
docs.text: Keep files out of the contract you publish. Put a .pactoignore file next to pacto.yaml, write patterns the way you would in .gitignore, and pacto pack and pacto push leave the matching files out. Use it for build output, editor files and anything secret, such as the sample config you inferred a schema from.

docs.title: Example .pactoignore
docs.text:
# Build artifacts
dist/
build/
*.log

# Editor files
.vscode/
.idea/
*.swp

# Temporary files
tmp/
*.tmp

# Large binaries not needed in the bundle
data/*.bin

# Include specific exception
!data/config.bin

The final !data/config.bin re-includes one file that an earlier pattern excluded (negation).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
.pactoignore follows the same pattern matching rules as .gitignore:

Pattern Behavior # at start of line Comment (ignored) Blank lines Ignored * Match any number of characters except / ? Match a single character except / [abc] Character class: match a, b or c ** Match zero or more directories / at start Anchor to the contract root / at end Match directories only ! at start Negate the pattern (include matching files even if earlier patterns excluded them)

The last matching pattern wins: if a file matches several, the last one decides whether it is left out or kept.

docs.title: Default ignores
docs.text:
These patterns are always applied, even when no .pactoignore file exists:

  • .git/
  • .pactoignore
  • .DS_Store

Note: pacto.lock is not in the default ignore list. When a lockfile is present it ships inside the bundle by default (see the lockfile). To keep it out of a pushed bundle, add an explicit pacto.lock line to .pactoignore.

docs.title: Immutable files
docs.text: pacto.yaml is never ignorable. Listing it in .pactoignore has no effect, because the bundle always includes the contract file.

docs.title: Referenced file validation
docs.text:
Ignoring a file that is referenced by the contract makes pacto validate, pacto pack and pacto push fail. You cannot ship a bundle missing a file it declares.

For example, if your contract references interfaces/openapi.yaml and your .pactoignore contains:

interfaces/openapi.yaml

Then pacto pack and pacto push exit with contract validation failed with N error(s) and nothing more. Under -v both add a debug line carrying the error count, never the file name. To see the message naming the file, run pacto validate: it prints FILE_NOT_FOUND (e.g. interface spec file "interfaces/openapi.yaml" not found in bundle). Neither command reports which ignore pattern excluded it.

The same rule applies to configurations[].schema, policies[].schema and any other file path declared in pacto.yaml.

docs.title: Commands affected
docs.text:
.pactoignore is applied by:

  • pacto pack: files matching ignore patterns are excluded from the tar.gz archive
  • pacto push: files matching ignore patterns are excluded from the OCI artifact
  • pacto init: files matching ignore patterns are not read when it drafts a contract from the folder, so none of them lands in the manifests artifact's build command

Every command that loads a local bundle reads through the ignore filter, so ignored files are invisible to all of them. The commands that validate the bundle (validate, pack, push) hard-fail on a missing referenced file, while graph, diff, doc and explain do not see the file and produce incomplete output. Only pacto pack and pacto push additionally package the filtered file set into the shipped artifact.

docs.title: Pattern examples
docs.text:
• /docs/: anchored: matches docs/ at the contract root only
  • *.log: unanchored: matches build.log and output/build.log
  • tmp/: trailing slash matches only the directory tmp/
  • !README.md after *.md: re-includes README.md; place negations after the broader exclude

docs.title: Pacto for platform engineers
docs.text:
You run the platform other teams deploy to. Pactify a service connects one service to delivery. This page is for the rest of the job: reading any team's contract to see what its service needs to run, such as its kind of workload, whether it keeps data, its APIs, the services it calls and its settings.

How a service is deployed stays in its own Kubernetes files. With delivery, pacto publish ships those files with each version and Flux applies them; the contract only points at them (publish.deploy). The contract says what the service is. Provisioning, scaling and wiring stay your decision.

docs.title: Your workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R[OCI Registry] --> PL[pacto pull]
    PL --> E[pacto explain]
    PL --> DI[pacto diff]
    PL --> G[pacto graph]
    PL --> GEN[pacto generate]
    GEN --> K[Files a plugin writes]
    DI --> CI[CI Gate]

docs.title: 1. Pull a service contract
docs.text:
pacto pull oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0

explain, diff, graph and generate accept oci:// references directly and cache what they download, so this pull step is optional.

A private repository needs credentials first: pacto login <registry>, or an already-authenticated gh for GHCR. Authentication gives the full resolution order.

docs.title: 2. Inspect it
docs.text:
pacto explain oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0

See pacto explain for the output format.

docs.title: 3. Check for breaking changes
docs.text:
pacto diff oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.0.0 \
  oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0

It exits non-zero if breaking changes are detected. See Diff and change classification for the full reference and worked examples.

docs.title: 4. Resolve the dependency graph
docs.text:
$ pacto graph oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0
payments-api@2.1.0
├─ auth-service@2.3.0
│  └─ user-store@1.0.0
└─ notifications@1.0.0 (shared)

Pacto follows each dependency to its own contract in the registry, all the way down, and caches the results. Add --with-references to also show configuration and policy references, or --only-references to show only those.

docs.title: 5. Generate deployment artifacts
docs.text: If you would rather generate Kubernetes files from contracts than keep them by hand, pacto generate <name> runs a plugin program called pacto-plugin-<name> and writes the files it returns. The two official plugins generate parts of an existing contract: openapi-infer writes the OpenAPI document and schema-infer writes the configuration schema. Both need a pacto.yaml in the folder first. To generate deployment files, write your own plugin: a small program in any language that reads a contract as JSON and returns file contents. See Plugin development.

docs.title: Workload type
docs.text: workload Kubernetes resource Notes service Deployment or StatefulSet Based on state.type job Job Runs to completion scheduled CronJob Schedule defined externally

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
The values below, such as shared/persistent, are short for the state.persistence.scope and state.persistence.durability fields, as pacto explain shows them. They describe the service. The table shows one sensible way to map them on Kubernetes:

state.type state.persistence Infrastructure stateless local/ephemeral Deployment, no PVC, free to scale horizontally stateful local/persistent StatefulSet + PVC, stable identity per replica stateful local/ephemeral StatefulSet with emptyDir (stable identity, no durable storage) stateful shared/persistent Network-attached or shared storage hybrid local/persistent StatefulSet + PVC, tolerates cold starts hybrid local/ephemeral Deployment with emptyDir, warm caches improve performance

The contract leaves out upgrade strategy, shutdown timing, replica counts and autoscaling on purpose. Those stay in your Kubernetes files.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration and policy: the full reference
  • Composition patterns: root + component contracts, infrastructure contracts, published policy + schema bundles and the rest
  • Diff and change classification: what counts as breaking
  • Put it in your repository: using Pacto in pipelines
  • GitHub Actions integration: the pacto-actions workflow
  • Fleet views: all your services at once (dashboard, pacto fleet, terminal UI)
  • Kubernetes operator: checks running services against their contracts, including what they actually do on the network
  • The operational graph: the fleet-wide read model
  • For developers: the other side of the same contract

docs.title: Plugin Development
docs.text: A plugin turns a contract into files: Helm charts, Terraform, Kubernetes manifests, a README. It is a separate program, written in any language. pacto generate <name> sends it the contract as JSON on stdin, and the plugin answers with a list of files on stdout. The Bash example below is a complete, working plugin.

docs.title: Official plugins
docs.text:
Plugin Description pacto-plugin-schema-infer Infers a JSON Schema from sample configuration files (JSON, YAML, TOML) pacto-plugin-openapi-infer Extracts OpenAPI 3.1 specs from source code (FastAPI, Huma)

Both read files you already have and write contract inputs, so you can skip writing a schema by hand. Pacto ships no deployment-artifact plugin. To use pacto generate helm, write or install a pacto-plugin-helm yourself. Without a pacto-plugin-helm on your PATH it exits 1 with plugin "helm" not found (looked for pacto-plugin-helm in $PATH and ~/.config/pacto/plugins/).

See Installation for how to install them. Refer to each plugin's README for usage:

  • pacto-plugin-schema-infer
  • pacto-plugin-openapi-infer

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Pacto loads the contract, finds the plugin program (pacto-plugin-<name>), writes a request to its stdin, reads the response from its stdout and writes the files. A plugin gets a copy of the contract and cannot change it. Pacto stops a plugin after 60 seconds or 64 MB of output.

docs.title: Plugin discovery
docs.text: Pacto searches for pacto-plugin-<name> in $PATH, then ~/.config/pacto/plugins/. Not found is an error: pacto generate helm without pacto-plugin-helm exits 1.

docs.title: Request (stdin)
docs.text:
Pacto writes a JSON object to the plugin's stdin:

{
  "protocolVersion": "1",
  "contract": {
    "pactoVersion": "2.0",
    "service": {
      "name": "my-service",
      "version": "1.0.0"
    },
    "interfaces": [...],
    "workload": "service",
    "state": {...},
    ...
  },
  "bundleDir": "my-service",
  "outputDir": "helm-output",
  "options": {
    "namespace": "production"
  }
}
Field Type Description protocolVersion string Always "1" contract object The full parsed contract bundleDir string Path to the bundle (may be relative) outputDir string Path for output files (may be relative) options object Optional. User-provided key-value options from --option key=value

docs.title: Response (stdout)
docs.text:
The plugin writes a JSON object to stdout:

{
  "files": [
    {
      "path": "deployment.yaml",
      "content": "apiVersion: apps/v1\nkind: Deployment\n..."
    },
    {
      "path": "service.yaml",
      "content": "apiVersion: v1\nkind: Service\n..."
    }
  ],
  "message": "Generated Kubernetes manifests for my-service"
}
Field Type Description files array List of generated files files[].path string Relative path within output directory files[].content string File content message string Optional message

files[].path must be relative. Absolute paths and .. are rejected. On error, write to stderr and exit non-zero.

docs.title: Example: Minimal plugin in Bash
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# pacto-plugin-readme: generates a README from a Pacto contract

set -euo pipefail

# Read the full JSON request from stdin
REQUEST=$(cat)

# Extract fields using jq
NAME=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.service.name')
VERSION=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.service.version')
WORKLOAD=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.workload // "n/a"')
STATE=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.state.type // "n/a"')

# Generate a README
CONTENT="# ${NAME}

**Version:** ${VERSION}
**Workload:** ${WORKLOAD}
**State:** ${STATE}

This file was auto-generated by pacto-plugin-readme.
"

# Write the response JSON to stdout
jq -n \
  --arg path "README.md" \
  --arg content "$CONTENT" \
  --arg msg "Generated README for ${NAME}" \
  '{files: [{path: $path, content: $content}], message: $msg}'

Make it executable and place it in your $PATH:

chmod +x pacto-plugin-readme
mv pacto-plugin-readme /usr/local/bin/
pacto generate readme my-service

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Read only from bundleDir. Do not access files outside the bundle.
  • Write only to stdout. Do not write files directly; return them in the response. Pacto handles file creation.
  • Follow the protocol. Return clean relative paths, write errors to stderr and exit non-zero on failure.
  • Be deterministic. Given the same input, produce the same output.
  • Handle missing optional fields. Only pactoVersion and service are required, so a contract may omit workload, state, configurations, dependencies or capabilities.

docs.title: Publish a version
docs.text:
This page describes how pacto publish works. To take a new service to its first release, follow Pactify a service.

pacto publish publishes what a contract's publish section declares: the contract bundle, the service's images, charts and the manifests Flux applies, all tagged with the version the contract states. Docker or a command you name does the build. Pacto pushes, signs and checks.

pacto publish --plan    # what is missing, and what would refuse it; writes nothing
pacto publish           # publish it

publish needs contract format 2.1, which earlier Pacto releases cannot read. Before your first publish, make sure the services that depend on yours run a Pacto and operator that read 2.1: see publish.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Pacto runs no tests. It refuses to publish when one of its own checks fails:

  • the contract is invalid, or uses a local reference or breaks its pacto.lock;
  • a provider does not meet what a required dependency requires (GUARANTEE_UNMET). Pacto fetches each provider that a dependency declares requires for, as pacto validate does, and --plan shows the unmet guarantee as the failed validation check. An unmet guarantee of an optional dependency and a provider Pacto cannot fetch (GUARANTEE_UNVERIFIED) are warnings: the validation check passes and names them;
  • publish.sign is missing, the signing key file would end up inside the bundle, or the signer does not open: a missing key file, a wrong COSIGN_PASSWORD or an unreachable KMS key refuses the plan, before anything is built;
  • there is no source revision (run it in a git checkout, or pass --revision). Pacto reads the commit from .git itself, worktrees and packed refs included;
  • the git checkout has uncommitted changes to tracked files, so the commit stamped and signed on every artifact would not hold what was built. Publish from a clean checkout. This check runs git status; --revision skips it, since you then name the revision yourself. Untracked files are not checked;
  • a dockerfile build has no usable docker buildx builder, or a command build's program is not an executable here;
  • two artifacts, or an artifact and the bundle, share one repository;
  • an SBOM is declared on a dockerfile build, which writes none, or sits in the contract directory without a .pactoignore line (--plan names it);
  • the version is too small for the change.

The signer, the clean checkout and the builders are checked only for what is still to write: a builder for each artifact not yet published, the signer and git status when anything is. Running publish again for a version already published (to --propose it, say) needs none of them.

A version too small for the change is also kept as a signed refusal in the contract bundle repository, signed with the publish key, so the dashboard's Published view shows it with the bump it needed. The refusal record leaves the outcome unchanged: if the registry rejects the record, publish reports that beside the refusal.

A release candidate's fixes ship as the version it was a candidate for: after 2.0.0-rc.1, 2.0.0-rc.2 and 2.0.0 are accepted whatever changed. The change since the last final release must still fit the version: after 1.0.0 and 1.1.0-rc.1, a breaking change cannot ship as 1.1.0. The version rule compares the contract with the highest version already published below it, using the same classification as pacto diff:

Change since the last version Smallest version allowed Breaking a new major version (before 1.0, a new minor) Potentially breaking: Pacto cannot tell a new minor version Not breaking any higher version

pacto diff prints the same rule as Required bump.

docs.title: Never overwritten
docs.text:
For every artifact the plan says what the registry holds for its tag:

State Meaning Publish does absent The tag does not exist builds, pushes and tags it identical The tag holds exactly what Pacto computed (the bundle) nothing adopt Its version and revision annotations match this publish reuses it if it is signed by the configured identity; refuses otherwise conflict The tag holds something else refuses; nothing is overwritten unreadable The registry could not be read refuses; unreadable is never absent

Annotations are not signed, so anyone who can push can write them. Pacto therefore never signs what it adopts: a tag it wrote was signed before it was tagged, and one without that signature is someone else's.

A run that stopped halfway finishes when you run it again from the same commit: the plan adopts what the first run pushed and writes only what is missing. Run it from another commit and every tag the first run wrote is a conflict, so that version is spent: publish a higher service.version.

The deploy artifact is tagged last: once its tag exists, everything it points at exists and is signed. The other tags, the bundle's included, may already exist when a run stops, but no Stage takes a version without its deploy artifact. Each tag is read again just before it is written, which narrows the window in which two runs racing on one version could both write. A registry has no compare-and-swap on tags, so the window stays open: give each version one publisher.

docs.title: What gets published
docs.text:
Each build gets PACTO_OUT, PACTO_VERSION, PACTO_REVISION and, for every artifact built before it, PACTO_DIGEST_<NAME> and PACTO_REF_<NAME>, so a manifests build can pin the image it deploys by digest. Pacto then:

  1. pushes each artifact by digest, with org.opencontainers.image.version and org.opencontainers.image.revision on its manifest;
  2. packages the deploy artifact as a Flux artifact whose delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/contract annotation names the digest-pinned contract bundle;
  3. attaches the SBOM file the build wrote to each image that declares one, and signs it, unless one signed by the configured identity is already there. Pacto never makes an SBOM, and refuses a file older than the build;
  4. signs every digest, unless a valid signature by the configured key, KMS key or keyless identity is already there, then verifies the new signature against that identity. A keyless signature carries whatever identity the CI token had, so a mismatch fails here, before any tag is written, so Pacto never publishes a version no Stage would take;
  5. pushes the bundle and writes the tags.

It needs docker buildx with a builder that can write an OCI layout (the docker-container driver can) for dockerfile builds, and git to check that the checkout is clean unless you pass --revision. It needs no syft or cosign. The build commands pacto init writes run sh, cp and sed, so they need a POSIX shell: on Windows, publish from WSL or a Linux CI runner. Registry credentials and plain-HTTP registries come from the same settings as pacto push.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
Pacto signs with the Sigstore library and needs no cosign binary. Each signature is a Sigstore bundle attached to the digest as a referrer, the way cosign 3 writes one, so cosign verify and Flux's spec.verify both check it.

sign What signs Notes key: cosign.key A PEM private key file A cosign key is decrypted with COSIGN_PASSWORD kms: awskms:///alias/ci A KMS key awskms://, gcpkms://, azurekms:// or hashivault://, with that cloud's usual credentials. The key must be ECDSA P-256, Ed25519 or RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256: Pacto refuses RSA-PSS and SHA-384 or SHA-512 keys. The released pacto binaries leave cloud KMS out to stay small: build one with go install -tags kms github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@<version>, or one provider's tag (kms_aws, kms_gcp, kms_azure, kms_hashivault). The error names the build to use keyless: true A short-lived certificate from public-good Fulcio The OIDC token comes from SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN or GitHub Actions (id-token: write)

A signature goes to the public transparency log unless transparencyLog: false. Keyless signing needs the log: its certificate lives ten minutes, so it verifies only at the time the log saw it, and Pacto refuses keyless with transparencyLog: false. Pacto verifies a keyless signature against the identity and issuer you configure, under the trusted root Sigstore publishes through TUF.

docs.title: In CI and from agents
docs.text: CI calls it as one step after the tests pass. An agent calls the same thing through MCP: pacto mcp --publish adds pacto_publish_plan and pacto_publish beside the authoring tools, over stdio only.

docs.title: Hand-off to delivery
docs.text:
With Pacto delivery installed, a Stage whose candidate OCIRepository follows the deploy artifact's repository sees each new version without an extra step, and --propose <namespace>/<stage> proposes it on a Stage that does not promote by itself. A Stage promotes only versions published this way: Flux checks the signature and the promoter checks the contract annotation. So --propose first waits until the Stage records the version as published, which happens once Flux polls the new tag and verifies its signature. It waits up to --propose-timeout (10 minutes by default), then gives up and says so.

To take a version back out of an environment, see Roll back by hand.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: In this tutorial you write a contract, check it and use it to catch a breaking change. It takes about five minutes. A contract is one file, pacto.yaml. Everything here runs on your machine, with no account and no registry.

docs.title: 1. Install Pacto
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh | bash

Installation covers the other ways to install and what to do if the script fails.

docs.title: 2. Create a contract
docs.text:
Run this from an empty directory and stay there through step 5; step 6 moves inside my-service.

pacto init my-service

This writes three files: pacto.yaml (the contract), interfaces/openapi.yaml (a placeholder API spec) and configuration/schema.json (a placeholder config schema). The argument is the folder to write into, and its last part becomes service.name, so pacto init fleet/checkout writes a contract for checkout in fleet/checkout. Run pacto init in a folder that already holds a service and it reads the Dockerfile and Kubernetes files instead: see Pactify a service.

Edit my-service/pacto.yaml and set service.version: 1.0.0. Then replace my-service/interfaces/openapi.yaml with an API that has required response fields:

openapi: "3.0.0"
info:
  title: my-service
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /orders/{id}:
    get:
      summary: Get an order
      responses:
        "200":
          description: OK
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [id, total]
                properties:
                  id:
                    type: string
                  total:
                    type: number

docs.title: 3. Validate
docs.text:
$ pacto validate my-service
my-service is valid

Validation checks three things: the file's shape, that fields agree with each other (a field that names an interface must name one the contract declares, for example) and your policies, the rules your platform team may set for every contract. See the Contract Reference for the full rules.

docs.title: 4. Add consumers
docs.text:
Two services depend on my-service, each with a different compatibility range. Copy the folder twice and declare the dependencies:

cp -r my-service checkout
cp -r my-service reporting

In checkout/pacto.yaml, set service.name: checkout and replace the dependencies: block that pacto init wrote as comments with:

dependencies:
  - name: my-service
    ref: ../my-service
    required: true
    compatibility: "^1.0.0"

In reporting/pacto.yaml, set service.name: reporting and use a wider range:

dependencies:
  - name: my-service
    ref: ../my-service
    required: true
    compatibility: ">=1.0.0"

checkout accepts ^1.0.0 (1.x only), reporting accepts >=1.0.0 (1.x and above). Step 7 shows what that difference changes.

docs.title: 5. Introduce a breaking change
docs.text:
Copy my-service to v2 and delete the total field from the response schema:

cp -r my-service v2

In v2/pacto.yaml, set service.version: 2.0.0. In v2/interfaces/openapi.yaml, remove total from required and from properties so the schema becomes:

schema:
  type: object
  required: [id]
  properties:
    id:
      type: string

docs.title: 6. Diff the two versions
docs.text:
Move into my-service and compare the original contract against v2:

$ cd my-service
$ pacto diff . ../v2
Classification: BREAKING
Required bump: major
Changes (3):
  [NON_BREAKING] service.version (modified): service.version modified [1.0.0 -> 2.0.0]
  [BREAKING] openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.total (removed): openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.total removed [- map[type:number]]
  [BREAKING] openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.required[total] (removed): openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.required total removed [- total]
breaking changes detected
$ echo $?
1

The classification is BREAKING, so the next published version must be a new major version, and the exit code is 1. That is the CI gate: pacto diff exits non-zero when the change is breaking for anyone who may use the service (pacto impact below says which consumers), so a branch-protection rule that requires passing checks blocks the merge.

docs.title: 7. Find the affected consumers
docs.text:
pacto impact takes that diff, finds every service that depends on my-service and tells you which ones break:

$ pacto impact . ../v2 --local ..
Impact: my-service 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 2
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Affected consumers (2):
  checkout                     direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=my-team
  reporting                    direct     confidence=contractual  compat=compatible   owner=my-team
    note: the range >=1.0.0 has no upper bound, so compatible only means the range >=1.0.0 accepts 2.0.0; this change is BREAKING, so check that reporting does not use what it removes or changes
Release gate: unverified
unverified: the change is BREAKING and 2 consumers depend on my-service, but none is shown to be both incompatible and running. Review each consumer, and add a source that knows where services run (for example --target-state) to tell deployed impact apart

checkout and reporting declare the same edge to the same service and get opposite verdicts. checkout pins ^1.0.0 (1.x only) and breaks. reporting accepts >=1.0.0 (any major), so its range still matches. The note says what that match does not prove: that reporting avoids what the change removes. Pacto tells the two apart because each contract carries its compatibility range.

The exit code is 2: the gate is unverified. The bundles say nothing about where the consumers run, so Pacto neither blocks the change nor calls it safe. Release gate and exit status explains the three outcomes.

owner=my-team is the placeholder team pacto init wrote. confidence=contractual means the answer comes from the declared ranges alone, without a runtime observation of the call. direct means each consumer declares my-service itself.

docs.title: Optional: publish to a registry
docs.text:
The steps above need no registry. To see the full round trip, start a local registry and push the contract:

docker run -d --rm -p 127.0.0.1:5001:5000 --name pacto-registry registry:3
pacto push oci://localhost:5001/demo/my-service-pacto -p .

Port 5001 because macOS binds 5000 for AirPlay. 127.0.0.1: because the registry accepts anonymous writes.

Read it back without pulling:

pacto explain oci://localhost:5001/demo/my-service-pacto:1.0.0

Or pull the bundle:

pacto pull oci://localhost:5001/demo/my-service-pacto:1.0.0 -o pulled

Clean up:

docker rm -f pacto-registry

For a real registry like GHCR, you need pacto login with a personal access token. See Installation for the supply-chain guarantees and Put it in your repository for what to commit.

docs.title: Watch a host with pacto agent
docs.text:
pacto agent is a small daemon that watches every workload on one Linux host and checks each one against its contract, round after round. Use it for long-running services on a Docker host, a VM or a bare-metal server. Runtime conformance explains what it watches and what the answers mean; this page shows how to run it.

On Kubernetes the operator deploys the same agent on every node. See the Kubernetes way.

docs.title: Quick start on a Docker host
docs.text:
Label the container you want checked with its contract and its ports:

docker run -d --name payments \
  --label dev.pacto.contract=oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments:1.4.0 \
  --label dev.pacto.bind.api=8080 \
  --label dev.pacto.dep.postgres=db.internal:5432 \
  ghcr.io/acme/payments:1.4.0

Then start the agent in a container of its own, from the Pacto runtime image. Set PACTO_VERSION to the Pacto release you run (pacto version prints it):

docker run -d --name pacto-agent --restart unless-stopped \
  --privileged --pid=host --cgroupns=host --network host --user 0 \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v /sys/fs/cgroup:/host/sys/fs/cgroup:ro \
  "ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard:${PACTO_VERSION}" \
  agent --sink local --docker --cgroup-root /host/sys/fs/cgroup

docker logs -f pacto-agent shows one round every 30 seconds:

2026-10-18T09:12:44Z
container/payments  Compliant  2/2 evaluated  oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments:1.4.0

Why each flag is there:

Flag Why --privileged, --user 0 loading the eBPF program needs root or the BPF, PERFMON and SYS_PTRACE capabilities --pid=host the agent reads every process's sockets and cgroup from the host's /proc --cgroupns=host and the /sys/fs/cgroup mount the agent names each socket's workload from the host's cgroup tree --network host health and metrics probes reach host-network services at 127.0.0.1; without it those probes are reported unsupported, with a note saying why the Docker socket the agent reads container labels; it only ever sends GET requests

On macOS and Windows, run the same command against Docker Desktop: the agent watches the containers inside Docker's Linux VM. Where that VM's kernel cannot load the program, the agent's snapshots keep reading collection Failed, with a reason such as LoadFailed.

docs.title: Docker labels
docs.text:
Label Meaning dev.pacto.contract the contract: an oci:// reference, or a bundle directory as the agent's container sees it dev.pacto.bind.<interface> the port the container serves the contract's interface on dev.pacto.dep.<dependency> the host:port the container reaches the contract's dependency at

Only running containers with dev.pacto.contract are checked. On a daemon several projects share, add --docker-label-filter to narrow that further: each one is a key or key=value label a container must also carry, all of them must match and the flag repeats. --docker-label-filter com.docker.compose.project=demo keeps the agent to one Compose project. Probes dial the container's address on its first network, or 127.0.0.1 for a host-network container. A directory contract is read from the agent's own filesystem, so mount it into the agent container at the same path the label names.

docs.title: Bindings file
docs.text:
For workloads that are not containers, such as systemd services, processes or pacto run sessions, describe them in a YAML file and pass it with --bindings:

# /etc/pacto/bindings.yaml
- match:
    unit: payments.service
  contract: /etc/pacto/contracts/payments
  interfaces:
    api: 8080
  dependencies:
    postgres: db.internal:5432
- match:
    container: 3f2a9c1b7d4e
  contract: oci://ghcr.io/acme/search@sha256:9b2d...
  host: 172.17.0.4
  interfaces:
    http: 9200
Field Meaning match exactly one of unit (a systemd unit), container (an id, at least 12 characters), cgroup (a cgroup v2 path), session (a pacto run session) or pid (a process; its workload is looked up at every round) contract an oci:// reference or a bundle directory; a relative directory is relative to the file host the address probes dial; default 127.0.0.1 interfaces contract interface name to port dependencies contract dependency name to host:port; host names are resolved at every round

Unknown fields are errors, so a typo fails at startup. --bindings and --docker can be used together. A bindings-file workload counts as started when its oldest running process started, so a connection from before that is ignored.

docs.title: Undeclared dependencies
docs.text: When a workload connects to another checked workload (a labelled container's address on a bound port, or a bindings entry's host and port) that its contract does not declare, the agent reports DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED, named by the other workload's contract service. A declared dependency is matched to a checked workload by service name, contract reference or bound address. If one matches none, it might be the very workload reached under another name, so the agent reports no undeclared dependency for that workload at all.

docs.title: Where results go
docs.text:
--sink picks what happens to each round:

  • local prints every workload's status and findings in --output-format (text, json or markdown). Nothing leaves the host.
  • evidence signs each workload's evidence and sends it to an Evidence Server, which stores it in your registry next to the contract revision. Your platform sees every host's results in one place.
  • stdout prints the raw observations as JSON, one line per round, for debugging or for your own tooling.
  • kubernetes is what the operator's node agent uses. The operator sets it.

docs.title: Sending evidence
docs.text:
Create a signing key on the host and give the public half to whoever runs the Evidence Server:

pacto evidence keygen --producer host-eu-1 --key-id host-eu-1-2026

The Evidence Server keeps evidence only about exact contract revisions, so every contract must be pinned by digest: oci://registry.example.com/acme/payments@sha256:<digest>. The agent refuses to start when a bindings-file contract is not pinned, and reports an error for a labelled container whose contract is not.

pacto agent --sink evidence --bindings /etc/pacto/bindings.yaml \
  --evidence-url https://evidence.example.com \
  --evidence-key /etc/pacto/host-eu-1-2026.key --evidence-key-id host-eu-1-2026 \
  --evidence-producer host-eu-1

Evidence covers the trust store and the server's --subject list.

docs.title: Run it as a systemd service
docs.text:
On a server without Docker, install the pacto binary and run the agent as a unit:

# /etc/systemd/system/pacto-agent.service
[Unit]
Description=Pacto runtime conformance agent
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/pacto agent --sink local --bindings /etc/pacto/bindings.yaml
Restart=on-failure
# Root loads the eBPF program; the agent opens no port and writes no files.
User=root

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now pacto-agent
journalctl -u pacto-agent -f

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Flag Default Meaning --publish-interval 30s how often a round is checked and printed --stabilization-window 2m how long a negative must last before it is reported --resync-interval 60s how often listeners are re-read from /proc, which heals a missed event --enable-probing off also check each listening interface speaks the protocol its type implies --node-name $NODE_NAME the host name in raw snapshots

The agent needs Linux with BTF and, to tell workloads that share the host's network apart, cgroup v2. Requirements has the details, and the CLI reference lists every flag.

docs.title: Runtime conformance
docs.text: A contract says what a service does: which ports it serves, which services it calls. Runtime conformance checks that the running service really does it. Pacto watches the service's network activity on the machine it runs on and compares it with the contract. It runs anywhere Linux runs: a laptop, a CI job, a Docker host, a bare-metal server or a Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The usual health signals miss the failures that hurt most:

  • A process passes its health check, but nothing listens on the port its contract declares, so every caller gets "connection refused".
  • A service keeps failing to reach a dependency it declared, and nobody notices until a user does.

Pacto turns each of these into a named finding against the contract, such as INTERFACE_ABSENT or DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE, the same finding codes the operator and the dashboard report.

docs.title: A one-minute example
docs.text:
Run your service through pacto run and tell it which port serves which interface:

pacto run --contract ./payments --bind api=8080 -- ./payments-server

If payments-server starts but never opens port 8080, the final report says:

session/pacto-run-4121  NonCompliant  1/1 evaluated  ./payments
  - [error] INTERFACE_ABSENT interface/api: interface "api" is not being served (pacto-run+ebpf)

No code changes, no SDK, no sidecar. Run a command under Pacto has the full guide.

docs.title: What Pacto watches
docs.text:
Pacto answers three questions about each service:

  • Who listens? Which TCP ports the service has open for callers.
  • Who connects? Which addresses the service dials.
  • Did it work? Whether each of those connections succeeded or failed.

The kernel watcher never reads message contents, request bodies, files, environment variables or secrets. The optional probes call the health, metrics and interface ports and read only the response they need to decide. A listener is recorded as an address, a port and a process name; a connection as a peer address and port, with counts and timestamps.

The watching is done with eBPF: a small program the Linux kernel runs safely each time a TCP connection changes state. It sees connections open, close and fail. It does not see the requests sent over them.

docs.title: Kept, broken or don't know
docs.text:
Every runtime check ends in one of three answers:

Answer Contract status Example Kept Compliant the declared port is open and the declared dependency answered Broken NonCompliant nothing listens on the declared port, or every recent connection to a dependency failed Don't know Unknown the observer stopped reporting, or could not see enough to decide
