Silence is never a violation. If Pacto cannot see, it says "don't know" and names why (for example EVIDENCE_STALE or COLLECTION_FAILED). A negative must also last for a stabilization window (two minutes by default) before it is reported, so a service has time to start before Pacto reports it broken.

docs.title: Three ways to run it
docs.text:
All three run the same watcher and the same evaluation; they differ in what they watch and where the answer goes.

pacto run pacto agent Kubernetes node agent What it watches one command and its child processes every workload on one host: containers, systemd units, processes every pod on every node How you name the workload --bind and --dep flags Docker labels or a bindings file the Pacto resource and its Service Privileges none required; root or eBPF capabilities for full results root or eBPF capabilities a root DaemonSet with eBPF capabilities, in a namespace labelled privileged for Pod Security What it can prove broken listeners in both modes; failed connections with eBPF only listeners and failed connections listeners and failed connections Where the answer goes your terminal and exit code; optionally an Evidence Server your terminal or log; optionally an Evidence Server the Pacto resource status Platform Linux; elsewhere the command runs unobserved Linux, or a Docker Desktop container on macOS and Windows any Linux node Guide Run a command Watch a host The Kubernetes way

Pick pacto run for a CI job or a single process you start yourself. Pick pacto agent for long-running services on a Docker host or a server. Pick the node agent when your services already run on Kubernetes with the Pacto operator. On Kubernetes the node agent is pacto agent too, which the operator can deploy on every node (opt-in: nodeAgent.enabled).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Full observation needs:

  • Linux 5.11 or later, or 5.8 to 5.10 with the SYS_RESOURCE capability (root has it), so the kernel lets Pacto load its program.
  • BTF, the type information the kernel publishes at /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux. Current distribution kernels ship it.
  • Root, or the BPF, PERFMON and SYS_PTRACE capabilities.
  • cgroup v2 to tell apart workloads that share the host's network, such as systemd units, host-network containers and pacto run sessions. A cgroup is the kernel's label for a group of processes; every container and systemd unit gets one. Without cgroup v2, only workloads with their own network stack (most containers, every pod) can be told apart.

Without these, pacto run still works in an unprivileged mode. It reads the command's open sockets from /proc once a second. It sees every listener, so a missing one is still reported. It sees a connection only while it is open at a read, and a failed connection never, so a dependency is reported reachable or "don't know", never unreachable. pacto agent has no unprivileged mode.

docs.title: What stays unverified off Kubernetes
docs.text:
On Kubernetes the operator also reads the cluster API, which knows things the network alone cannot show. On a plain host these fields stay unverified:

Contract field On Kubernetes Elsewhere interfaces[].visibility read from the Service, Ingress and load balancer unverified, listed in coverage.unverified; the status does not change dependencies[].compatibility the provider's deployed contract version unverified, listed in coverage.unverified state.persistence.scope read from the pod's volume claims unverified, listed in coverage.unverified workload, state.persistence.durability: persistent, required configurations read from the workload, volumes and bound ConfigMaps no source: the contract reads Unknown with EVIDENCE_MISSING a call to another Pacto service no dependency declares DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED pacto agent: the same, for a call to another workload it checks; pacto run: not reported, it checks one command

Off Kubernetes, pacto run and pacto agent probe the bound port of the health and metrics capabilities with no flag, and --enable-probing also checks the protocol an interface speaks (interfaces[].type). On Kubernetes, active probing and metrics observation are off by default; see Opt-in features.

The field coverage reference says, for every contract field, what each of the three ways can verify, and names the tests that prove it.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Evidence: how a remote host signs what it saw and reports it to your platform.
  • The model: how observations become findings.

docs.title: Run a command under Pacto
docs.text: pacto run starts your command, watches its network activity while it runs and tells you whether it kept its contract. It is the quickest way to try runtime conformance: one command, no daemon, no cluster. Use it on a laptop, in a CI job or in front of any process you start yourself.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pacto run --contract ./payments \
  --bind api=8080 \
  --dep postgres=127.0.0.1:5432 \
  --fail-on noncompliant \
  -- ./payments-server --port 8080

What each part means:

  • --contract is the contract: a bundle directory or an oci:// reference.
  • --bind api=8080 says the contract's interface api is served on port 8080. Bind every interface the contract declares; an unbound one reads "don't know".
  • --dep postgres=127.0.0.1:5432 says the contract's dependency postgres is reached at that address. A host name is resolved at every check.
  • --fail-on noncompliant turns a broken contract into a failed run.
  • Everything after -- is your command, untouched.

A name in --bind or --dep that the contract does not declare is rejected before the command starts, so a typo cannot hide an unchecked interface.

Every 10 seconds (--interval) Pacto prints a round to stderr. When the command exits it prints a final round, judged from the last view taken while the command was still running:

2026-10-18T09:12:44Z  ebpf  final
session/pacto-run-4121  Compliant  2/2 evaluated  ./payments

2/2 evaluated means both checks the contract requires got an answer. A broken check adds a line per finding, such as - [error] INTERFACE_ABSENT interface/api: interface "api" is not being served (pacto-run+ebpf). The part in brackets at the end names who saw it.

docs.title: Use it in CI
docs.text:
Run your integration tests against the service while pacto run wraps it. The job fails if the service broke its contract:

pacto run --contract ./payments --bind api=8080 --dep postgres=db:5432 \
  --stabilization-window 10s --interval 5s --fail-on noncompliant \
  --output-format json --report pacto-rounds.jsonl \
  -- ./payments-server &
PACTO=$!
./run-integration-tests.sh
kill -TERM "$PACTO"   # passed on to the server; Pacto prints its final round
wait "$PACTO"

wait returns the server's exit code, so a server that dies on SIGTERM returns 143 and fails the job on its own. Make it exit 0 on SIGTERM. Two settings matter in CI:

  • --stabilization-window. A negative is reported only once it has lasted this long (two minutes by default). Keep it shorter than the job, or a missing listener never gets reported.
  • --fail-on. noncompliant fails the run when the contract is broken; unknown also fails it when Pacto could not decide. The default none never changes the exit code.

docs.title: What you see with and without privileges
docs.text:
Pacto picks the best mode the machine allows and says which one on stderr before the command starts.

With privileges (root, or the BPF, PERFMON and SYS_PTRACE capabilities plus write access to its own cgroup, on Linux with BTF and cgroup v2), the command starts in its own cgroup pacto-run-<pid> and an eBPF program sees every listener and every connection attempt of the command and its children, failures included. Findings cite the collector pacto-run+ebpf. In a container this needs --privileged and its own cgroup namespace. If the program loads but the kernel refuses to start the command in that cgroup, Pacto says so and falls back to the mode below.

Without privileges, Pacto falls back to reading the command's sockets from /proc once a second and says so:

pacto run: unprivileged mode (eBPF: ...): polling the process tree's sockets in /proc every 1s. ...

The fallback sees listeners in full, so INTERFACE_ABSENT is still reported. It sees a connection only while it is open at a poll and never sees one fail, so a dependency is reported reachable or "don't know", never unreachable. Findings cite the collector pacto-run.

Outside Linux (macOS, Windows), the command runs unobserved and every runtime check reads OBSERVATION_UNSUPPORTED. Run it inside a Linux container to get real results.

eBPF mode Unprivileged mode Missing listener (INTERFACE_ABSENT) reported reported Reached dependency reachable reachable if the connection is open at a poll Refused dependency (DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE) reported never: reads "don't know" A child that leaves the process tree still watched: it stays in the cgroup still watched: Pacto adopts orphaned children

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Exit code When the command's own the command exited; --fail-on did not trigger 128 + n the command was killed by signal n, as a shell reports it 1 the command exited 0, but the final verdict met --fail-on 1 Pacto could not start: a bad flag, a contract that does not load or a binding the contract does not declare

The command runs in a process group of its own, so a Ctrl-C reaches it once. When Pacto owns the terminal, it hands the terminal to the command: the command reads it and gets Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z straight from it, and Pacto takes it back once the command exits. Otherwise SIGINT and SIGTERM sent to Pacto are passed on to the command's whole group. Either way Pacto waits for the command and then prints the final round.

docs.title: Keep the rounds: --report
docs.text:
Your command keeps its own stdin, stdout and stderr. Pacto writes rounds to stderr, each in a single write so they never interleave with the command's lines. With --report <file> the rounds go to that file instead. The file is emptied when the run starts and every round is appended whole, so a reader following it never sees half a round. With --output-format json each round is one JSON object per line:

{"evaluatedAt":"2026-10-18T09:12:44Z","mode":"ebpf","final":true,"targets":[{"target":"session/pacto-run-4121","contract":"./payments","status":"Compliant","coverage":{"evaluated":2,"required":2}}]}

The round with "final": true is the verdict. --output-format markdown writes a heading and a bullet per finding, handy for a CI job summary.

docs.title: Send the result to your platform
docs.text:
Add the --evidence-* flags and every round is also signed and sent to an Evidence Server. The server stores evidence only about exact contract revisions, so --contract must be pinned by digest:

pacto run --contract oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments@sha256:4f1c... --bind api=8080 \
  --evidence-url https://evidence.example.com --evidence-key ci.key \
  --evidence-key-id ci-2026 --evidence-producer ci-payments \
  -- ./payments-server

Evidence explains the keys and how the server trusts them.

docs.title: Other flags
docs.text:
• --host (default 127.0.0.1) is the address health, metrics and protocol probes dial, at the bound interface's port.
  • --enable-probing also checks that each listening interface speaks the protocol its type implies (HTTP for openapi, HTTP/2 for grpc).

The CLI reference lists every flag.

docs.title: Verify a record
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

This page is for an auditor or security reviewer who must check what Pacto did, using standard tools only. It shows how to read a record, check its signature, check the whole history and check that a released version was signed. Without access to the cluster you still take three things from the team that runs Pacto: the public key records are checked against, the address where a Stage's records hang and the id of its newest record (a hash of that record, explained in Check the whole history). Ask for all three in writing and keep them: a later mismatch is evidence. Two optional checks below need one more key each: the eval runner's for exams and the publisher's for released versions. The full detail is in Signed records and history.

Words in links are defined in the glossary: a record is signed by the recorder and stored in your registry as a referrer of a digest. Each one is about one change to one Stage. A Stage's records form its stream, numbered and hung on one fixed digest, its anchor. A follower is a Stage in another cluster that takes the versions this Stage verified by reading its stream.

docs.title: What a record says
docs.text:
A record answers: what was asked, by whom, for which Stage, what each check said and why, who approved and how it ended. Refusals are recorded too. It holds references, never secrets. A record is an in-toto statement with the type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/operation/v1.

Every field sits under .predicate:

Field What it says kind operation for a change, gap for a placeholder (see below), unrecordable for a signed stand-in for a change whose own record failed a check. A stand-in takes that change's number in the chain and hangs on the anchor only. A follower takes no more versions from the stream at a stand-in until a person acknowledges it (an acknowledge record on that Stage names its record id in intent.params.record) intent What was asked: the change's name, its Stage (intent.stage.namespace and intent.stage.name) and its reason actor.user, actor.class Who asked, and whether that is a human, an agent, break-glass (a member of the emergency group, whose change skips every check and approval and freezes the Stage) or Pacto itself (controller) actor.onBehalfOf The person an agent said it acted for. Only claimed, never checked, and marked so approvals[] Who answered (by), the answer (decision: approve, reject or accept-unknown, which means a person let the change go ahead although a check said Unknown) and when they last signed in (authTime) verdicts[] Each check (gate), when it ran (phase: pre before the move, verify after) and its result: Pass, Fail or Unknown verdicts[].citation.runner, .runnerBundle For an eval check: who ran the exam, and the answer that runner signed itself (see "Check who ran an exam") outcome.result How it ended, such as Succeeded, Failed, Rejected or Cancelled outcome.pointer.before, .after The version digest the Stage ran before and after guarded Read this first. true when the cluster's admission policies confirmed who asked and who approved. Without it, those names are only what the writer claimed chain.seq, chain.parent The record's number in its Stage's history and the id of the record before it (see "Check the whole history")

Records exist only when your platform team turns on the recorder.

docs.title: Where records live
docs.text:
Each record is stored in your registry as a referrer, attached to the version the change moved to, the version it moved from, the new contract and one fixed digest per Stage called the anchor. These four digests are the record's signed subjects (.subject[], named to, from, contract and anchor). The anchor is where the whole history of one Stage hangs. All anchors live in one repository, the streams repository. The anchor's full address is in the Stage:

kubectl get stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod payments -o jsonpath='{.status.stream.anchor}'
# registry.example/pacto/streams@sha256:3a7f...

If you have no cluster access, ask the platform team for this address. It never changes for a Stage.

docs.title: Get the public key
docs.text:
You check signatures against the recorder's public key, a file such as recorder.pub. Get it from the platform team, not from the registry, so a forger cannot hand you their own. The platform team makes it with one of these (you need neither):

openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout -out recorder.pub          # from a key file
cosign public-key --key awskms:///alias/pacto > recorder.pub # from a cloud KMS key

If the recorder signs with no key file (keyless), ask instead for its certificate identity, issuer and trusted root; the records reference shows the flags.

docs.title: Check one record without Pacto
docs.text:
You need oras, cosign, jq and base64, and read access to the registry (oras login registry.example). List the records on the anchor, fetch one and check its signature. Records are the entries of type application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json; --artifact-type lists only those:

ANCHOR=registry.example/pacto/streams@sha256:3a7f...   # from the step above
oras discover --artifact-type application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json "$ANCHOR"
REC=sha256:...                                         # the digest of one entry in the list (not the record id below)
REPO=${ANCHOR%@*}
oras blob fetch --output record.json \
  "$REPO@$(oras manifest fetch "$REPO@$REC" | jq -r '.layers[0].digest')"
cosign verify-blob-attestation --bundle record.json --key recorder.pub \
  --type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/operation/v1 --insecure-ignore-tlog \
  --digest "${ANCHOR##*sha256:}" --digestAlg sha256
jq -r .dsseEnvelope.payload record.json | base64 -d | jq .predicate   # read it

--digest is the anchor's digest: the check passes only if this record names this Stage's anchor among its signed subjects, so a record moved from another Stage fails. cosign prints Verified OK when the signature holds and exits non-zero when it does not. --insecure-ignore-tlog is expected: the recorder never writes to a public log, because records name your services. The signature alone proves the record is unchanged.

docs.title: Check the whole history
docs.text:
Each Stage's records are numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on (.predicate.chain.seq). A record's id is sha256: followed by the SHA-256 of its signed statement, the decoded payload:

jq -r .dsseEnvelope.payload record.json | base64 -d | shasum -a 256   # the id, without "sha256:"

oras discover lists a different digest for the entry. That digest names the stored file, and the id names what was signed. Compare ids with ids.

Fetch and check every record on the anchor as above, then check three things:

  1. The numbers run 1, 2, 3 with no hole and no number twice.
  2. Each record's .predicate.chain.parent is the id of the record numbered one lower. Record 1 has no parent.
  3. The newest record's id equals the Stage's .status.stream.head, which the platform team can read for you. If it does not, newer records are missing.

A record with .predicate.kind gap is a signed placeholder for a number no change used. It fills its number, so the stream stays continuous. Ask the platform team about every gap. With cluster access, Pacto does the same check in one command and exits non-zero if anything is wrong:

pacto delivery record verify -n prod --stage payments --trust recorder.pub
pacto delivery blame -n prod --stage payments --trust recorder.pub   # who asked and approved what runs now

When Pacto cannot read every record, its answer says partial. Then a missing change may still have happened: no answer means "unknown", never "nobody".

docs.title: Check who ran an exam
docs.text:
An eval runner runs each eval check, such as an AI agent's eval suite. The runner signs its own answer: which version it ran, the sha256 of the suite, how many cases passed and where the run can be read again. The record keeps that signed answer in the verdict's citation.runnerBundle, inside the recorder's signature. So you can check the runner's signature yourself, without trusting the recorder or the promoter. Get the runner's public key from the team that runs the evals, not from the record or the registry:

jq -r .dsseEnvelope.payload record.json | base64 -d \
  | jq -r '.predicate.verdicts[] | select(.citation.runnerBundle) | .citation.runnerBundle' > runner.json
VERSION=$(jq -r .dsseEnvelope.payload record.json | base64 -d | jq -r '.subject[] | select(.name=="to") | .digest.sha256')
cosign verify-blob-attestation --bundle runner.json --key runner.pub \
  --type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/eval/v1 --insecure-ignore-tlog \
  --digest "$VERSION" --digestAlg sha256
jq -r .dsseEnvelope.payload runner.json | base64 -d | jq .predicate   # what it signed

The commands take the first eval check of the record; a record with more than one keeps one signed answer per check. Then check what the runner signed against the record:

  • operation is the record's .predicate.intent.uid and the subject its to digest
  • the counts and the suite match the verdict's citation
  • the verdict's result follows from the counts and the Stage check's minPassRate in the record's .predicate.policy (a model the runner named can only make it worse)

An eval verdict that says Pass or Fail with no runnerBundle has no runner signature. Do not trust it. With cluster access, pacto delivery record verify --trust keys.yaml does all of this when that file lists the runner's key with role: runner beside the recorder's, and prints who ran each exam. It finds the eval verdicts from the record's Stage policy and citations. To decide that yourself, list on the runner key the providers whose verdicts it must sign, as the trust config in Verify records shows.

What this cannot catch: a promoter that reuses an answer the runner signed earlier in the same operation, for the same version. Each answer carries the one-time value the promoter asked with, and only the promoter knows which one it used last.

docs.title: Check a version was signed
docs.text:
Every version Pacto promotes was published and signed with pacto publish. A break-glass override can skip this: look for actor.class break-glass in the records and check its to digest the same way. pacto publish signs each digest it pushes: the contract, each image and the files Flux applies. Check any of them with cosign and the publisher's public key, which the team that publishes gives you:

cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example/acme/payments@sha256:...

For keyless signing, from CI with no key file, check the identity instead:

cosign verify --certificate-identity https://github.com/acme/payments/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  registry.example/acme/payments@sha256:...

If the team publishes with transparencyLog: false, add --insecure-ignore-tlog to the key command; the publishing team can tell you which it uses. pacto publish refuses to publish a version it cannot sign.

To tie a record to a release, take the digest of the subject named to (jq -r '.subject[] | select(.name=="to") | .digest.sha256' on the decoded statement; it prints the bare hex, so put sha256: in front of it for cosign verify). It is the deploy artifact, the package of Kubernetes files Flux applies. It lives in the repository the service's contract names for that artifact, for example registry.example/acme/deploy/payments. Ask the publishing team for that address, as for the anchor. Check it there with the cosign verify command above. Get the publisher's key out of band too, never from the registry. See Publish a version for the signing settings.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Someone who controls both the registry and the cluster can delete the newest records and report an older newest id. Compare with the id you kept from your last audit.
  • With no public log, nothing outside the record proves when it was signed. Someone holding the recorder's key could write a record with any date.
  • A change running while its Stage is deleted is never recorded.
  • Two different names on a record do not always mean two people. When actor.class is agent and actor.onBehalfOf is empty, the person behind the agent may be the one who approved. Even when it is set, it is only the agent's claim.
  • Registry clean-up rules can delete records. The platform team must keep the streams repository out of them.
  • A record from an earlier promoter that ran without the cluster's admission checks has no guarded: true.
  • A runner's signature proves which runner key signed the answer, not that the runner ran every case honestly, and not which model really answered. A runner that reports observedModel vouches for it with its own key.
  • A mira or http verdict is unsigned, and the record signs only what the promoter read. Mira counts telemetry the service reports about itself (its own server spans, keyed on the service.name and service.version it sends), so code under test, or any pod that can reach the OTLP endpoint, can hide its errors or flood clean spans to force a Pass, or a Fail and with it a rollback. See what a health verdict can prove.

docs.title: Why Pacto
docs.text:
A team ships a change to its service, and a service another team owns breaks. The pull request looked safe: a minor version bump and a few lines of YAML. Review answers whether the change is correct. It rarely answers who the change breaks, because that knowledge sits in other teams' code.

Pacto tells you which services a change breaks before it ships, and checks what is actually running. This page follows one change through review twice, first without Pacto and then with it.

docs.title: One change, two ways
docs.text:
The commerce team owns orders. It publishes version 2.4.0 with two changes:

  • The order status in the orders-api response gains a new value, refunded. The value lives in a shared component that the response references with $ref.
  • The deprecated orders-v1 interface now goes away on 2026-12-01 instead of 2027-06-01.
orders-2.4.0/interfaces/orders-api.yaml (excerpt)
components:
  schemas:
    OrderStatus:
      type: string
      enum: [pending, paid, shipped, refunded]   # 2.3.0 had pending, paid, shipped

The finance team owns billing. Its contract accepts any 2.x version of orders and relies on per-key ordering of the order-events stream:

billing/pacto.yaml (excerpt)
dependencies:
  - name: orders
    ref: ../orders
    required: true
    compatibility: "^2.0.0"
    requires:
      - interface: order-events
        ordering: per-key

docs.title: Without Pacto
docs.text:
The reviewer sees one added enum value in a components file, a date moved in a deprecation notice and a minor version bump. Adding a value looks additive, so the reviewer approves. Nothing in the diff names billing, and nobody on the commerce team knows that billing decodes status into a closed type.

The release goes out. The first refunded order reaches billing, which rejects the response, and invoices for that order stop. On 2026-12-01 the orders-v1 endpoint disappears, and billing learns about the new date from its error rate.

docs.title: With Pacto: validate the new revision
docs.text:
pacto validate checks the contract in stages and names the next command to run:

$ pacto validate orders-2.4.0
orders-2.4.0 is valid
PASS load
SKIP lock         no pacto.lock
PASS structural
PASS cross-field
PASS policy
SKIP environments no environments declared
SKIP guarantees   no dependency declares requires
SKIP readiness    not requested (--readiness)
SKIP closure      not requested (--closure)
Next: pacto impact PUBLISHED_REF orders-2.4.0

docs.title: With Pacto: diff the two revisions
docs.text:
pacto diff compares 2.3.0 with 2.4.0. It resolves the $ref and judges the enum where the response uses it. A new value in a response is BREAKING, because a consumer that reads the old set of values cannot read the new one:

$ pacto diff fleet/orders orders-2.4.0
Classification: BREAKING
Required bump: major
Changes (3):
  [NON_BREAKING] service.version (modified): service.version modified [2.3.0 -> 2.4.0]
  [BREAKING] openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.status.enum[refunded] (added): openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.status.enum refunded added (in #/components/schemas/OrderStatus) [+ refunded]
  [POTENTIAL_BREAKING] interfaces.lifecycle.sunset (modified): interfaces.lifecycle.sunset modified: orders-v1 sunset moved earlier, from 2027-06-01 to 2026-12-01 [orders-v1: 2027-06-01 -> orders-v1: 2026-12-01]
breaking changes detected

The command exits 1. The Required bump line says the change needs a major version, so 2.4.0 claims less than the change does. The reason names the component, #/components/schemas/OrderStatus, so the reviewer knows which file to read.

docs.title: With Pacto: list the consumers
docs.text:
pacto impact joins the diff with the contracts in the fleet folder and names the services that depend on orders:

$ pacto impact fleet/orders orders-2.4.0 --local fleet
Impact: orders 2.3.0 -> 2.4.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 1
Potentially breaking changes: 1
Affected consumers (1):
  billing                      direct     confidence=contractual  compat=compatible   owner=finance
    note: compatible only means the range ^2.0.0 accepts 2.4.0; this change is BREAKING, so check that billing does not use what it removes or changes
Release gate: unverified
unverified: the change is BREAKING and 1 consumer depends on orders, but none is shown to be both incompatible and running. Review each consumer, and add a source that knows where services run (for example --target-state) to tell deployed impact apart

The command exits 2. The reviewer now has a name and an owner: ask finance whether billing handles refunded. The range ^2.0.0 accepts 2.4.0, and the note says that a range match leaves the breaking change to check. A local folder knows no deployments, so the gate is unverified. With a source that knows where services run, such as --target-state or --k8s, the gate can tell deployed consumers apart. See impact analysis.

docs.title: With Pacto: the consumer's next build
docs.text:
Once 2.4.0 is published, the billing pipeline checks the contracts it depends on. The new sunset reaches finance as a warning with the date and the successor:

$ pacto validate --closure billing
billing is valid
…
PASS guarantees
SKIP readiness    not requested (--readiness)
PASS closure
  WARN  [DEPENDENCY_INTERFACE_DEPRECATED] dependencies[0]: orders@2.4.0 interface orders-v1 is deprecated since 2026-09-01, sunset 2026-12-01; successor orders-api
Next: pacto impact PUBLISHED_REF billing

The guarantees stage passes because orders still offers per-key ordering. When a provider stops meeting a requirement, the stage fails. Here billing asks for global ordering instead:

$ pacto validate billing
billing is invalid
…
FAIL guarantees
  billing/pacto.yaml:16:5: ERROR [GUARANTEE_UNMET] dependencies[0].requires: billing requires order-events ordering global from orders, which offers per-key
…
Next: fix dependencies[0].requires at billing/pacto.yaml:16:5 [GUARANTEE_UNMET], then run pacto validate billing
validation failed with 1 error(s)

docs.title: What changes for each role
docs.text:
• Provider team. Run pacto diff before you tag a release. The Required bump line tells you which version the change needs, and interfaces[].lifecycle tells consumers when an interface goes away.
  • Consumer team. Declare a compatibility range and the guarantees you rely on in dependencies[].requires. pacto validate --closure warns you about each deprecated interface and fails when a provider stops meeting a requirement.
  • Reviewer. Read the pacto impact output on the pull request. It names the classification, each affected consumer and its owner.
  • Platform team. Run pacto impact in CI with the sources that know your fleet, such as --oci, --k8s or --target-state. See who breaks in CI.
  • On-call. The operator and pacto run compare a running service with its contract and report findings such as INTERFACE_ABSENT and DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE. See runtime conformance.
  • Agents. The MCP tools pacto_check and pacto_impact return the same stages, Next line and consumer list a person sees. See AI assistants (MCP).

docs.title: Start with a pilot
docs.text:
Pick two or three services you already run where one calls another. A pilot needs no change to service code.

  1. Pactify each service: give it a contract that describes what it offers and which versions of its providers it accepts.
  2. Add pacto diff and pacto impact to each pull request. See CI and GitHub Actions.
  3. Add pacto validate --closure to each consumer's build, so deprecations and unmet guarantees reach the consumer team.

Measure the pilot for a few release cycles:

  • Breaking changes pacto diff reports before merge, and how many of them the author did not expect.
  • Review time on pull requests that bump a provider version.
  • Consumers that hear about a sunset from pacto validate --closure before the sunset date.

Expand when the pilot teams act on the impact output during review. Add the services that call the pilot services next, because each new consumer makes the impact answer more complete. The tenets explain the design choices behind each check.

docs.title: Limits and other tools
docs.text: Pacto lists what it cannot do yet in the known limitations. How Pacto relates to other tools compares it with the tools you may already use.

docs.title: Contract Reference (v2.3)
docs.text:
A Pacto contract is one YAML file, pacto.yaml, that says what a service is and what it needs to run: its interfaces, dependencies, configuration, capabilities and readiness. This section is the field-by-field reference. The smallest valid contract is four lines:

pactoVersion: "2.0"
service:
  name: my-library
  version: 1.0.0

The fields are split across contract sections, configuration and policy, dependencies and state, readiness, publish, checks and environments. The rules are in validation layers, overrides and change classification. This page covers the bundle layout all of them assume.

Each interfaces, configurations and policies entry points at a schema you already have: an OpenAPI document, an AsyncAPI event definition, a gRPC service descriptor or a JSON Schema. Every referenced file must parse as JSON or YAML; see interface types.

The model explains what the contract states and what it leaves to the platform.

The canonical JSON Schemas are pacto-v2.0.schema.json, pacto-v2.1.schema.json, which adds publish, checks, external dependencies and the mcp interface type, and pacto-v2.2.schema.json, which adds the interface lifecycle, compatibilityEpoch and guarantees and dependency requires, and pacto-v2.3.schema.json, which adds environments. Every contract declares pactoVersion and is validated against that version's schema.

docs.title: Bundle structure
docs.text:
A Pacto bundle is a self-contained directory (or OCI artifact) with the following layout:

/
├── pacto.yaml
├── interfaces/              ← optional
│   ├── openapi.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   └── events.yaml
├── configuration/           ← optional
│   └── schema.json
├── environments/            ← optional
│   ├── staging.yaml
│   └── production.yaml
├── policy/                  ← optional
│   └── schema.json
├── docs/                    ← optional
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── architecture.md
│   ├── runbook.md
│   └── integration.md
└── sbom/                    ← optional
    └── sbom.spdx.json

Only pacto.yaml is required. All other directories are optional. Include a directory when your contract references files in it. Validation checks that every file referenced by pacto.yaml exists within the bundle.

When you run pacto push, Pacto packages the bundle as a versioned, content-addressed OCI artifact. You can store it in any OCI registry and pull it from any team, service or environment.

docs.title: docs/: optional documentation
docs.text:
Files in docs/ are informational metadata. They travel with the contract and are ignored by validation and diff classification.

Typical content:

  • Service overview: what the service does and its purpose within the platform
  • Architecture notes: internal design, data flow and key dependencies
  • Operational runbooks: incident response, scaling procedures and known failure modes
  • Integration guides: how consumers use the service's interfaces

docs.title: sbom/: optional Software Bill of Materials
docs.text:
Files in sbom/ are also informational metadata. They travel with the contract and are ignored by validation.

pacto diff includes SBOM files in its output. When both the old and new bundles contain an SBOM, pacto diff reports package-level changes (added, removed, version, license or supplier modified). These changes are informational and leave the overall diff classification unchanged.

Supported formats:

Format File extension Spec version SPDX .spdx.json 2.3 CycloneDX .cdx.json 1.5

Pacto auto-detects the format by file extension. Place one or more SBOM files directly in the sbom/ directory. Pacto reads only the top level of sbom/.

Generating an SBOM:

Use any standard tool (Syft, Trivy, cdxgen) writing SPDX/CycloneDX JSON into sbom/.

docs.title: Minimal contract
docs.text: Only pactoVersion and service are required, as in the four-line example at the top of this page. All other sections are optional: workload, state, interfaces, configurations, environments, policies, dependencies, capabilities, readiness, metadata and extensions. A minimal contract is useful for lightweight dependency declarations, shared libraries or contracts where runtime semantics are managed externally.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: checks lists the test and eval suites a version ships. Delivery runs them after release through the same Stages as any other check. The other sections are in Contract sections and Dependencies and state.

docs.title: checks
docs.text:
Optional. Needs pactoVersion: "2.1": a 2.0 contract with it fails validation with NEEDS_PACTO_2_1. 2.1 needs Pacto core 4.1.0 or later and operator 6.1.0 or later; see Versions.

pactoVersion: "2.1"
service:
  name: support-agent
  version: 1.3.0
  owner: {team: support}
checks:
  - name: evals                  # a Stage runs it by this name
    file: evals/suite.yaml       # ships in the bundle
  - name: smoke
    file: tests/smoke.yaml
Field Meaning name The suite's name, unique in the contract (DUPLICATE_CHECK_NAME otherwise). A Stage names it to run it file The suite's file in the bundle (FILE_NOT_FOUND when missing)

Pacto treats a suite as opaque. It packs the file in the bundle, records a sha256 of the suite and hands file and digest to the runner the Stage names. It accepts only a verdict about that exact digest. No verdict, a timeout or an answer about another suite is Unknown, and Unknown never passes. The environment picks the runner for a suite.

A suite is every file in the directory that holds its file, because a runner may read cases, fixtures or golden answers from beside it. Keep each suite in its own directory, such as evals/. A suite file at the bundle root takes in the whole bundle. The digest is what sha256sum prints for those files, sorted by path, hashed once more:

cd evals && find . -type f | sed 's|^\./||' | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum | sha256sum

docs.title: What a change needs
docs.text:
pacto diff compares the suites by name:

Change Classification A suite added Non-breaking: it only adds a check A suite removed, moved or edited Potentially breaking: a release that drops the cases it fails would loosen the check it ships behind, so a person reviews it

pacto diff compares the suite's digest, including every file beside it. It detects an edit, and the reviewer decides whether the suite got stricter or weaker.

In delivery, any suite change (added, removed, moved or edited) holds the version for a person on every level, including autonomous.

docs.title: Running a suite in delivery
docs.text:
A Stage runs a suite with an eval provider, configured in the delivery chart like any other check (see health checks):

gates:
  verify:
    checks:
      - name: evals
        provider: evals                # gates.providers: {name: evals, type: eval, url: ...}
        suite: evals                   # the checks[].name to run
        suiteDigest: sha256:...        # optional: the exact suite to accept
        params: {minPassRate: "0.95"}

suite names the check to run. You can omit it when the version ships exactly one suite. A version that lacks the named suite is held before it ships, with a message that names the missing suite, until a person accepts it. The check records no verdict. pacto delivery plan and the dashboard predict this hold too: the chart publishes each provider's name and type (and keeps its URL and keys private) beside the identity policy, so a client knows which checks run on an eval provider. The runner says how many cases passed and the sha256 of the suite it ran, and only an answer about that exact sha256 counts. minPassRate must be above 0.

The runner signs its answer, and the provider lists the runner keys it trusts. An unsigned answer, or one signed by a key outside the provider's list, is Unknown. The signed answer stays in the delivery record, so an auditor can see who ran the exam and check that runner's signature.

suiteDigest pins the suite to bytes the Stage owner chose. A version that ships a suite with another sha256 is held for a person before it ships, and its eval check is Unknown, never Pass.

docs.title: An agent is a service
docs.text:
An AI agent uses the same sections as any other service:

  • The tools it exposes are an interface of type mcp: a tools/list result such as {"tools": [{"name": "refund", "inputSchema": {...}}]}, every tool named once (INVALID_MCP_TOOLS otherwise). Removing a tool is breaking, adding one is non-breaking, and Pacto compares tool schemas like an OpenAPI request and response.
  • The model it calls is a dependency. A model with a contract is compared by its range; one without is an external dependency named by its version, so swapping it is potentially breaking.
  • Its eval suite is a checks entry, run by an eval runner that signs its result.

To pin an agent completely:

  • Put its prompt and its agent policy (allowed tools, safety rules) as files in the bundle. The contract digest then covers their bytes.
  • Declare its tools in the mcp interface.
  • Name the model by an exact version, such as a dated model ID, and avoid aliases such as latest. Set it in the deploy manifests, which delivery moves by digest. A ConfigMap or Secret outside them escapes the digest.
  • Have the eval runner report the model that answered (observedModel). The eval check then fails when no external dependency version in the contract names that model, and a Stage check with requireObservedModel: true stays Unknown until the runner says.

Two things stay outside the pin: a prompt or tool list the agent fetches at runtime, and the model the agent calls in production. The eval runner's observedModel records what it saw during the exam, signed with its own key. Pacto compares it only with the contract's external dependency versions.

docs.title: Configuration and policy
docs.text: Two fields: configurations lists the settings a service reads at runtime, and policies lists the rules its contract must follow. Both point at a JSON Schema, so tools can check values and contracts before anything ships. The other sections are in Contract sections, Dependencies and state and Readiness.

docs.title: configurations
docs.text:
Declares the named configuration inputs the service reads at runtime. Platform provisioning APIs, Helm deployment values and Kubernetes ConfigMaps describe related but separate things; see Reusing a schema you already have. Optional: a service with no configuration input can omit this section.

Field Type Required Constraints name string Yes Non-empty identifier for the configuration entry required boolean Yes Whether the configuration is mandatory. true = its confirmed absence at runtime is a violation; false = optional. Has no default, so every entry must set it schema string Conditional Non-empty. Must reference a file in the bundle. Required if ref is not set ref string Conditional Non-empty. OCI or local reference to another Pacto contract. Required if schema is not set values object No Must conform to the schema defined in schema

With schema, the configuration schema is a local file, and validation checks that it exists in the bundle and parses. With ref, the entry points at another Pacto contract. Pacto checks that the reference is a well-formed OCI or local reference, records it as a reference edge in the graph and pins it by digest in pacto.lock. A ref records which contract owns the schema. Pacto leaves the schema in the referenced bundle and validates nothing against it. schema and ref are mutually exclusive: when ref is set, schema and values must be absent.

Required configuration keys are derived from the JSON Schema's required array.

The optional values field provides default configuration values validated against the local schema. A ref: entry carries no values. To attach values, vendor a local schema:. Values document expected defaults or provide environment-specific overrides through the --set and --values flags (see Contract overrides). To check the values each environment uses against the schema, list them in environments.

Tip

pacto push packages every file the contract references, the configuration schema included, into a self-contained OCI artifact.

docs.title: External configuration schema reference
docs.text:
You can reference another Pacto contract that owns a configuration schema, so you keep only one copy of it. By convention the referenced bundle keeps that schema at configuration/schema.json, which is where pacto init scaffolds it:

configurations:
  - name: platform
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform-config-pacto:1.0.0
    required: true

A platform team publishes one configuration contract and every service references it. pacto lock follows the chain with cycle detection, so a referenced contract that has its own configurations[].ref is resolved and pinned to the end of the closure.

Tip

Configuration references create reference edges in the dependency graph, separate from dependencies[].ref edges. pacto graph --with-references shows them alongside dependencies, --only-references shows them alone and the dashboard graph draws them dashed. The graph records these edges and traverses only dependencies[].ref, so a service coupled to another only through a shared configuration schema shows no dependents. pacto.lock resolves and pins the transitive reference closure.

Warning

pacto push rejects local configuration references (file:// and bare paths). Use them for development and switch every ref to oci:// before you publish.

docs.title: Secret references
docs.text:
Keep secrets out of a contract. Store a reference that the platform resolves at deployment time. The contract declares what the service needs; the platform decides how to provide it.

configurations:
  - name: default
    required: true
    schema: configuration/schema.json
    values:
        DB_HOST: prod-db.internal
        DB_PORT: 5432
        DB_PASSWORD: secret://vault/payments/db-password
        API_KEY: secret://vault/payments/stripe-api-key

The secret:// prefix is a convention. Pacto treats it as an opaque string value. Your platform tooling (Kubernetes operators, Terraform modules, deployment scripts) interprets these references and injects the actual secret at runtime. This keeps sensitive values out of the contract while making the dependency on secrets explicit and auditable.

Your configuration JSON Schema should declare secret fields as strings:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "DB_PASSWORD": { "type": "string", "description": "Database password (secret reference)" },
    "API_KEY": { "type": "string", "description": "Stripe API key (secret reference)" }
  },
  "required": ["DB_PASSWORD", "API_KEY"]
}

docs.title: Reusing a schema you already have
docs.text:
These artifacts are related, and some of them use JSON Schema, but each one describes something different:

Artifact Describes Service runtime configuration keys the running service reads (for example a ConfigMap it mounts) Platform provisioning API inputs to a provisioning claim Helm deployment values inputs to helm install/upgrade Kubernetes ConfigMap/Secret content the runtime configuration object itself

A Helm chart's values.schema.json may be reused as a configurations[].schema only when the named scope has the same semantic shape as those values, or when an explicit mapping exists between them. Composition patterns explains whether the service or the platform owns that schema.

docs.title: What the Kubernetes collector validates
docs.text: The Kubernetes integration binds a configurations[] scope to a runtime object only when the Pacto CR sets spec.target.configBindings. When it does, it validates the decoded content of the bound ConfigMap key against the declared schema. It validates the whole decoded JSON or YAML value at that key. For a Secret it verifies only that the object exists and never reads Secret values. A required scope whose bound object or key is confirmed absent is a violation (NonCompliant), and so is a schema mismatch on observed content. A binding that the operator cannot observe is insufficient evidence (Unknown).

docs.title: policies
docs.text:
Defines or references policy constraints for the contract. Optional: a service with no policy can omit this section. A policy is a JSON Schema that validates the contract itself, so an organization can state its standards as rules. Examples: require a health capability, require a declared owner, restrict interface visibility or require a readiness gate.

When present, each entry must have a name and either schema or ref specified.

Field Type Required Constraints name string Yes Non-empty identifier for the policy entry schema string Conditional Non-empty. Path to a JSON Schema file in the bundle (convention: policy/schema.json). Required if ref is not set ref string Conditional Non-empty. OCI or local reference to another Pacto contract. If the referenced contract declares policies[], those schemas are used directly; otherwise Pacto uses the fixed path policy/schema.json. Required if schema is not set target string No What the policy is evaluated against. contract is the only accepted value and the default. The field exists so a later release can add a second target without a breaking change. Any other value fails Layer 1 with SCHEMA_VIOLATION

schema and ref are mutually exclusive. An entry defines its policy inline or references an external one.

docs.title: Policy as a contract author
docs.text:
To define a policy, create a JSON Schema that describes constraints on pacto.yaml contracts and place it at policy/schema.json in the bundle:

# pacto.yaml: a policy contract
pactoVersion: "2.0"
service:
  name: platform-policy
  version: 1.0.0
  owner:
    team: platform
policies:
  - name: platform-policy
    schema: policy/schema.json

Example policy schema (policy/schema.json) requiring every contract to declare an owner:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["service"],
  "properties": {
    "service": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["owner"]
    }
  }
}

A policy schema validates the contract itself, so it can require any contract field, for example a health capability through a capabilities contains rule or a readiness gate. A contract is always checked against its own inline schema policies, so this policy contract satisfies the rule above by declaring service.owner.

docs.title: Policy as a contract consumer
docs.text:
To adopt a policy, reference the policy contract via OCI:

policies:
  - name: platform-policy
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform-policy-pacto:1.0.0

The ref row above lists the schemas a referenced contract contributes. Layer 3 lists the commands that walk that chain and what happens when a link in it fails to fetch.

The policies apply to the contract that references them. pacto validate --closure also checks every contract in its dependency closure against them; see Dependency closure.

Tip

Like configurations[].ref, policy references create reference edges in the dependency graph (pacto graph --with-references) and are pinned in pacto.lock alongside dependencies.

Warning

pacto push rejects local policies[].ref values (file:// and bare paths). Use them for development and switch every ref to oci:// before you publish.

Info

pacto push resolves every remote policies[].ref before publishing and rejects the push if the contract violates one of those schemas.

A policy author's own bundle carries the schema at policy/schema.json, the fixed path a policies[].ref resolves against; see bundle structure for where that sits among the other optional directories.

docs.title: Dependencies and state
docs.text: Three fields: dependencies lists the other services this one calls, workload says how it runs (a long-running service, a job or a scheduled job) and state says what data it keeps. Impact analysis, the lockfile and the Kubernetes operator all read them. The other sections are in Contract sections, Configuration and policy and Readiness.

docs.title: dependencies
docs.text:
Declares dependencies on other services via their Pacto contracts.

Field Type Required Constraints name string Yes Non-empty identifier for the dependency ref string Yes, unless external Non-empty. OCI reference (oci://...) or local path (file://... or bare path) required boolean Yes Whether the dependency is mandatory. Has no default, so every entry must set it compatibility string With ref Non-empty. Valid semver constraint external boolean No true when something outside this Pacto system delivers the dependency. Needs pactoVersion: "2.1" version string Only for external without ref The version it runs against, as free text requires list No Guarantees this service relies on from the provider. See Required guarantees. Needs pactoVersion: "2.2"

Note

true means the service cannot function without the dependency. false means it degrades gracefully when the dependency is unavailable. The field is declared intent: consumers read it and the dashboard uses it to work out the affected consumers. Pacto checks nothing about it at deployment time.

docs.title: Required guarantees
docs.text:
Each requires entry names a provider interface and the guarantees this service relies on. The provider must declare each one at least as strong as written.

dependencies:
  - name: orders
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/pacto/orders
    compatibility: "^2.0.0"
    required: true
    requires:
      - interface: order-events
        delivery: at-least-once
        dedupeWindow: 5m

pacto validate reads the provider contract and reports every unmet guarantee in one run as GUARANTEE_UNMET, naming both services, the guarantee and both values. It is an error on a required dependency and a warning on an optional one. When Pacto cannot read the provider contract, nothing confirms the requirement, so validation warns with GUARANTEE_UNVERIFIED and reports the guarantees stage as SKIP with a reason naming the dependency. The stage passes only when every requirement was checked. pacto publish and pacto push run the same check: an unmet guarantee of a required dependency refuses them, and a warning is shown in their output. pacto pack builds an archive offline and does not fetch providers. pacto graph marks each refused edge. pacto impact lists the consumers whose requirement a change breaks and blocks the release when one of them runs. Delivery holds a promote that leaves a consumer's required guarantee unmet for that consumer's team, wherever the consumer runs. A Pacto status an older operator wrote records no guarantees or requires, so delivery reads it as unknown until the new operator reconciles it: a requirement on that provider is not refused, and a breaking or possibly breaking change to one of its providers waits for a person to accept the unknown.

docs.title: External dependencies
docs.text:
external: true marks a dependency that something outside this Pacto installation delivers. Your company may still run it. Pacto expects no running instance of it, never proposes moving it first and leaves it out of the unresolved list. It takes one of two forms:

dependencies:
  - name: ledger                 # someone wrote a contract for it
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/pacto/ledger
    compatibility: "^4.0.0"      # compared like any other dependency
    required: true
    external: true
  - name: model                  # no contract: name the version instead
    external: true
    version: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5
    required: true

With ref, versions are compared as usual. Without it, version is required: it shows in the graph and in pacto diff, where any change is potentially breaking. Pacto has no contract to compare it with, so anything that relies on it is Unknown and never passes. A dependency with no ref and no external: true fails validation with DEPENDENCY_REF_REQUIRED. An external dependency with no ref and no version fails with EXTERNAL_VERSION_REQUIRED.

docs.title: A dependency whose contract is not published yet
docs.text:
For a service your Pacto system delivers whose contract nobody has published yet, leave external out. Set ref to the repository its contract will be published at and compatibility to the versions you accept:

dependencies:
  - name: ledger
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/ledger   # published later
    compatibility: "^1.0.0"
    required: true

The contract validates. Until ledger publishes, Pacto lists the dependency as unresolved, so the gap stays visible. With external: true and a version in its place, compatibility stays Unknown for good.

docs.title: Dependency reference schemes
docs.text:
Scheme Example Description oci:// oci://ghcr.io/acme/auth-pacto:1.0.0 OCI registry reference (required for pacto push) oci:// (no tag) oci://ghcr.io/acme/auth-pacto Resolved to the highest semver tag satisfying compatibility file:// file://../shared-db Local filesystem path (bare path) ../shared-db Local filesystem path (shorthand for file://)

When an oci:// reference omits the tag, pacto queries the registry for available tags and selects the highest semver version that satisfies the compatibility constraint. For example, with compatibility: "^2.0.0" and available tags 1.0.0, 2.0.0, 2.3.0, 3.0.0, pacto resolves to 2.3.0. Pacto caches tag listings in memory for the duration of the command, so dependencies that point to the same repository share one registry query.

compatibility applies only to untagged references

Pacto reads the constraint only when the reference omits its tag. A ref that names a tag or a digest resolves to exactly that version, and validation skips the compatibility check. This example validates with no warning:

dependencies:
  - name: auth
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/auth-pacto:1.0.0   # resolves to 1.0.0 …
    required: true
    compatibility: "^2.0.0"                    # … which this does not satisfy

Pinning and constraining are separate decisions. If you pin, the pin wins. Keep compatibility accurate anyway, because consumers and the lockfile read it as your declared range.

At runtime the Kubernetes operator does check the range: when the provider runs under its own Pacto resource, the contract version it reports outside compatibility is DEPENDENCY_VERSION_MISMATCH, an error for a required dependency and a warning for an optional one. An unknown version stays unverified.

Note

Validation rejects OCI references whose tag or digest is malformed. Tags must follow the OCI tag grammar ([A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}), and digests must be well-formed (sha256:<64 hex> or sha512:<128 hex>). The same check applies to config and policy refs.

docs.title: Compatibility constraint examples
docs.text:
Pacto uses Masterminds/semver constraint syntax:

Constraint Matches Use case ^2.0.0 >= 2.0.0, < 3.0.0 Accept patches and minors within a major version ~2.1.0 >= 2.1.0, < 2.2.0 Accept only patches within a minor version >= 2.0.0 2.0.0 and above (including 3.x, 4.x, …) Track the latest version above a floor >= 2.0.0, < 4.0.0 2.x and 3.x only Constrain to a range of major versions * Any version Always resolve to the absolute latest

Warning

Use local dependency references (file:// and bare paths) during development. pacto push rejects contracts with local dependencies, so switch every ref to oci:// before you publish.

Practices:

  • Pin by digest in production. Use oci://...@sha256:.... A tag-based reference produces a validation warning.
  • Give cloud-managed resources a contract when you can. A lightweight Pacto contract for GCP Cloud SQL, AWS SNS or Azure Service Bus, referenced as an external dependency, makes it version-tracked alongside your own. When nobody writes one, name its version with version.
  • Pin the whole closure with pacto lock. When a pacto.lock file is present, every resolved dependency must match the pinned digest or the command fails. See Lockfile.

docs.title: workload
docs.text:
Top-level string describing the execution pattern of the workload. Optional. Enum: service, job, scheduled.

Value Description service A long-running process that serves requests continuously job A one-shot task that runs to completion and then exits scheduled A task that runs on a recurring schedule (for example cron) 
workload: service

docs.title: state
docs.text:
Top-level section declaring how the service manages state. Optional: a minimal contract, such as a lightweight dependency declaration, can omit it. The contract tells the platform whether the service needs persistent storage or a stable network identity.

Field Type Required Enum values type string Yes stateless, stateful, hybrid persistence Persistence Yes dataCriticality string Yes low, medium, high

State types:

Value What it means Example services stateless No data retained between requests. Any instance can handle any request. Instances are interchangeable. REST APIs, reverse proxies, API gateways stateful Retains data between requests. Requires stable storage or instance affinity. Databases, message brokers, distributed caches hybrid Handles requests statelessly but keeps selective in-memory or local state that enriches behavior. Losing that state degrades the service but leaves it running. APIs with local caches, services with in-memory session stores

How platforms interpret state:

The combination of state.type, persistence.scope and persistence.durability tells a platform what infrastructure a service needs. These signals are platform-agnostic. See Platform engineers for the full contract-field → platform-decision mapping (Deployment, StatefulSet, PVC and the equivalents on Nomad, ECS or a custom platform).

Data criticality:

Value What it means low Loss of data has minimal impact. Can be regenerated or is non-essential. medium Loss has moderate impact. May require manual recovery. high Loss has severe business impact. Must be prevented. Implies backups, replication, stricter disruption budgets.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Field Type Required Enum values scope string Yes local, shared durability string Yes ephemeral, persistent
  • local: data stays on a single instance. Each replica has its own.
  • shared: all instances share data through a common store.
  • ephemeral: data can be lost on restart without impact. Caches, temp files and reconstructible state.
  • persistent: data must survive restarts. Requires durable storage.

At runtime the Kubernetes operator reads scope from the workload: one PersistentVolumeClaim in the pod template of a workload with more than one replica is shared, so local scope with such a claim is PERSISTENCE_MISMATCH. shared scope with per-replica storage stays unverified, because the shared store may live outside the cluster.

docs.title: State invariants
docs.text:
Condition Constraint type: stateless durability must be ephemeral

The JSON Schema rejects a stateless service with persistent storage.

state:
  type: stateful
  persistence:
    scope: shared
    durability: persistent
  dataCriticality: high

docs.title: pacto diff and change classification: what counts as a breaking change
docs.text:
pacto diff compares two versions of a contract and tells you which changes can break the services that depend on it. Run it in CI to catch a breaking change before it merges:

pacto diff oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments-api:1.4.0 ./payments-api

Every change goes through a fixed rule table, so the same two contracts always give the same answer. The tables below are the complete list: every field Pacto compares and the verdict it reaches.

Each change is classified as:

  • BREAKING: a change that breaks consumers or platforms relying on the previous contract
  • POTENTIAL_BREAKING: a change that may break consumers, depending on how they use the field
  • NON_BREAKING: a safe change that keeps compatibility

A change that matches no specific rule below defaults to POTENTIAL_BREAKING. Inside an interface schema the default is BREAKING; see Schema position.

docs.title: Service identity
docs.text:
Field Change Classification service.name Modified BREAKING service.version Modified NON_BREAKING service.owner.team Added / Modified / Removed NON_BREAKING service.owner.dri Added / Modified / Removed NON_BREAKING service.owner.contacts[] Added / Modified / Removed NON_BREAKING

The owner block is compared field by field, so changing a dri or adding a contact while the team is unchanged reports that specific change. Contacts are keyed by type:value, and a purpose change on an existing contact is a modification. service carries identity only, so the contract has no image or chart field to diff. A pactoVersion change, such as "2.0" to "2.1", is NON_BREAKING.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
Field Change Classification interfaces Added NON_BREAKING interfaces Removed BREAKING interfaces.type Modified BREAKING interfaces.ref Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING interfaces.visibility Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING interfaces.lifecycle Added / Removed NON_BREAKING interfaces.lifecycle.deprecated Modified NON_BREAKING interfaces.lifecycle.sunset Added / Removed NON_BREAKING interfaces.lifecycle.sunset Modified, earlier POTENTIAL_BREAKING interfaces.lifecycle.sunset Modified, later NON_BREAKING interfaces.lifecycle.successor Added / Modified / Removed NON_BREAKING interfaces.guarantees Added NON_BREAKING interfaces.guarantees Removed BREAKING interfaces.guarantees.weakened Modified BREAKING interfaces.guarantees.strengthened Modified NON_BREAKING interfaces.compatibilityEpoch Modified (raised or lowered) BREAKING

Interfaces are keyed by name. The type enum is openapi/asyncapi/grpc/mcp, and the spec pointer is ref. Deprecating an interface changes nothing a consumer calls, so it is a notice. An earlier sunset shortens the time consumers have to migrate. Removing an interface before its sunset is still BREAKING, and the reason says that the sunset has not been reached.

Each guarantee is compared on its own: a longer dedupeWindow or retention, a shorter timeout, global ordering in place of per-key and a new idempotent: true are stronger. A delivery change is weaker in both directions, because a consumer relying on the old value breaks.

A compatibilityEpoch change marks a behavior change that no spec diff can see.

docs.title: Configurations
docs.text:
Field Change Classification configurations[] Added NON_BREAKING configurations[] Removed BREAKING configurations[].schema Added POTENTIAL_BREAKING configurations[].schema Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING configurations[].schema Removed BREAKING configurations[].ref Added NON_BREAKING configurations[].ref Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING configurations[].ref Removed BREAKING configurations[].values.* Added / Modified / Removed NON_BREAKING

Dropping a schema is BREAKING: the configuration a consumer supplies stops being validated. Introducing a schema where there was none is POTENTIAL_BREAKING, because a configuration that was unchecked before can now fail validation.

Inline configuration values and environment values are the provider's own inputs. Pacto diffs them key by key (for example configurations[app].values.replicas) and classifies each change NON_BREAKING.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: Field Change Classification environments[] Added NON_BREAKING environments[] Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING environments[].*, a value in the environment's file, for example environments[production].chart.ingress.host Added / Modified / Removed NON_BREAKING

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
Field Change Classification policies[] Added NON_BREAKING policies[] Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING policies[].schema Added / Modified / Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING policies[].ref Added NON_BREAKING policies[].ref Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING policies[].ref Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING

Introducing a policy schema where there was none is POTENTIAL_BREAKING for the same reason it is on a configuration: a contract that no policy checked before can now fail against it.

docs.title: Workload and state
docs.text:
Field Change Classification workload Modified BREAKING workload Added / Removed NON_BREAKING state.type Modified BREAKING state.persistence.scope Modified BREAKING state.persistence.durability Modified BREAKING state.dataCriticality Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING state.dataCriticality Added / Removed NON_BREAKING

workload and state are top-level sections. Scheduling and scaling are delivery concerns, so the contract has no runtime, lifecycle or scaling section to diff.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Field Change Classification capabilities Added NON_BREAKING capabilities Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING

Capabilities (health, metrics, extension) are compared as a set, keyed by type, plus ref for an extension. Adding a capability is a new signal (NON_BREAKING). Removing one loses an observability guarantee (POTENTIAL_BREAKING). The diff compares only set membership and ignores binding, so re-pointing an existing capability's binding.interface or binding.path produces no change entry.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Field Change Classification dependencies Added NON_BREAKING dependencies Removed BREAKING dependencies.ref Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING dependencies.compatibility Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING dependencies.required Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING dependencies.requires Added / Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING dependencies.requires Removed NON_BREAKING

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text: pacto diff performs deep comparison of referenced OpenAPI specs, detecting changes at the path, method, parameter, request body and response level.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Field Change Classification openapi.paths Added NON_BREAKING openapi.paths Removed BREAKING

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Field Change Classification openapi.methods Added NON_BREAKING openapi.methods Removed BREAKING

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Field Change Classification openapi.parameters Added (optional) POTENTIAL_BREAKING openapi.parameters Added (required: true) BREAKING openapi.parameters Removed BREAKING openapi.parameters Modified (optional → required) BREAKING openapi.parameters Modified (schema narrowed) BREAKING openapi.parameters Modified (any other) POTENTIAL_BREAKING

Introducing a new required parameter, or flipping an existing one from optional to required, is BREAKING because existing clients omit it. A parameter's schema sits in request position, so narrowing it, for example dropping an enum value or lowering a maxLength, is BREAKING too. Relaxing required to optional is POTENTIAL_BREAKING.

Parameters are identified by name + in (location: query, path, header, cookie). A parameter renamed or moved to a different location counts as a removal plus an addition.

docs.title: Request body
docs.text: Field Change Classification openapi.request-body Added POTENTIAL_BREAKING openapi.request-body Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING

docs.title: Responses
docs.text:
Field Change Classification openapi.responses Added NON_BREAKING openapi.responses Removed BREAKING

Neither table has a Modified row. A request body or a status code present on both sides is deep-diffed field by field. A request body schema sits in request position and a response schema in response position, and the schema position rules classify each inner difference. A documentation edit, such as a response description or an example, is NON_BREAKING. Any other change around the schema, such as a media type or a header, is POTENTIAL_BREAKING, except that removing a response's whole content, one of its media types or its schema is BREAKING.

Change paths use a hierarchical format that pinpoints the exact location, for example:

openapi.paths[/users].methods[GET].parameters[filter:query]
openapi.paths[/users].methods[POST].request-body.content.application/json.schema.required[email]
openapi.paths[/users].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.email

docs.title: AsyncAPI
docs.text: pacto diff compares referenced AsyncAPI documents at the channel and operation level. Both AsyncAPI 2.x and 3.x are supported, in YAML or JSON.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Field Change Classification asyncapi.channels Added NON_BREAKING asyncapi.channels Removed BREAKING asyncapi.channels.publish, subscribe (a 2.x flip removes one) Removed BREAKING

A channel present on both sides is compared field by field, so each payload difference surfaces as its own change. Old and new publishers and subscribers run side by side, so a message's payload and headers schemas sit in record position: a new optional property is NON_BREAKING and every other schema difference is BREAKING. Documentation, tags included, and a new 2.x publish or subscribe operation are NON_BREAKING. Any other difference, such as a binding or a message name, is POTENTIAL_BREAKING. For that reason the table has no asyncapi.channels Modified row.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Field Change Classification asyncapi.operations Added NON_BREAKING asyncapi.operations Removed BREAKING asyncapi.operations.action, channel.$ref Modified BREAKING

An operation present on both sides is deep-diffed exactly like a channel, so flipping action from send to receive surfaces as asyncapi.operations[sendOrder].action (BREAKING).

Top-level operations are an AsyncAPI 3.x concept. A 2.x document has no operations map, so only its channels are compared.

The diff ignores info, servers and defaultContentType, which change on most releases and leave what a consumer can publish or subscribe to unchanged. Components are compared where they are used.

Change paths pinpoint the exact location, for example:

asyncapi.channels[payment.completed]
asyncapi.channels[payment.refunded].publish.message.payload.required[charge_id]
asyncapi.operations[sendOrder].action

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
pacto diff compares referenced .proto files at the service, rpc, message, field and enum level.

Field Change Classification grpc.services Added NON_BREAKING grpc.services Removed BREAKING grpc.rpcs Added NON_BREAKING grpc.rpcs Removed BREAKING grpc.rpcs Modified BREAKING grpc.messages Added NON_BREAKING grpc.messages Removed BREAKING grpc.messages.fields Added NON_BREAKING grpc.messages.fields Removed BREAKING grpc.messages.fields Modified BREAKING grpc.enums Added NON_BREAKING grpc.enums Removed BREAKING grpc.enums.values Added POTENTIAL_BREAKING grpc.enums.values Removed / Modified BREAKING

proto3 has no required, so an added rpc, message or field is always wire-compatible with existing clients. An added enum value is POTENTIAL_BREAKING: the scan cannot tell whether the enum reaches a reader that switches over every value. A removed or renumbered value is BREAKING. Everything else here is BREAKING. Removing a service, rpc, message or field breaks every caller. A changed rpc signature (including a switch between unary and streaming), or a field whose type or number changed, breaks the wire format for clients built against the old descriptor. For that reason a modified field is BREAKING.

Change paths pinpoint the exact location, for example:

grpc.services[FraudService]
grpc.rpcs[FraudService.EvaluateTransaction]
grpc.messages[EvaluateTransactionRequest].fields[metadata]

docs.title: Limits of the proto comparison
docs.text:
The comparison scans proto3 source as text. It runs no protobuf compiler, which has these effects:

  • imports stay unresolved. Pacto compares only the declarations in the referenced file. A message that moves into an imported file reads as a removal.
  • Nested messages, nested enums and oneof bodies are skipped. Their fields are left out of the enclosing message, so a change inside one produces no change entry.
  • Identity is the declared name. A renamed field or rpc reads as a removal plus an addition even when the field number is unchanged.
  • Type identity is textual. The scanner compares names as written, without package or import resolution, so fully qualifying a type (Inner → pkg.v1.Inner) reads as a modified field even though the descriptor is unchanged.
  • Inline field options are ignored. Adding or removing [deprecated = true] produces no change entry, while a retype behind one still does. A field whose option block contains braces (a nested text-format value such as [(validate.rules).string = {min_len: 1}]) is dropped from the revision that carries it, and only from that one. Adding such an option to an existing field therefore reads as a removal and is classified BREAKING.
  • Comments and string literals are inert. A //, a } or a /* inside a string literal, such as a URL in an option line, is read as part of the string.

docs.title: JSON Schema (configuration & policy schemas)
docs.text:
Schema files referenced by configurations[].schema, policies[].schema or the auto-detected policy/schema.json are compared recursively. Pacto detects and classifies every structural difference, including properties, types, constraints, defaults and enums.

Field Change Classification schema.properties.* Added POTENTIAL_BREAKING schema.properties.* Removed POTENTIAL_BREAKING schema.properties.* Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING schema.required Added / Removed BREAKING schema.description, title, examples and other documentation Added / Removed / Modified NON_BREAKING schema.* (any other path) Added / Removed / Modified POTENTIAL_BREAKING

A configuration or policy schema carries no position. A configuration schema constrains a value the platform supplies, so both required transitions take the conservative answer and stay BREAKING.

docs.title: Schema position
docs.text:
An interface schema is judged by the position it sits in, because the same edit helps one side of an exchange and hurts the other.
