A remote ref, or one whose target is missing, is POTENTIAL_BREAKING with a reason saying Pacto could not resolve it, and so is a ref whose target goes away while its text stays the same. A component nothing references is reported as NON_BREAKING. An x- extension keyword inside an interface schema is POTENTIAL_BREAKING in every position: tools read it, and Pacto cannot tell whether a change to one reaches a reader of the data. The safe direction of each edit above is NON_BREAKING, and so is a new optional property in a request or a response. Documentation edits (description, title, summary, example, examples, $comment, externalDocs, deprecated, tags) are NON_BREAKING everywhere, configuration and policy schemas included. - 039d160: pacto validate reports one PASS, FAIL or SKIP line per stage (load, lock, structural, cross-field, policy, guarantees, readiness and closure), lists each error under its stage with its file:line:column when it can be located (never with --set or -f, which validate a merged document), and ends with a Next: line naming the one command to run now. A failed load or lock stage skips every stage after it, and a failed structural or cross-field stage skips the stages after it up to policy. The guarantees, readiness and closure stages run even when an earlier stage fails. The JSON output adds stages, next, file and each error's line and column, and pacto_check returns the same stages, next and locations. An unknown field or a mistyped enum value carries a did you mean hint naming the closest valid one.

The text output of pacto validate now goes to stdout as one stream: the error and warning lines moved there from stderr. The one-line failure summary stays on stderr, and exit codes are unchanged.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 9d4ec34: Make Pacto easier for an agent to drive from the CLI help and the MCP tool text alone.

pacto impact has a new exit status. It now exits 2 when a breaking change cannot be shown to be safe. A CI job that treated any non-zero exit as a failure fails on these runs too; one that gates on deployed impact alone can treat 2 as a pass.

pacto impact and the fleet tools no longer give answers that read as safe when they are not.

  • pacto impact adds the new revision to the snapshot when no fleet source holds the changed service, so --local ./fleet with only the consumers finds them instead of answering "No affected consumers".
  • Every impact answer ends in a release gate, gate and gateReason, and the exit status follows it: 0 clear, 1 blocked (a breaking change reaches an incompatible consumer on a known target) and the new 2 unverified (a breaking change on a partial answer, or with consumers none of which is shown to be safe). A declared-only run of a breaking change with consumers now exits 2 instead of 0. The pacto_impact MCP tool, the dashboard's Change analysis view and the terminal UI show the same gate and its reason.
  • On a breaking change, a consumer whose range accepts the new version carries a note: the range match does not show that it avoids what the change removes. An open range such as >=1.0.0 is named as open.
  • A declared dependency carries rangeStatus (satisfied, unsatisfied or unknown) beside resolved. A provider in the fleet at a version outside the range is reported by pacto fleet status, pacto_fleet_status, explain and the dashboard's attention list as DEPENDENCY_RANGE_UNSATISFIED, in the new out-of-range category (--unsatisfied-ranges, unsatisfied_ranges).
  • pacto_fleet_status with no category selected, including empty input, reports every category, as pacto fleet status does. It returned items: null before.
  • owner has one shape in search and get, the contract's {team, dri, contacts}, and is left out when no contract declares one. A service read only from Kubernetes takes its owner from the operator's status.contract.owner, where it was empty before.

Delivery plans are readable to an agent from the tools alone. The CLI and the MCP delivery tools now say the same thing. The operator's promoter shares this code, so its messages and the Rejected-plan behaviour change with it.

  • pacto delivery candidates and the pacto_delivery_candidates tool list the versions a Stage may take, with their digests: what its candidate source offers that pacto publish published. The to of plan and propose takes a version (3.0.0), a tag or a digest. A version or a tag must name exactly one candidate; Pacto refuses one that names none or several, or that it cannot match because a candidate cannot be read, and says why. A missing to says where to find a valid value.
  • A plan carries next: which teams must sign (and that their approval also meets a Stage's rule that a person approves every promote), that an agent cannot answer and the operation is then Held, and that an operation nobody decides before its approval deadline concludes Expired with nothing changed. pacto delivery get, pacto_delivery_get and pacto delivery explain say what happens at the deadline of a held operation.
  • A plan predicted Rejected asks nobody anything, and its failing verdict says what to do first, such as promoting the version on the upstream Stage.
  • The message for a consumer that must move first names the Stage to promote it on in plain words.
  • PlanStale names the reason or the on-behalf-of person when a propose adds one the plan did not have, and otherwise lists what the intent digest binds instead of saying the Stage moved.

pacto init and pacto_create with pactify read more of a service into its contract. The workload's environment, including the ConfigMaps it reads, becomes a configuration schema with each value as its default. A URL in it that names another service in the cluster becomes a dependency: with that service's contract in --fleet, its bundle and a range from its version; without it, a placeholder range that the contract comment and Unknown name. A readiness, liveness or startup probe becomes a health check.

pacto init --describe-only (describe_only in pacto_create) writes a contract that only describes the service: no publish section, no signing key and no .pactoignore. Without it, init still writes the publish section and now says how to leave it out.

pacto init, pacto_create and pacto_edit flag an owner written as team/billing, and pacto_check suggests the pacto_edit call that writes billing. pacto_check also explains how to declare a service of your own whose contract is not published yet, so it shows as unresolved until it is. The contract schema and the DEPENDENCY_REF_REQUIRED message say the same.

The MCP server instructions, pacto_schema and pacto --help now describe what a contract holds and say delivery is opt-in, and pacto_schema returns how to describe an AI agent as a service. - 67de328: pacto validate --closure checks every contract in the dependency closure against the policies the root contract resolves. A dependency that cannot be resolved fails the run, and each finding names the dependency it came from.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 67de328: The dashboard delivery tab that lists Stages and its page are now named Stages, as the glossary calls them. The URL #/delivery/environments and the API path stay the same, so existing links keep working.
  • 67de328: Redeploy pacto.run/latest with the rewritten documentation: the front door, the comparison page, the delivery security model and the guide to generate contracts from what you already have. This changeset carries documentation only. This core patch is the release that redeploys pacto.run/latest.
  • 67de328: pacto init skips the files .pactoignore lists, and it no longer takes a Backstage catalog-info.yaml or a skaffold.yaml for a Kubernetes manifest, so neither lands in the manifests artifact Flux applies.
  • 67de328: pacto init no longer reads a Helm chart's templates as Kubernetes manifests, so unrendered templates stay out of the manifests artifact and never become the contract's workload. A chart's crds/ folder is skipped too, whether the chart sits in a subfolder or at the service root. Unknown names every chart found and says how to render it.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 407c06e: A dashboard people sign in to now reads delivery Stages and Operations from one shared cache, which its ServiceAccount lists and watches, instead of listing them again with every person's token. Each person sees only what their own RBAC allows: the dashboard asks the API server who their token is and, with a SubjectAccessReview, whether they may make the same list or get, keeping each answer 10 seconds; a list across every namespace needs a cluster-wide allow. Every action (propose, approve, cancel, roll back, unfreeze) and every read it is built on still uses the person's own token, and the dashboard reads with that token until the cache has loaded and for a moment after the person changes something. With 2,000 Stages and 10,000 Operations, fifty people opening the inbox at once wait about a second instead of 12. The operator grants the dashboard's ServiceAccount get, list and watch on Stages and Operations, nothing more in the delivery group, and holds that right itself while the dashboard is enabled.
  • 407c06e: A shared dashboard can sign people in, and then shows nothing until they do. pacto dashboard takes an OpenID Connect issuer (--oidc-*, the client secret in PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET), a private issuer CA (--oidc-ca-file), an internal issuer address (--oidc-internal-issuer-url), the API server's claim mapping, session lifetimes (--session-idle-timeout, --session-max-age) and --token-login, which takes a pasted Kubernetes token for clusters that trust no identity provider. The API server names each signed-in person (SelfSubjectReview), and every view and action runs with their token and RBAC. /api/session says who is signed in and how; every other endpoint answers 401 with the code LoginRequired until they sign in. The header names who they are, and the sign-in button says Sign in with OIDC or names the provider (--oidc-display-name). A remote pacto mcp reads the same claim mapping flags and logs each caller as the mapping names them.

The pacto-operator chart gains dashboard.auth: oidc (issuerURL, internalIssuerURL, caBundle, clientID, clientSecretRef, redirectURL, extraScopes, displayName and the claim mapping usernameClaim, usernamePrefix, groupsClaim, groupsPrefix), session (idleTimeout, maxAge) and tokenLogin.enabled. See Dashboard authentication. - 407c06e: A dashboard people sign in to now shows each person only what Kubernetes RBAC lets them read. A namespace's services, revisions, targets, edges and evidence appear only if the person may list Pactos there, checked with a SubjectAccessReview for their username and groups, as the API server names them, and kept a minute. One filter covers every fleet view, counts, search, the graph, change analysis and a remote pacto mcp --fleet with --auth-issuer. The dashboard says when services are hidden without naming them, and a service page counts the hidden services on each side. A service known only from a registry, with no namespace, shows only to people who may list Pactos in every namespace. Local and sign-in-free dashboards are unchanged. The operator grants the dashboard's ServiceAccount create on subjectaccessreviews and holds that right itself while the dashboard is enabled. - 407c06e: Add Pacto delivery, the opt-in part of Pacto that decides which version each environment runs and earns autonomy one confirmed level at a time, plus pacto publish, contract format 2.1 and a pacto init that pactifies existing services, one folder, several or a whole cluster. Nothing changes for a project that does not use them, with one exception: a consumer on an older Pacto or operator cannot read a provider's contract once the provider moves to format 2.1 (see below).

Delivery is Alpha. The new packages (pkg/delivery, pkg/publish, pkg/signing, pkg/deliveryrecord and pkg/ocireferrer) are experimental and not covered by semantic versioning, so their API may change in a minor release.

Pactify a service. pacto init [dir] now reads a folder that already holds a service instead of failing. It fills in the contract from the Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests: name, version and registry from the workload and its image, the owner from --owner or a team label, the interface from an OpenAPI file and a publish section that builds the image and ships the manifests with the workload's image swapped for the one each version builds, pinned by digest in every manifest that runs it, so nobody raises the image tag by hand. A bare image name such as checkout, a Docker Hub official image, leaves the registry Unknown. On a folder whose own contract has no publish section, init says how to add one. Services the workload's environment points at are listed as dependencies, commented out until you set the versions you accept; --fleet <dir> also lists the services that declare this one. Anything it cannot tell is reported as Unknown. A file holding Secret values, or a kustomization with a secretGenerator, is never shipped. --delivery also writes the cluster pieces: the Pacto resource and, for each environment (--env, default test and prod), the Flux OCIRepository objects, a Kustomization that waits for the rollout and the Stage. Every Stage starts on observe and its OCIRepository stays pinned to the tag you deploy, so nothing changes until a person raises it. The last environment's Stage asks a person to approve every promote until you add a health check there and delete its approval; --insecure-registry marks those Flux objects for a plain-HTTP registry, --registry-secret <name> gives them and the Pacto resource the login for a private registry (secretRef and pullSecretRef) and --no-transparency-log writes transparencyLog: false for a key whose signatures stay out of Rekor. --plan prints exactly what would be added and writes nothing. pacto init only adds files and missing .pactoignore lines, so running it twice is safe and it never overwrites your edits. An empty folder still gets the blank contract. Agents get the same through pacto_create with pactify: true (plus delivery, registry, environments, fleet_roots, no_transparency_log, insecure_registry, registry_secret and dry_run).

Pactify many services. pacto init takes several folders and ends with a summary table. pacto init --cluster [--namespace <ns>]... --out <dir> drafts a contract for every workload in the current kubeconfig context that no Pacto describes, in <dir>/<namespace>/<name>. With the node agent running, the services a workload was seen calling become dependencies pinned to the version seen running (=2.3.0) for you to widen. Drafts are never published, and an invalid one fails the command. pacto_create takes paths, cluster and namespaces for the same.

Contract format 2.1. pactoVersion: "2.1" adds a publish section (the contract bundle repository, the image, chart or manifests the service publishes, how each is built and signed and the deploy artifact Flux applies), a checks list of test and eval suites shipped in the bundle (Pacto only hashes each one and takes a runner's verdict about that exact file), an mcp interface type for the tools a service exposes and external: true on a dependency this Pacto system does not deliver. An external dependency either points at a contract and is compared by its range as usual, or has no ref and names a free-text version that nothing can check, so anything relying on it is Unknown. An AI agent is a normal service: tools as an mcp interface, its model as an external dependency, its evals as a check. pacto diff compares tools one by one and treats a new external version, and a suite removed, moved or edited, as needing at least a minor. A 2.0 contract keeps working unchanged; publish, checks, an external dependency or an mcp interface in a 2.0 contract fails validation with NEEDS_PACTO_2_1, which says to set pactoVersion: "2.1". Older Pacto versions reject a 2.1 contract, and that reaches consumers too: once a provider publishes a 2.1 bundle, a consumer whose Pacto or operator predates 2.1 fails to resolve it as a dependency, though the consumer changed nothing. Upgrade the consumers' Pacto and operator before a provider moves to 2.1.

pacto publish publishes what the contract declares as the version it states. --plan shows, for every artifact, whether its tag is absent, identical, adoptable, in conflict or unreadable and which checks refuse the publish. A publish builds what is absent (docker buildx or a command writing to $PACTO_OUT), pushes by digest with the version and the git commit (read from .git, or --revision; it refuses a checkout with uncommitted changes unless --revision names the revision), attaches the SBOM file the build wrote (Pacto does not generate SBOMs), signs every digest and checks each new signature against the configured identity before any tag is written. It never overwrites a tag, so a second run changes nothing and a run that stopped halfway finishes when run again from the same commit; a conflict says to publish a higher service.version. The plan also opens the signer and checks for a docker buildx builder and each build program, so a missing key or builder refuses it before anything is pushed. pacto publish [dir] takes the directory as init and validate do. It refuses a version too small for the change: a breaking change needs a major (a minor before 1.0) and a change Pacto cannot classify at least a minor. A refused publish is kept as a signed refusal in the bundle repository. pacto diff reports the same requiredBump and pacto validate refuses an sbom on a dockerfile build. --propose <namespace>/<stage> hands the version to delivery. pacto mcp --publish adds pacto_publish_plan and pacto_publish over stdio.

Signing. Pacto signs and verifies with sigstore-go and needs no cosign binary; signatures are Sigstore bundle referrers that cosign verify and Flux's spec.verify check. It signs with a key file (COSIGN_PASSWORD decrypts a cosign key), keyless through public-good Fulcio and Rekor, or a cloud KMS key. The KMS providers are optional: the default build leaves the AWS, GCP, Azure and Vault SDKs out (the linux/amd64 binary drops from 75.3 MB to 64.3 MB), and a KMS key in that build fails with an error naming the build to use (go install -tags kms ..., or kms_aws, kms_gcp, kms_azure, kms_hashivault).

Delivery. pkg/delivery holds the operations (delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/promote, rollback, override, freeze, unfreeze, autonomy and acknowledge) and PlanFor, the one planning function the promoter, the CLI, the MCP tools and the dashboard call. A promote is refused as NotPublished unless pacto publish published it and Flux verified its signature, or its upstream Stage verified and offered it. It then compares the running contract with the new one and checks the new version against every consumer's declared range. A consumer the change breaks holds it, asks only that consumer's owners and says which service must move first and to which verified version. Compatibility comes from each consumer's declared version range; Pacto does not check which fields or endpoints a consumer uses. Anything Pacto cannot see holds the change for a person to accept the unknown, a breaking change no contract depends on included; Unknown never passes. Health checks keep running after release: a mira provider judges the error ratio of the service's traces, http is the plug-in format for any other tool, eval runs one of the checks the version ships (the Stage check's suite names it, and a version that does not ship it is held for a person), a verdict counting only about that suite's sha256, and pacto.runtime fails a version the node agent saw calling a service it never declared and passes only after a soak. A workload the node agent saw calling a service with no contract of its own counts as an unknown consumer: a breaking change waits for a person to accept it or for that caller to get a contract, and the question prints the pacto init --cluster command that drafts one; while the agent's view is partial (for example a pod on the host network), every breaking change waits the same way. The fleet snapshot lists these callers (uncontractedCallers). A confirmed failure rolls back once, then freezes the Stage.

Every operation that ends becomes a signed record: an in-toto statement in a Sigstore bundle, chained per Stage and verifiable with standard Sigstore tools without Pacto, against a trust config that says which keys may sign which streams. pkg/signing and pkg/ocireferrer are the shared signing and referrer-write paths; the Evidence Server uses the latter.

pacto delivery types, describe, plan, propose, get, cancel, approve, explain, history, blame, undo and record verify drive and read delivery over the ambient cluster. approve records only a decision the promoter would count, or it says why not; where the Stage asks for a recent sign-in, it logs the person in again in the browser and records the decision with that login alone, trusting a private issuer CA with --oidc-ca-file. plan gathers its input as the promoter does, so it predicts what the promoter will do. history and record verify read the signed records, say asOf, source and completeness and list forks, gaps and anything unreadable; --all walks every Stage you can list. pacto mcp --delivery serves the read tools to anyone and propose and cancel only to agents; there is no approve tool. Over HTTP, pacto mcp verifies a bearer token on every request (--auth-issuer, --resource, --audience) and exchanges it for one the apiserver accepts, so each caller acts as itself.

The autonomy ladder. Each Stage is on one level: observe plans every new version and moves nothing, recording what it would have done; advise ships only what a person asked for or approved; auto-nonbreaking promotes non-breaking changes on its own; autonomous promotes any change the graph clears. An autonomy operation moves a Stage one level: lowering needs nobody (an agent never lowers to observe), raising needs a person of the running service's team other than whoever asked, leaving observe needs the applyRef labelled and an observed digest, and an automatic level needs the recorder, so every grant of autonomy is a signed record. Pacto proposes the next level once a Stage earned it (10 verified changes by default) and lists what blocks it; a raise it has not proposed asks the approver to accept the unknown. When a version Pacto shipped on its own fails and rolls back, the promoter lowers the Stage one level; an Unknown never does. pacto delivery propose --type autonomy --to <level> asks for a move.

Dashboard. pacto dashboard gains a Delivery tab for signed-in people (--delivery-namespace, --delivery-trust, --mira-url): an inbox of what waits on your teams, an environments board, a page per change with its plan, verdicts and proof, history with blame and undo, published versions with recent refused publishes and a path to autonomy: each Stage's level, what Pacto would have done on observe, the next proposal and what blocks it, with the command that fixes each blocker. Promote, roll back, unfreeze, cancel and decisions run there under the person's own token. A decision needs membership of a team the question names and is never taken from an agent or a pasted token; the dashboard offers and records only a decision the promoter would count. Where the Stage asks for a recent sign-in, the dashboard says when a person's sign-in is too old, asks in a dialog to sign in again and keeps their choice and note for one more click, and says up front when a cluster reports no login time, so nobody can approve there. The dashboard also takes a new look: serif titles and numbers, a grouped data-sources menu and labelled status bars.

Demos. The browser demo plays the payments story from examples/story on Pacto's own code over fixed data and labels it simulated; the story now starts fraud on observe and adds the advise raise and the automatic step-down; its Wasm is about 4 MB to download. The Compose demo has no cluster or sign-in, so it shows no Delivery tab; it now shows pacto diff and pacto init --plan.

Behaviour change: pacto push fails on a conflicting reference. Before, pushing to a reference that already held a bundle printed a warning, wrote nothing and exited 0, whatever the bundle held. Now different content under an existing reference exits non-zero, so a script that relied on the old exit status fails; pass --force to overwrite the reference instead. The same content pushed again still exits 0 and writes nothing.

New direct dependencies: github.com/coreos/go-oidc/v3 (dashboard sign-in), github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go, github.com/sigstore/sigstore, github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs, github.com/theupdateframework/go-tuf/v2, github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4 and github.com/digitorus/timestamp (signing and verifying without cosign), and golang.org/x/oauth2 and google.golang.org/protobuf (once indirect, now direct). The four github.com/sigstore/sigstore/pkg/signature/kms/{aws,azure,gcp,hashivault} modules pull in the AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Vault SDKs; they are linked only into builds with -tags kms (or kms_aws and the like), which the pacto-delivery image uses and the default pacto CLI does not. Together they add about 100 indirect modules.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 9d96a75: Update the dashboard frontend's dependencies. The bundle the pacto binary and the dashboard image serve moves to Mermaid 12.2, Cytoscape 3.34.4, cytoscape-dagre 4.0.1, Marked 18.1 and Svelte 5.57. Mermaid 12 lays diagrams out with ELK and draws them in its new neo look by default, so bundle docs keep the dagre layout and classic look they had before.

The dashboard's accessible names now begin with the visible text of the control (the navbar search, the graph's Reset layout button and the change count in delivery history), as WCAG 2.5.3 asks and axe-core 4.14 checks.

Build and test tooling moves to Playwright 1.64, axe-core 4.14, jsdom 30, svelte-check 4.7, the Svelte Vite plugin 7.3 and mermaid-cli 12. TypeScript stays on 5.9: svelte-check and openapi-typescript do not support TypeScript 7 yet. - 9f5f638: Update github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4 to v4.1.6 to fix CVE-2026-116587, a denial of service when parsing JWKs that contain RSA keys. It reaches the pacto binary and the operator through OIDC sign-in and Sigstore signing.

golang.org/x/net moves to v0.62.0 (GO-2026-6860, GO-2026-6866) and the operator's github.com/google/cel-go to v0.30.0 (GO-2026-6094). govulncheck finds none of the three reachable, so this is hygiene rather than an exposure fix.

The dashboard frontend's dependencies are updated too, which fixes the known advisories in the bundle the pacto binary and the dashboard image serve: DOMPurify 3.4.17, KaTeX 0.18 (used by Mermaid diagrams), devalue 5.9.4 and source-map-js 1.2.2. The build and test tooling moves to Vite 8.3 and Vitest 4.1.12.

docs.title: Major Changes
docs.text:
• 9b84eda: Fixes from a whole-repo architecture review, and the breaking cleanups of the v4 major: camelCase JSON everywhere, the deprecated v3 API removed and a few APIs reshaped. Every breaking change is listed under Breaking changes with its migration.

Behaviour changes

  • An extension capability no longer keeps a contract at Unknown forever. Pacto has no evaluator for one, so validation.Evaluate now lists it in Coverage.Unverified as capabilities[ref=<ref>] instead of counting it as a required assertion and emitting EXTENSION_EVALUATOR_UNAVAILABLE. A contract declaring an extension can reach Compliant; that verdict says nothing about the extension. The code is removed (see below).
  • An evidence observation with outcome Observed must carry every verdict-bearing payload key for its kind (present, type, reachable or durable, plus conformant for a present configuration). A missing or null key used to decode to false and read as a confirmed violation; it is now rejected. The payloads Pacto's own producers emit always carry these keys.
  • PACTO_NO_ANIM and PACTO_NO_UPDATE_CHECK share one parser: Go's boolean spellings, with any other non-empty value read as set. PACTO_NO_ANIM=0 or false now leaves animations on, and PACTO_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=true now disables the update check. 1 works as before.

Fixes

  • MCP pacto_check runs the same validation path as pacto validate, including pacto.lock verification, so a drifted lockfile no longer passes.
  • MCP pacto_edit add_config_properties writes the properties into the first configuration's schema file, merging with what is there, instead of declaring a configuration and dropping them. Edited files are written through a uniquely named temporary file that keeps the target's permissions.
  • pacto agent --docker-label-filter key=value (repeatable) narrows --docker to containers carrying every given label, so one agent on a shared daemon can keep to one Compose project. The Compose demo now does.
  • Evidence ingestion keys a record's domain by the same rule the fleet sources use (contract.OCIDomain), and keeps the evidence validation detail in the server log. Sending evidence uses a client with a timeout and a bounded response read.
  • Free text in pacto doc tables escapes | and folds line breaks.
  • The CLI reference now states that PACTO_INSECURE_REGISTRIES applies to every registry access and that an unknown --output-format is rejected.

API additions

  • contract.OCIScheme, TrimOCIScheme, SplitOCIDigest, SplitOCITag, SplitOCIRef and OCIDomain: one lenient set of reference helpers, now used everywhere Pacto split references by hand.
  • contract.DocsDir and contract.WalkDocs, lock.ReadFS and capability.ToolsForContract: the bundle readers the fleet, the offline view and MCP share.
  • finding.Registry returns every registry row; fleet.Paginate and fleet.Page page a sorted list; fleet.AttentionCategoriesList returns the attention order as a copy; fleet.SourceKindKubernetes names the Kubernetes source kind.

Breaking changes

  • The Go module path becomes github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4 (was .../v3). Update every import, and install the CLI with go install github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@latest.
  • camelCase JSON. finding.Finding, finding.SubjectRef and finding.EvidenceRef (code, severity, category, subject.kind, contractPath, message, evidenceRefs[].source …), readiness.Result and readiness.CheckResult (score, minScore, checks[].id …), contract.ValidationError/ValidationWarning, validation.ValidationResult and the --output-format json of pacto init, validate, pack, pull and push (dir, path, valid, errors, name, version, ref, digest) were PascalCase on the wire. That reaches pacto agent and pacto run output, MCP answers, the dashboard /api/fleet/* answers and the Evidence Server's records and target projection. Migration: read the camelCase keys. Evidence records already stored in a registry and answers from an older Evidence Server still decode, because the decoder matches keys without regard to case. The evidence envelope (pacto.dev/evidence/v1) is a versioned protocol and does not change.
  • pkg/dashboard.Server takes an options struct. NewServer(dashboard.Options{UI, Host, Port, Version, CORSOrigin, Logger, Fleet, Impact, Refresh}) and Serve(ctx) replace NewServer(ui), the seven setters (SetFleetProvider, SetImpactProvider, SetFleetRefresher, SetListenAddr, SetVersion, SetCORSOrigin, SetLogger) and Serve(ctx, port, host...). The OpenAPI server URL is derived from Host and Port.
  • Fleet HTTP filters are enums. status on /api/fleet/services, /api/fleet/entities and /api/fleet/attention accepts only the seven compliance states, and kinds on /api/fleet/entities is a comma-separated list of service, revision, target, owner and source checked item by item. An unknown value or an empty item (a trailing comma) is answered with 422 naming the parameter (query.kinds[1]). Migration: send only listed values and no empty items.
  • /api/sources reports Kubernetes as kubernetes, the fleet source kind, instead of k8s. The dashboard's source pill follows.
  • Product impact moved to pkg/impact. impact.Product, impact.ProductConsumer, impact.ConsumersPage, impact.TallyBucket, impact.ProductChange, impact.ChangesPreview, impact.ProductRevisions, impact.ImmutableRef and impact.BuildProduct hold the route-neutral logic; dashboard.ProductImpact embeds impact.Product and adds hrefs. Gone from pkg/dashboard: ProductChange, ProductChangesPreview, ProductRefsPreview (owners and active targets are ProductRefPreview), ImpactTallyBucket and the MaxImpact*, DefaultImpactConsumers and MaxChangeValueRunes constants (now impact.MaxProduct*, impact.DefaultProductConsumers and impact.MaxChangeValueRunes). The JSON field names of POST /api/fleet/impact do not change; three OpenAPI component names do (Impact.ChangesPreview, Impact.ProductChange, Impact.TallyBucket).
  • MCP pacto_create no longer infers state from the description. Words such as postgres, db, redis, cache, persistent or "stores data" used to make the contract stateful; a runtime that disagrees is now a confirmed contradiction, so a guess would turn into a false violation. Migration: pass stores_data, data_survives_restart and data_shared_across_instances when the service keeps state. Without them the contract is stateless.
  • Removed deprecated API.
    • pkg/finding: CategoryInterfaceMismatch; CodeExtensionEvaluatorUnavailable and its registry row (a stored finding with that code no longer has a category); the retired CodeInvalidInterfaceType, CodeInterfaceRefRequired, CodeInvalidCapabilityType, CodeCapabilityRefRequired and CodeUnsupportedPolicyTarget (all reported as CodeSchemaViolation); DefaultSeverity (use SeverityFor(code, true)).
    • pkg/fleet: BuildOptions.AllowPartial (use DisallowPartial), AttentionCategories (use AttentionCategoriesList()), ParseTargetKey, IsDigestPinnedRef (use ParseCanonicalOCIRef or ClassifyContentIdentity), FleetSnapshot.ObservedDependents and ObservedDependencies (use the query neighborhood), MemorySource.WithCollectFunc, ProductSeverityUnknown (use ProductSeverity(finding.SeverityUnknown)), LimitationRevisionConflict and LimitationRevisionContentMutable (nothing emitted them).
    • pkg/contractview: LookupValidation, ValidationCatalogEntry, NormalizeContractStatus, the Condition, EndpointStatus, ResourcesInfo, PortsInfo, ChecksSummary, ComplianceCounts and SectionInfo types, the Section* and VersionPolicy* constants and the ServiceDetails fields nothing populated (Endpoints, Conditions, ChecksSummary, Resources, Ports, RuntimeEvaluated, SectionMeta, VersionPolicy, LatestAvailable, UpdateAvailable). ComputeCompliance takes only the contract status, and ComplianceInfo carries only status.
    • pkg/dashboard: the forwarders ServiceFromContract, ServiceDetailsFromBundle, GlobalGraphFromResult, NormalizeContractStatus, ComputeCompliance, LookupValidation and ApplyLock (call pkg/contractview), the inert ComputeDiff, DiffResultFromEngine, GraphFromResult and ComputeRuntimeDiff (call diff.Compare and contractview.GlobalGraphFromResult) and the aliases of the removed contract-view types and constants.
    • pkg/oci: WithNameOptions (use WithInsecureRegistries); LocalOnly, RemoteAllowed and the ResolveMode type, so Resolver.Resolve, ResolveConstrained and ResolvePinned drop their mode argument; CachedStore.PullCached and PullCachedPinned (use Pull and PullPinned); ReadCachedRef (use ReadCacheEntry); Resolver.ListVersions and FetchAllVersions (use BundleStore.ListTags with FilterSemverTags); ExportedUserHomeDirFn and SetUserHomeDirFn (use t.Setenv("HOME", dir)).
    • pkg/evidenceingest: Source and NewSource (read the evidence-source HTTP projection at TargetsPath), MemoryStore, NewMemoryStore and the onAccept argument of NewHandler (wrap Store.Commit to observe accepts).
    • graph.RenderTree (use RenderTreeColored(r, graph.TreeColors{})), sbom.HasSBOM (check ParseFromFS for a nil document), otelobserver.Observe (use ParseTraces, DependencyEdges and EvidenceSets), semver.LessDesc (use Compare) and catalog.ContentID.Zero (compare with catalog.ContentID{}).

API additions in v4

  • runtimefacts.CollectorKubernetes, CollectorKubernetesKernel and CollectorKernel name the Kubernetes collectors; the operator uses them and go run ./cmd/gendocs registry publishes them.
  • 9b84eda: Judge more of the contract at runtime, without turning an inability to observe into a violation.

Evidence payloads gain facts a producer may report: InterfaceObservation carries protocol (http1, http2, tls, other) and exposure (external, cluster), DependencyObservation carries the provider's version and undeclared and PersistenceObservation carries shared. All are omitempty, so a producer that does not set them emits the same JSON as before.

validation.Evaluate checks them as facets of an observed assertion:

  • INTERFACE_PROTOCOL_MISMATCH — openapi answering neither HTTP/1 nor HTTP/2, or grpc answering anything but HTTP/2.
  • INTERFACE_VISIBILITY_MISMATCH — an internal interface (the schema default, now applied when visibility is omitted) exposed outside the cluster.
  • DEPENDENCY_VERSION_MISMATCH — the provider's version outside compatibility; an error for a required dependency, a warning for an optional one.
  • PERSISTENCE_MISMATCH now also covers local scope with storage shared between replicas.
  • DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED — a reachable peer no dependency declares; always a warning, because a contract does not claim its dependency list is complete.

A facet with no usable fact is listed in the new Coverage.Unverified and never changes the status. Every finding's EvidenceRef now names the collector and detectedAt of the observation it came from.

pkg/validation/schema/field-coverage.yaml inventories every schema path and runtime-relevant enum value with its runtime class, evidence, rule, outcomes, limitations and tests; a test fails when the schema and the inventory disagree. Every runtime-checked field also says how far each way of running runtime conformance verifies it (platforms: kubernetes, agent, run, each verified, partial or unverified with a reason and its tests).

New pacto agent command (Linux): a host daemon that watches TCP listeners and connection outcomes with eBPF and attributes each socket to the workload whose cgroup created it (a Kubernetes pod, a container, a systemd unit or a pacto-run-<n> session), falling back to its network namespace when the cgroup names none. --sink stdout prints one JSON snapshot per line; --sink kubernetes writes the node's NodeRuntimeObservation and is what the operator's node agent DaemonSet runs. Attribution reads the socket's cgroup id in the kernel, so on cgroup v2 workloads that share the host's network (systemd units, host-network containers) are told apart too.

--sink local and --sink evidence check workloads against their contracts on the host itself. Workloads come from --bindings (a YAML list of match (unit, container, cgroup, session or pid), contract, host, interfaces and dependencies) and, with --docker, from running containers labelled dev.pacto.contract, dev.pacto.bind.<interface> and dev.pacto.dep.<dependency>. Interfaces and dependencies are judged from the kernel, health and metrics capabilities and (with --enable-probing) the interface protocol by probing the bound port. local prints every workload's compliance each round; evidence signs each workload's evidence and sends it to an Evidence Server, which needs contracts pinned by digest. Exposure, provider version and persistence scope have no source off Kubernetes and stay unverified; a declared workload, persistent durability or required configuration reads EVIDENCE_MISSING. A workload that reaches another checked workload its contract does not declare reports DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED named by that workload's contract service, with the operator's suppression rule. A bindings-file workload starts with its oldest process, so earlier connections are ignored. An agent off the host's network reports probes of loopback-bound workloads unsupported, with a note, instead of probing its own loopback.

New pacto run --contract <dir|oci ref> [--bind iface=port] [--dep name=host:port] -- command: runs one command and checks its process tree against the contract while it runs, printing a round every --interval and a final one after the command exits, then exits with the command's exit code (--fail-on noncompliant|unknown turns a bad final verdict into exit 1). With the privileges for it on Linux the command starts in its own cgroup and is observed with eBPF (collector pacto-run+ebpf); otherwise it falls back to polling /proc, says so, and never reports a dependency unreachable because it cannot see a failed connection (collector pacto-run); it falls back the same way when the program attached but the command cannot start in the cgroup. The command runs in a process group of its own: on a terminal pacto run owns, the group takes the terminal over, otherwise SIGINT and SIGTERM are passed on to the whole group, so a Ctrl-C reaches it once. Elsewhere the command runs unobserved and every runtime assertion is unsupported. The command's stdin, stdout and stderr stay its own: rounds go to stderr, or with --report <file> to a file, one whole round per write. --evidence-* signs and sends every round to an Evidence Server.

New public packages: pkg/runtimefacts, the platform-neutral runtime snapshot, workload bindings and the verdicts that turn them into observations (the operator now uses them too), and pkg/probe, the SSRF-safe HTTP health, metrics and protocol probes, moved out of the operator.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 79de1ba: This week's dependency bumps in one go: bubbletea 2.0.10 → 2.1.0 and x/sync 0.23.0 → 0.24.0 in the engine, OpenTelemetry 1.46.0 → 1.47.0 (and the Prometheus exporter 0.68.0 → 0.69.0) in the operator module. No source changes.

Go goes 1.26.6 → 1.26.9 and x/net 0.59.0 → 0.60.0 in both modules, because govulncheck flagged reachable net/http and x/net/http2 vulns (GO-2026-6607 to GO-2026-6617) and wouldn't let any of the bot's PRs through. Both shipped binaries were exposed, so it's worth the patch release.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 1ee5a37: Retitle the homepage section that compared Pacto to a service catalog, and fix four dead links.

"What a service catalog does not do" headed a section on both the README and the homepage without anything setting the comparison up — neither page mentions a catalog before it — and the section then did not describe catalogs. What follows it is a worked pacto impact run answering which consumers a major version bump breaks, so the heading now says that. The comparison keeps the two places that have the context for it: the "What Pacto is not" list in the model, and the comparison table in the README.

Four links were dead. The operator chart's README pointed at an api-reference.md that exists nowhere in the repo, which mattered because that README is the package description on Artifact Hub; it now points at the CRD reference page. Two links named a pacto-dashboard repository that does not exist. The Cosign overview and the Kubernetes resource-quantity pages had both moved. Nothing checked any of them: docs_lint.check_links walks root-level Markdown only, and mkdocs validates only what it builds.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• ae1c923: Rebuild the documentation around what a reader is trying to do, and cut it in half.

The site used to be organised by subsystem, so finding out what Pacto does meant reading about how it is built. Twelve top-level navigation sections are now eight: the homepage, the changelog and the six a reader moves through in order — Try it, Get started, Guides, How Pacto decides, Reference, Integrations. Concepts and the operational graph merged into How Pacto decides, patterns moved under Guides, examples split across the two entry sections and Project internals left the site altogether.

Someone who lands on the homepage can open the live dashboard demo without installing anything, and the quickstart that follows reaches a validated contract, a breaking change and the list of affected consumers entirely on a local filesystem. Publishing to a registry moved to the end of that page as an optional step, because it was the first thing standing between a new reader and a result. Committing the contract to a repository is now its own short page, CI integration, rather than a section buried in installation.

Twenty-eight pages are gone. Most of what they said lives on the page that already owned the subject; nothing was silently dropped:

  • Seven concept and graph pages — concepts, concept boundaries, collectors, observation sources, fleet queries, fleet sources and impact surfaces — are now sections of the model, the operational graph, impact analysis and fleet tools.
  • Six pattern pages are one page, composition patterns, and the developer and platform-engineer guides no longer restate those patterns.
  • Three evidence pages — the OCI storage layout, the protocol and the security model — are one page, evidence.
  • Three MCP pages — agent capabilities, authoring tools and catalog discovery — are folded into AI assistants (MCP), and the per-tool argument tables moved to the CLI reference alongside the commands.
  • The separate agent walkthrough is folded back into the guided tour, which now covers both ways through the demo in one pass.
  • The architecture, tooling-architecture, release and testing pages were never for site readers. They are contributor documentation and now sit in ARCHITECTURE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and release/README.md in the repository, next to the code they describe.
  • The dashboard-architecture and compliance-scenario pages are removed, not moved. ARCHITECTURE.md carries one short dashboard section, not the fourteen the old page had, and the scenario-to-proof map is gone.

The corpus falls from 71 pages to 47 and from 101,000 words to 57,000 — -43% measured over everything a page contains, -47% measured over running prose alone. The surviving pages are shorter as well, because most of what came out was the same thing said on three pages.

This repository has no mkdocs-redirects, so every one of those twenty-eight URLs is permanently dead, as is any bookmark to a heading that moved onto a different page. Readiness is the one most likely to be linked: it was a section of the contract reference and is now a page of its own, so contract-reference/#readiness no longer resolves to anything. If you have linked to a Pacto documentation page from a runbook or a wiki, this release is the one that breaks it. mike keeps prior versions live at their own URL prefixes, which is the only mitigation there is: every version deploys under its own number, so a bookmark to pacto.run/latest/collectors/ still resolves at pacto.run/3.3.3/collectors/. The list above is the map from what was removed to the page that now carries it.

Three claims the documentation used to make are now rejected by the linter. Vale gained tokens for "policy enforcement" and "enforcement layer" — Pacto checks policy, it does not act on a live system, and the layer that does the checking is named "Policy checks" — and for "blast radius", which is borrowed jargon for something the tools report precisely as the consumers a change affects. Three more tokens catch prose habits rather than claims: "leverage" is always "use" here, "load-bearing" never named what it held up, and an opening that announces the page instead of starting it is now a lint error. The disclaimers that say what Pacto is not are deliberately still allowed to use the words they disclaim, and the finding codes consumers branch on are not claims either, so no token matches them.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• fa6d27a: Take the week's dependency bumps in one go: modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk 1.7.0 → 1.8.0 in the engine, and controller-runtime 0.25.0 → 0.25.1, ginkgo 2.32.2 → 2.33.0 and gomega 1.43.0 → 1.43.1 in the operator module. No source changes — all four are drop-in.

Dependabot also learns to group: Kubernetes libraries move as one train because client-go, apimachinery and controller-runtime pass each other's types, Charm moves as one because bubbletea, bubbles and lipgloss share the v2 renderer, everything else minor-or-patch lands in a single weekly PR. Five open PRs for one afternoon of bumps is how a bot teaches you to stop reading it.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 12b7c03: Gate the documentation deterministically, and cut the corpus to fit the gate.

make docs-lint is a new leg of make docs-check, so CI and a laptop run the identical command. Three tools, three concerns, no overlap — a rule has exactly one home:

  • markdownlint (.markdownlint-cli2.jsonc) owns Markdown syntax.
  • Vale (.vale.ini, .vale/styles/Pacto/) owns prose: marketing language, buzzwords, filler, weasel words, unsupported claims and the terminology this project has already settled on.
  • release/scripts/docs_lint.py owns structure: 1200 prose words per page, 250 per section, headings no deeper than ####.

No model is involved in any of it. The same input always produces the same verdict, which is the point — a documentation rule nobody can forget is worth more than one every contributor is asked to remember. Both linters are pinned by version and neither is vendored; a missing tool is a hard failure, never a silent skip.

The word budgets count running prose only. Front matter, HTML comments, fenced code (including mermaid), tables and lists are exempt by design: what makes a section unreadable is unbroken running text, and a table or a bulleted reference list is already broken up. Counting them punished pages for being reference pages. docs_lint.py self-tests the counter on every run, because a counter that quietly stops counting reads exactly like a corpus in good shape.

Scope lives in one place — scope() hands both external tools an explicit file list rather than a glob, covering the published site, each integration's hand-written docs and the root Markdown a reader meets on GitHub. Generated pages are out: docs/cli-reference.md and the per-integration generated/ trees are already drift-gated against their real sources, and prose rules would only fight the generator.

A fourth leg resolves the links and anchors in the root Markdown files. mkdocs build --strict already validates everything inside docs/, and the integration hook copies integrations/*/docs into it, so those were covered; the six files at the repository root were outside docs_dir and gated by nothing.

Eleven pages were split into twenty-seven to fit the page budget — architecture, concepts, contract-reference/sections, impact, mcp-integration, operational-graph, platform-engineers, the demo tour, the release and testing pages under maintainers/, and the Kubernetes installation page. Each split promoted its extracted sections to a new page, added the mkdocs.yml nav entry and rewrote every inbound link. Everything else came off by deleting prose, not by moving it.

Eleven pages were removed and what they said survives on the page that already owned the subject. The eight one-contract example stubs are now sections of Example contracts; the ingestion endpoints are a section of evidence tooling, ingestion and security; override files are a section of configurations as composable claims; and the developer day-to-day page repeated the contract reference, the breaking-change section of the platform-engineer guide and the MCP page, so it is gone and the three links point at those.

This repository has no mkdocs-redirects, so a page that was removed and a heading that moved to a new page are both permanently dead deep links for anyone who bookmarked them. mike keeps prior versions live at their own URL prefixes, and each origin page names where its content went.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 36e2ef2: Stop the OCI bundle cache from reporting a failure when a concurrent pull of the same reference commits first.

A cache entry is built in a staging directory and swapped into place with one rename, so a reader sees a whole entry or none. Two pulls of the same reference aim at the same destination, though, and nothing serializes them — the second pull is usually a second pacto process sharing one cache directory. Both clear the destination, one rename lands, and the loser's fails onto the winner's fresh entry with directory not empty.

Nothing was wrong: the entry the losing pull set out to write was on disk, put there whole by the other one. But the loser reported the rename error, and the caller logs it, so a healthy parallel pull told the user could not cache the pulled bundle. The commit now asks the filesystem what is actually there and treats a lost race as the success it was.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 771574b: Add --root to pacto fleet, pacto tui and pacto impact: a contract root whose whole dependency closure joins the snapshot.

Every other definition source stops at what someone remembered to list. --local scans a directory and finds the bundles that happen to be in it; --oci pulls exactly the references you typed. So a bundle declaring a dependency on oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments:2.1.0 left a dangling edge unless you also passed that reference yourself — and the graph reported a service with no dependents when the truth was that nobody had looked.

--root resolves the root you name and then follows its declarations, transitively, the way pacto mcp --root already did. It is the same discovery through the same resolver, so a catalog session and a fleet snapshot cannot disagree about what a reference means. Roots and dependencies that fail to resolve stay visible as limitations rather than vanishing, so a short closure is never served as a whole one.

pacto fleet graph payments --root ./orders          # follows orders' declarations
pacto tui --root oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform:1.4.0  # the whole platform closure

On pacto mcp, --root keeps its existing meaning — it selects the read-only catalog server, and stays mutually exclusive with --fleet.

Fixes a related identity bug this exposed: --local hashed the raw directory while the lockfile, the catalog and a pushed artifact all hash the packaged file set. One developer's stray .DS_Store was therefore enough to make the same bundle look like two different revisions of one service at one version — a content conflict reported against a fleet where nothing had changed. Local revisions now hash the .pactoignore-filtered file set, like everywhere else. - 771574b: Fix two ways a fleet snapshot could report itself healthier than it was, and report a contested lockfile instead of silently dropping its pins.

A source that dropped or invalidated a record used to keep saying it was available, and the snapshot kept calling itself complete. The two halves of one collection were graded differently: a deployment target kept after one bad enum value was normalized marked its source partial, while a revision discarded outright — no immutable digest and a bundle that could not be hashed — left the source looking fully read, even as the snapshot's own limitations said a record was missing. Both now count. If a source could not deliver a record, every answer drawn from it carries the incomplete-knowledge envelope that fact deserves, so an absent service is never read as proof the service does not exist.

Two sources that disagree about one revision's pacto.lock are now reported with a new REVISION_LOCK_CONFLICT limitation. A lock decides which bundle a declared dependency or reference actually resolves to, and the same revision can reach a snapshot from a registry and from a working copy with different lock bytes. Serving whichever arrived first would let source completion order change the resolved graph under an unchanged snapshot ID, so the pins are discarded — and the reference detail now says they were discarded because contributors disagreed, rather than reporting that the lockfile recorded no resolution at all. That distinction matters: the old wording sent operators off to re-run pacto lock, regenerate identical pins and watch nothing change. Locks are compared on the resolutions they record, so two contributors who produced byte-identical pins on different Pacto releases still agree.

Two limitation codes are deprecated and no longer emitted by anything. REVISION_CONTENT_CONFLICT described two sources pinning one revision key to different contract bodies, which a content-addressed key rules out; the real disagreements it stood for are REVISION_DOCUMENT_CONFLICT and the new REVISION_LOCK_CONFLICT. REVISION_CONTENT_MUTABLE described a revision resolved through a tag or a path, which REVISION_IDENTITY_UNRESOLVED already says at the point the identity is derived. Both Go constants remain exported through v3 so existing code keeps compiling, and both are removed at v4. - 771574b: Stop a warm OCI cache from answering for a registry it has not checked, and make --no-cache mean the same thing everywhere.

A cached tag is revalidated before it is served. A digest names its own bytes, so an entry written under one can never go stale. A tag is mutable: the disk entry records what the tag pointed at when some earlier process wrote it, and re-pushing the tag left the cache handing back the old artifact under the new name. That is worse than stale — it is what disarmed pacto lock, whose whole job is to notice a dependency's bytes changing under a fixed reference. A developer with a warm cache got "no drift" on a dependency that had been republished.

PullPinned now resolves the tag's current digest before serving a disk entry. It costs one manifest lookup and re-downloads nothing when the tag has not moved. A registry that cannot be reached is not evidence that it did, so the entry is still served and an offline reader keeps reading the cache. Only the disk leg asks: an in-memory hit was put there by this same process, which already observed the registry for that reference, so one command still resolves one tag to one artifact. pacto pull --local-only and the other offline readers are untouched and still never contact a registry.

--no-cache now reaches the fleet sources, and says so when it cannot help. The flag was read straight off the command line by pacto fleet, pacto tui and pacto impact, so setting it through PACTO_NO_CACHE or through no-cache: true in the config file disabled the bundle store's cache but left the cached-bundle fleet source running — the disk cache the caller asked to ignore still contributed services to the snapshot. The resolved decision is now written back onto the flag, so all three spellings mean one thing.

And a bundle store with no cache to disable is now an error rather than a silent no-op. Proceeding quietly ran the whole command against the very cache the caller asked it to ignore, and reported success. - 771574b: Resolve a dependency from the contract that declared it, grade every interface difference from one table, and stop pacto login from failing open.

Relative dependency references now resolve against their declarer. The graph resolver built one base directory from the root and used it at every depth, so ./b written by a bundle one level down pointed at the root's sibling rather than at its own. A root pulled from a registry got no directory at all, so its relative references resolved against the process working directory — a remote contract choosing which local files Pacto reads. A local reference declared inside a registry bundle now fails closed, under the same rule the catalog resolver already applied. graph.OriginContractFetcher is the additive port that carries the declaring origin; a plain ContractFetcher still resolves exactly the graph it always did.

Node identity moves with it. Two contracts in different directories can both declare ./shared and mean different bundles, and two can declare one registry reference under ^1.0.0 and ^2.0.0 and mean different versions. The visited map is keyed on the declaring base, the reference and the constraint, so those no longer collapse into a single node with the second declaration discarded.

pacto login no longer fails open on a config it cannot read. It treated an unreadable credentials file as an empty one and rewrote from a zero value, so a transient permission or I/O error deleted every other stored credential and reported success. pacto logout failed closed on the identical condition and skipped the chmod login applied. Both go through oci.SetCredential and oci.RemoveCredential now — new writers beside the reader that already owned the format — with one error policy and one chmod.

A lock entry pins a digest to the bytes it names. Building an entry asked the store what a tag pointed at and separately downloaded that tag. Those are two observations, and a warm cache plus a re-pushed tag made them disagree deterministically, after which pacto lock --check certified the result clean. The lock builder and the catalog resolver both take the bundle and its digest from one oci.PullPinned call now. An artifact whose identity the registry will not state is recorded as unresolved rather than pinned to an empty digest.

A lock error reports its own code. The machine-readable code CI and the operator branch on was derived by splitting the rendered message at its first colon, so a file-read failure produced codes like open /home/me/svc/pacto and a YAML parser's prose produced whatever it happened to say. Every pkg/lock error type has a Code() method, Error() renders it, and anything carrying no code is LOCK_ERROR.

Responses are deep-diffed, and every classification resolves through one table. Request bodies were walked field by field while responses were not, so a status code present on both sides reported one opaque POTENTIAL_BREAKING no matter what changed inside it. Classification itself was written in three places and the copies had drifted, and .schema was hardcoded as a modification, which made the added and removed rules for that field unreachable — dropping a schema graded as if it had merely been edited. Two invariants are pinned by tests: removing part of a thing never grades worse than removing the whole thing, and a schema reached through an example is documentation rather than the payload's field set. docs/contract-reference/diff.md gains the rows that could not fire and loses the two that never described real behaviour.

Every MCP tool call is validated against its declared schema. The SDK documents that as the caller's job and nothing did it, so a declared schema was decoration: {"max_depth":"3"} — a string where the schema says integer, which models emit constantly — decoded to 0, and pkg/fleet reads 0 as unbounded, so a caller asking to bound a traversal got an unbounded one. required was equally advisory. Every tool registers through the typed generic form now, bundle-derived capability tools included, and a schema that will not resolve is registered as a visible unavailable tool rather than dropped or left to panic the server. pacto_check runs the resolving validator the CLI runs, so an agent looping until it reports valid can no longer terminate on a contract CI rejects.

A registry's tag list is no longer memoized for the life of the process. ListTags cached a mutable registry fact forever, six lines below a Resolve that documents why it deliberately does not. A dashboard rediscovers on a loop, so every pass after the first answered from the first observation: a release published after startup stayed invisible, and /api/versions with fetch:true pulled nothing while reporting success. The memo expires on half the rediscovery interval, so an entry written just after one pass cannot survive the next.

Smaller, and visible from outside: snapshot limitations print to stderr rather than stdout, so a partial answer no longer contaminates piped output; markdown table cells built from contract-controlled strings are escaped, so a pipe in a config pattern no longer breaks the table around it; and fleet.Build fills the freshness timestamps a source's own declared state left unset, so a source that reports its health no longer reaches the snapshot looking like it never synced.

Additive API: oci.CacheLocator, oci.CacheDisabler and oci.CacheObserver name the three capabilities a bundle store may extend BundleStore with. They were anonymous interface assertions, so a store that missed one silently did nothing — which is how --no-cache came to be accepted and ignored. Also oci.PullPinned, oci.SetCredential, oci.RemoveCredential and graph.OriginContractFetcher.

Exported symbols left with no production caller are marked Deprecated with their replacement and Removed at v4 rather than deleted, because v3 is published and this ships as a minor: sbom.HasSBOM, oci.SetUserHomeDirFn, the LocalOnly resolver surface, the standalone sidecar reader and the ingestion store's own fleet.Source adapter among them.

Keeping them means keeping them honest, so two that had drifted from the code they now defer to are repaired rather than left to rot behind the marker:

  • sbom.HasSBOM skips directories, as ParseFromFS already did. A directory named deps.spdx.json used to make it answer true where ParseFromFS answers nil, which is precisely the question its deprecation note says the two settle the same way.
  • The ingestion store's fleet.Source adapter drops a record whose compliance is outside the canonical vocabulary and raises SOURCE_RECORD_INVALID, matching the live evidence source. It used to copy the status straight through, so the two disagreed about the same record and an uninterpretable one entered the graph as though it had been understood.
  • 771574b: Retire the dashboard's second ingestion stack, and make the static export and the published API document tell the truth about what they answer.

The dashboard used to run two independent ways of turning references into services in one process: the original DataSource stack (source_local.go, source_oci.go, source_cache.go, source_k8s.go, detect.go, its own cache and its own multi-source resolver) and the operational graph in pkg/fleet, reached through SetFleetProvider. They disagreed about freshness, about partiality and about what "this source is available" means, and only one of them carried the completeness envelope every fleet answer is supposed to carry. The DataSource stack is gone. Every source the dashboard serves — local, OCI, cached, Kubernetes and observation — now arrives through pkg/fleet, so /api/sources reports the same health the fleet reports and an incomplete read is never rendered as an empty one.

The contract-view types the static export and pacto doc render moved out to pkg/contractview, a leaf with no HTTP and no Huma in it. pkg/dashboard keeps every released name as an alias, so existing imports compile unchanged.

Breaking, and deliberate: the whole pkg/dashboard multi-source surface is removed. Everything else in this release is additive, so this ships as a minor with the break called out here rather than held for v4. A shim is not possible for any of it: these names have no successor inside pkg/dashboard to forward to. What replaced them lives in internal/fleetsrc, behind pkg/fleet, and is reached through SetFleetProvider. A wrapper that accepted a DataSource and ignored it would turn a compile error into a dashboard that silently serves nothing, which is the worse failure.

// before
srv := dashboard.NewServer(src, dashboard.EmbeddedUI())

// after
srv := dashboard.NewServer(dashboard.EmbeddedUI())
srv.SetFleetProvider(func(ctx context.Context) (*fleet.Query, error) { ... })

The full list, so nobody discovers it at compile time:

  • Constructors: NewServer loses its DataSource parameter, NewResolvedServer is removed.
  • Server methods: SetResolver, SetCacheDir, SetCacheSource, SetOCISource, SetK8sRedetect, SetLazyEnrich, RefreshCacheSources, UpdateSourceInfo, WaitForVersionEnrich. Source wiring, cache wiring and the enrichment handshake are all the fleet's job now.
  • The source interface and its implementations, with their methods: DataSource, LocalSource, OCISource, K8sSource, K8sClient, CRDDiscovery, CacheSource, ResolvedSource, and the constructors NewLocalSource, NewOCISource, NewK8sSource, NewCacheSource, NewResolvedSource, BuildResolvedSource, plus ContractRefProviderFromSource and RepoProviderFromSource.
  • The source-local cache: Cache, CachedDataSource, NewMemoryCache, NewCachedDataSource. The fleet snapshot is the cache now.
  • Detection: DetectSources, RedetectK8s, CurrentKubeContext, DetectOptions, DetectResult, and the diagnostics types SourceDiagnostics, LocalDiagnostics, OCIDiagnostics, K8sDiagnostics, CacheDiagnostics.
  • ClassifyVersions and BundlePair, which classified versions for a stack that no longer produces them.

pacto dashboard --diagnostics is removed, with the PACTO_DASHBOARD_DIAGNOSTICS environment variable and the DashboardConfig.Diagnostics field behind it. The flag existed to register /api/debug/sources and /api/debug/services, which reported on the source stack; both endpoints went with it. The field is the one removal here from a type that survives, and it is not kept as an inert bool on purpose: DashboardConfig is published as a JSON Schema, so a retained field would advertise a diagnostics panel that no longer exists. /api/sources now carries the fleet's own health and completeness, which is what the panel was reading for. Scripts passing the flag will fail with an unknown-flag error rather than silently changing behaviour.

CRDDiscovery in the list above is a re-export of an internal/k8sclient type, and it goes for a second reason beyond its stack: pkg/dashboard is now gated k8s-free by tests/architecture/boundary_test.go, so keeping the alias would pull client-go back into a package that must stay consumable without it.

If you were importing any of these, you were driving the dashboard's private ingestion. Build a fleet.Query and hand it to SetFleetProvider instead; that is the same data with a completeness envelope attached.

Everything else that moved kept its name. ApplyLock, AggregatedService, SourceInfo, ServiceNameInput, ComputeDiff, DiffResultFromEngine, GraphFromResult and ComputeRuntimeDiff are all still exported from pkg/dashboard with their v3 signatures, the last four marked deprecated because nothing in Pacto calls them any more.

ServiceDetails.SectionMeta and the Section* vocabulary around it are deprecated. Their two writers went with the ingestion stack and the field has had no producer since; it is omitempty, so it is simply absent on the wire. The names stay through v3 and are removed at v4.

get-service-graph is removed from the published OpenAPI document. Nothing answered it: the live host serves /api/fleet/services/{name}/graph and the offline export serves the global /api/graph. The generated TypeScript client's serviceGraph facade had no callers and goes with the operation. Three operations that the document listed and the export could not answer — a specific version, the per-source breakdown and a same-version diff — now have real fixtures instead, so the offline single-service app no longer meets a 501 on a call it makes itself.

Behaviour change in pacto doc. Every service page now renders all eleven domain sections; an empty one says "None declared" instead of vanishing. The contents rail always listed all eleven, and the presence map it consulted had no writer, so it was offering jump targets that scrolled nowhere.

Also in pacto doc: a dependency's display name is derived by parsing the reference rather than by scanning it for the last colon. A reference carrying a registry port rendered as localhost, and one with no tag at all rendered as oci — both now render the repository's last path component, like every other reference already did. - 771574b: Add pacto tui, a full-screen terminal front-end over the CLI.

pacto dashboard answers "what is the fleet doing" in a browser and only reads. pacto tui answers it in the terminal you are already in, and it also writes — because the point of a front-end over the CLI is that you do not have to leave it to run the command. It takes the same source flags as pacto fleet and navigates the same snapshot: services, revisions, targets, owners and sources, opening on the Services tab. Whatever row is highlighted becomes the argument, so you never type a path.

Read verbs run in-process against the loaded snapshot — validate, explain, fleet explain, lock check, diff, impact and the neighborhood graph. Write verbs — push, pull, lock update and generate — shell out to this same binary so they own the terminal, and each names what it is about to change before it waits for a y: the directory a pull will overwrite, the resolved plugin binary and the output directory a generate will write. A successful write reloads the snapshot rather than leaving a confidently stale list on screen. --read-only hides the four write verbs entirely rather than refusing them at the last moment, and y copies the equivalent pacto command — shell-quoted, so a contract value carrying a space or a semicolon pastes as one argument — for anything the TUI does not offer.

Building it made a gap in shell completion obvious: the closed vocabularies the code already owned were never declared to cobra. Seven flags now complete from their real source of truth — --status and --compliance from fleet.CanonicalStatuses(), --workload from the contract.Workload* constants, and --direction, --ui, --transport and --output-format from the values their own validators accept — and the four pacto fleet positionals no longer offer filenames for arguments that are never paths.

One behaviour change comes with that, and a script can trip over it. pacto doc's three mutual-exclusion checks are now cmd.MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive("serve", "ui", "output") instead of hand-rolled value comparisons. Cobra tests whether a flag was set, not what it was set to, so all three of these now error where they used to be accepted:

pacto doc --serve=false -o out.md
pacto doc --ui= -o /tmp/o.md .
pacto doc -o "" --serve .

Nothing in the repo relied on any of those spellings. The one check cobra has no primitive for — --interface requires --ui — stays hand-rolled. --ui's help string now names the closed set it enforces instead of advertising an open one. - 771574b: Resolve every policy reference from the contract that declared it, and fail closed when the referenced schema cannot be read.

Relative references now resolve against their declarer, not the working directory. A ref: written in a bundle three hops down the dependency chain was resolved from wherever pacto happened to be invoked, so the same contract validated differently depending on which directory you ran the command in. Worse, a contract pulled from a registry could name a local directory and have Pacto read a policy schema out of the invoking machine's filesystem. Resolution now carries the declaring origin: a reference reached from a registry bundle can only ever resolve to another registry bundle, and a local reference resolves relative to the contract file that wrote it.

validation.OriginBundleResolver is the new port — RootBase() plus ResolveBundleFrom(base, ref) — mirroring graph.OriginContractFetcher. The widening is additive: ResolveBundleFrom is discovered at runtime, so ValidateWithResolver and ResolvePoliciesWithResolver keep their signatures and an existing BundleResolver implementation behaves exactly as it did. Cycle detection keys on the pair (declaring base, reference text) rather than the text alone, so a diamond in the reference graph is no longer misreported as a cycle.

A referenced bundle whose policy schema cannot be read is now an error. Three conditions — an unreadable schema file, one that is not JSON and one that does not compile — returned nil and dropped the policy silently whenever the referenced bundle declared policies[], while the sibling branch raised POLICY_REF_UNRESOLVED on exactly the same three. A platform bundle shipped without its declared schema therefore made every consumer's pacto validate and pacto push pass with zero policies enforced. All three now raise POLICY_REF_UNRESOLVED.

A contract that used to pass may now fail. That is the point: it was passing because nothing was being enforced. If pacto validate starts reporting POLICY_REF_UNRESOLVED against a bundle that was green before, the referenced bundle is not shipping the schema its own policies[] block promises.

service.version must be a single safe path component. pacto pack interpolates it straight into its output filename, so a version carrying a path separator or naming the parent directory let a contract authored in a pull request write its archive outside the build root. The pattern lands in the JSON Schema rather than in the pack command because every consumer runs the schema — a guard in pack alone would leave the operator, the dashboard and the MCP server open. Every shape semver produces still passes, prerelease and build metadata included, and so does a plain label like latest.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 771574b: Give the dashboard a real document outline: a collapsible section's title is now a heading, not just a button.

Every accordion on a service page — Overview, Interfaces, Dependencies, Configurations, Policies, Readiness and the rest — rendered its title as a bare <button>. Visually that reads as a section title; to a screen reader it was a control with no structural meaning, so the page went straight from its <h1> to the <h3>s buried inside a section body. Users who navigate by heading got a flat list of subsection names with nothing to say which section each belonged to, and the skipped level is a WCAG 1.3.1 failure. The toggle is now wrapped in an <h2>, the WAI-ARIA accordion pattern, so the outline reads h1 → section → subsection. Nothing moves on screen.

Three heading levels that were only legal by accident are corrected with it: "Skills" and "Secret Keys" were <h4>s that read as valid only when some earlier section happened to supply the missing <h3>, and the empty services list titled itself <h3> directly under the page <h1>. A service page that fails to load — "Service not found", a failed remote resolve — now titles itself with an <h1> rather than leaving the page with no top-level heading at all.

The route sweep that should have caught these was auditing an error state: it reached the non-Fleet views by telling the browser the host had no fleet, but the host it said that to answers no contract-view request, so every page under audit was a failed fetch. It now runs against a real pacto doc --format html export, which is the only place those views are served. - 771574b: Fix a bundle scan reporting no services because one directory refused to open.

Both filesystem-walking fleet sources aborted the whole walk on the first read error and marked themselves unavailable. For --local that meant pacto tui, pacto fleet and pacto impact answered "0 services" from a home directory: the walk reaches TCC-guarded paths like ~/Library/Accounts within milliseconds, long before it reaches any contract, and gave up there. The same scan now finds 64 services on the machine this was found on. For --cache the same abort emptied the entire offline baseline when a single cache entry was unreadable, which is what one sudo pacto pull leaves behind.

A refused directory is a gap, not a verdict. Both sources now record it as a SOURCE_PARTIAL limitation naming the path relative to the scan root, then step over it, exactly as an unparseable bundle already was.
