Past ten of them the rest are summarised as a count, so a home directory's hundred-odd privacy directories cannot bury the gaps a reader can act on. The walk root itself remains the one fatal case: nothing was read, so there is no partial answer to report.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• ddb6a46: Publish four documentation fixes that have been correct on main but absent from the site.

docs/examples/dashboard-demo.md named v1.2.0 → v2.0.0 as the breaking step of the demo fleet. OCI tags are immutable, so republishing that fixture under changed bytes renumbered it to v1.2.1 → v2.0.1 and left the page pointing at two tags that no longer exist. The same stale literals were what broke the WASM demo smoke test and turned the docs pipeline red; that test now finds the breaking step by behaviour rather than by version, and this ships the half a reader can see.

The rest of the batch rides along because release.yml's docs job is the only publisher and it builds the whole site: the mkdocs-material 9.6.21 → 9.7.7 bump, the two aria-labels.js fixes that keep it accessible and a testing note. 9.7 wraps every code block's buttons in an unnamed <nav> and labels the breadcrumb with the same string the primary navigation uses, so every page carrying two code blocks fails landmark-unique. The theme bump has never been published without its fixes, and shipping them in one transaction keeps it that way.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• a6fe2a3: A guided tour of what Pacto tells a human and an agent, and the five fixes building it uncovered.

docs/examples/demo-tour.md walks a sixteen-service fleet as six user stories, in the order the questions arrive: I inherited this fleet, something says Unknown, I am about to ship a break, who do I have to tell, my diagram and my traffic disagree, and I want an agent on this without handing it write access. Every command on the page is real. The terminal transcripts are generated from a live run by make gen-demo-transcripts, snippet-included rather than pasted, and compared by the docs drift gate — so a page claiming output Pacto no longer produces fails CI. The two commands no generator can cover — an MCP server holding stdin open and a live dashboard — are copied in by hand, and the page says so. Every one of them runs in tests/acceptance/local/demo-arc.sh on each pull request, and both readers plus the generator share one argument table, so the page and the test can never drift apart on what was actually run. A release test asserts the two sets cover each other exactly: nothing runs in CI untaught, and nothing on the page includes a transcript that does not exist.

Building it against a fleet large enough to be interesting surfaced five bugs that a three-service fixture never reaches:

  • pacto diff iterated Go maps directly in eleven collections, so its change list came out in a different order each run: twenty runs of one diff produced six distinct byte sequences in text, six in JSON and five in Markdown. A tool whose output people paste into review comments and gate CI on cannot print different bytes each time. It is now byte-deterministic.
  • pacto impact keyed the changed service by a ref classifier that disagreed with the one that actually loads the bundle: one treats a ref as local only on ., / or ~, the other treats it as OCI only on oci://. A bare relative path loaded as a local bundle but was keyed under an invented OCI domain, so its identity never joined the fleet and every consumer silently vanished. The same two bundles found four consumers and exited 1 when passed as ./a ./b, and reported none and exited 0 when passed as a b.
  • pacto impact left completeness untouched when the changed service was missing from the graph, so a breaking change printed "No affected consumers.", nothing on stderr and exit 0 — a silent all-clear that actually meant "I could not tell". The answer is now marked partial and says so. The exit code is deliberately unchanged; that interacts with the documented declared-only contract and is filed separately.
  • pacto fleet picked a service's owner by sorting revisions on RevisionKey, which is ServiceKey@sha256:<content digest> — digest order, not chronology. Editing any byte of any bundle could silently change who Pacto says to notify, which lands directly on the blast-radius answer. It now uses the semver-first revision chronology the package already documents for this exact hazard.
  • pacto mcp --fleet read --traces but never registered it: the flag was persistent on the fleet parent, and mcp is not its child, so the lookup error was discarded and the snapshot got nil. An agent could never see provenance=observed — the observed edges that find undeclared consumers were absent from the agent-facing surface entirely.

The limitation that made the tour honest is now gone: AsyncAPI and gRPC interfaces are compared spec-against-spec, not just by ref. AsyncAPI channels and operations are deep-diffed so a payload property or a required entry surfaces on its own, and a .proto is scanned for services, rpcs, messages and fields. The proto scan is a text scan, not a compile, so a single pre-scan blanks comments and string-literal contents before anything is matched — a // or a } inside a string neither truncates a line nor closes a block early — and a field's inline [...] option block is parsed off and dropped, so adding [deprecated = true] is not a change while a retype behind one still is. docs/contract-reference/diff.md states what each comparison does and, in "What the proto comparison does not do", what it does not.

The in-browser dashboard demo now teaches itself. Where the fixture notice was a banner and nothing more, it offers a guided tour: six steps, each naming one thing to do and each gated on the dashboard actually reaching the state that proves it was done. The gate is an observation, so no step is ever pressed to confirm a thing the tour just watched happen — it detects the action, holds the verdict until the gate has been quiet long enough that a search typed one character at a time is never interrupted mid-word, then says so.

What follows depends on where the answer is. Where the result is read on the next screen, the tour moves itself after a moment's confirmation. Where the result IS the answer — the service in full, the field-by-field comparison that says Breaking, the neighborhood a change reaches — the next step navigates away from it, so those hold: the confirmation hands over a Continue the reader presses once they have finished reading, and the spotlight moves off the control onto what it produced. Showing someone a breaking change and taking it away a second later is the one outcome worse than making them press a button. The two steps with nothing to observe keep a real button throughout. Every gated step carries Skip, which performs the action for the reader rather than jumping past it — on a holding step that means they still get to read the result — and Exit leaves at any point. It is opt-in, and it ships only with the WebAssembly demo: examples/demo/boot.js is loaded by nothing else, so it cannot appear in front of a real fleet.

The image tags a reader copy-pastes no longer age. The Compose demo page named ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/demo:3.2.7, the dashboard page named its image five times and the operator's install page quoted a startup log naming dashboard:3.2.1 — three releases behind — and nothing compared any of them to what was published. apply-release-plan now rewrites those coordinates the way it already rewrote the chart's --version pin, so the Version PR carries the new tag instead of leaving a command that resolves to nothing, and the idempotency proof covers the pages. That list is not the guarantee: the docs gate holds every page on the site to the tag its release unit published, so a page pinning a coordinate the rewriter has never heard of fails CI rather than rotting. Both pages now say the tag is the current release and that swapping it is how you run an older one, instead of repeating the number in prose where nothing can check it.

The published pacto-dashboard bundle described half of its own API. The OpenAPI document it shipped was maintained by hand and had fallen to 18 paths against the 32 the server registers, so a consumer reading the contract could not see the fleet endpoints at all. make gen-openapi now generates it from the live Huma registrations, which makes the published bundle byte-identical to the drift-gated SDK contract instead of a second copy that ages on its own.

Two fixture versions moved: payments-service 1.2.0 and 2.0.0 are already published to ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto, and the capabilities[] and sbom/ additions this tour needs change their bytes, so they ship as 1.2.1 and 2.0.1 and a published tag keeps meaning what it meant.

CI now runs on the demo. examples/demo/**, its transcript generator, the five subsystems that produce the committed transcripts and the two those reach through are in the docs-check path filter, the transcripts are inside generated_paths() so the drift gate covers them, and an MCP integration test drives the demo fleet over a real stdio session — including the case where pacto_fleet_status called with no arguments returns a null item list, which an agent asking the obvious way reads as a clean bill of health. That is pinned as the trap it is, so it cannot change quietly before it is fixed.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 5046822: Make the dashboard move, and make what it draws honest.

Motion is a closed system rather than a per-component decision. Four roles — feedback, flip, reveal, dismiss — are declared once in tokens.css, and a ration governs who may use them: only an error state may enter on its own and carry the alarm ring, a warning may enter but never rings, and every other tone stays still. The number of moving things on a screen is the number of things wrong with it. Every entrance respects prefers-reduced-motion.

The graph stops being a picture and becomes an instrument. The subject of the page carries a standing halo, so arriving on a graph tells you what it is about; a click pins a directional spotlight and re-frames the camera without ever re-laying-out; edges answer the pointer; a fit can no longer zoom past the point where labels are text. The legend was a caption listing distinctions the canvas actually draws — every entry is now a toggle that dims exactly that distinction, because a dense neighborhood is read by taking things out of it. Picking from the accessible text list points the canvas at the same node, so the two halves of the screen can no longer describe different things, and a summary line states the counts, what the legend is hiding and what is selected.

Three bespoke charts are gone. A treemap, a donut and a second bar chart are replaced by the two house forms already used elsewhere, and cytoscape-expand-collapse — a dependency behind a toolbar nothing rendered — is removed with it.

Chart corrections, each a case of the drawing contradicting the data:

  • The priority quadrant measured every service against a fixed midpoint while the gate is per service, so a service scoring 60 against a threshold of 80 sat on the healthy side of the line while failing. Points are now plotted as distance from their own threshold, and the divider says what it is.
  • Dot radius encoded blast radius, which is already the y position — the same number drawn twice. One radius for every dot.
  • The version timeline positioned markers by date and drew no date axis, so the only way to read one was to hover it.
  • Compliance status was three separate tables — the row badge, the legend swatch and the graph node — and they disagreed. "Unknown" was a blue badge, an amber swatch and a grey node on one screen. One table now decides both the wording and the tone, and every surface reads it.
  • Distribution shares printed a decimal below a population of a hundred, stating "12.5%" where the smallest step the data can take is 12.5 points. The same rounding ran out at the other end: one invalid target in a fleet of three thousand printed as "1 (0% of 3000)", a row contradicting the count beside it, and it is exactly the row a triage page exists to surface. A non-zero share now prints as the bound it is under rather than as nought.

A drawer opening beside the graph pushed the page off the right of the screen. Cytoscape writes its current pixel width onto a wrapper inside the canvas, so the graph's minimum width was whatever it was last laid out at, and no track holding it could shrink. The graph now contains its own inline axis and sizes from the outside in, which fixes every layout that embeds it rather than the one that happened to notice. A claim's source revision is abbreviated rather than printed as a full digest, and the responsive gate reads the body's scroll width as well as the document's — clipped overflow is invisible to the document — at desktop widths as well, where the drawer that started this actually opens.

Change analysis joins the long pages on the shared "On this page" rail. A finished analysis runs several screens deep — the revision pickers, the change table, then the consumer table under it — and getting back up to compare a different pair was a scroll. It is the navigator the overview and the entity pages already use, so there is no second contents list, and it lists only what the page actually rendered: there is no "What it affects" entry until there is a result.

The overview draws populations it can count. Nine operational targets on a proportional bar is a shape the reader has to convert back into nine things; drawn as nine marks, two of them red, the count is the picture. Past a hundred and twenty members the marks stop being countable and the proportion is the honest reading again, so the bar comes back — and a population that over-counts itself is never drawn as marks at all, because it has no individuals to draw. The prose around them is cut: a sentence under the posture bars restated two bucket values that were already on the screen, so there are no longer two copies of the same number to check against each other.

Those marks are now sized from the population, so a small one is big: nine targets drawn as nine fixed sixteen-pixel squares was a smudge in a four-hundred-pixel column — countable in principle and nothing to look at — and the size steps down only as fast as it has to for the row to keep fitting. The gutter and the corner are fractions of the mark, so a field of nine and a field of ninety are the same drawing at two scales rather than two different charts. The three posture questions sit in three columns where there is room, instead of two and an orphan below an empty half-row. And every distribution now puts its picture first: the description used to sit between the heading and the graphic, so a band of three charts was read as six lines of caveat with drawings between them, and each figure announced itself to a screen reader by reciting the whole paragraph. The prose is a footnote to the drawing, so it is printed under it.

The WebAssembly demo's notice can be dismissed. It floats over the bottom of the dashboard and never left, which on a short window is where the content is. A failed engine load brings it back: that is the one message the reader cannot be allowed to have closed.

Ten scale limits are closed. Measured against a fleet of five hundred services, two thousand revisions, three thousand targets and eight thousand relationships, each of these was a place where the cost of an answer grew with the size of the fleet rather than with the size of the question:

  • Every concurrent request that missed a cold service index ran its own full serial resolution of the whole fleet. One rebuild is admitted at a time and the callers queued behind it return the index it stored, doing no work at all.
  • A Fleet host issued a whole-fleet /api/services it never reads, every two seconds. The capability probe used to race the load it decides the shape of, so the first pass always read "capabilities unknown", took the legacy branch and paid for an answer it threw away. It is probed first now, at the cost of one round trip on first load. The poll also no longer stacks a second pass on top of one still in flight, while a manual refresh is still never dropped.
  • The whole-fleet dependency graph had no node bound. It takes one, defaulting to the engine's ceiling, and every node carries the path taken to reach it — so an unbounded deep answer was quadratic on the wire, not linear.
  • Meta applied none of the envelope caps ProductMeta applies, so two answers from the same snapshot could disagree about how much they left out.
  • The per-target revision match rebuilt its candidate set from every revision in the fleet; it is grouped once per service and reused.
  • The bulk snapshot export round-tripped through a marshal-and-unmarshal defensive copy on its way to a wire it is then written to and dropped.
  • A truncated graph said only that it had been truncated. It now says how much is missing, and offers the next node budget — sixty, a hundred and fifty, five hundred, the same steps the backend will honour, because a control that offers a step the server then clamps is a control that lies about what it just fetched. The budget is part of the URL, so a shared link reopens the graph being discussed rather than a smaller one.
  • A fit clamped at the legibility floor left part of the graph off screen and said nothing, and a cropped canvas looks exactly like a complete one. It says so.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• e36b181: Reframe the README, the pacto.run homepage and the pages that define what Pacto is around a positive category noun: operational contract system.

The definitional slot on both front doors was held by an analogy ("Pacto is to service operations what OpenAPI is to HTTP APIs") and, on the homepage, by an eyebrow reading "Open contract standard". The first installed "file format" as the category and discarded the engine; the second promised governance and a second implementation that do not exist. Both are replaced by a definition that states what a contract records, how it is published and what it is compared against.

The category noun says what Pacto is; one sentence beside it now says what that is for. Pacto gives software a machine-readable operational interface — a versioned description of what a service is, what it exposes, what it depends on and what it promises — so platforms, CI systems, controllers, automation and agents consume the same interface instead of each reconstructing operational knowledge from deployment files, documentation and runtime state.

Structural changes:

  • README.md leads with the category, then the problem (operational facts with nowhere to live, and a dependency edge that carries no version range), then the mechanism, then who reads a contract, then why software operating software raises the price of not having one. "What Pacto is NOT" drops from four bullets to three and moves behind all of it.
  • docs/index.md moves "What Pacto is not" below "The problem" — non-goals disambiguate a model the reader already holds and cannot build one. The heading and its anchor are unchanged, so #what-pacto-is-not still resolves.
  • The hero's only jump link now points at #what-is-pacto rather than at the list of exclusions.
  • The IDP contrast is cut back to a single non-goal bullet. What replaces it as the differentiator is version shape: a catalog entry records that an edge exists, a Pacto dependency records the range it accepts and pins the closure by digest.

Corrections found while verifying the copy against the implementation:

  • Diff · Graph · Enforce · Verify becomes Diff · Graph · Validate · Verify. There is no pacto enforce; policy is Layer 3 inside validate, and MANIFEST.md disowned "enforcement" eight lines below the slogan.
  • docs/contract-reference/sections.md claimed a configurations[].ref is resolved from the referenced bundle at the fixed path configuration/schema.json. No code reads that path. The reference is validated as well-formed, recorded as a reference edge and pinned in pacto.lock; the recursive-resolution claim is scoped to the lockfile, which is the surface that actually walks the closure.
  • docs/index.md said pacto generate produces deployment artifacts. It invokes a pacto-plugin-<name> binary you supply; Pacto ships no generators.
  • "Blast-radius analysis" as an MCP capability becomes impact analysis, the feature that exists.
  • The Kubernetes overview stated "never modifies" and then retracted it. It now leads with the actual grant — get, list, watch on watched workloads — and keeps the managed-component escalation as the second half of the same paragraph rather than as a retraction.

docs.text:
• 840a183: Move both Go modules onto the Kubernetes 0.37.0 library line and patch the runtime image's OpenSSL.

k8s.io/api, k8s.io/apimachinery and k8s.io/client-go are now v0.37.0 in go.mod and integrations/kubernetes/go.mod, together with the transitive k8s.io/kube-openapi, k8s.io/utils, k8s.io/streaming, sigs.k8s.io/structured-merge-diff/v6 and go-openapi/swag moves the line pulls in. The three library modules only work in lockstep, so bumping them one at a time — as the individual Dependabot pull requests did — leaves k8s.io/api behind and fails to compile.

The runtime stage of the CLI/dashboard image now runs apk upgrade before installing its packages, so the image picks up the fixed libssl3/libcrypto3 3.5.8-r0 instead of the 3.5.7-r0 baked into the alpine:3.22 tag (CVE-2026-14456, HIGH).

No API or behaviour change.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 3987568: Restructure the documentation as one information system.

An editorial and information-architecture pass over the whole surface: the nav is ordered as a reader's path, each concept has one canonical home, duplicated worked examples and repeated statements of the thesis are gone, and development history is out of the product pages. Three pages were split out of pages that were carrying two subjects — the Pacto model, dashboard architecture and observation sources. The published surface loses about 1,500 words while staying roughly the same length in lines: the prose is tighter and the split-out pages add the structure back. No technical claim was dropped, and no file changed path, so every existing URL still resolves.

Docs-only; no functional change to the engine, CLI or dashboard. This core patch is the release that redeploys the site, which docs.yml deliberately does not do.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• b11de31: Move both Go modules onto the Kubernetes 0.36.4 library line.

k8s.io/client-go, k8s.io/api and k8s.io/apimachinery are now v0.36.4 in go.mod and integrations/kubernetes/go.mod. The bumps landed on main without a changeset, so neither the core line nor the kubernetes line would have shipped them — this patch is what actually publishes a core module and an operator image built against 0.36.4.

No API or behaviour change: the 0.36.4 patch releases only refresh the golang.org/x dependencies underneath.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 9f27024: Keep date scalars verbatim across generic YAML round-trips.

pacto_edit could not edit a pristine pacto init scaffold. Edit reads pacto.yaml into a map[string]any, and yaml.v3 resolves an unquoted readiness.expires: 2099-12-31 to a time.Time, so re-encoding wrote 2099-12-31T00:00:00Z and the tool rejected the contract it had just produced. The same round-trip happens in pkg/override (pacto pack --set) and in the structural validator, which was handing the JSON Schema layer an RFC3339 string for a value the document spells as a bare date.

The three sites now decode through contract.DecodeYAML, which retags !!timestamp scalars as !!str before decoding, so the text the author wrote survives untouched — the same thing contract.Parse has always done by decoding dates into string fields. Nothing is reformatted: a non-canonical 2099-1-1 stays rejectable instead of being canonicalised by an unrelated edit, an explicit 2024-01-15T00:00:00Z keeps its time instead of being truncated to a date, and the schema layer never checks a value that is not in the file.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• c230de9: Make a demo-fixture edit unable to half-ship a release.

Release run 32560058692 published four irreversible units and then died. Two independent defects had to line up for that, and both are closed here.

The demo bundles publish to immutable tags. payments-service 2.1.0 was edited in place — a mermaid diagram added to a version already published — so the byte-exact gate correctly refused the tag, but it refused it mid-release, because nothing ran that gate before the release. The fixture is restored to its published bytes and the diagram ships as a new payments-service 2.1.1, and publish-demo-bundles.sh --check now runs the identical gate read-only at PR time as the demo-bundle-immutability CI leg.

Separately, the demo-compose job lost its ORAS install when the unit moved to docker compose publish, on the reasoning that ORAS stayed where the ledger used it — while that job still read and wrote the ledger, which is the ORAS user. ledger.sh returned the empty string for a missing binary, the empty string means "nothing recorded", and the unit failed closed. ledger.sh now refuses to run without its tools and distinguishes a 404 from an unreadable registry; the two if [ "$(ledger.sh …)" ] call sites that discarded its exit status now assign first; and a new gate walks every job's shell through its make targets and scripts and fails when a job can reach a CLI it never installed. That gate found a second, quieter instance: the release dry run was rehearsing without syft, silently skipping the SBOM the real release produces.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 8352060: Add the Pacto operational graph: what is declared, what is actually running and how the two differ.

Pacto could describe a contract. It could not describe a fleet. This release adds the read model for that, and the surfaces on top of it.

pkg/fleet composes many contracts, contract revisions and operational targets into an immutable, deterministic FleetSnapshot with a pure, network-free Query over it. It keeps three identities distinct — the logical service, the contract revision and the operational target — and it keeps them domain-qualified, so two teams may own a checkout without becoming one node. It makes incompleteness explicit: every snapshot and every answer carries an as-of time, a completeness and structured limitations, so an unreachable source is reported as an unavailable source that turns the answer's completeness into partial — surfacing in the dashboard as unavailable knowledge, taken from the worst source health — and never as an authoritative empty graph. unknown stays a distinct state, for when there is no completeness envelope at all.

Around that read model:

  • Evidence reporting. pacto evidence serve accepts signed evidence sets from environments Pacto cannot reach, verifies the producer signature, checks the report against the resolved contract revision and records the result. An environment that stops reporting goes stale rather than disappearing. pkg/evidenceenvelope is the signed wire format and pkg/evidenceingest the accept pipeline.
  • Evidence lives in the registry. An accepted record is stored as an OCI 1.1 referrer of the exact contract digest it is about, so the registry that already holds the contract is the only durable evidence system. No bucket, no database, no second persistence path.
  • Contract catalog. pkg/catalog answers what a set of contract roots and their closure contain, bounded and free of any delivery mechanism. It reaches agents over MCP as exactly two fixed read-only resources, pacto://catalog and pacto://catalog/closure, plus one tool, pacto_catalog_revision — and no resource templates, because a revision identity is four structured fields and a URI template would force the ad hoc encoding that identity discipline exists to prevent. The session is frozen, so a catalog answer cannot change underneath a conversation.
  • Change impact. pkg/impact and pacto impact answer who is affected by a change, computed over canonical identities and refusing a mutable reference.
  • Reconciliation and observation. pkg/reconcile compares the declared graph with the observed one; pkg/otelobserver reads an OpenTelemetry span export to discover calls nobody declared.
  • CLI. New pacto fleet (with fleet reconcile), pacto evidence, pacto impact and pacto otel command groups, all backed by the same read model.
  • Dashboard. A product-shaped interface over the graph: services, revisions, targets, owners and sources as first-class pages with canonical links between them, an attention view that ranks what is actually wrong, and a graph view that stays readable at fleet size. The wire contract is generated from OpenAPI end to end, so the frontend cannot invent semantics the backend does not have.

Everything reports what it does not know. Evidence that is absent, stale, partial or unreadable is reported as such and is never rendered as a passing result.

Backwards compatible: no existing flag, API or JSON shape changes.

docs.text:
• dd4dab1: Repo-wide audit remediation (engine, CLI, dashboard). Closes the OpenAPI breaking-change diff false-negatives — path-item-level parameters are now diffed, the request body is deep-diffed so a newly required property is BREAKING, and optional→required / added-required parameters are BREAKING — so a BREAKING-only release gate can no longer be bypassed. Further security and dashboard fixes land in the same PR.

As the first release since v3.1.0, this also ships the previously-merged but unreleased dashboard Ctrl+C shutdown fix and the demo version-label fix.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 0813b6e: Delivery matches contract environments to Stages. A promote runs a new pacto.environment check that compares the Stage's spec.environment with the environments the version's contract declares, using the same environments stage as pacto validate on the version's bundle.

  • A contract that declares no environments passes the check, which says it does not apply, so services that do not use environments are unaffected.

  • A contract that declares environments but none named like the Stage's spec.environment waits for the service's team to approve it, for example version 1.1.0 declares no environment prod for Stage payments-prod (it declares dev, staging). So does one whose values for that environment fail with ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_INVALID, ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_MISSING or ENVIRONMENT_UNKNOWN_CONFIGURATION, each located in the values file. When the version also waits for a consumer's team, the service's team is asked too, and the question names every team.
  • Values Pacto cannot check (ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_UNVERIFIED) wait for a person to accept the unknown.

The promoter also holds a promote that leaves a consumer with a required guarantee unmet, the consumers pacto impact lists for the change. Like a consumer whose range refuses the version, it holds wherever the consumer runs, including when Pacto cannot place it. The consumer's team is asked, and the question names consumer, provider and guarantee. A rollback to such a version waits the same way. An unmet guarantee of an optional dependency holds nothing.

The dashboard labels the check "Environment values" and shows N/A when it does not apply. The Stage's spec.environment field documents the match. - 0813b6e: Add pactoVersion: "2.3" and environments, so pacto validate checks the configuration values each environment uses against the schema of every configuration they name. Every 2.2 contract is valid under 2.3. A 2.3 contract needs Pacto core 4.4.0 or later and operator 6.4.0 or later. A "2.0", "2.1" or "2.2" contract that declares environments reports NEEDS_PACTO_2_3.

pactoVersion: "2.3"
configurations:
  - name: chart
    schema: chart/values.schema.json
    required: true
environments:
  - name: staging
    file: environments/staging.yaml
  - name: production
    file: environments/production.yaml

An environment's file maps each configuration name to that environment's values, for example chart: {replicaCount: 5, ingress: {host: shop.example.com}}. It ships in the bundle like any other referenced file. Values hold references to secrets, such as a Secret name; keep secret material out of the file.

  • pacto validate reports a duplicate environment name (DUPLICATE_ENVIRONMENT_NAME), and a file that is missing or whose path leaves the bundle (FILE_NOT_FOUND). A new environments stage, after policy, merges each environment's values over the configuration's default values and checks the result against its schema (ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_INVALID). A null in an environment's file removes that key from the merged values. The stage reports values for a configuration the contract does not declare (ENVIRONMENT_UNKNOWN_CONFIGURATION) and a required configuration whose defaults alone fail its schema when an environment omits it (ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_MISSING). Each error names the environment, the configuration and the JSON Pointer of the value, and carries the environment's file. A schema violation and an unknown configuration also carry the line and column of the value, and a file that does not parse carries the line the parser names. A configuration whose schema is behind a ref, or a run with no bundle files, reports ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_UNVERIFIED, a warning, and the stage is skipped with a reason naming it. Without environments the stage is skipped.
  • pack, push, publish, the operator, the dashboard and pacto_check run the environments stage too, so a version whose values break an environment is refused there as well.
  • pacto diff reports an environment added as non-breaking, one removed as potentially breaking and every changed value in its file as non-breaking, at environments[<name>].<configuration>.<path>.
  • pacto explain and the MCP contract summary list the environments.
  • A validation error carries file when it points into a file other than pacto.yaml, in pacto validate and in pacto_check. The text output of pacto validate widens its stage column by one character.

  • 0813b6e: The Pacto status records the guarantees of the contract, so the fleet the promoter builds from Pacto status evaluates them as a fleet built from published bundles does.

  • status.interfaces[] adds guarantees, lifecycle and compatibilityEpoch, under the contract's own field names.

  • status.dependencies[] adds requires, one entry per interface of the provider with the guarantees the dependency relies on.

  • The promoter's fleet rebuilds each Pacto's interfaces from its status. A dependency whose provider runs in the cluster reports its guarantees as met or unmet, and as unknown when no Pacto of the provider runs there. The impact analysis lists a guarantee the candidate does not meet under each consumer whose status records the requirement.

  • status.statusFormat is 1 on every status this operator writes. It says the status records guarantees, so a missing one means none is offered.

The fields are optional and the CRD version stays v1alpha1. Pactos last reconciled by an older operator carry none of them until the operator reconciles them again, which it does for every Pacto when it starts. In that window the promoter reads a status without statusFormat as guarantees unknown: a dependency on that provider reports its guarantees as unknown, never unmet, and a breaking or possibly breaking change to a service whose consumer has such a status waits for a person to accept the unknown.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 039d160: Add pactoVersion: "2.2" and an interface lifecycle, so a provider can retire an interface on a schedule its consumers can see. Every 2.1 contract is valid under 2.2, which also carries an interface's compatibilityEpoch and guarantees and a dependency's requires. A 2.2 contract needs Pacto core 4.3.0 or later and operator 6.3.0 or later. A "2.0" or "2.1" contract that uses a 2.2 field reports NEEDS_PACTO_2_2 for each.
pactoVersion: "2.2"
interfaces:
  - name: orders-v1
    type: openapi
    ref: interfaces/orders-v1.yaml
    lifecycle:
      deprecated: "2026-10-01"
      sunset: "2027-04-01"
      successor: orders-v2
  • pacto validate checks that both dates are YYYY-MM-DD, that the sunset is not before the deprecation (INVALID_INTERFACE_LIFECYCLE) and that the successor names another interface or is an absolute URL (INTERFACE_SUCCESSOR_UNKNOWN). A 2.0 or 2.1 contract with a lifecycle reports NEEDS_PACTO_2_2.
  • pacto validate --closure warns a consumer about each deprecated interface of a service it depends on directly, naming the interface, its sunset and its successor (DEPENDENCY_INTERFACE_DEPRECATED). From the sunset date the code is DEPENDENCY_INTERFACE_SUNSET.
  • pacto diff reports deprecating an interface as non-breaking and moving its sunset earlier as potentially breaking. Removing an interface before its sunset stays breaking, and the reason says so.
  • pacto explain, the MCP contract summary and the dashboard API show an interface's lifecycle.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 67de328: Delivery always installs its admission policies, and a promoter started without --admission-policies admits no operation and counts no approval: its Operations and Stages show Unguarded.

Breaking for delivery (alpha): the chart removes delivery.admissionPolicies.enabled and delivery.admissionPolicies.allowUnguarded, and fails to render while either key is set. Delete both from your values. To render offline for helm lint or a helm template without --api-versions, set delivery.admissionPolicies.skipCapabilityCheck=true, which skips only the Kubernetes 1.30 and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy API check. An upgrade with --reuse-values carries the old enabled: true over, so use --reset-then-reuse-values.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 9d4ec34: Make Pacto easier for an agent to drive from the CLI help and the MCP tool text alone.

pacto impact has a new exit status. It now exits 2 when a breaking change cannot be shown to be safe. A CI job that treated any non-zero exit as a failure fails on these runs too; one that gates on deployed impact alone can treat 2 as a pass.

pacto impact and the fleet tools no longer give answers that read as safe when they are not.

  • pacto impact adds the new revision to the snapshot when no fleet source holds the changed service, so --local ./fleet with only the consumers finds them instead of answering "No affected consumers".
  • Every impact answer ends in a release gate, gate and gateReason, and the exit status follows it: 0 clear, 1 blocked (a breaking change reaches an incompatible consumer on a known target) and the new 2 unverified (a breaking change on a partial answer, or with consumers none of which is shown to be safe). A declared-only run of a breaking change with consumers now exits 2 instead of 0. The pacto_impact MCP tool, the dashboard's Change analysis view and the terminal UI show the same gate and its reason.
  • On a breaking change, a consumer whose range accepts the new version carries a note: the range match does not show that it avoids what the change removes. An open range such as >=1.0.0 is named as open.
  • A declared dependency carries rangeStatus (satisfied, unsatisfied or unknown) beside resolved. A provider in the fleet at a version outside the range is reported by pacto fleet status, pacto_fleet_status, explain and the dashboard's attention list as DEPENDENCY_RANGE_UNSATISFIED, in the new out-of-range category (--unsatisfied-ranges, unsatisfied_ranges).
  • pacto_fleet_status with no category selected, including empty input, reports every category, as pacto fleet status does. It returned items: null before.
  • owner has one shape in search and get, the contract's {team, dri, contacts}, and is left out when no contract declares one. A service read only from Kubernetes takes its owner from the operator's status.contract.owner, where it was empty before.

Delivery plans are readable to an agent from the tools alone. The CLI and the MCP delivery tools now say the same thing. The operator's promoter shares this code, so its messages and the Rejected-plan behaviour change with it.

  • pacto delivery candidates and the pacto_delivery_candidates tool list the versions a Stage may take, with their digests: what its candidate source offers that pacto publish published. The to of plan and propose takes a version (3.0.0), a tag or a digest. A version or a tag must name exactly one candidate; Pacto refuses one that names none or several, or that it cannot match because a candidate cannot be read, and says why. A missing to says where to find a valid value.
  • A plan carries next: which teams must sign (and that their approval also meets a Stage's rule that a person approves every promote), that an agent cannot answer and the operation is then Held, and that an operation nobody decides before its approval deadline concludes Expired with nothing changed. pacto delivery get, pacto_delivery_get and pacto delivery explain say what happens at the deadline of a held operation.
  • A plan predicted Rejected asks nobody anything, and its failing verdict says what to do first, such as promoting the version on the upstream Stage.
  • The message for a consumer that must move first names the Stage to promote it on in plain words.
  • PlanStale names the reason or the on-behalf-of person when a propose adds one the plan did not have, and otherwise lists what the intent digest binds instead of saying the Stage moved.

pacto init and pacto_create with pactify read more of a service into its contract. The workload's environment, including the ConfigMaps it reads, becomes a configuration schema with each value as its default. A URL in it that names another service in the cluster becomes a dependency: with that service's contract in --fleet, its bundle and a range from its version; without it, a placeholder range that the contract comment and Unknown name. A readiness, liveness or startup probe becomes a health check.

pacto init --describe-only (describe_only in pacto_create) writes a contract that only describes the service: no publish section, no signing key and no .pactoignore. Without it, init still writes the publish section and now says how to leave it out.

pacto init, pacto_create and pacto_edit flag an owner written as team/billing, and pacto_check suggests the pacto_edit call that writes billing. pacto_check also explains how to declare a service of your own whose contract is not published yet, so it shows as unresolved until it is. The contract schema and the DEPENDENCY_REF_REQUIRED message say the same.

The MCP server instructions, pacto_schema and pacto --help now describe what a contract holds and say delivery is opt-in, and pacto_schema returns how to describe an AI agent as a service.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 407c06e: The pacto-operator chart renders every CRD as a template from files/crds/, which make sync-crds fills from config/crd/bases. helm upgrade now updates the Pacto, PactoRevision and NodeRuntimeObservation CRDs and adds new ones, and helm uninstall keeps every CRD (helm.sh/resource-policy: keep). The delivery CRDs still follow delivery.enabled. Set crds.install=false to manage the CRDs yourself.

Upgrading: CRDs an older chart installed from its crds/ directory are not part of the release, so helm upgrade stops with invalid ownership metadata. Label and annotate them for your release once, as Upgrade the operator shows, then upgrade. - 407c06e: The pacto-operator chart has a global block shared by every workload it runs (the controller, the delivery promoter and the recorder): global.imageRegistry (default ghcr.io), global.imagePullSecrets, global.commonLabels, global.podSecurityContext and global.securityContext. A component's own podSecurityContext or securityContext replaces the global one, and its imagePullSecrets follow the global ones. The delivery pods take delivery.podAnnotations and delivery.podLabels.

Changed values: image.repository and delivery.image.repository no longer carry the registry (trianalab/pacto/operator, trianalab/pacto/delivery). Set image.registry or delivery.image.registry for one image, global.imageRegistry for all, or global.imageRegistry="" to give each repository as a whole reference. A repository that already starts with a registry host (ghcr.io/..., localhost:5001/...) stays the whole reference, so older values keep working. The top-level podSecurityContext and securityContext, and their delivery. counterparts, default to empty and fall back to the global ones. - 407c06e: The pacto-operator chart can install zot and Dex from their official charts (zot.enabled, dex.enabled, both off by default). The chart ships the profile values-quickstart.yaml, which turns both on for an evaluation cluster: zot holds the delivery record streams, Dex signs people in to the dashboard and the chart generates the dashboard's client secret, the first sign-in password and the recorder's signing key (delivery.recorder.signing.ed25519.generate) at install. See Quickstart with a bundled registry and sign-in. - 407c06e: A dashboard people sign in to now reads delivery Stages and Operations from one shared cache, which its ServiceAccount lists and watches, instead of listing them again with every person's token. Each person sees only what their own RBAC allows: the dashboard asks the API server who their token is and, with a SubjectAccessReview, whether they may make the same list or get, keeping each answer 10 seconds; a list across every namespace needs a cluster-wide allow. Every action (propose, approve, cancel, roll back, unfreeze) and every read it is built on still uses the person's own token, and the dashboard reads with that token until the cache has loaded and for a moment after the person changes something. With 2,000 Stages and 10,000 Operations, fifty people opening the inbox at once wait about a second instead of 12. The operator grants the dashboard's ServiceAccount get, list and watch on Stages and Operations, nothing more in the delivery group, and holds that right itself while the dashboard is enabled. - 407c06e: A shared dashboard can sign people in, and then shows nothing until they do. pacto dashboard takes an OpenID Connect issuer (--oidc-*, the client secret in PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET), a private issuer CA (--oidc-ca-file), an internal issuer address (--oidc-internal-issuer-url), the API server's claim mapping, session lifetimes (--session-idle-timeout, --session-max-age) and --token-login, which takes a pasted Kubernetes token for clusters that trust no identity provider. The API server names each signed-in person (SelfSubjectReview), and every view and action runs with their token and RBAC. /api/session says who is signed in and how; every other endpoint answers 401 with the code LoginRequired until they sign in. The header names who they are, and the sign-in button says Sign in with OIDC or names the provider (--oidc-display-name). A remote pacto mcp reads the same claim mapping flags and logs each caller as the mapping names them.

The pacto-operator chart gains dashboard.auth: oidc (issuerURL, internalIssuerURL, caBundle, clientID, clientSecretRef, redirectURL, extraScopes, displayName and the claim mapping usernameClaim, usernamePrefix, groupsClaim, groupsPrefix), session (idleTimeout, maxAge) and tokenLogin.enabled. See Dashboard authentication. - 407c06e: A dashboard people sign in to now shows each person only what Kubernetes RBAC lets them read. A namespace's services, revisions, targets, edges and evidence appear only if the person may list Pactos there, checked with a SubjectAccessReview for their username and groups, as the API server names them, and kept a minute. One filter covers every fleet view, counts, search, the graph, change analysis and a remote pacto mcp --fleet with --auth-issuer. The dashboard says when services are hidden without naming them, and a service page counts the hidden services on each side. A service known only from a registry, with no namespace, shows only to people who may list Pactos in every namespace. Local and sign-in-free dashboards are unchanged. The operator grants the dashboard's ServiceAccount create on subjectaccessreviews and holds that right itself while the dashboard is enabled. - 407c06e: Add the Pacto delivery promoter and recorder, an opt-in component with its own image and API group, installed by the pacto-operator chart under delivery.enabled into its own namespace, and tie every Pacto check result to the version it evaluated. The operator holds no role in the delivery namespace, so it cannot run a pod as the promoter or the recorder or mint their tokens.

Pacto status. Pacto.status.evaluatedRevision names the contract digest and the workload object and generation an evaluation read, and its kernelCoverage says how far the node agent's view could be trusted (Complete, Partial, Failed or Stale). A consumer acting on contractStatus must check evaluatedRevision first, as the promoter does. The Pacto status also accepts mcp interfaces, so a service that exposes tools reconciles. status.observedCallers lists the workloads the node agent saw calling the target's Service that no Pacto describes, and status.observedCallersCoverage says whether that list is complete, partial (with a reason such as shared-netns or stale-node) or unavailable; delivery holds a breaking change on either. Host-network pods in kube-system and the other cluster namespaces and in the node agent's own namespace do not make that coverage partial; controller.kernelEvidence.callerIgnoreNamespaces adds more.

Check results change for every operator user, delivery on or off. A dependency that resolves to the same service in several namespaces now resolves to the one in the consumer's own namespace when there is one (a service in test calls the provider in test), where before the match was ambiguous (Insufficient) unless exactly one of them satisfied the declared range. The node agent's evidence leaves out pods being deleted, so a pod still shutting down no longer counts toward kernel coverage or findings, and a workload with no running pod has Partial kernel coverage.

The API. delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1 (Alpha, in the kubectl category pacto-delivery) adds Stage (one service in one environment, whose pointer is the artifact digest it runs), Operation (one decision, with an immutable spec) and Approval (a person's decision bound to an operation's uid and intent digest and to the approver's groups).

The promoter (ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/delivery, subcommand promoter) admits each operation and promotes only a version pacto publish published: the Stage's candidate OCIRepository must set spec.verify naming the publisher, and a downstream Stage takes only what its upstream Stage verified and offered (status.published, status.offered). Anything else is refused as NotPublished, and a Stage that cannot check its candidates says why in its Ready condition. It then compares the contracts, checks every consumer's declared range, holds for a person when a consumer in the Stage's environment would break or Pacto cannot see enough and writes to status.plan.order which consumer must move first, planned again while the change waits. It accepts an approval only from a person in a team the question names (chart delivery.identities.teamGroupPrefix); a question that names no team is answered by nobody unless delivery.identities.requireOwnerTeam is false, and with delivery.identities.humanGroups set only those groups count as people. The chart publishes these identities in the ConfigMap pacto-delivery-identities, which the promoter runs with and the CLI, the MCP server and the dashboard read, with the name and type of each gate provider (never its URL or signers) so a client's plan predicts an eval check's hold as the promoter does. It takes the Stage lock with one compare-and-swap, moves the pointer, waits for the apply and runs the verify checks the Stage lists in spec.gates.verify.checks: the Pacto contract check, providers from delivery.gates.providers (mira, http or eval, whose check names the contract suite it runs in suite) and the built-in pacto.runtime. Checks run again every spec.gates.verify.recheck after release. Unknown never passes and never rolls back. A confirmed failure is never promoted again (the Stage keeps its last 50) and gets one bound rollback; a second failure, a version a person chose, nothing safe to go back to, a refused automatic rollback, an outcome that cannot be established or an edit of the pointer the promoter did not make freezes the Stage. A Stage starts on spec.startLevel (observe by default; an admin creating a Stage may pick any level) and only an autonomy operation moves status.level after that; on auto-nonbreaking and autonomous the promoter promotes the newest eligible candidate itself. It records what an observe Stage would have done in status.shadow (the newest 20), proposes the next level in status.proposal after spec.autonomy.proposeAfter verified changes (10 by default) and, after an automatic rollback of a version it shipped on its own, lowers the Stage one level through an operation named <failed operation>-stepdown. kubectl get stages shows the level. spec.auto is gone. A breaking change no contract depends on also waits for a person, since a service without a contract may call it, unless the Stage sets gates.impact.declaredConsumersOnly.

The promoter emits Events when it holds, concludes, rolls back or freezes and exports pacto_delivery_operations_total, pacto_delivery_verdicts_total, pacto_delivery_stage_frozen and pacto_delivery_stage_watched (chart delivery.metrics.*). Each Stage says in Watched whether its running version passed its latest re-check and in Mediated whether its pointer alone decides what runs, gives every condition an observed generation and publishes the promoter's login freshness in status.authFreshness. The freshness is off by default, so a person decides with the sign-in they have; set delivery.promoter.authFreshness (a duration such as 15m) to make deciding need a recent sign-in. An approval the promoter passes over is named on the operation with the reason. A Stage reconciles when its operations, its upstream Stage, its OCIRepositories, the Kustomizations that apply them or its Application change, and every delivery.promoter.resync (a minute) otherwise. The promoter reads the apply OCIRepository's digest from the apiserver wherever it decides on it, and its client allows 50 requests per second, bursting to 100 (--kube-api-qps, --kube-api-burst).

Reach (experimental). A Stage applies through a Flux OCIRepository by default, or, as an experimental option, through an Argo CD Application with an OCI source (applyRef.kind: Application, chart delivery.argocd.enabled). candidates.upstreamRecords lets a Stage follow a Stage in another cluster from that cluster's signed records, read with delivery.promoter.upstreamTrust; without it the Stage is not Ready (UpstreamUntrusted), and while those records cannot be read or lost their newest entries it is not Ready either (UpstreamUnreadable). An unrecordable stand-in upstream stops the follower too, until a person of the service's team checks it and raises an acknowledge naming its record id with a reason (status.upstreamAcknowledged), or break-glass overrides. Ready also names an applier the promoter cannot write through. Only a Flux OCIRepository with spec.verify admits a new version, so the first Stage of a service needs Flux even when Argo CD applies it. A freeze is local: it does not stop followers. Argo CD and cross-cluster reach may change more than the rest of delivery.

The recorder (subcommand recorder, chart delivery.recorder.*, off by default) is the only delivery component that holds the signing key and the registry push credentials. With an Ed25519 key the operator, which reads every Secret, can read the key too, so prefer a KMS key or keyless signing. It writes a signed record of every operation that ends, in order per Stage, attaches it to the versions and contract involved, confirms the Referrers API lists it and only then advances the Stage's stream. A record can be late, and every operation that ends gets one. It signs with an Ed25519 key, a KMS key or keyless through a projected service account token, verifies each stream against its trust config before extending it, freezes a Stage whose stream is in conflict and can post a CDEvent per record. A record of an autonomy operation carries outcome.level (from and to). RecordStoreReady says whether records are being written, and pacto_delivery_records_pending shows the lag. With the recorder on, the promoter deletes recorded operations after delivery.recorder.operationTTL (a week), never the one a Stage runs.

The delivery section of the pacto-operator chart (delivery.enabled, off by default; the default render is unchanged) installs both in delivery.namespace (pacto-delivery, created by the chart and never the release namespace) with the Stage, Operation and Approval CRDs, their own ServiceAccounts and RBAC, the <release>-delivery-agent and <release>-delivery-approver roles and ValidatingAdmissionPolicies that bind an operation's actor to the requesting user, keep approvals to people (with delivery.promoter.authFreshness set, people with a login time, which the apiserver maps to userInfo.extra["delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time"]), keep the pointer to the promoter or break-glass, keep the promoter itself to the pointer field and keep the record fields to the recorder. Every delivery object is named <release>-delivery[-part]. It refuses to render below Kubernetes 1.30, without the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy API or without the policies unless delivery.admissionPolicies.allowUnguarded is set; the promoter admits no operation and counts no approval while they are missing. delivery.promoter.registryCredentials.secretName lets the promoter read a private contract or deploy repository. The delivery CRDs are chart templates with helm.sh/resource-policy: keep: helm upgrade updates them and helm uninstall leaves them and their history in place. The delivery image is published, signed and versioned with the operator.

The chart's images gain image.digest and delivery.image.digest: set one to a sha256: digest and that image is pulled as tag@digest, so the pod runs exactly that image whatever the tag later points at.

The pacto-operator chart gains dashboard.delivery for the managed dashboard's delivery views: namespace (where delivery publishes its identity policy), trust (the ConfigMap holding the trust config History verifies records with) and miraURL. The dashboard's role gains no delivery right and no impersonation. The operator now passes the managed dashboard its namespace scope in PACTO_DASHBOARD_NAMESPACE, the variable the dashboard reads.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 9f5f638: Update github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4 to v4.1.6 to fix CVE-2026-116587, a denial of service when parsing JWKs that contain RSA keys. It reaches the pacto binary and the operator through OIDC sign-in and Sigstore signing.

golang.org/x/net moves to v0.62.0 (GO-2026-6860, GO-2026-6866) and the operator's github.com/google/cel-go to v0.30.0 (GO-2026-6094). govulncheck finds none of the three reachable, so this is hygiene rather than an exposure fix.

The dashboard frontend's dependencies are updated too, which fixes the known advisories in the bundle the pacto binary and the dashboard image serve: DOMPurify 3.4.17, KaTeX 0.18 (used by Mermaid diagrams), devalue 5.9.4 and source-map-js 1.2.2. The build and test tooling moves to Vite 8.3 and Vitest 4.1.12.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text: • fe07e42: Fix the operator's go.sum checksum for github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4 v4.0.0. The operator v6.0.0 tag recorded a checksum for a core tree that was never tagged, so a standalone build of integrations/kubernetes failed with a checksum mismatch and the v6.0.0 operator image and chart never published.

docs.title: Major Changes
docs.text:
• 9b84eda: Fixes from a whole-repo architecture review of the operator. Two of them change what you see.

Behaviour changes

  • Controller logs default to JSON (production mode). Pass --zap-devel to get the old console format back.
  • The RuntimeObserved condition is now False with reason ObservationFailed whenever any runtime read failed during collection, and the message lists what failed. Before, it could read True while parts of the collection had failed.

Fixes

  • PactoRevision names and version labels are valid for every semver version, including build metadata (1.0.0+build.1), uppercase pre-releases and very long versions. Names that were already valid do not change.
  • ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor endpoints that name their port (the usual case in real clusters) are now resolved, so metrics discovery through them works.
  • An unset numeric targetPort now means the Service port everywhere, as the API server defaults it.
  • Configuration schemas are compiled once per contract revision instead of on every reconcile.

Breaking changes and migration (operator v6)

  • The Go module path becomes github.com/trianalab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6 (was .../v5) and requires github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4. Go code importing api/v1alpha1 updates its imports; go get github.com/trianalab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6@v6.0.0.
  • Apply the v6 CRDs before helm upgrade, which never touches them: kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f charts/pacto-operator/crds/. v6 adds the NodeRuntimeObservation CRD and the operator exits at startup without it (no matches for kind "NodeRuntimeObservation"), whether or not the node agent is enabled.
  • Removed --webhook-cert-path, --webhook-cert-name and --webhook-cert-key. The operator registers no webhook and starts no webhook server; drop the flags from any manifest that still passes them, or the operator refuses to start on an unknown flag.
  • Removed --dashboard-oci-secret and the dashboard.ociSecret chart value, superseded by --dashboard-oci-secrets and dashboard.ociSecrets. Migrate with dashboard.ociSecrets: [<name>]; the chart schema rejects the old key.
  • Removed the condition reasons no reconciler emitted (NotFound, AllPortsMatch, MissingPorts, the seven endpoint probe reasons OK, ConnectionFailed, InvalidStatusCode, EmptyResponse, NotDeclared, InterfaceHasNoPort, InterfaceNotFound, and Match, Mismatch, Missing, Skipped) and the SeverityError and SeverityWarning constants from api/v1alpha1. Nothing in a cluster carries them; Go code importing them uses finding.Severity and the reasons in troubleshooting.md.

Samples

  • The scenario samples under config/samples/scenarios/ use pactoVersion: "2.0" contracts. The duplicate showcase samples were removed in favour of config/samples/demo/.
  • 9b84eda: Add an opt-in eBPF node agent and the runtime checks it and the Kubernetes API make possible.

nodeAgent.enabled deploys a DaemonSet (pacto agent --sink kubernetes from the pacto runtime image the operator already runs the Evidence Server from; --node-agent-image overrides it) that watches TCP socket state through one BTF tracepoint and publishes each node's listeners and connections as a NodeRuntimeObservation object, a new CRD. It reads no payloads, files or Secrets and opens no port. It needs Linux 5.8 or later with BTF, hostPID, the node's /sys/fs/cgroup mounted read-only, root and the BPF, PERFMON and SYS_PTRACE capabilities, so it runs in its own namespace (nodeAgent.namespace, default pacto-node-agent), which the chart creates with the privileged Pod Security level; the release namespace keeps whatever level you set. Each agent renews a coordination.k8s.io Lease named after its node every publish interval and rewrites its NodeRuntimeObservation only when the view changes (or every tenth interval); the operator reads the node's heartbeat from the Lease. Where the API serves ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (Kubernetes 1.30 or later), the chart binds each agent's writes to the node named in its token, so one agent cannot speak for another node. The operator merges the evidence into interface and dependency observations: a ready pod with nothing listening on a TCP port becomes INTERFACE_ABSENT, the latest connection success or failure within the staleness bound decides dependency reachability (never against a provider with no ready endpoint) and a stale or failed node reads Unknown, never a violation. The agent's Role is get, create and patch on its observations and get, create, patch and update on its Leases, the DaemonSet runs on Linux nodes only and the operator deletes the objects of a node that no longer exists.

Findings carry evidenceRefs[].collector and detectedAt; status.evaluationCoverage.unverified lists facets with no usable fact.

Behaviour change: the complementary checks run with or without the node agent, because none of them depends on it: the interface protocol (with controller.enableProbing), the interface exposure, the provider version for dependencies[].compatibility (which also picks the target when several providers match the ref) and the persistence scope (read-only claims ignored). Exposure is external only on positive evidence of a public address: a public externalIPs entry, or a LoadBalancer Service without an internal load balancer annotation or an Ingress whose status carries a public IP or hostname. A NodePort Service or an HTTPRoute leaves it unknown. An interface with no visibility is internal, so one behind such a public address now reports INTERFACE_VISIBILITY_MISMATCH. Declare visibility: public for it.

Fixes: interface availability compared the Service port with the EndpointSlice port, which carries the target port, so a Service with port different from targetPort read absent; oci:// dependencies never matched a sibling Pacto and read Unsupported; passive health ignored the declared path. The chart now exposes controller.enableProbing and controller.enableMetricsObservation, grants list and watch on ConfigMaps, which the cached reads needed, and adds read access to pods, Ingresses, HTTPRoutes and NodeRuntimeObservation objects. Cached pods are trimmed to the fields the operator reads.

The kernel merge and the probes now come from core pkg/runtimefacts and pkg/probe, so the same verdicts hold on Kubernetes and on any host.

The operator uses evidence types from this release's core, so ship it in the same release as @pacto/core: the core tag is created first and the operator go.mod must pin it.

Breaking changes and migration (operator v6)

  • The node agent moved to a dedicated namespace. Set nodeAgent.namespace if pacto-node-agent does not suit you; it must not be the release namespace and must not already exist outside this release. Remove the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged label you may have put on the release namespace for the agent. The operator deletes the agent it ran in the release namespace (DaemonSet, RBAC and observations) at its first sync. A private imagePullSecrets entry must also exist in the agent namespace.
  • --kernel-evidence-namespace (and controller.kernelEvidence.namespace) now defaults to the agent namespace, not the operator's. New flag: --node-agent-namespace.
  • The managed components' lifecycle permissions moved out of the ClusterRole: a Role in the release namespace (dashboard and Evidence Server, plus the teardown of the old agent) and a Role in the agent namespace (the agent's DaemonSet, RBAC, observations and Leases). The ClusterRole keeps the reads, the dashboard's ClusterRole and binding, node reads, Lease reads and a by-name read and relabel of the agent namespace. The operator no longer creates namespaces at all, and no longer needs namespaces list or watch. An operator installed without the chart needs the new Roles (config/rbac/role.yaml generates them).
  • Objects the operator creates for the agent no longer carry an owner reference to the operator Deployment: it lives in another namespace, and Kubernetes garbage-collects a dependent whose owner is in another namespace.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 79de1ba: This week's dependency bumps in one go: bubbletea 2.0.10 → 2.1.0 and x/sync 0.23.0 → 0.24.0 in the engine, OpenTelemetry 1.46.0 → 1.47.0 (and the Prometheus exporter 0.68.0 → 0.69.0) in the operator module. No source changes.

Go goes 1.26.6 → 1.26.9 and x/net 0.59.0 → 0.60.0 in both modules, because govulncheck flagged reachable net/http and x/net/http2 vulns (GO-2026-6607 to GO-2026-6617) and wouldn't let any of the bot's PRs through. Both shipped binaries were exposed, so it's worth the patch release.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• fa6d27a: Take the week's dependency bumps in one go: modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk 1.7.0 → 1.8.0 in the engine, and controller-runtime 0.25.0 → 0.25.1, ginkgo 2.32.2 → 2.33.0 and gomega 1.43.0 → 1.43.1 in the operator module. No source changes — all four are drop-in.

Dependabot also learns to group: Kubernetes libraries move as one train because client-go, apimachinery and controller-runtime pass each other's types, Charm moves as one because bubbletea, bubbles and lipgloss share the v2 renderer, everything else minor-or-patch lands in a single weekly PR. Five open PRs for one afternoon of bumps is how a bot teaches you to stop reading it.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• 35c37f6: Carry the checksums for the pinned engine core in the operator's go.sum.

The published v5.4.0 module requires github.com/trianalab/pacto/v3 v3.3.0 while its go.sum only covers v3.2.7, so building the operator module on its own — outside the workspace, which is how a consumer or a fresh clone builds it — fails with missing go.sum entry for every pacto/v3 package. The fix landed on main in #369; this release ships it, and moves the published pin to v3.3.1.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 771574b: Make the operator's status tell the truth about overrides, force-pushed tags and per-tag failures, and stop the registry fan-out riding on the reconcile loop.

spec.overrides are now validated. An override patched the parsed contract struct only, so validation layers 1 and 3 — the JSON Schema check and policy enforcement — still ran against the original document. An override that violated a policy reported ContractValid=True. The patch now applies to the raw YAML as well, so every layer sees the contract the operator actually reconciles.

Force-push detection works on the cases it was missing. Two of them. A tag force-pushed twice compared the registry digest against an arbitrary PactoRevision rather than the newest one, so TagOverwritten re-fired on every reconcile forever. And a registry tag of v1.2.0 for a contract declaring service.version: 1.2.0 missed the label lookup entirely, so the drift check never ran for any v-prefixed tag.

A tag that fails to load is now reported. Every per-tag failure during mirroring was a log.V(1) and a continue: invisible at default verbosity, and one bad tag aborted nothing but told nobody. Failures are aggregated and surface as the same events the main path already uses — ContractUnavailable for a transient obtain failure, ContractInvalid for everything else.

.status.contractStatus and the dashboard now agree. The operator derived the status ladder from findings with its own local copy of the rule. It calls validation.DeriveStatus instead, so a contract cannot read Warning in kubectl and Compliant in the dashboard.

A configuration's schema is read from the bundle. The runtime config dimension treated configuration.schema as inline JSON when it is a bundle-relative path, so a real schema never compiled and the dimension reported insufficient evidence instead of a verdict.

Tag mirroring runs on its own schedule. Enumerating a registry's tags and loading each one used to happen inline in Reconcile, which every watched workload write triggers — so a busy namespace turned into registry traffic proportional to unrelated churn. It is now a manager runnable on a five-minute tick, independent of reconciliation.

Pull Secrets are read straight from the API server. A cached typed Get on a Secret builds an informer for every Secret in scope and parks its .data in the operator's memory. Secret reads go through the uncached reader and the Secret watch carries metadata only, so the operator holds no credential it is not using right now.

The dashboard and Evidence Server components moved to the same runnable shape behind a shared component lifecycle, with the same five-minute tick and an ownership check before any delete.

Deprecated, with no replacement needed: the condition reasons no reconciler emits — NotFound, AllPortsMatch, MissingPorts, every ReasonEndpoint*, every runtime-reconciliation reason and the three severity constants. The outcomes they used to name are reported as evidence and findings now. They stay through v5 for API compatibility and are removed at v6.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 92a064f: Make the contract verdict usable as a GitOps promotion gate, and emit the event that says a contract recovered.

The operator has always reached a verdict and written it to status.contractStatus. Neither Flux nor Argo CD reads that field. Flux decides health with kstatus, which recognises Ready, Reconciling and Stalled and discards every condition Pacto publishes, so a Kustomization holding a NonCompliant Pacto reports healthy. Argo picks health checks from a closed list of built-in kinds and returns nothing for the rest, and the roll-up ignores nothing — a violated contract is not unhealthy to Argo, it is invisible. Both tools have an extension point for this; neither ships one for Pacto.

The new GitOps promotion gates page is those two snippets, plus the timing they depend on. The Flux one is a spec.healthCheckExprs entry with no inProgress expression, so an unrecognised verdict holds the deploy instead of going falsely green. The Argo one is a Lua health customization written for the sandbox Argo actually runs it in, which has the string library disabled.

Neither snippet is an illustration. Both live under tests/acceptance/kind/fixtures/gitops/, the page includes those files rather than copies of them, and each has a kind acceptance shard that applies it to a real cluster running the tool it targets.

gitops-flux.sh proves the Flux gate changes what ships: a contract that contradicts the workload must leave the dependent Kustomization's manifest out of the cluster entirely, and correcting the contract must let it through. It runs at the operator's default stabilization window on purpose, because the page claims a mismatch does not wait one out.

gitops-argocd.sh runs in two passes, because the Argo snippet's failure mode is silence — a data key Argo does not recognise is ignored, and an ignored key looks exactly like having configured nothing. The first pass needs no cluster: the argocd CLI evaluates the customization in the same Lua sandbox the controller uses, which is what gives every contract status an assertion, including the states a running cluster passes through too quickly to catch — no status yet, a verdict behind the contract, a status added in some future release. The second pass serves an Application from an OCI source in kind and requires it to go Degraded naming the finding, then Healthy once the contract is corrected. The page's read-back recipe is that same CLI command, and the shard runs it against the live cluster rather than only publishing it.

Building that second pass turned up something the page has to say out loud: the merge patch alone is not enough. Argo's application controller caches health customizations at startup and compares that cached verdict to decide whether a changed object is worth re-examining, so a controller that started without the customization treats every verdict the operator writes as no change and only catches up on the next periodic resync, minutes later. The page now pairs the patch with a controller restart, and says why the two read-back checks cannot detect the difference — both read the ConfigMap, not the controller.

ContractRecovered is new. The three contract warnings — ValidationFailed, ContractInvalid, ContractUnavailable — are transition-gated, so a contract that goes back to Compliant used to fall silent with no event marking the recovery. It now has one, matching the pair that ReadinessGateUnmet and ReadinessRecovered already formed. ValidationFailed also fired only when status.summary happened to be set; it now fires on the transition itself.

Two documentation corrections ride along, both load-bearing for the timing advice on the new page. The stabilization window applies to absences only — INTERFACE_ABSENT, DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE, CAPABILITY_ABSENT and CONFIGURATION_ABSENT. A mismatch — WORKLOAD_MISMATCH, PERSISTENCE_MISMATCH, CONFIGURATION_MISMATCH — is NonCompliant on the first reconcile that observes it. The events table said seven events and listed seven; there are eight.

• 840a183: Move both Go modules onto the Kubernetes 0.37.0 library line and patch the runtime image's OpenSSL.

k8s.io/api, k8s.io/apimachinery and k8s.io/client-go are now v0.37.0 in go.mod and integrations/kubernetes/go.mod, together with the transitive k8s.io/kube-openapi, k8s.io/utils, k8s.io/streaming, sigs.k8s.io/structured-merge-diff/v6 and go-openapi/swag moves the line pulls in.
