docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• c230de9: Make a demo-fixture edit unable to half-ship a release.

Release run 32560058692 published four irreversible units and then died. Two independent defects had to line up for that, and both are closed here.

The demo bundles publish to immutable tags. payments-service 2.1.0 was edited in place — a mermaid diagram added to a version already published — so the byte-exact gate correctly refused the tag, but it refused it mid-release, because nothing ran that gate before the release. The fixture is restored to its published bytes and the diagram ships as a new payments-service 2.1.1, and publish-demo-bundles.sh --check now runs the identical gate read-only at PR time as the demo-bundle-immutability CI leg.

Separately, the demo-compose job lost its ORAS install when the unit moved to docker compose publish, on the reasoning that ORAS stayed where the ledger used it — while that job still read and wrote the ledger, which is the ORAS user. ledger.sh returned the empty string for a missing binary, the empty string means "nothing recorded", and the unit failed closed. ledger.sh now refuses to run without its tools and distinguishes a 404 from an unreadable registry; the two if [ "$(ledger.sh …)" ] call sites that discarded its exit status now assign first; and a new gate walks every job's shell through its make targets and scripts and fails when a job can reach a CLI it never installed. That gate found a second, quieter instance: the release dry run was rehearsing without syft, silently skipping the SBOM the real release produces.

docs.title: Minor Changes
docs.text:
• 8352060: Run the operational graph in a cluster: an operator-managed Evidence Server and observed-dependency input for the dashboard.

  • Managed Evidence Server. Set evidence.enabled and the operator reconciles a separate Evidence Server Deployment and an internal Service, with optional Ingress or Gateway API HTTPRoute exposure. It is single-writer, so its replica count is fixed at one, and it runs the same runtime image as the managed dashboard. evidence.registry.subjects names the exact immutable contract revisions evidence may be reported against; the registry holding them is the durable store, so the chart installs no volume, database or bucket of its own.

  • Observed dependencies. dashboard.observation.sources mounts offline OTLP/JSON trace exports read-only into the managed dashboard, so its operational graph can reconcile declared dependencies against observed ones. Each entry is one named data source with a stable identity, read through a root the process cannot follow a symlink out of, never written to and never scanned. This is offline input only: no OTLP receiver ships and no collector is deployed.
  • insecureRegistries. Reach named host:port registries over plain HTTP for a controlled in-cluster registry, scoped per host so every other registry stays HTTPS-only. The controller, the managed dashboard and the managed Evidence Server all inherit it.

Also adds a pacto-dev-gateway chart that installs Envoy Gateway and a GatewayClass for local development, so the Gateway API path can be exercised on a laptop cluster.

Backwards compatible: every new capability is off by default and no existing value, CRD field or status shape changes.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text: • bbc7b9c: Rebuild the operator and dashboard container images through the new native per-arch build pipeline: each architecture builds on its own runner (no QEMU emulation) and is merged into the multi-arch manifest. No functional change to the engine, operator, or dashboard — this release ships and validates the faster image pipeline.

docs.title: Patch Changes
docs.text:
• dd4dab1: Repo-wide audit remediation (engine, CLI, dashboard). Closes the OpenAPI breaking-change diff false-negatives — path-item-level parameters are now diffed, the request body is deep-diffed so a newly required property is BREAKING, and optional→required / added-required parameters are BREAKING — so a BREAKING-only release gate can no longer be bypassed. Further security and dashboard fixes land in the same PR.

As the first release since v3.1.0, this also ships the previously-merged but unreleased dashboard Ctrl+C shutdown fix and the demo version-label fix.

docs.title: Who sees what in the dashboard
docs.text:
With sign-in, the fleet views reuse Kubernetes RBAC. You see a namespace's services, revisions, targets, edges and evidence only if you may list Pactos there. The dashboard asks the apiserver with a SubjectAccessReview for your username and groups, keeps each answer a minute and applies one filter to every view: counts, search, the graph, change analysis and the remote MCP fleet tools. A visitor who has not signed in gets the sign-in screen and no fleet data.

Your username and groups are what the API server answers for your token (match the API server's claim mapping). A remote pacto mcp --fleet takes the same mapping as --oidc-username-claim, --oidc-username-prefix, --oidc-groups-claim and --oidc-groups-prefix, so a person is the same identity in both. When your RBAC lets you read no namespace, the dashboard says so and names your groups.

docs.title: What stays hidden
docs.text:
Change analysis on raw references answers only for services you can see: a hidden one, on either side of the change, reads as not found. A service known only from a registry, with no Pacto in any namespace, belongs to no namespace: only people who may list Pactos in every namespace see it, and for everyone else it is hidden like the rest. A hidden service is never named: the dashboard says some services are hidden, and a service page counts the hidden services it depends on and that depend on it. If the apiserver cannot answer, the views show an error, not a smaller fleet.

Without sign-in nothing is filtered. On loopback the dashboard reads the fleet as your kubeconfig user and shows all of it. A shared dashboard without sign-in shows everything its ServiceAccount reads to anyone who reaches it.

docs.title: What the dashboard needs
docs.text:
The operator's chart grants the dashboard's ServiceAccount create on subjectaccessreviews and get, list and watch on delivery Stages and Operations, for the shared cache. The operator holds the same rights while the dashboard is enabled, since Kubernetes lets it grant only what it has. A dashboard you run yourself with pacto dashboard --oidc-issuer-url needs the same rights for the credentials it runs with; without the delivery reads, it reads delivery with each person's token. A remote pacto mcp --fleet with --auth-issuer needs create on subjectaccessreviews.

For delivery, the ServiceAccount also lists namespaces. A person who may not list Stages in every namespace sees the Stages of each namespace where their own RBAC lets them list Stages, including a namespace that runs no Pacto yet. The ServiceAccount learns only the namespace names; the person's own RBAC decides which Stages they read. Without this right the dashboard reads Stages only in the namespaces of the fleet's workloads and marks the answer partial.

docs.title: Dashboard authentication
docs.text:
A shared dashboard signs people in before it shows anything. Every view then follows that person's Kubernetes RBAC and every action runs as them:

  • Reads come from a shared cache, filtered by your RBAC. The dashboard keeps one copy of the delivery Stages and Operations, read and watched with its own ServiceAccount. Before it answers you from that copy, it asks the API server (SubjectAccessReview) whether you may make the same list or get there, so a namespace your RBAC denies stays out of every view, and a list across every namespace needs your cluster-wide permission.
  • Actions use your token. Propose, approve, cancel, roll back and unfreeze go to the API server with your own token, so RBAC and admission decide and the audit log names you. The reads an action is built on use your token too. The dashboard offers an action only where your RBAC allows it, with the same 10-second review as the reads.
  • The fleet views show only the namespaces you may read (who sees what). A service known only from a registry belongs to no namespace, so only people who may list Pactos in every namespace see it, and counts and totals leave it out for everyone else.

The dashboard's ServiceAccount stays read-only: it may get, list and watch Stages and Operations and ask the API server what a person may read. There is no impersonation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A person opens the dashboard and sees only its sign-in screen. Every API endpoint and /metrics answer 401 with the code LoginRequired until they sign in; the page itself, /health, /api/session and /auth/* stay open.
  2. They sign in with your identity provider (OpenID Connect, authorization code with PKCE) or, where you allow it, paste a Kubernetes bearer token.
  3. The dashboard keeps the tokens in a server-side session behind an HttpOnly, Secure cookie. Browser JavaScript never sees a token.
  4. Each request uses the session's token. The API server says who it belongs to and RBAC decides, exactly as for kubectl. The dashboard keeps each answer about the delivery objects you may read for 10 seconds and each answer about the namespaces the fleet views show for a minute, so a removed RoleBinding hides its namespace within that time. Until the shared cache has loaded, and for a moment after you change something, the dashboard reads with your token instead.

On every page, the person button in the header opens who you are, your groups and Sign out. Approving a held change needs an identity provider sign-in, and a recent one where delivery asks for it (a recent sign-in to decide). The delivery views read their own settings under dashboard.delivery (the dashboard's delivery settings).

A dashboard on your own machine (pacto dashboard on loopback, with no sign-in configured) acts as your kubeconfig user and shows no sign-in screen.

docs.title: Configure the chart
docs.text:
dashboard:
  auth:
    oidc:
      issuerURL: https://idp.example.com
      clientID: pacto-dashboard
      clientSecretRef: {name: dashboard-oidc, key: client-secret}
      redirectURL: https://pacto.example.com/auth/callback
      extraScopes: [offline_access]   # what your provider needs beyond openid, profile and groups
      displayName: Keycloak           # the button says "Sign in with Keycloak"; empty: "Sign in with OIDC"
      # The claim mapping: the same values as the API server's claimMappings.
      usernameClaim: sub              # empty: sub
      usernamePrefix: ""              # empty: the issuer URL and #, none for email; "-" for none
      groupsClaim: groups             # empty: groups
      groupsPrefix: ""
    session:
      idleTimeout: 1h                 # empty: 1h
      maxAge: 12h                     # empty: 12h
    tokenLogin:
      enabled: false

For an evaluation cluster, the chart can bundle Dex and wire it for you (quickstart).

The sign-in screen's button says Sign in with OIDC. Set displayName to the name people know the provider by and it says Sign in with that name instead.

Register https://<dashboard>/auth/callback as the client's redirect URL and terminate TLS in front of the dashboard. pacto dashboard takes the same settings as --oidc-*, --session-* and --token-login flags (CLI reference), with the client secret in PACTO_DASHBOARD_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. A remote pacto mcp with --auth-issuer takes the same claim mapping flags (who sees what).

docs.title: Reach the issuer
docs.text:
The dashboard reads the issuer's discovery document, keys and tokens itself. Two settings cover an issuer it cannot reach the way browsers do:

dashboard:
  auth:
    oidc:
      issuerURL: https://idp.example.com
      # Discovery, tokens and keys are read here; browsers still go to issuerURL.
      internalIssuerURL: http://dex.dex.svc:5556
      # PEM certificates of the CAs that sign the issuer's certificate.
      caBundle: {configMap: corporate-ca, key: ca.crt}   # or {secret: corporate-ca}
  • caBundle names a ConfigMap or a Secret in the operator namespace whose key holds a PEM bundle. The dashboard trusts those CAs on top of the image's public roots, for an issuer whose certificate a corporate or self-signed CA signs.
  • internalIssuerURL sends every request for the issuer's scheme and host to that address, with the issuer's path replaced by the internal URL's. The discovery document and every ID token must still name issuerURL, so the issuer must be configured with its public URL.

pacto dashboard takes them as --oidc-ca-file and --oidc-internal-issuer-url.

docs.title: Match the API server's claim mapping
docs.text:
The API server decides who a token is. At sign-in and on every renewal the dashboard asks it (SelfSubjectReview) with the person's ID token, and every view uses the answer. The claim mapping names the person only while the API server does not accept the ID token, for example before it trusts the issuer, so it must equal the API server's. With the defaults above, the API server's structured authentication reads:

apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AuthenticationConfiguration
jwt:
- issuer: {url: https://idp.example.com, audiences: [pacto-dashboard]}
  claimMappings:
    username: {claim: sub, prefix: "https://idp.example.com#"}
    groups: {claim: groups, prefix: ""}

Then a mismatch shows as the wrong fleet: the views ask about a user the API server never sees. To check, sign in and compare the header with kubectl auth whoami run with a token from the same issuer. The dashboard drops any group starting with system: from a token, as the API server does.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
The dashboard renews the ID token with the refresh token before it expires, so a session lasts until idleTimeout passes without a request or maxAge after sign-in. A provider that issues refresh tokens only for offline_access needs it in extraScopes; without a refresh token the session ends when the ID token expires. Renewal keeps the original login time, which is what a recent sign-in to decide measures when delivery asks for one (delivery.promoter.authFreshness).

Sign out ends the session, revokes the refresh token where the provider supports revocation and, where the provider publishes an end_session_endpoint, sends the browser there to end the provider's session too. Sessions live in the memory of one dashboard process. The operator runs the dashboard as one replica, and a restart signs everyone out. A pacto dashboard you deploy yourself with sign-in needs one replica too, or a load balancer with session affinity (for example sessionAffinity: ClientIP on its Service) so each person keeps reaching the replica that holds their session.

docs.title: Token sign-in
docs.text:
Set tokenLogin.enabled: true for a cluster whose API server trusts no identity provider you can use. The sign-in screen then takes any bearer token the API server accepts, such as a ServiceAccount token from kubectl create token. The dashboard checks it with a SelfSubjectReview, keeps it in the server-side session and checks it again every five minutes, so a token that expires or is revoked ends its session. A token session reads and acts with that token's RBAC and never decides on a held change: it proves no recent sign-in. Token sign-in works with or without oidc.

To get a token:

  • For a ServiceAccount, run kubectl create token <service-account> -n <namespace>. Add --duration for a token that lasts longer than the default hour, up to what the API server allows.
  • For yourself with a static token in your kubeconfig, run kubectl config view --raw --minify -o jsonpath='{.users[0].user.token}'.
  • For yourself on EKS, run aws eks get-token --cluster-name <cluster> and take its status.token field.
  • For yourself on GKE, run gcloud auth print-access-token.

Cloud provider tokens are short-lived, and the session ends when its token expires.

docs.title: Identity providers
docs.text:
Provider issuerURL Claim mapping Notes Dex https://dex.example.com defaults Add offline_access for renewal. For approvals add audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli (why). Keycloak https://keycloak.example.com/realms/<realm> usernameClaim: preferred_username Add a Group Membership mapper named groups with full group path off. Microsoft Entra ID https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0 usernameClaim: oid Add the groups optional claim; groups arrive as object IDs, so bind RBAC to those. Add offline_access for renewal. Okta https://<org>.okta.com/oauth2/<server-id> defaults Add a groups claim to the authorization server and offline_access for renewal. Google https://accounts.google.com usernameClaim: email The ID token carries no groups, so bind RBAC to users. Sessions end when the ID token expires, after about an hour.

Use oid with Entra ID because its sub differs per application.

docs.title: Managed clusters
docs.text:
The API server must trust the same issuer with the same mapping.

  • EKS: associate an OIDC identity provider with the cluster (aws eks associate-identity-provider-config) and give it the same usernameClaim, usernamePrefix, groupsClaim and groupsPrefix.
  • GKE: configure your provider in Identity Service for GKE and match its userClaim, userPrefix, groupsClaim and groupPrefix.
  • AKS: managed Entra ID integration accepts tokens for its own server application. To sign in with the dashboard's client, use structured authentication where the cluster offers it, or token sign-in.

Approvals need more from the API server than sign-in does; the approval table lists which clusters can provide it.

docs.title: Delivery reference: eval providers
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

An eval provider is a suite runner: it runs one of the checks the version ships, such as an AI agent's eval suite. The Stage check names it in suite:

spec:
  gates:
    verify:
      checks:
        - name: quality
          provider: evals
          suite: evals
          suiteDigest: sha256:...   # optional
          params:
            minPassRate: "0.95"

Without suite the runner runs the only check the version ships. A version that does not ship the named check, or with no suite ships no check or more than one, is held before it ships (the pacto.suites gate): a person accepts it or it does not ship.

suiteDigest pins the sha256 of the suite the version ships, which covers every file in the suite's directory (see Checks): a version with another suite is held the same way, and its eval is Unknown. A suite must be self-contained in its directory.

docs.title: The runner's answer
docs.text:
The promoter posts the same {"input": ..., "params": ...} as to an HTTP provider, the input also naming the contract the version ships and the suite in it: "contract": "oci://...@sha256:...", "suite": {"name": "evals", "path": "evals/suite.yaml", "digest": "sha256:..."}. The runner runs that suite on the version under check and answers with a Sigstore bundle: a DSSE envelope over a statement it signs.

{
  "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v1",
  "subject": [{"name": "pay-agent", "digest": {"sha256": "..."}}],
  "predicateType": "delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/eval/v1",
  "predicate": {
    "operation": "<the input's operationUID>",
    "challenge": "<the input's challenge>",
    "suite": "sha256:...",
    "run": "https://evals.example/runs/7",
    "passed": 48,
    "total": 50,
    "observedModel": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5",
    "message": "two refunds wrong"
  }
}

docs.title: Trusted runners
docs.text:
operation and challenge echo the input's: the challenge is new for every check, so an old answer cannot be replayed. suite is the sha256 of the suite it ran and observedModel (optional) the model it saw answer. The provider lists the runners it trusts in signers, each a public key or a keyless identity:

delivery:
  gates:
    providers:
      - name: evals
        type: eval
        url: https://evals.internal
        signers:
          - name: evals-ci
            publicKey: |
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              ...
          - name: evals-keyless
            identity: https://github.com/acme/evals/.github/workflows/run.yaml@refs/heads/main
            issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
            trustedRoot: '{"mediaType": "application/vnd.dev.sigstore.trustedroot+json;version=0.1", ...}'

The Stage sets the pass bar:

Param Default Meaning minPassRate 1 The share of cases that must pass, above 0 and up to 1. Fewer fails

These answers count as Unknown:

  • an answer no listed signer signed
  • an answer about another version or another suite
  • an answer for another operation or another challenge
  • a suite whose sha256 is not the Stage's suiteDigest
  • no cases, or no run to cite
  • a version whose contract cannot be read or does not ship the suite

The verdict cites the contract, the suite, the run and the runner (runner), and keeps the signed answer (runnerBundle) for record verify.

docs.title: Which model answered
docs.text:
When the runner reports an observedModel that no external dependency version of the version under check names, the check fails and says both. Pacto takes the runner's signed word for it; nothing else checks it. A Stage check can require the runner to say:

        - name: quality
          provider: evals
          suite: evals
          requireObservedModel: true

Then no observedModel, or no dependency version to compare it with, is Unknown.

docs.title: Delivery reference: health checks
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Beyond the Pacto contract check, a Stage can check a version's errors and response times in your monitoring, an AI agent's evals and that the service calls only what its contract declares (its claims). Every check answers Pass, Fail or Unknown and cites what it read, so anyone can run it again. An Unknown check holds the change for a person, who can accept the unknown.

The Pacto resource ships inside every version and names its own target, so pacto.contract and pacto.runtime count only a Pacto that evaluated the workload the Stage says the service runs: spec.workload (kind and name in the Stage's namespace), or the Deployment named spec.service.name when it is empty. A Pacto that checked another workload, a decoy a version shipped for example, is Unknown. pacto init --delivery writes spec.workload.

docs.title: Add checks to a Stage
docs.text:
List the checks under spec.gates.verify.checks. Each names a provider:

apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: prod
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamStage: {name: payments, namespace: test}
  startLevel: advise
  gates:
    verify:
      window: 5m
      recheck: 1m
      checks:
        - name: health
          provider: mira
          params: {minSpans: "50", maxErrorRatio: "0.02", soak: "3m"}
        - name: claims
          provider: pacto.runtime

The checks run on the time since Flux applied the version, all at once, and one that takes longer than a minute is Unknown. The promoter works on delivery.promoter.workers (4 by default) operations and Stages at a time, so a slow provider does not hold up the others. Any Fail rolls it back, all Pass verifies it and anything else waits; when window runs out a person is asked to accept the unknown or reject the version. While that question waits, the checks run again every recheck: a Fail still rolls the version back and all Pass verifies it without the person.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
pacto.runtime is built in. Every other provider is configured in the operator chart's delivery section, so a Stage or an agent can name a provider and only the chart sets the host it calls:

delivery:
  gates:
    providers:
      - {name: mira, type: mira, url: "https://mira.observability:4318"}

The URL must be https. A verdict ends up in a signed record, so an answer forged on the way could get a Pass signed. Plain http works only on loopback, or with allowPlainHTTP: true on a test cluster. The promoter never follows a redirect: a provider that answers one gets Unknown.

A provider inside the cluster often has a certificate from an internal CA. Put that CA's PEM certificates in a ConfigMap in delivery.namespace and name it, so the promoter trusts it on top of the public roots:

delivery:
  gates:
    caBundle: {configMap: internal-ca, key: ca.crt}

docs.title: Mira
docs.text:
A mira provider counts the service's spans in Mira by service.name, one span kind at a time: server spans by default, so one span per request served. Its params:

Param Default Meaning spanKind server The spans counted: server, consumer, producer, client, internal, unspecified or any minSpans 20 Fewer spans than this is Unknown maxErrorRatio 0.05 A larger share of failed spans fails soak 1m A clean result passes only after this long latencyThreshold off Spans slower than this count as slow maxLatencyRatio 0.05 A larger share of slow spans fails where none Extra Mira terms as JSON, for example the namespace matchVersion false Count only spans whose service.version is the contract's service.version

By default the provider counts every span of the service in the window, so while a rollout is still replacing pods the old version's spans count too: they can hide a breach or fail a clean version. The window starts when Flux or Argo CD reports the version applied, not when the rollout finished. Set matchVersion: "true" to judge only the version under check, once the service sets the service.version resource attribute to its contract's service.version (for example through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES). Without a contract version to match, the check is Unknown.

A read that fails or stops short is Unknown. Mira's query API has no count, so the provider pages through the spans and stops at 200,000 per query. A window holding more is judged on its newest soak only, and the message says so; if even that holds more, the check is Unknown, so narrow it with where. The citation holds the exact queries with absolute time bounds, so posting them to Mira again reads the same spans.

docs.title: What a verdict can prove
docs.text:
Mira and http verdicts are unsigned and, by default, self-reported. Mira counts the spans the service sends about itself, keyed on the service.name and service.version the sender sets. The version under check, or any pod that can reach the OTLP endpoint, can leave out its errors or send clean spans to force a Pass, or send failed ones to force a Fail and a rollback. An http provider's answer is believed as it arrives over https. To make a verdict worth more:

  • accept telemetry only from authenticated senders at the collector;
  • add a where on attributes the collector sets, not the sender, such as the k8s.pod.uid or k8s.namespace.name the k8sattributes processor adds;
  • count the spans of the service's callers (spanKind: client on the caller's side) instead of the service's own.

docs.title: HTTP providers
docs.text: An http provider is the plug-in format for any other tool. The promoter posts {"input": ..., "params": ...}, where the input names the operation, the Stage, the service, the digests under check and the time window. The tool answers {"subject": "sha256:...", "result": "Pass|Fail|Unknown", "message": "...", "citation": {...}}, where subject is the digest it judged. An answer that names no subject, or a version other than the one under check, is Unknown.

docs.title: Eval providers
docs.text: An eval provider runs an AI agent's eval suite that the version ships. See Delivery reference: eval providers.

docs.title: Claims against the running service
docs.text: pacto.runtime uses the node agent. It fails a version the kernel saw calling a Pacto-managed service its contract never declares, or not listening on a port it declares. It reads the Pacto evaluation of exactly this version and passes only when status.evaluatedRevision.kernelCoverage is Complete and the version has run for soak (a Go duration, default 1m); otherwise the answer is Unknown. A Pass means only that the node agent saw neither of those two things: right after a rollout the version may not have handled traffic yet, which is what the soak is for. A contradiction the kernel saw fails at once.

docs.title: After release
docs.text: After release the checks run again every recheck (default 1m) on the last window. A confirmed Fail marks the version failed and raises one rollback citing the check. The Stage freezes instead when that cause already had its rollback, when there is nothing to roll back to or when a person or an agent chose the running version (a rollback, or a promote during auto-hold). It also freezes, naming the operation, when an operation Pacto did not raise holds the name of the rollback or freeze it raises (<operation>-rollback, <operation>-freeze). Unknown after release never rolls back, and a result about a version the Stage stopped running is dropped. The newest result is in status.lastCheck, which also says when the operation that shipped the running version is gone. The Stage's Watched condition is True while that result passed. It turns False with reason RecheckUnknown while nothing watches the running version (a provider down, too many spans, no coverage) and RecheckFailed after a Fail. The promoter emits an Event when it turns False, and the pacto_delivery_stage_watched gauge drops to 0, so you can alert on it.

docs.title: Explain
docs.text:
pacto delivery explain -n prod <operation>

explain shows where an operation is and every verdict with its citation and how to run it again. --cause-verdict on propose cites a verdict as its cause, for example on a frozen Stage; the promoter runs it again and refuses a cause that comes back with another result.

docs.title: Delivery reference: approvals and agents
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

People decide in the dashboard and agents reach Pacto over the network, each under their own Kubernetes identity. The dashboard and the MCP server pass the caller's own token on, so the apiserver decides what the caller may do and its audit log names the person. There is no impersonation.

docs.title: The cluster trusts your identity provider
docs.text:
A person decides with the sign-in they have. If you also ask for a recent sign-in to decide, approving needs the login time, read by the apiserver itself. Structured authentication maps the OIDC auth_time claim to userInfo.extra["delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time"], only for tokens issued to the two clients that make a person log in again: the dashboard and pacto delivery approve's own client, pacto-approve. A client-credentials or exchanged token never has it, and neither does a kubeconfig login (pacto-cli): any process in your shell, an agent included, can reuse that one.

apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AuthenticationConfiguration
jwt:
- issuer: {url: https://idp.example.com, audiences: [pacto-dashboard, pacto-cli], audienceMatchPolicy: MatchAny}
  claimMappings:
    username: {expression: "'https://idp.example.com#' + claims.sub"}
    groups: {claim: groups, prefix: ""}
    extra:
    - key: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time
      valueExpression: >-
        has(claims.auth_time) && has(claims.azp) && claims.azp in ['pacto-dashboard', 'pacto-approve']
        ? string(int(claims.auth_time)) : ''

The identity provider must put azp on these tokens. Dex sets it only on a token with two audiences, so give the dashboard and pacto delivery approve the extra scope audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli and make pacto-cli trust pacto-dashboard and pacto-approve. Register pacto-approve as a public client (PKCE, no secret) whose redirect is the loopback address http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback, and use it for nothing else. Without that trust, people decide from the terminal with their own kubeconfig.

docs.title: Where approving works
docs.text:
Only a recent sign-in needs the login time. The apiserver must load this file (flag --authentication-config), and its claimMappings must be able to set extra. That is in your hands wherever you set the apiserver's flags, as with kind, kubeadm or k3s; Pacto's own tests run it on kind. Managed clusters mostly decide it for you:

Cluster Can it map delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time? kind, kubeadm, k3s and others where you set apiserver flags Yes, tested on kind AKS Not verified: structured authentication is in preview EKS, GKE Not verified

To check a cluster, sign in again and run kubectl auth whoami -o yaml. If extra holds no delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time, nobody can approve there with a recent sign-in required. Delivery still promotes every change that needs no decision. People can still freeze, unfreeze, roll back and cancel. The dashboard and the CLI still read everything. What you need to be allowed lists the three ways a held change still ends.

docs.title: Who counts as a person, an agent or a team
docs.text:
Set the groups once, in the operator chart's delivery section:

delivery:
  identities:
    agentGroups: [pacto:agents]          # agents propose, never approve or unfreeze
    breakGlassGroups: [pacto:break-glass]
    teamGroupPrefix: ""                  # owner team T is group T, or this prefix plus T
    requireOwnerTeam: true               # a question naming no team is answered by nobody
    humanGroups: [staff]                 # everyone outside these groups is an agent
    allowEmptyHumanGroups: false         # true lets humanGroups stay empty

The chart renders the admission policies from these values and publishes them in the ConfigMap pacto-delivery-identities in delivery.namespace, which every signed-in user may read. The promoter runs with that ConfigMap and restarts when it changes. pacto delivery, pacto mcp --delivery and the dashboard read it too, from --delivery-namespace (default pacto-delivery; the chart points its own dashboard at delivery.namespace), so what they offer matches what admission and the promoter decide. A client that cannot read it falls back to the defaults above; admission and the promoter still decide.

A held question goes to the teams that own the affected services. When neither the service nor its consumers declare an owner, nobody may answer it with requireOwnerTeam: true, and only break-glass can override. The plan says so in its question. Set it to false to let any person answer instead.

Service accounts are always agents, but a person-like agent identity is an agent only while it is in an agent group. Left out by mistake, it counts as a person, and an unenrolled identity that completes a pacto-approve login counts as a person when it approves too: pacto-approve is a public client, so a bot user with stored credentials can log in without anyone at the keyboard and get a login time. Set humanGroups to the groups your people are in, and anyone outside them is an agent. The chart refuses delivery with humanGroups empty unless you set allowEmptyHumanGroups: true.

docs.title: The dashboard's delivery settings
docs.text:
The delivery views need dashboard sign-in. For approvals, add the extra scope audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli (see above). The delivery settings sit under dashboard.delivery:

dashboard:
  auth:
    oidc:
      extraScopes: [audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli]
  delivery:
    namespace: ""      # where the identity policy is; empty means delivery.namespace when delivery.enabled
    trust: {configMap: delivery-trust, key: trust.yaml}   # verifies History
    miraURL: http://mira.observability:4318

trust is the trust config the CLI reads (trust and key rotation). The dashboard's ServiceAccount gains nothing in delivery and cannot impersonate. A dashboard on loopback without sign-in never decides, because any process on your machine could do it as you; it shows the pacto delivery approve command instead.

docs.title: Follow delivery in the dashboard
docs.text: The Delivery tab (what it shows) appears only where the cluster serves the delivery API and the dashboard knows who you are. Every action shows the plan first, and the fresh plan if anything moved since. When you may not list delivery objects across the cluster, the views say they may be incomplete.

docs.title: Approve from the dashboard
docs.text: A held change asks one question of the teams that own the affected services. Only their members may answer. A contract owner team T is the group T, or teamGroupPrefix followed by T. A person decides with the sign-in they have. The dashboard and pacto delivery approve check a decision with the promoter's own rule before they record it, and refuse one it would not count, saying why. Agents are refused, and so is a pasted token in the dashboard.

docs.title: A recent sign-in to decide
docs.text: Set delivery.promoter.authFreshness to a duration such as 15m to make deciding need a recent sign-in. The promoter then ignores an approval given more than that long after its author's login, and every Stage publishes the setting in status.authFreshness for the dashboard and pacto delivery approve to follow. Once a login is older than two thirds of it, the dashboard says so next to the decision buttons, and a decision opens a dialog that sends the person to sign in again (prompt=login), keeping their choice and note for one more click. A token with no login time cannot approve.

docs.title: Approve from the terminal
docs.text:
pacto delivery approve -n prod <operation> --decision approve

It decides as your kubeconfig signs you in. Where the Stage asks for a recent sign-in or cannot be read, it never sends your kubeconfig's credentials:

export PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL=https://idp.example.com
pacto delivery approve -n prod <operation> --decision approve \
  --oidc-extra-scopes audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli --oidc-redirect-port 8001

It prints an address with prompt=login and max_age=0, waits up to ten minutes on the loopback port for you to log in again in your browser, refuses a token whose auth_time is older than the command, and sends the Approval with that token alone. The token is not stored. --oidc-client-id defaults to pacto-approve; a confidential client's secret comes from PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. Without --oidc-redirect-port it picks a free port, which suits a provider that allows any loopback port (RFC 8252).

docs.title: Agents over the network
docs.text:
PACTO_MCP_EXCHANGE_CLIENT_SECRET=... pacto mcp --delivery -t http --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --auth-issuer https://idp.example.com --resource https://pacto-mcp.example.com/mcp \
  --exchange-client-id pacto-mcp

Every request must carry a bearer token for the resource; the server publishes where to get one at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. It exchanges each caller's token at the identity provider (RFC 8693) for one the apiserver accepts and asks the apiserver who the caller is on every request. Everyone gets the read tools, an agent also propose and cancel, nobody an approve tool. Put agent clients in pacto:agents (or your agent group), or set humanGroups. Without token exchange the server refuses --delivery over HTTP. With --fleet and --auth-issuer, the fleet tools answer as the dashboard does.

Both servers log every refused token, sign-in and signed-in request as a warning with the issuer, audience or client, the reason and where it came from (X-Request-Id too, when a proxy sets it), never the token. With --verbose the MCP server also logs each caller's class and whether it got the write tools.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• An agent holding a person's credentials, session or refresh token is that person to the cluster, and by default it can approve as them. A recent sign-in raises the bar; it does not close the gap. pacto delivery approve asks for the login with prompt=login, but the cluster cannot see what a login asked for: a process that drives your browser could run the pacto-approve login itself and ride your identity provider's session, and it gets a login time only as old as your last real login there. An identity provider that ignores prompt=login widens this.
  • A stolen dashboard session can take that person's actions until it ends. With a recent sign-in required, it approves only in the first two thirds of delivery.promoter.authFreshness after they signed in again.
  • Sessions live in the dashboard's memory: it runs as one replica and a restart signs everyone out (sessions).
  • A change's timeline shows only the Operation's own times, not Kubernetes events. Published versions are those your Stages know, and refused publishes are listed as the registry holds them, without checking their signatures.

docs.title: Delivery reference: plan, propose and approve
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

How a change is planned, proposed and approved, for Pacto delivery. Setting up a Stage is in Delivery reference: setup and gates.

pacto delivery candidates -n prod --stage payments
pacto delivery plan -n prod --stage payments --to 3.0.0
pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --to 3.0.0 --intent-digest sha256:...
pacto delivery approve -n prod <operation> --decision approve

candidates lists the versions a Stage may take, with their digests. --to takes a version, a tag or a digest; a version or a tag must name exactly one candidate, or Pacto refuses it and says why. The operation records the digest.

approve decides as your kubeconfig signs you in. Where the Stage asks for a recent sign-in, it makes you log in again in your browser through its own pacto-approve client instead, so it needs the issuer the cluster trusts (--oidc-issuer-url or PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL). See approve from the terminal.

plan predicts each gate's verdict and the one question a person would be asked. Its next lines say which teams must sign, that an agent cannot answer and that an operation nobody decides before its approval deadline (24 hours unless the Stage's deadlines.approval says otherwise) concludes Expired. A Rejected plan asks nobody anything; its failing verdict says what to do first. propose with the plan's intent digest refuses with PlanStale if anything moved since. The digest also binds the reason and the on-behalf-of person, so pass the same ones you planned with: when they explain the difference, PlanStale names them.

docs.title: Cancel and roll back
docs.text:
cancel works until the pointer moves; after that, propose --type rollback --undoes <operation>. A rollback runs no gates, so only a person or break-glass may roll back a rollback or an override: an agent proposes a promote of that version instead, which the gates judge. One check applies to a rollback a person or agent raises: when a consumer's range does not accept the version it returns to (checkout moved to ^3 and the rollback goes back to 2.x), that consumer's team approves it first. Nothing Pacto cannot see holds a rollback, and the promoter's own rollbacks never wait. An agent may cancel only an operation it proposed; a rollback or freeze the promoter raised, or anyone else's operation, is cancelled by a person or break-glass. Once an operation has moved the pointer nobody deletes it, not even break-glass: re-checks, rollbacks and history cite it. Only the promoter (after delivery.recorder.operationTTL, and never the one the Stage runs) and the namespace controller remove it. With the recorder off, history names any seq whose Operation is gone. Names ending in -rollback, -freeze or -stepdown, and <stage>-auto- or <stage>-witnessed- names, are the promoter's own: admission refuses them to everyone else, so nobody can take the name of a rollback before the promoter raises it.

pacto mcp --delivery gives agents the tools Which tools exist lists, with propose and cancel only when the apiserver says the caller is an agent.

docs.title: When another service must move first
docs.text:
When a promote breaks a consumer, the plan names a version of that consumer to ship first: one that accepts both the running and the new provider version, fits the other services there, is newer than what runs and was offered by its upstream Stage. It shows in plan, explain, status.plan.order and the dashboard's Update these first. While a change waits, the promoter plans again, so a consumer that moved stops being asked and one newly broken is asked. Pacto never promotes the other service itself.

Only consumers in the same environment count. A Pacto's delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/environment label places it; without one, it is where a Stage's Kustomization applies (targetNamespace), even if you deployed it there for another environment, so label it then. A Pacto that cannot be placed counts everywhere and, as a consumer, asks a person.

docs.title: Who may do what
docs.text:
Identity May May not Agent (its service account or pacto:agents) propose, read and cancel its own operations approve, freeze, unfreeze, write status, edit the pointer Person propose, read and cancel any operation, approve a question their team is asked, freeze, unfreeze write status (beyond clearing a Stage's upstreamSeen) Break-glass (pacto:break-glass) override and edit spec.ref.digest Promoter write status and raise its own operations sign or push Recorder write the record fields and finalizer; sign and push records anything else

Admission requires an Approval's spec.by and spec.groups to match the requesting user, and a spec.authTime to match its login time. The promoter does not count a login older than delivery.promoter.authFreshness when you set one, an approval from the operation's own actor or whoever it acts for, one from outside the teams asked, one given before the question was last asked, an accepted unknown where an approval is needed or an approval once the version shipped. The operation's status.message says why an Approval does not count. Once given, an Approval's spec cannot change; the promoter makes its operation its owner, so deleting the operation deletes its Approvals. A break-glass edit of the pointer is never undone: it is recorded as a witnessed override and the Stage freezes.

docs.title: Delivery reference: Argo CD and several clusters
docs.text:
Pacto delivery applies versions through Flux by default. This page covers the two other set-ups: a Stage applied by Argo CD, and a Stage that follows a Stage in another cluster.

Experimental

Both set-ups are experimental, within an Alpha component: they may change more than the rest of delivery. Every pull request that changes delivery runs each of them live once, in the delivery demo; Flux runs in every delivery scenario.

docs.title: Apply through Argo CD
docs.text:
A Stage can point at an Argo CD Application instead of a Flux OCIRepository. Turn it on in the operator chart's delivery section:

delivery:
  argocd:
    enabled: true

This gives the promoter patch on Argo CD Applications and adds an admission policy. On a labelled Application only the promoter or break-glass may change spec.source.targetRevision.

The Application must:

  • live in the Stage's namespace. Argo CD calls this Applications in any namespace. Add the namespace to application.namespaces and to the project's sourceNamespaces.
  • have one OCI source (spec.source.repoURL: oci://…), not spec.sources, and set no Kustomize images, patches or components, Helm parameters, values or value files, or plugin. Otherwise the Stage's Mediated condition is False: something besides the digest decides what runs.
  • sync on its own (syncPolicy.automated), because the promoter never runs a sync.
  • carry the delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref label, set to the Stage's name. Without it the Stage has Ready False with the reason ApplierUnlabelled.
  • start with targetRevision empty or at the digest the Stage runs. Any other value is a write the promoter did not make, so the first promote freezes the Stage.

The Stage is not Ready while the Application breaks one of these, and the reason names which: ApplierUnreadable (missing, the promoter may not read it, or its CRD is not installed, such as Argo CD in a Flux-only cluster), ApplierUnlabelled, ApplierMultiSource, ApplierNotOCI or ApplierNotAutomated. A Flux OCIRepository the Stage applies through needs the same label, so ApplierUnreadable and ApplierUnlabelled apply to it too.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: prod
  labels: {delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref: payments}
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: oci://registry/deploy/payments
    path: .
  destination: {server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: prod}
  syncPolicy: {automated: {}}
---
apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata: {name: payments, namespace: prod}
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {kind: Application, name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamStage: {name: payments, namespace: test}

docs.title: How a promote applies
docs.text:
The promoter sets spec.source.targetRevision to the new digest and asks Argo CD to refresh. The move counts as applied once the Application is Synced and Healthy at that digest; status.sync.revision alone is not proof, since it moves on refresh while the old version still runs. A sync of the digest that ends Failed or Error, or Degraded health after that sync, fails the promote and starts the usual rollback.

Argo CD does not check signatures. The candidate source checks them, and the promoter only ever writes a digest, so Argo CD fetches exactly the checked bytes. Admission keeps the rest of spec.source, spec.sources and the label to break-glass, so nobody else changes what those bytes become. Only a Flux OCIRepository with spec.verify admits a new version, so the first Stage of a service needs Flux's source controller in its cluster even when Argo CD applies it. Stages after it can take versions from that Stage, in the same cluster or through its records, with no Flux at all. An Argo CD Stage places no consumers, so label the Pactos it runs with delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/environment.

docs.title: Follow a Stage in another cluster
docs.text:
A Stage in one cluster can take its versions from a Stage in another cluster, such as prod in one cluster following staging in another. The clusters do not talk to each other. The downstream promoter reads the upstream Stage's signed records from the registry.

You need:

  1. The recorder running in the upstream cluster (see Signed records).
  2. The upstream recorder's public key in the downstream promoter's trust config, bound to the upstream stream:
promoter:
  upstreamTrust: |
    keys:
      - name: staging-recorder
        publicKey: |
          -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
          ...
          -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
        streams: ["8d1e…/staging/*"]
  1. The downstream Stage naming the upstream stream and the repository that holds its records. The stream is the upstream Stage's status.stream.id.
apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata: {name: payments, namespace: prod}
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamRecords:
      repository: registry/delivery/streams
      stream: 8d1e…/staging/payments

docs.title: What the follower takes
docs.text: The promoter rebuilds from the records what the upstream verified: a promote that Succeeded, Verified and passed the published gate there is offered here, and a failure the follower has read is never taken: a version that failed there, or was rolled back after release. That includes a version that fails a check after release when the promoter cannot roll it back there (a person or agent chose it, or its rollback is used up): the promoter freezes that Stage with a freeze operation whose record names the failed version. Its own gates, approvals and checks still run. The digest must also exist in the Stage's own apply repository: use the same repository or a mirror that keeps digests. pacto delivery plan reads these records only with --trust and the upstream recorder's key.

docs.title: When the records cannot be trusted
docs.text:
The promoter offers nothing when it cannot check the history: without delivery.promoter.upstreamTrust the Stage is not Ready (UpstreamUntrusted). A gap, a fork or an unreadable registry make it not Ready (UpstreamUnreadable, saying why) until a read succeeds, and refuse a promote as NotPublished. A record no trusted key signed is skipped, since anyone with push access could attach one. A trusted record that stops verifying leaves a gap.

What the follower cannot see, it cannot refuse. It detects records removed from before status.upstreamSeen, but not a record hidden after it was written and before the follower first read it, nor one signed with a key upstreamTrust does not list, which is skipped like a forgery. A version that failed upstream through such a record can still be taken. So rotate the recorder's key in every follower first (list the new key beside the old one in upstreamTrust), then upstream. The Stage's Ready message counts the referrers on the upstream anchor it could not verify, so a skipped record does not go unsaid.

docs.title: When records were removed or rewritten
docs.text:
The Stage remembers the newest upstream record it read in status.upstreamSeen. A later read that ends before it, or holds another record at its seq however far the stream has grown since, is refused the same way: records were removed or rewritten, and one of them could be a failure. Every pacto.published verdict on such a Stage cites the record it relied on as upstreamHead and upstreamSeq, so an auditor can replay the stream up to it.

Sometimes the cut is intended: the upstream stream was recreated, or a StreamConflict repair removed its newest record. Nothing clears the mark on its own, so the follower stays not Ready until a person does. Once an auditor confirms the cut, clear it, with the right to patch stages/status. Admission lets that right do nothing else: only the promoter writes the rest of a Stage's or an Operation's status, so the write must remove upstreamSeen and change nothing more. The next read, within 30 seconds, sets it again:

kubectl patch stage <stage> -n <namespace> --subresource=status --type=merge \
  -p '{"status":{"upstreamSeen":null}}'

The promoter reads the upstream registry at most every 30 seconds for auto-promotion, and afresh when it plans a promote. It fetches and verifies each record once.

docs.title: Freezes
docs.text: A freeze is local, in one cluster or across two. Freezing the upstream Stage does not stop a follower from taking a version the upstream already verified: freeze the follower too. When the promoter freezes a Stage because a check failed after release, its record names the failed version, so followers never take that version.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A Stage sees the upstream's history only as far as its records reach the registry, so a failure not yet recorded is not seen.
  • A cut is noticed only against a record the Stage already read. A Stage that starts following a stream whose newest records were already removed cannot tell.

docs.title: Delivery reference: record keys
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

docs.title: Trust and key rotation
docs.text:
Readers and the recorder check every signature against a trust config. To rotate, sign with the new key and keep the old one listed:

delivery:
  recorder:
    trust: |
      keys:
        - name: old-recorder
          publicKey: |
            -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
            ...
            -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
          streams: ["*/prod/*"]

streams are patterns over stream ids (<cluster>/<namespace>/<stage>), so a dev key cannot sign prod history. A keyless entry names identity, issuer and the required trustedRoot. The recorder's own key is always trusted. List the old key before the recorder signs with a new one, also when a KMS alias moves. Otherwise the old records stop verifying and the Stage freezes. Pass the same file (or the recorder's PEM public key) to the CLI with --trust or PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST, and to pacto mcp --delivery and pacto dashboard with --delivery-trust. A dashboard the operator deploys reads it from the ConfigMap in the operator namespace that dashboard.delivery.trust names, as in {configMap: delivery-trust, key: trust.yaml}. Without it, records are read unchecked and every answer says it is partial.

docs.title: Revoke a key
docs.text:
When a key leaks, rotate the recorder to a new key first. Then keep the old key listed with untilRecord, the id of the last record it signed on that stream, and untilSeq, that record's seq. The old key then verifies only that record and those it chains from, so history stays readable. Anything else it signs is skipped as untrusted, whether a record after untilSeq or a forgery backdated to a seq it already used. So a forgery neither extends nor forks the stream and the Stage does not freeze:

keys:
  - name: leaked
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...
      -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
    streams: ["<cluster>/prod/payments"]
    untilSeq: 41
    untilRecord: 3f9c...e1 # the record at seq 41

Seqs count per stream, so give a key that signed several streams one entry per stream. The last seq and record of each are in the Stage's status.stream.recordedSeq and status.stream.head, or in pacto delivery record verify. Set both fields or neither. A read of one version's records, not the whole stream, cannot walk the chain, so it shows what the old key signed as not verified. Followers need the same trust config: one that does not trust the new key sees the stream end at the last record it can verify.

Removing the key instead makes its records unverifiable: the recorder stops on the missing head and every follower sees a hole.

docs.title: Delivery reference: signed records and history
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

The recorder writes a signed record of every operation that ends, refusals included, into your registry next to the versions it touched. Off by default. Only the recorder can sign and push records. With it on, history, blame and undo read the records in place of the Operations left in the cluster.

docs.title: What a record is
docs.text:
An in-toto statement of predicate type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/operation/v1: what was asked, by whom and for whom, the Stage policy, every check result with its proof, every approval and the outcome. It holds references, never secrets. It is a sigstore bundle attached as an OCI referrer to the version moved to, the one moved from, the new contract and the Stage's stream anchor. guarded: true says the admission policies checked who asked and who approved. The promoter admits an operation only while its admission policies guard the cluster, so every record it writes carries it. A record from an earlier promoter that ran without them lacks it, and its names are only what their writers claimed.

An eval verdict carries two signatures:

  • the eval runner's, on its own answer, kept in citation.runnerBundle (eval providers), with the runner named in citation.runner
  • the recorder's, on the whole record around it

docs.title: Streams, stand-ins and gaps
docs.text:
Each Stage has one stream: records are numbered (seq) and each names the one before (parent). An unrecordable record stands in for an operation that failed a check before signing (a value that looks like a secret, an approval no longer bound); status.record.refused says why. It keeps none of what the operation did, so record verify reports it as a problem, and a Stage in another cluster that follows the stream offers nothing from then on: the stand-in could be the failure that marks a version failed. The follower's Ready message names the stand-in's record id. A person of the team that owns the service checks what the operation did upstream, then acknowledges that one stand-in on the follower:

pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type acknowledge \
  --record sha256:... --reason "checked upstream: the rollback failed nothing"

The acknowledge takes effect at once and is recorded like any other operation, with who asked, the record id and the reason. The follower then skips that stand-in and offers versions again; any other stand-in still stops it. Only a person of that team or break-glass may acknowledge, never an agent or the promoter, and a reason is required. When nothing runs on the follower yet, or what runs names no team or cannot be read, only break-glass may acknowledge, whatever requireOwnerTeam says. Break-glass can still move the follower with an override instead. A gap record marks a number no operation holds. A record can be late but is never skipped: an Operation keeps its delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/record finalizer until the registry lists its record.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Your registry must serve the OCI Referrers API natively. zot does; GitHub's registry and released distribution do not, so they hold no records.

delivery:
  recorder:
    enabled: true
    streamsRepository: registry.example/pacto/streams
    registryCredentials:
      secretName: recorder-push       # a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret
    signing:
      ed25519:
        secretName: recorder-key      # holds key.pem, a PKCS#8 Ed25519 key
      allowOperatorReadableKey: true  # the operator can read this Secret too

The push Secret needs write access to the streams, deploy and contract repositories. Create a test key with openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out key.pem. The operator reads every Secret, so the chart refuses such a key without allowOperatorReadableKey, and refuses a recorder that shares the promoter's ServiceAccount.

In production, sign with a KMS key (delivery.recorder.signing.kms: awskms:///alias/pacto; ECDSA P-256, Ed25519 or RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256; AWS, GCP, Azure and Vault) or keyless (delivery.recorder.signing.keyless: certificate identity and issuer, a Fulcio, a required timestamp authority and a trustedRoot). Workload identity goes in delivery.recorder.serviceAccount.annotations. The recorder checks a probe record at startup, so a wrong key stops it before anything lands.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
Each Stage gets a RecordStoreReady condition:

Reason Meaning ReferrersSupported Records are being written ReferrersUnsupported The registry has no Referrers API RegistryUnavailable The registry did not answer; it tries again SignerUnavailable The signer (KMS key, keyless token, Fulcio or timestamp authority) failed; it tries again StreamConflict Two trusted records with one number, a broken chain or a missing head (the one the Stage names). The recorder stops and the Stage freezes

A record signed by no key trusted for its stream is not part of its history: the recorder and followers skip it, and the condition names the first one. Anyone who can push can attach a referrer, so an untrusted one never freezes a Stage.

Pacto never resolves a StreamConflict for you. Find the bad record with pacto delivery record verify, delete its referrer manifest from the streams repository, wait for RecordStoreReady to turn True, then unfreeze. After an etcd restore the recorder continues from the newest record.

docs.title: Require records
docs.text:
By default automation keeps moving a Stage while the recorder cannot write, and records catch up later. To stop that, set records.required:

spec:
  records:
    required: true

Then every promote or rollback an agent or the promoter raises waits for a person's approval while RecordStoreReady is not True, or while more than five of the Stage's operations wait for a record. People, break-glass and freezes are not held. With delivery.recorder.monitoring.enabled, the chart scrapes the recorder and ships a PrometheusRule. PactoDeliveryRecordsPending fires when a stream has waited 15 minutes for a record, and PactoDeliveryRecorderDown when no recorder answers a scrape.

docs.title: Trust, key rotation and revocation
docs.text: Readers and the recorder check every signature against a trust config. How to write it, rotate the recorder's key and revoke a leaked one is in Delivery reference: record keys.

docs.title: History, blame and undo
docs.text:
pacto delivery history -n prod --stage payments --trust recorder.pub
pacto delivery history --all --trust recorder.pub
pacto delivery blame -n prod --stage payments
pacto delivery undo -n prod <operation>

Every answer says when it was read (asOf), its source (records, or status when only the cluster's Operations could be read) and its completeness: complete only when every record verifies and the chain is whole. problems lists what the records show is wrong, and unreadable what could not be read. On a partial answer a missing change may still have happened. --all walks every Stage you can list, up to 500 in two minutes.

blame names the change that moved the Stage to what it runs: who asked, who approved, what each check said. No change on a partial history means unknown, never nobody. undo proposes nothing; it returns the plan and the command that would undo an operation. pacto delivery plan also lists what the new version's records say happened on other Stages, so a version that failed in test shows when you plan it for prod.

docs.title: Verify records
docs.text:
pacto delivery record verify -n prod --stage payments --trust recorder.pub

It checks every signature and the whole chain, exits non-zero if anything is wrong and prints a command that checks one record without Pacto, with oras and cosign. record verify --all checks every stream.

Eval runners:

  • A record with an eval runner's signed answer verifies only when the trust config also lists that runner's key with role: runner. A keyless runner takes identity, issuer and trustedRoot.
  • The output names who ran each exam.
  • An eval verdict that says Pass or Fail fails the check when it keeps no runner-signed answer, when the answer is for another operation or version, or when the signed counts and the Stage's minPassRate give another result.
  • providers on a runner key lists the gate providers whose verdicts a runner must sign, so you decide which verdicts are exams.
  • A runner key verifies only runner answers, and a recorder key only records.
  • To check a runner's signature with cosign, see Verify a record.
keys:
  - name: recorder
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...
  - name: evals-ci
    role: runner
    providers: [evals]
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...

  seq 4    operation     sha256:9c1f... promote-pay-agent-1-1-0
           evals: the exam was run and signed by evals-ci

Check one record without Pacto gives the oras and cosign commands for a recorder key file.

For a keyless recorder it uses these flags instead of --key recorder.pub, with the entry's trustedRoot saved as trusted_root.json:

--trusted-root trusted_root.json --certificate-identity <identity> \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer <issuer> --use-signed-timestamps \
  --insecure-ignore-sct

--insecure-ignore-sct appears only when the trusted root lists no certificate transparency log, as in many private Sigstores: then a certificate carries no SCT and cosign needs the flag. The TSA timestamp is still checked.

docs.title: Retention and events
docs.text: A recorded Operation is deleted after delivery.recorder.operationTTL (a week), except the one a Stage runs. Nothing in Pacto deletes a record, but registry retention rules can, leaving history partial: keep the streams repository and the referrers out of them. With delivery.recorder.cdeventsSink set, the recorder posts a CDEvent for every record, best effort.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The recorder notices a tampered record only when it next records on that Stage; record verify checks any time.
  • Deleting a Stage while a change runs leaves that change unrecorded. Wait for its changes to conclude first.
  • A follower in another cluster notices records removed from a stream's tail only against the newest record it already read (details).
  • No record goes to a transparency log such as Rekor. A keyless record's signed time comes from the timestamp authority the recorder must name, and the certificate is checked at that time.

docs.title: Delivery reference: security model
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Every change Pacto delivery makes goes through an Operation. A person, a CI job and an AI agent over MCP each create one, and the promoter plans and checks it. The operator chart's admission policies check who writes each Operation and Approval and who moves a Stage's pointer. This page lists what those policies close and what your platform closes itself.

docs.title: How Pacto tells who is acting
docs.text:
Admission and the promoter read the identity the Kubernetes API server authenticated. They sort it into four classes, and the first row that matches wins:

Class Who Promoter The promoter's own ServiceAccount Break-glass Members of delivery.identities.breakGlassGroups Agent Any other ServiceAccount, members of agentGroups and, when you set humanGroups, anyone in none of them Person Everyone else

A CI job that runs under a ServiceAccount counts as an agent. An agent that holds a person's credentials acts as that person. Approvals and agents sets the groups.

docs.title: What each admission policy checks
docs.text:
The chart installs these ValidatingAdmissionPolicies whenever delivery is on. Each one fails closed.

Policy What it checks operation An Operation's actor is the user who creates it. Only the promoter raises a witnessed operation (an override it records for a digest it did not write; see Plan, propose and approve). Only break-glass raises an override, apart from the promoter's witnessed override. Agents may not freeze, unfreeze, acknowledge or lower a Stage to observe. cancel An agent cancels only an Operation it proposed. Once the pointer has moved, nobody cancels the Operation, and only the promoter or the namespace controller deletes it after it concludes. approval An Approval's author is the user who creates it. Agents and ServiceAccounts may not approve. pointer On a labelled Flux OCIRepository, only the promoter or break-glass changes spec.ref.digest. Only break-glass changes its URL, layer selector or ignore rules, or removes the label. pointer-argocd The same rules for spec.source.targetRevision on a labelled Argo CD Application. Only break-glass changes its source, destination or project. Installed with delivery.argocd.enabled. applier On a labelled Flux Kustomization, only break-glass changes what it applies or removes the label. status Only the promoter writes the status of a Stage or an Operation, apart from the recorder's record fields and system:masters. A person may clear a Stage's status.upstreamSeen. records Only the recorder writes record fields, and it writes nothing else. Installed with the recorder. promoter-writes The promoter writes only to labelled pointers, and only their digest. promoter-writes-argocd does the same for the target revision of an Application. Installed with delivery.argocd.enabled.

Only break-glass, system:masters, the GitOps controllers in delivery.admissionPolicies.gitopsUsers, the namespace controller and the garbage collector create or delete a labelled pointer or Kustomization.

docs.title: When a policy is missing
docs.text: The promoter reads its policies before it acts. If one is missing, fails open, has a binding that does not deny or binds another policy, or is narrowed by matchResources or paramRef, the promoter holds every operation and counts no approval. Cluster-admin and system:masters can delete the policies. The promoter then holds every operation until they are back. A promoter started without --admission-policies admits nothing, and every Stage shows Unguarded.

docs.title: The checks each operation type runs
docs.text:
Every Operation of the same type runs the same checks, whoever raised it. Who must approve it can depend on who raised it. The types run different checks:

  • A promote runs the published, diff, impact and suite checks before it applies, and the contract check after.
  • Before it applies a rollback, the promoter runs only the impact check, which holds it for the consumers' owners when a consumer does not accept the older version. The impact check skips the promoter's own rollbacks.
  • A break-glass override runs no checks and freezes the Stage until a person unfreezes it.

Plan, propose and approve lists every type.

docs.title: What stays outside the policies
docs.text:
• The policies match only objects that carry the delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref label. A Stage leaves observe only once its pointer carries it.
  • Fields outside the rules stay open, such as an OCIRepository's interval and verify or an Argo CD Application's syncPolicy.
  • The GitOps controllers may create and delete a labelled pointer with no digest check. When the promoter finds a digest it did not write, it records an override and freezes the Stage.
  • No policy matches workloads or the Stage spec. RBAC alone limits kubectl apply on a Deployment.

Close the rest with RBAC on workloads, Stages and pointer objects, and with your own admission on workloads.

docs.title: Signed records
docs.text: A change leaves a signed record only when the recorder is on and your registry serves the OCI Referrers API. The recorder is off by default. Signed records and history sets it up.

docs.title: Delivery reference: setup and gates
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Reference for Pacto delivery. To pactify a service end to end, follow Pactify a service instead. The API group is delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1 (alpha). Plans, approvals and who may do what are in Delivery reference: plan, propose and approve.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text: The two automatic levels need signed records, and records need a registry that serves the OCI Referrers API natively. The recorder attaches each record to its streams repository and to the versions and contract it touched, so keep all of them on such a registry. GHCR does not serve the API.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Delivery is the pacto-operator chart's delivery section, off by default. It needs Flux (source and kustomize controllers). Turn it on:

helm upgrade pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --version 6.4.0 \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system \
  --reset-then-reuse-values --set delivery.enabled=true \
  --set delivery.identities.humanGroups={staff}

Replace staff with the group your people are in: anyone outside it counts as an agent, which may propose but never approve. The chart refuses an empty humanGroups unless you set delivery.identities.allowEmptyHumanGroups=true (see identities).

If you set crds.install=false to manage the CRDs yourself, apply the delivery CRDs before you turn delivery on. The promoter and the recorder do not start without them:

kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6.4.0/integrations/kubernetes/config/crd/bases/delivery.pacto.trianalab.io_approvals.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6.4.0/integrations/kubernetes/config/crd/bases/delivery.pacto.trianalab.io_operations.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6.4.0/integrations/kubernetes/config/crd/bases/delivery.pacto.trianalab.io_stages.yaml

This needs Helm 3.14 or later. Delivery runs in delivery.namespace (pacto-delivery, never the release or node agent namespace), where the operator holds no role, so it cannot act as the promoter. It still reads every Secret: prefer KMS or keyless recorder signing. Set delivery.createNamespace=false to create the namespace, with the recorder key, yourself. Bind pacto-operator-delivery-agent to agents and pacto-operator-delivery-approver to approvers. The image is signed.

The admission policies make the actor of an Operation and the person behind an Approval true, so the chart always installs them with delivery and refuses Kubernetes below 1.30 and a cluster without the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy API. With helm template, pass --api-versions admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1/ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, or set delivery.admissionPolicies.skipCapabilityCheck=true to skip only that check. While a policy the chart rendered is missing or weakened, the promoter admits no operation, counts no approval and shows Unguarded (when a policy is missing).

To run an unreleased build, from the repository root:

docker build -f integrations/kubernetes/Dockerfile --target delivery --build-arg CMD=cmd/delivery \
  -t registry.example.com/pacto-delivery:dev .
helm upgrade --install pacto-operator integrations/kubernetes/charts/pacto-operator \
  -n pacto-operator-system --create-namespace --set delivery.enabled=true \
  --set delivery.image.registry=registry.example.com --set delivery.image.repository=pacto-delivery \
  --set delivery.image.tag=dev

docs.title: Metrics and Events
docs.text:
The promoter and the recorder serve Prometheus metrics over plain HTTP on port 8080. The promoter's are behind the <release>-delivery-metrics Service; set delivery.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true to create a Prometheus Operator ServiceMonitor for it. delivery.recorder.monitoring.enabled=true gives the recorder's their own Service, ServiceMonitor and alerts.

Metric What it counts pacto_delivery_operations_total concluded operations by type, outcome, verification and actor_class: how much shipped with no person, and how often a person accepted an unknown pacto_delivery_verdicts_total gate verdicts of concluded operations and re-checks, by gate, phase and result pacto_delivery_stage_frozen 1 while a Stage is frozen pacto_delivery_stage_watched 0 while the newest re-check of the running version did not pass pacto_delivery_records_pending concluded operations per stream that have no record yet (recorder)

The promoter emits a Kubernetes Event on an operation when it waits on a person (Held) and when it concludes (its outcome). It emits one on a Stage when it raises a rollback (RollbackRaised), freezes (Frozen) or stops being watched (RecheckUnknown, RecheckFailed).

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Upgrade the operator as usual: helm upgrade updates the delivery CRDs, and helm.sh/resource-policy: keep keeps them and their history on uninstall.

docs.title: How a change moves
docs.text:
A Stage names the Flux OCIRepository that applies it, and its status.pointer is the digest it moved the environment to. Only the promoter moves it, and the only field it writes on an object it does not own is that repository's spec.ref.digest. Every change is an Operation whose spec never changes:

flowchart LR
  P[Pending] -->|gates pass| L[lock]
  P -->|a person must decide| H[Held]
  H -->|approved| L
  L --> R[Running]
  R -->|Flux applied it| V[Verifying]
  V -->|Pass| S[Succeeded]
  V -->|Fail| F[Failed, rolled back]
  S -->|re-check fails| F
  • Before: pacto.published admits only a version pacto publish published, pacto.diff compares the contracts and pacto.impact checks every consumer in the environment that declares a range on the service, as Who is asked and why explains.
