Anything unseen (an unreadable Pacto, a registry silent for 10 seconds) is Unknown. pacto.suites holds a version that does not ship a suite one of the Stage's checks names, for a person to accept the unknown. It also holds a version that changes a suite it ships, on every level. pacto.environment holds a version whose contract declares environments but none named like the Stage's spec.environment, or values there that fail their schemas. A contract with no environments passes it.
  • After: the Pacto contract check counts only when status.evaluatedRevision names this version's contract digest and the current workload generation. Compliant and Warning pass, NonCompliant and Invalid fail, anything else is Unknown. Health checks can join it.
  • Rollbacks, freezes and the 50 failed versions never tried again work as What happens to a change says. A rollback that is refused or unclear also freezes the Stage, and a person's rollback puts an auto-hold on a Stage on an automatic level.

Only six built-in operation types exist: promote, rollback, override, freeze, unfreeze and autonomy, which moves the Stage up or down the autonomy ladder. Stage approval policy is approval.always, not an expression.

docs.title: What the pointer guarantees
docs.text: Pacto mediates the pointer and signed records name it. The pointer alone decides what runs only when nothing else can change it; the Stage's Mediated condition says whether that holds. It is True when exactly one Flux Kustomization applies the apply OCIRepository, both carry the delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref label, the Kustomization sets a serviceAccountName and sets none of images, patches, components, postBuild, namePrefix, nameSuffix, kubeConfig, suspend or decryption, and the OCIRepository sets no spec.ignore. Without a serviceAccountName Flux applies each version as kustomize-controller, which is cluster-admin in a default install, so a version whose contract did not change could ship a ClusterRoleBinding and an automatic level would apply it: the levels judge only the contract. pacto init --delivery writes a namespaced deployer account for each environment. On Argo CD it is True when the Application carries the label, has one source and sets no Kustomize images, patches or components, Helm parameters, values or value files, or plugin. Otherwise it is False and the reason (ApplyRefUnguarded, NoApplier, SeveralAppliers, ApplierUnguarded, ApplierUnscoped, ApplierOverrides, SeveralSources) names what else decides what runs.

docs.title: What only break-glass may change
docs.text: On labelled objects, only break-glass may change: removing the label, the OCIRepository's spec.url, spec.layerSelector and spec.ignore, the rest of an Application's spec.source, its spec.sources, spec.destination and spec.project, and a Kustomization's sourceRef, path, images, patches, components, postBuild, namePrefix, nameSuffix, targetNamespace, serviceAccountName, kubeConfig, suspend and decryption. A GitOps tool that applies those objects must leave these fields alone or run as break-glass. Deleting a labelled object, or creating one with the label, is an edit too: only break-glass, system:masters, the namespace controller, the garbage collector and the users in delivery.admissionPolicies.gitopsUsers (Flux's kustomize-controller and Argo CD's application controller by default) may. On kubeadm clusters, kind included, the admin kubeconfig is in kubeadm:cluster-admins, not system:masters, so let GitOps create the pointers or add that user to gitopsUsers. If one of them is ever recreated without the label, the Stage shows Ready False with the reason ApplierUnlabelled and Mediated False with the reason ApplyRefUnguarded. kubectl set image on the workload itself is not mediated: Flux puts it back on its next reconcile, and Argo CD does with selfHeal; until then it runs beside the pointer. The security model lists what each admission policy checks and what stays open.

docs.title: Set up a Stage
docs.text:
The candidate OCIRepository follows the deploy artifact's repository and its spec.verify names the publisher, so Flux checks every signature. The Stage lists each digest Flux verified in status.published and refuses anything else as NotPublished. Without a secretRef or matchOIDCIdentity Flux accepts a keyless signature from anyone, so such a Stage promotes nothing. Flux reads a matchOIDCIdentity issuer and subject as regular expressions, so each must be anchored (^...$) and must not match an identity nobody has: .*, or a subject left open at the end, counts as no identity at all. A Stage that cannot promote has Ready False with the reason CandidateUnverified, CandidateNotFound, NoCandidateSource or UpstreamUntrusted.

apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: OCIRepository
metadata: {name: payments-candidates, namespace: test}
spec:
  url: oci://registry/apps/payments
  ref: {semver: ">=0.0.0"}
  verify: {provider: cosign, secretRef: {name: cosign-pub}}
  # keyless: matchOIDCIdentity with the issuer and subject of publish.sign

Label the OCIRepository that applies the Stage with delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref=<stage name>, so admission keeps everyone but the promoter and break-glass off its digest, and give it the same spec.verify. The value names the one Stage that applies through it, so a second Stage cannot drive the same pointer. Without the label, or with another Stage's name in it, the promoter may not write the digest either: the Stage has Ready False with the reason ApplierUnlabelled, and a refused write shows in the operation's status.message. A downstream Stage takes only what its upstream lists in status.offered: versions that passed the published gate and were verified there, never one let through on an accepted unknown.

apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata: {name: payments, namespace: prod}
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamStage: {name: payments, namespace: test}
  startLevel: advise
  gates:
    verify: {window: 5m}

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Pacto delivery decides which version of each service runs in each environment, such as test and prod. It uses your contracts to tell a safe change from a risky one, asks a person only when it must and rolls back a version that fails its checks. Flux does the actual switch from one version to the next (Argo CD can do it instead, as an experimental option). Words in links are defined in the glossary.

Delivery is opt-in. It is a separate install, and only with it does Pacto change what runs. To set it up for a service, pactify it: give it a contract and connect it to delivery.

Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

docs.title: What happens to a change
docs.text:
A change is a request such as "run payments 2.4.0 in prod". A person, your build pipeline or an AI agent can ask for one. Every change takes the same path:

flowchart LR
  A[Request] --> B[Checks before]
  B -->|safe| D[Apply]
  B -->|could break someone| C[A person decides]
  C -->|approved| D
  D --> E[Checks after]
  E -->|pass| F[Done]
  E -->|fail| G{Safe to roll back?}
  F -->|a later check fails| G
  G -->|yes, once| R[Rolled back]
  G -->|no| Z[Frozen until a person decides]

Before it moves, Pacto checks that this version was published with pacto publish, Pacto's release command, and signed, which proves who published it. It compares the new contract with the one running and looks at every service in that environment that uses this one. If none of them would break, the change goes ahead on its own on an automatic level.

After Flux applies it, Pacto checks that the running version does what its contract says. You can add health checks too, such as error rates from your monitoring. These checks keep running after release, so a problem found an hour later still rolls the version back once, whoever asked for it: the version that ran before is put back. The Stage freezes instead when there is nothing safe to go back to, the rollback itself fails, someone chose the running version by hand (a rollback, or a promote during auto-hold) or someone else already took the name of the rollback Pacto raises. It then waits for a person to roll back or unfreeze it, from the dashboard or the command line. A failure of a version Pacto shipped with no person also costs the Stage one level: see Step-down. None of a Stage's last 50 failed versions is tried again there.

docs.title: Stages and records
docs.text:
A version reaches prod only after it passed in the environment before it, such as test. Each service in each environment is called a Stage, and moving a Stage to a new version is called promoting it. A Stage can promote on its own only once a person has raised it up the autonomy ladder.

Every change that ends, refusals included, can leave a signed record in your registry. The signature shows the record was not changed later. Anyone can check who asked for what, who approved and what each check said. Records are off until you turn on the recorder, and they need a registry that serves OCI Referrers.

docs.title: Who is asked and why
docs.text:
Each contract lists the services it depends on and the versions of each it accepts (its consumer range), for example "checkout accepts payments 2.x". That is how Pacto knows who a change can break.

Say payments 3.0.0 removes a field. In prod, checkout and orders still accept only payments 2.x. The change waits for the checkout and orders teams, whose services it would break.

A breaking change that no contract depends on still waits for a person, who can accept the unknown, because a service without a contract may call it. A Stage whose every consumer has a contract can say so with gates.impact.declaredConsumersOnly: true.

Pacto also says what to update first. If checkout 1.9.0 accepts both payments 2.x and 3.0.0 and already passed in test, Pacto's plan says to ship it first. Then only the orders team is still asked.

Pacto judges by declared version ranges, per consumer. Traffic shows which service calls which; Pacto has no view of the fields or endpoints each call uses. Why you were asked lists every case in which a change waits for a person.

docs.title: Who may approve
docs.text:
AI agents can plan, ask for and cancel their own changes, but only people can approve. The person who asked cannot approve, and neither can the person an agent says it acts for (--on-behalf-of, which the agent claims and Pacto never checks). An agent that leaves it out hides who is behind it, so the two-person rule holds only for changes a person asks for directly or an agent asks for in their name.

A person approves with the sign-in they have, and the record names them. You can also ask for a recent sign-in to decide. That needs a cluster that trusts your company login, untested on EKS, GKE and AKS; where approving works says how to check and what to do without it.

docs.title: What Unknown means
docs.text:
Every check answers Pass, Fail or Unknown. Unknown means Pacto could not see enough to say: too little monitoring data, a registry that did not answer, a breaking change that no contract depends on. Pacto sees only the consumers that have a contract, so a service with no contract may still call the one that changed.

An Unknown check holds the change for a person, who can reject it or accept the unknown. The record marks that check as accepted and names who accepted it.

docs.title: Where you follow it
docs.text:
• The dashboard, the web page pacto dashboard starts, gains a Delivery tab once it knows who you are (you sign in, or run it on your own machine): the changes waiting for your team, what each environment runs, past changes with who asked and who approved, and the publishes Pacto refused.
  • The command line: pacto delivery plan shows what would happen before you ask, and pacto delivery history what already did. kubectl get pacto-delivery -A lists every Stage, Operation and Approval; name a kind in full, such as stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io, where another tool also defines a Stage.
  • AI agents get the same tools through pacto mcp --delivery. MCP is the common way AI agents call tools. There is no approve tool.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
None of these is required reading:

  • Setup and gates: install and Stages by hand
  • Plan, propose and approve: what moves first and who may do what
  • Health checks: monitoring, the suites a version ships and the calls a service makes
  • Eval providers: suite runners and their signed answers
  • Approvals and agents: who may approve, agents over the network and the dashboard's delivery settings
  • Signed records and history: records, blame, undo and verification
  • Record keys: trust, key rotation and revocation
  • Argo CD and several clusters (experimental)
  • Ladder reference: levels, proposals and blockers
  • Publishing details and the contract's publish section

To see all of it run on your machine, try the Kubernetes demo.

docs.title: The Evidence Server
docs.text:
The Evidence Server lets places the operator cannot watch, such as CI runners or edge sites, send signed reports about a service into your cluster. Pacto checks each report against the contract and stores it in your registry. Evidence here means a record of what a tool saw in a running system.

It is off by default (evidence.enabled: false). Turning it on needs three things the chart cannot guess. Settle the first before you publish anything: it decides which registry the contract itself has to live in.

docs.title: Check the registry serves the native Referrers API
docs.text: Each report is stored next to the contract version it is about, in the same registry repository, as an OCI 1.1 referrer (an artifact that points at another artifact). Pacto has no fallback to the older tag-based scheme, so the registry holding the contract must support Referrers lookup. GHCR does not qualify, and neither does CNCF distribution (registry:2, registry:3); see Evidence in OCI. This matters because every other page on this site publishes to ghcr.io. Choose a conformant registry for the contract before you run pacto push.

docs.title: Create the trust store
docs.text:
pacto evidence keygen mints an Ed25519 pair and names the public key after the trust binding the server reads: <producerId>__<keyId>.pub, or a bare <keyId>.pub when there is a single producer:

pacto evidence keygen --out ./keys --producer acme-ci --key-id release-2026

key id:      release-2026
private key: keys/release-2026.key
public key:  keys/acme-ci__release-2026.pub

The Secret is mounted whole and read-only at /etc/pacto/trust, so each Secret key has to be the public-key filename, which is what --from-file gives you. One --from-file per trusted producer:

kubectl create secret generic pacto-evidence-trust \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system \
  --from-file=keys/acme-ci__release-2026.pub

The private .key stays with the producer that signs; the cluster needs only the public key. Evidence security covers rotation and multi-producer trust.

docs.title: Get the subject digest
docs.text:
A subject is one immutable contract revision, and pacto push prints the digest of the revision it just published:

Pushed payments-api@2.1.0 -> registry.example.com/your-org/your-service-pacto:2.1.0
Digest: sha256:<64 hex characters>

Then install:

helm install pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace \
  --set evidence.enabled=true \
  --set 'evidence.registry.subjects[0]=oci://registry.example.com/your-org/your-service-pacto@sha256:<digest>' \
  --set evidence.trust.existingSecret=pacto-evidence-trust
  • At least one subject. evidence.registry.subjects lists the exact, immutable contract revisions evidence may be reported against, each an oci://<repo>@sha256:<digest> reference. The chart's schema rejects an empty list, so helm install fails before anything reaches the cluster: at '/evidence/registry/subjects': minItems: got 0, want 1. It rejects a short or tag-shaped reference the same way: the digest has to be all 64 hex characters.
  • A trust store. evidence.trust.existingSecret names the Secret you created above. The chart does not check this one, so an install without it succeeds and the operator then exits at startup with evidence enabled but no trust secret set: signature verification is mandatory. Verification is mandatory.
  • A registry that serves the native Referrers API, as above. Nothing checks it at install time: the chart installs, the operator starts and the failure surfaces later as an Evidence Server that never becomes ready.

If that registry is private, there is a fourth thing you create yourself: a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret named by evidence.registry.credentialsSecret, mounted read-only as a DOCKER_CONFIG directory so the server authenticates the way pacto pull does. Leave the value empty for an anonymous or in-cluster registry.

See the Helm reference for the full value list and Operator configuration for the controller flags each value maps to.

docs.title: Verifying the install
docs.text:
evidence.enabled=true adds a third Deployment, pacto-evidence, created by the controller the same way the dashboard is:

NAME              READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
pacto-dashboard   1/1     1            1           16s
pacto-evidence    1/1     1            1           14s
pacto-operator    1/1     1            1           21s

1/1 means more than "the process started". Readiness is GET /api/evidence/v1/ready, which answers 503 until every subject resolves in the registry and answers native Referrers discovery. A pacto-evidence stuck at 0/1 is nearly always a subject the cluster cannot pull or a registry without the Referrers API. Read the server's own log:

kubectl -n pacto-operator-system logs deploy/pacto-evidence

The Service is pacto-evidence on port 8686. Producers inside the cluster POST signed envelopes to it:

http://pacto-evidence.pacto-operator-system.svc:8686/api/evidence/v1/envelopes

A pacto fleet outside the cluster consumes the same server's read-only contribution by base URL. --evidence-url appends /api/evidence/v1/targets itself, so leave it out:

kubectl port-forward -n pacto-operator-system svc/pacto-evidence 8686:8686 &
pacto fleet search --evidence-url http://127.0.0.1:8686

Nothing durable lives in the cluster: no PersistentVolumeClaim, no data volume, because the registry is the store. Delete and recreate the Deployment and the accepted evidence is still there. Evidence in OCI covers what is written and where; the ingestion API lists all five endpoints.

docs.title: GitOps promotion gates
docs.text:
Make Flux or Argo CD stop the next rollout step when a service breaks its contract. Copy one snippet below and a NonCompliant Pacto turns the Kustomization unready or the Application Degraded.

These snippets stop the next step, not the current deploy: by the time the operator has a verdict the pods are already serving. The Kustomization goes unready, the dependent one waits and the Argo Application goes Degraded. To catch a breaking change before it lands, use pacto impact in the pull request.

Flux and Argo CD read status.contractStatus only through an extension point. Without one, a Kustomization holding a NonCompliant Pacto reports healthy. The two snippets below configure that extension point.

docs.title: Flux
docs.text:
Flux decides health with kstatus, its built-in status reader, which recognises only the Ready, Reconciling and Stalled conditions. Pacto publishes ContractValid, RuntimeObserved and ReadinessSatisfied, so kstatus discards all three and the object falls through to Current: the gate looks configured and passes everything. spec.healthCheckExprs (kustomize-controller v1.5.0, flux2 v2.5.0 and later) replaces that fallback with a CEL expression:

# Flux promotion gate driven by the Pacto contract verdict.
#
# This file is published verbatim in integrations/kubernetes/docs/gitops.md and
# applied verbatim by tests/acceptance/kind/gitops-flux.sh. Edit it and you edit
# both; the documented snippet cannot drift from the tested one.
---
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: orders-staging
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  # Must exceed the operator's stabilization window (default 2m) plus one
  # requeue interval, or a real violation arrives as an ambiguous timeout
  # instead of a clean failure.
  timeout: 5m
  prune: true
  wait: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: OCIRepository
    name: orders
  path: ./staging
  healthCheckExprs:
    - apiVersion: pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
      kind: Pacto
      failed: status.contractStatus in ['NonCompliant', 'Invalid']
      current: status.contractStatus in ['Compliant', 'Reference', 'Warning']
---
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: orders-production
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  timeout: 5m
  prune: true
  wait: true
  # Production does not start until staging is healthy, and healthy now
  # includes the contract verdict. This line is the promotion gate.
  dependsOn:
    - name: orders-staging
  sourceRef:
    kind: OCIRepository
    name: orders
  path: ./production

sourceRef is whatever you already use. Three things about that snippet, each checked against fluxcd/pkg runtime/cel/status_evaluator.go:

  • The snippet leaves out inProgress on purpose. When no expression matches, Flux falls through to in-progress, so an unrecognised verdict holds the deploy until it times out. It fails closed.
  • Warning sits in the passing set. Move that one word to failed if you want contract warnings to block promotions. That is the whole knob.
  • timeout must exceed the operator's stabilization window, or a real violation reaches you as an ambiguous timeout. See Timing.

A freshly created Pacto has no status and the expression errors while that is true; Flux treats the error as not-yet-healthy and keeps polling.

tests/acceptance/kind/gitops-flux.sh applies that exact file to a kind cluster and asserts the dependent Kustomization never reaches it while the contract is violated.

docs.title: Argo CD
docs.text:
Argo picks a health check from a fixed list of built-in kinds and returns no health for any other kind. The roll-up into Application health skips a resource with no health, so Argo ignores a Pacto. A resource health customization in argocd-cm supplies the missing check:

# Argo CD health customization that makes a violated Pacto contract turn its
# Application red.
#
# This file is published verbatim in integrations/kubernetes/docs/gitops.md.
# Apply it as a MERGE PATCH, never as a plain `kubectl apply` -- argocd-cm holds
# Argo's own keys and a full apply would drop them:
#
#   kubectl -n argocd patch configmap argocd-cm --type merge \
#     --patch-file argocd-cm-pacto-health.yaml
#
# The data key must be typed exactly. Argo silently ignores a key it does not
# recognise, which looks identical to having configured nothing at all.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  resource.customizations.health.pacto.trianalab.io_Pacto: |
    -- Argo runs this with the Lua string library disabled.
    -- Only concatenation, comparison, ipairs and tostring() are available.

    -- Set to "Degraded" to make contract warnings block a promotion.
    local warningHealth = "Healthy"

    local hs = {}

    if obj.status == nil or obj.status.contractStatus == nil then
      hs.status = "Progressing"
      hs.message = "waiting for the first contract evaluation"
      return hs
    end

    if obj.status.observedGeneration ~= obj.metadata.generation then
      hs.status = "Progressing"
      hs.message = "contract not yet evaluated at this generation"
      return hs
    end

    local s = obj.status.contractStatus

    if s == "Compliant" or s == "Reference" then
      hs.status = "Healthy"
      hs.message = "contract satisfied"
      return hs
    end

    if s == "Warning" then
      hs.status = warningHealth
      hs.message = "contract satisfied with warnings"
      return hs
    end

    if s == "NonCompliant" then
      hs.status = "Degraded"
      hs.message = "contract violated"
      if obj.status.findings ~= nil then
        for _, f in ipairs(obj.status.findings) do
          if f.severity == "error" then
            hs.message = "contract violated: " .. tostring(f.code) .. ": " .. tostring(f.message)
            break
          end
        end
      end
      return hs
    end

    if s == "Invalid" then
      hs.status = "Degraded"
      hs.message = "contract is invalid and could not be evaluated"
      return hs
    end

    -- Unknown, NotEvaluated, and anything added later.
    hs.status = "Progressing"
    hs.message = "contract verdict pending: " .. tostring(s)
    return hs

Apply it as a merge patch, because argocd-cm holds Argo's own configuration and a plain kubectl apply would drop it. Then restart the controller:

kubectl -n argocd patch configmap argocd-cm --type merge \
  --patch-file argocd-cm-pacto-health.yaml
kubectl -n argocd rollout restart statefulset/argocd-application-controller

The restart is required. The application controller reads health customizations into its resource cache at startup, and that cached verdict is what it compares to decide whether a changed object needs re-examining. Until it has the customization, every verdict the operator writes compares equal to the last and the Application only catches up on the next periodic resync. On a core install, without argocd-server, a restart is the only way in: hot reload of argocd-cm needs server.secretkey, which only argocd-server creates.

In the Lua, anything unrecognised becomes Progressing. Argo's Unknown ranks worse than Degraded and would mask broken workloads, so the script never returns it. The string library is also disabled, so string.format and s:gsub() fail at runtime, after the script loads.

tests/acceptance/kind/gitops-argocd.sh runs that exact file through the Lua sandbox with no cluster, and then inside a kind cluster where an Application must go Degraded naming the finding and back to Healthy once corrected.

docs.title: Check that it took
docs.text:
Argo ignores a data key it does not recognise, and an ignored key looks exactly like having configured nothing:

# The key must read back exactly, group and kind included.
kubectl -n argocd get cm argocd-cm \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.resource\.customizations\.health\.pacto\.trianalab\.io_Pacto}'

Then ask Argo what it makes of a real object. argocd admin settings evaluates the customization against files on disk, in the same Lua sandbox the controller uses, so it answers without waiting for a sync:

kubectl -n argocd get cm argocd-cm -o yaml > /tmp/argocd-cm.yaml
kubectl -n <namespace> get pacto <name> -o yaml > /tmp/pacto.yaml

argocd admin settings resource-overrides health /tmp/pacto.yaml \
  --argocd-cm-path /tmp/argocd-cm.yaml

A Compliant Pacto prints STATUS: Healthy and MESSAGE: contract satisfied. A key that did not take prints Health script is not configured while exiting 0, so read the output and ignore the exit code. Both checks read the ConfigMap, so they also pass on a controller that started before the patch.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
The gate is as fresh as the verdict behind it, and verdicts land at different speeds.

Change When it becomes NonCompliant A mismatch: workload, persistence or configuration conformance The first reconcile after the workload is observed An absence: a missing interface, capability, dependency, Secret or ConfigMap After the stabilization window (default two minutes) plus one requeue interval

That split is why timeout has a floor: five minutes against the default two-minute window leaves room for the window, one requeue and the apply.

Argo re-examines a Pacto when its health status changes, so Healthy to Degraded shows up in about a second. But one NonCompliant reason replaced by another keeps the stale message until the next periodic resync. The status changes at once and the message catches up later.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Argo health customizations are instance-global. One Argo serving several teams cannot give one a blocking Warning and another a passing one.
  • Neither tool can refuse an artifact for what is inside it. "Reject this because its contract breaks three consumers" is a pull-request check.
  • The verdict is about the contract. Compliant says the workload matches its contract. It says nothing about request errors or saturation.
  • status.lastReconciledAt cannot gate on freshness. Neither tool hands the expression a clock.

docs.title: Install the Kubernetes operator
docs.text:
Install the operator with one Helm command, then point it at a contract and it tells you whether the running service matches. This page takes you from an empty cluster to your first verdict.

The operator ships as a Helm chart and a controller image. Coordinates are on the published artifacts page; every value is on the Helm reference.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster (the operator watches cluster-wide by default). The chart declares no kubeVersion floor. The acceptance suite runs on whatever kind ships by default, so older clusters are untested. The chart still installs on them.
  • Helm 3.8 or newer (OCI registry support).
  • Cluster-admin permissions to install the CRDs, the operator's ClusterRole and its namespaced Role (see RBAC). A CRD (custom resource definition) teaches Kubernetes a new kind of object, here Pacto.
  • No Pod Security exemption for the release namespace: the operator, the dashboard and the Evidence Server run under restricted. The optional node agent gets its own namespace, which the chart creates privileged.
  • The pacto CLI for the steps after the install. The Helm install itself does not need it.
  • Network access from the cluster to the registry holding your contracts. For a private repository, put credentials in a Secret and name it in spec.contractRef.pullSecretRef on each Pacto resource; without one the operator pulls anonymously and a private contract reports Unknown.

docs.title: Install with Helm
docs.text:
The chart lives in an OCI registry. Installing it also installs the CRDs and, by default, a dashboard the operator runs for you. The CRDs are part of the release: helm upgrade updates them and helm uninstall keeps them.

At chart defaults the operator can escalate its own privileges

Managing the dashboard means creating the dashboard's own RBAC, so the default install grants the operator unrestricted create on clusterroles and clusterrolebindings, enough to grant itself anything in the cluster. Its observation of your workloads is read-only, and the install as a whole can write. Use --set dashboard.enabled=false if that does not fit your threat model, and deploy the dashboard yourself from the container manifest. RBAC lists every rule, generated from the chart.

helm install pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace

Pin a chart version with --version for a reproducible install (see the compatibility table). The currently published chart:

helm install pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --version 6.4.0 \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace

To manage the CRDs yourself, for example from a separate GitOps source, set crds.install=false and apply them before the install. The operator does not start without them:

kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6.4.0/integrations/kubernetes/config/crd/bases/pacto.trianalab.io_noderuntimeobservations.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6.4.0/integrations/kubernetes/config/crd/bases/pacto.trianalab.io_pactorevisions.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/integrations/kubernetes/v6.4.0/integrations/kubernetes/config/crd/bases/pacto.trianalab.io_pactos.yaml

With delivery.enabled=true, also apply the delivery CRDs. crds.install covers them too.

For an evaluation cluster, use the quickstart profile.

docs.title: Common overrides
docs.text:
helm install pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace \
  --set controller.watchNamespace=my-namespace \
  --set metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true \
  --set dashboard.enabled=false
  • controller.watchNamespace watches one namespace only (empty means the whole cluster).
  • metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled creates a Prometheus ServiceMonitor.
  • dashboard.enabled turns the operator-managed dashboard on or off.

The CRDs are cluster-wide and belong to one release. For a second release, for example one per watched namespace, set crds.install=false, or its install fails with invalid ownership metadata. The same happens on a reinstall under a new release name after an uninstall, because the kept CRDs still name the old release. Point them at the new one first:

for crd in $(kubectl get crd -o name | grep pacto.trianalab.io); do
  kubectl annotate "$crd" --overwrite \
    meta.helm.sh/release-name=NEW_RELEASE \
    meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=NEW_NAMESPACE
done

Three checks are off by default because they cost something:

  • controller.enableProbing lets the operator send requests to your Services to check health and protocol.
  • controller.enableMetricsObservation checks the metrics capability.
  • nodeAgent.enabled runs a small agent on every node that watches which ports your pods really listen on and which services they really connect to. It has requirements of its own, listed in Runtime conformance.

Opt-in features explains each one. Name-match discovery has no chart value.

Keep the dashboard private unless sign-in protects it

By default anyone who can reach the dashboard reads every contract, dependency and compliance result. The chart therefore defaults dashboard.service.type to ClusterIP with dashboard.ingress.enabled and dashboard.httpRoute.enabled off. Reach it with kubectl port-forward. Before you turn any of those on, put an authenticating proxy in front of it or configure sign-in. See Security.

docs.title: Resources and probes
docs.text:
The controller, the delivery promoter and the delivery recorder set CPU requests and memory limits, and no CPU limit, which would throttle a busy process until its liveness probe fails. The liveness probe allows 5 seconds per answer and restarts a process after 2 minutes of failures. Set resources, delivery.promoter.resources or delivery.recorder.resources to change the defaults, listed in the Helm reference.

The promoter wakes a Stage when an object it reads changes and rechecks it once per delivery.promoter.resync (1m by default). An operation waiting on Flux is checked once per delivery.promoter.poll (3s by default), so the promoter's CPU grows with the number of waiting operations. On a large fleet raise the poll or the promoter's CPU request.

docs.title: Offline trace sources for the dashboard
docs.text:
Observed dependencies reach the dashboard as offline OTLP/JSON trace exports. The operator mounts them for you:

dashboard:
  enabled: true
  observation:
    sources:
      - name: orders                      # stable Data Source identity
        file: traces.json                 # relative to this source's mount
        existingClaim: orders-trace-export

Each source is mounted read-only at /var/lib/pacto/observation/<name>/ and read as exactly <mount>/<file>, with no directory scan and no writes. Give each source either existingClaim (real exports, written by some other workload) or configMap (small static exports), never both. name is the Data Source identity and must be unique across every source the dashboard assembles, so local, catalog, target-state, evidence-http, oci and cache are already taken, as is the Kubernetes source's identity: your current kube context name, or k8s when no context is set. A collision is refused, naming both claimants. Whoever owns the storage owns producing and rotating the exports: Pacto ships no OTLP receiver, so nothing listens on 4317 or 4318.

Sources lists every source the graph reads, and Knowledge tells an unreadable source from a stale one.

docs.title: The Evidence Server is off by default
docs.text: evidence.enabled is false. See The Evidence Server.

docs.title: Keep the delivery namespace to cluster admins
docs.text: With delivery.enabled, the promoter and the recorder run in delivery.namespace (pacto-delivery). Anyone who can create a pod there can run it as the promoter's service account, which moves any labelled pointer and writes every Stage's and Operation's status, or as the recorder's, which signs records. Anyone who can edit a ConfigMap there can change the identity policy and the upstream trust config. Grant write access in that namespace to cluster admins only, and give nobody else a binding there.

docs.title: Verify the install
docs.text:
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system get deploy

NAME              READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
pacto-dashboard   1/1     1            1           16s
pacto-operator    1/1     1            1           21s

Two Deployments: pacto-operator is the controller Helm created, pacto-dashboard is the one the controller created in turn. With nodeAgent.enabled=true you also get a pacto-node-agent DaemonSet (one pod per node). With --set dashboard.enabled=false you get pacto-operator alone: the log below has no dashboard reconciler lines, you skip the port-forward and Bind your first contract needs a contract of your own. The three CRDs are registered either way:

kubectl get crds | grep pacto.trianalab.io

noderuntimeobservations.pacto.trianalab.io   2026-08-22T21:24:59Z
pactorevisions.pacto.trianalab.io   2026-08-22T21:24:59Z
pactos.pacto.trianalab.io           2026-08-22T21:24:59Z

If a Deployment never becomes available, read the controller's log:

kubectl -n pacto-operator-system logs deploy/pacto-operator

A healthy start ends with the workers and the dashboard reconciler:

INFO  dashboard  Starting dashboard reconciler  {"enabled": true, "image": "ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard:4.4.0", ...}
INFO  Starting Controller  {"controller": "pacto", "controllerKind": "Pacto"}
INFO  Starting workers     {"controller": "pacto", "worker count": 1}
INFO  dashboard  Dashboard resources reconciled successfully

Open the dashboard by forwarding its Service; there is no Ingress by default:

kubectl port-forward -n pacto-operator-system svc/pacto-dashboard 3000:3000

docs.title: Scraping the metrics
docs.text:
metrics.enabled is true, so the install already publishes a pacto-operator-metrics Service on port 8443. Five gauges are exported, all labelled name and namespace after the Pacto resource:

Metric What it is pacto_contract_status Info-style: 1 for the resource's current status, 0 for every other. The status label takes all seven CRD values, so NotEvaluated is always 0: the operator never writes it. pacto_readiness_score The derived readiness score, 0-100. pacto_readiness_gate 1 when the gate passes, 0 when it does not. pacto_readiness_status Info-style over the gate state: Satisfied, BelowMinScore or Expired. pacto_readiness_checks How many claims sit at each declared status: done, partial, not-done, deferred.

The four readiness gauges are emitted only for contracts that declare a readiness: block. For a contract without one the series is absent, so write alerting rules that tolerate a missing series.

Two things the chart does not do for you. metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled is false, so nothing is scraped until you turn it on. And metrics.secure is true, so the endpoint sits behind the controller-runtime authn/authz filter: an unauthorised scrape gets 403. The chart packages no reader role, so grant one to the ServiceAccount that scrapes:

kubectl create clusterrole pacto-metrics-reader \
  --non-resource-url=/metrics --verb=get
kubectl create clusterrolebinding pacto-metrics-reader \
  --clusterrole=pacto-metrics-reader \
  --serviceaccount=monitoring:prometheus-k8s

metrics.secure=false also works and is the wrong trade for a shared cluster: the gauges name every contract and namespace you have bound.

docs.title: Bind your first contract
docs.text:
A Pacto resource points at a contract and at the Service to observe. The dashboard the operator just deployed publishes its own contract, so you can bind a real one without pushing anything. Save this as pacto-dashboard.yaml:

apiVersion: pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Pacto
metadata:
  name: pacto-dashboard
  namespace: pacto-operator-system
spec:
  contractRef:
    oci: ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard-contract
  target:
    serviceName: pacto-dashboard

kubectl apply -f pacto-dashboard.yaml
kubectl get pactos -n pacto-operator-system

NAME              STATUS    SERVICE           VERSION   ERRORS   WARNINGS   LAST RECONCILED   AGE
pacto-dashboard   Unknown   pacto-dashboard   3.2.1     0        0          19s               30s

The reference carries no tag, so the operator resolved the highest semver tag (3.2.1). It snapshotted every tag it saw as an immutable PactoRevision (kubectl get pactorevisions -n pacto-operator-system), observed the Deployment and Service behind pacto-dashboard and wrote status.contractStatus.

Unknown is the expected first result. Zero errors and zero warnings means nothing contradicted the contract; the operator could not observe four of the things it declares. kubectl describe pacto pacto-dashboard -n pacto-operator-system names each one:

message: interface "http-api" cannot be observed in this environment
code:    OBSERVATION_UNSUPPORTED

An interface has no port until you say which Service port serves it. That is Kubernetes knowledge, and the platform-agnostic contract leaves it to the binding. Add the binding and the interface and its health capability resolve:

  target:
    serviceName: pacto-dashboard
    interfaceBindings:
      - interface: http-api
        servicePort: 3000

Two findings remain: the metrics capability needs controller.enableMetricsObservation (see Opt-in features), and the default configuration needs a configBindings entry naming the ConfigMap or Secret behind it. See Contract bindings for both, and Runtime observations for how a finding maps to a status.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
helm uninstall pacto-operator --namespace pacto-operator-system

That removes the controller and everything owner-referenced to it, dashboard and Evidence Server included. Five things survive, in any order:

  • The CRDs and your Pacto resources. The chart marks every CRD helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, because deleting one takes every Pacto, PactoRevision and NodeRuntimeObservation with it. With delivery enabled this includes the delivery CRDs, so every Stage, Operation and Approval and their history stay too. No finalizers, so the delete returns immediately.
  • The dashboard's cluster-scoped RBAC, which a namespaced owner cannot own.
  • Anything you created by hand: the Evidence Server's trust Secret, your registry-credentials Secret, a metrics-observation-role ClusterRole you applied yourself.
  • The leader-election Lease a4917283.pacto.io, inert once the controller is gone and reused on reinstall.
  • The namespace, if --create-namespace created it.
# Look first: everything that answers is on the list above, plus Kubernetes'
# own default ServiceAccount and kube-root-ca.crt ConfigMap.
kubectl get all,sa,secret,lease,role,rolebinding -n pacto-operator-system
kubectl get clusterrole,clusterrolebinding | grep pacto

Then remove what is left:

kubectl delete crd pactos.pacto.trianalab.io pactorevisions.pacto.trianalab.io \
  noderuntimeobservations.pacto.trianalab.io
kubectl delete crd stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io \
  operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io approvals.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io  # if delivery was enabled
kubectl delete clusterrole,clusterrolebinding pacto-dashboard
kubectl delete clusterrole metrics-observation-role               # if granted
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding metrics-observation-rolebinding # if granted
kubectl delete namespace pacto-operator-system   # takes the Lease and Secrets

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: What the operator cannot see, what you must switch on yourself and where its answers lag. Two rules sit behind all of it: the operator reports a violation only when it can prove it, and it leaves the workloads it watches unchanged.

docs.title: Read-only towards your workloads
docs.text:
The operator never modifies the workloads it observes: it does not restart pods, edit Deployments or change anything it was pointed at. Observation is read and report only. Deciding which version runs is Pacto delivery, an opt-in component of the same chart (delivery.enabled); installing the operator without it grants none of it.

The operator does write to its own components. At chart defaults it manages the Pacto dashboard for you, which means creating a Deployment, Service, ServiceAccount, Secret, ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding of its own. The grants that allow that are broad enough to escalate privilege. RBAC has the full rule list and the flags that switch the managed components off.

docs.title: Observation boundaries
docs.text:
When the operator has no reliable way to check something, it reports Unsupported. Unsupported makes the contract Unknown, never NonCompliant. That happens for:

  • External or non-Pacto Services -- a dependency backed by an ExternalName Service, or a Service the operator does not manage, cannot be reached reliably and is reported Unsupported.
  • Non-HTTP capability bindings -- health and metrics probing supports HTTP bindings only; gRPC capability probing is not implemented and returns Unsupported.
  • Unbound interfaces and capabilities -- the target port cannot be resolved and the result is Unsupported. That happens when an interface has no interfaceBindings entry (and name-match discovery is off), or when a capability's owning interface has no binding.

docs.title: Opt-in features
docs.text:
Some observation is off by default because it costs cluster calls or opens an in-cluster request surface:

  • Metrics observation requires --enable-metrics-observation; otherwise the metrics dimension returns Unsupported.
  • Active health probing requires --enable-probing: the operator issues an in-cluster HTTP GET against the health capability's own port and path. Without it, health falls back to what the cluster already knows: an httpGet readiness probe on the container behind that port, plus a Ready EndpointSlice endpoint. That observes the workload rather than the declared endpoint. The flag help and the observation reference call these two Tier A and Tier B; nothing the operator reports uses those labels.
  • Interface name-match discovery requires --interface-name-match-discovery and only ever assists positive availability -- it never produces an absent or error result.

See Operator configuration for these flags.

The chart exposes the first two as controller.enableProbing and controller.enableMetricsObservation; the second also grants read access to ServiceMonitors and PodMonitors. Name-match discovery has no chart value.

Name-match discovery needs a manual patch

The chart renders a fixed argument list with no extraArgs value, so the only way to turn --interface-name-match-discovery on is to add it to the running Deployment yourself:

kubectl patch deployment pacto-operator -n pacto-operator-system \
  --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--interface-name-match-discovery"}]'

This does not survive helm upgrade. Helm re-renders args and the flag disappears silently. Re-apply the patch after every upgrade.

An operator installed without the chart needs its own grant for --enable-metrics-observation. Add a separate ClusterRole, never a patch of manager-role, whose rules are an atomic list a strategic merge would wipe:

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: metrics-observation-role
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["monitoring.coreos.com"]
    resources: ["servicemonitors", "podmonitors"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: metrics-observation-rolebinding
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: metrics-observation-role
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: pacto-operator                  # the chart's ServiceAccount
    namespace: pacto-operator-system      # the release namespace

The repository also carries a kustomize overlay at config/rbac/metrics-observation/, but config/ is kubebuilder scaffolding: it is not published with a release, and no test or CI job deploys from it. Use it as a source for the YAML above; it is unsupported as an install path.

docs.title: Runtime conformance boundaries
docs.text:
The node agent and the complementary checks report only violations they see. These things stay out of reach:

  • Visibility now defaults to internal. An interface with no visibility is internal, so one served through a LoadBalancer Service or an Ingress that publishes a public address reports INTERFACE_VISIBILITY_MISMATCH after upgrading, node agent or not. Declare visibility: public for it.
  • hostNetwork pods share the node's network namespace, so their sockets cannot be attributed. With the agent on, their interfaces read Insufficient unless another backing pod is seen listening. Their outbound calls cannot be attributed either, so a hostNetwork pod in a workload namespace makes the caller coverage of every Service partial (shared-netns) and delivery holds breaking changes for review. hostNetwork pods in kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease and the node agent's namespace do not count: kube-proxy is taken not to call your services. Other namespaces like that go in controller.kernelEvidence.callerIgnoreNamespaces (the operator flag --caller-coverage-ignore-namespace). The chart lists kube-flannel, calico-system and tigera-operator there by default. A call from a pod in a listed namespace goes unseen, so keep only namespaces that exist on your cluster and that you control: on a cluster without Calico, anyone who may create namespaces could create calico-system and call your services from it unseen.
  • Loopback-only listeners do not serve the pod IP and do not count as serving the port.
  • TCP only. UDP sockets are not observed, so a UDP or SCTP Service port gets no kernel opinion; the Kubernetes result stands.
  • Connection history. A dependency is judged from the latest success and failure within the staleness bound. A dependency the workload has not called recently has no kernel opinion, and a recent success never overrides a provider with no ready endpoint; the two together read Insufficient.
  • TLS hides the protocol inside, so a TLS port leaves interfaces[].type unverified, and asyncapi names no wire protocol to check.
  • Socket-level load balancing (for example a kube-proxy replacement) connects to the backend pod directly. The operator matches every current endpoint IP too, so a connection to a backend that has since left the EndpointSlice no longer counts.
  • Exposure is external only when a Service or Ingress status shows a public address (how exposure is decided). The operator does not read node or gateway addresses, so a NodePort Service or an HTTPRoute leaves exposure unknown. A route outside its watch scope, another route kind or a mesh gateway is not seen, so internal can miss an exposure; it never invents one.
  • Kernel requirements. A node without BTF (the kernel type information the agent needs) reports Failed, which turns its pods' interface checks into COLLECTION_FAILED. A kernel older than 5.11 can report it too, since the agent pod has no SYS_RESOURCE.
  • Docker Compose and bare hosts. The node agent is the Kubernetes way to run pacto agent. On a Docker host or a server, run pacto agent yourself; the cluster-only checks then stay unverified (what stays unverified off Kubernetes).
  • Private registries. The agent's ServiceAccount carries the chart's global.imagePullSecrets and imagePullSecrets, which must also exist in the agent namespace (nodeAgent.namespace): a pull secret is read from the pod's own namespace. An operator installed without the chart passes --node-agent-image-pull-secret itself.

docs.title: Node agent heartbeat and identity
docs.text:
• Heartbeat. Every publish interval the agent renews a coordination.k8s.io Lease named after its node, held by the node and valid for three intervals. It rewrites its NodeRuntimeObservation only when the view changed (lastPublished aside) or every tenth interval, and renews the Lease only after the view is written, so a fresh Lease never vouches for a stale view. The operator takes the heartbeat from the Lease renewTime, or from lastPublished when there is no Lease. An observation deleted by hand on a quiet node comes back within ten intervals; until then the node reads stale.
  • One node, one writer. RBAC cannot say which node's objects an agent may write. Where the API serves ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, the chart adds one that lets the agent's ServiceAccount create or update a NodeRuntimeObservation or Lease only under the node name its token carries (authentication.kubernetes.io/node-name). The policy refuses a token without that name, and the node then reads stale.
  • Kubernetes 1.30 or later. Tokens carry the node name from 1.30, the release ValidatingAdmissionPolicy became generally available. On an older cluster the policy is not rendered and RBAC alone lets any agent write any node's object in the agent namespace.

docs.title: NotEvaluated is reserved
docs.text: NotEvaluated is a valid contractStatus enum value that the operator does not currently emit. A valid, targeted contract with no runtime evidence yields Unknown. The value exists for parity with the engine dashboard, which uses it for offline OCI or local sources that were never runtime-evaluated.

docs.title: Stabilization delay
docs.text:
The stabilization window (--stabilization-window, default two minutes) trades immediacy for resistance to transient blips: a single negative observation reads Unknown until the negative streak spans the whole window.

It applies to absences only: something the operator expected to find and did not:

  • INTERFACE_ABSENT
  • DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE
  • CAPABILITY_ABSENT (active probing only)
  • CONFIGURATION_ABSENT, for a declared Secret or ConfigMap

A mismatch, something that is there and contradicts the contract, is NonCompliant on the first check that observes it, with no delay: WORKLOAD_MISMATCH, PERSISTENCE_MISMATCH, CONFIGURATION_MISMATCH, INTERFACE_PROTOCOL_MISMATCH, INTERFACE_VISIBILITY_MISMATCH and DEPENDENCY_VERSION_MISMATCH. There is nothing transient to wait out; the evidence is already conclusive.

This split matters if you gate deployments on the verdict. See GitOps promotion gates.

docs.title: Delivery and private registries
docs.text:
Images can stay private with only a pull Secret. A private contract or deploy repository needs a login in three places, or the checks that read it answer Unknown, every change waits for a person to accept the unknown and an accepted unknown never moves on to the next environment:

  • delivery: set delivery.promoter.registryCredentials.secretName on the operator chart to a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret in the release namespace;
  • Flux: secretRef on each OCIRepository in delivery/<env>.yaml;
  • the operator: spec.contractRef.pullSecretRef in delivery/pacto.yaml.

pacto init --delivery --registry-secret <name> writes the last two, naming a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret you create in each environment's namespace; the chart value stays yours to set. See Pactify a service for the commands.

docs.title: Delivery records have no outside witness
docs.text: The recorder does not send records to a transparency log such as Rekor. Your registry is the only place they are kept. Anyone who can delete from it can drop the newest records of a stream. Only a follower that already read those records notices they are gone; a new follower, or one that never read them, does not. See signed records.

docs.title: API version
docs.text: The CRDs are served at v1alpha1. Fields are added conservatively and additively; see the CRD reference for the current schema.

docs.title: Kubernetes integration
docs.text:
The Pacto operator tells you, for every service in your cluster, whether what is running still matches its contract. You deploy with Helm or Kustomize as usual. Nothing ties that deployment back to the contract, so the two drift apart without anyone noticing. The operator closes that gap: you point a small Pacto resource at a contract and a workload, and its status says Compliant, NonCompliant or Unknown, with a finding for each problem.

kubectl get pactos -A

With the optional node agent, Pacto also checks what your service does on the network against what its contract says, and tells you only what it can prove. It catches a pod that reports ready while nothing listens on its port, a dependency it keeps failing to reach and a service it calls without declaring it. The node agent is pacto agent, the same watcher that checks Docker hosts and servers, deployed on every node.

On your workloads it only reads (get, list and watch); it never changes them. On its own components it holds more: at chart defaults it deploys Pacto's dashboard, which means creating a Deployment, Service, ServiceAccount, Secret and cluster-wide RBAC of its own. Those grants are broad enough to allow privilege escalation, and turning the managed components off removes them. Read RBAC before installing into a cluster where that matters. The Evidence Server, the operator's other managed component, is off by default; it needs evidence.enabled=true plus a trust store and a subject list (see The Evidence Server).

docs.title: How a reconciliation works
docs.text:
A reconciliation is one pass in which the operator re-checks a Pacto resource. It runs on every change and on a timer, and follows the same steps:

  1. Loader resolves the contract from an OCI registry (auto-selecting the highest semver tag) or parses inline YAML, and snapshots each resolved version as an immutable PactoRevision.
  2. Observer (the collector) reads runtime state from the Kubernetes API and turns it into evidence: typed observations of what is running. With the opt-in node agent it also merges kernel socket evidence (see Runtime conformance and Runtime observations).
  3. Validator is the engine's pure evaluator. It compares the contract with the evidence and returns findings (one per problem) plus coverage (what it could and could not check). It is stateless: the operator owns evidence collection and status writes.
  4. Controller coordinates the pipeline, writes the PactoRevision snapshots and updates the Pacto resource status with structured conditions, a contract compliance status and Prometheus metrics.

The revisions in step 1 accumulate, and they are keyed by content. The name is <pacto>-<version>-<7 hex of the sha256 of the contract YAML>, and the controller looks it up before creating it. Reconciling the same bytes a thousand times therefore produces one PactoRevision. Republishing a different contract under the same tag produces a second one alongside it, which is how a mutated tag becomes visible after the fact. status.currentRevision names the one in force. Each revision is set as a child of its Pacto, so deleting the Pacto garbage-collects its whole history with it. Nothing else prunes them, so a long-lived resource whose contract changes often keeps every distinct version it has ever seen.

flowchart LR
    CR[Pacto CR] --> Loader
    Observer -- reads --> API[(K8s API)]
    Loader --> Validator
    Observer --> Validator
    Validator --> Status[Status + Conditions]
    Validator --> Metrics[Prometheus metrics]

docs.title: What it reports
docs.text:
The operator sets status.contractStatus on each Pacto resource to one of six values (Compliant, Warning, NonCompliant, Reference, Unknown, Invalid), derived from the findings. It measures whether the service matches its contract. Health is a separate question. The schema (CRD) accepts a seventh, NotEvaluated, which the operator never writes. Runtime observations lists every status, finding code and what is observed.

Unknown here means checked, and one required claim of the contract could not be decided: a verdict about this contract. Elsewhere in Pacto, unknown describes how much of the world an answer saw (see Knowledge). The two are separate fields.

Alongside the status the operator exports five Prometheus gauges. The names, labels and the scrape permission you have to grant yourself are in Scraping the metrics.

Start with Install the Kubernetes operator.

docs.title: Quickstart with a bundled registry and sign-in
docs.text:
For an evaluation cluster, the chart ships the profile values-quickstart.yaml. It installs zot as an in-cluster registry with persistence and native OCI referrers, installs Dex as the dashboard's identity provider and turns on delivery with its recorder writing to zot. The chart generates the dashboard's client secret, the first sign-in password and the recorder's signing key at install and keeps them across upgrades.

helm pull oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator --untar
helm install pacto-operator ./pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace \
  -f pacto-operator/values-quickstart.yaml

The profile is for evaluation. zot and Dex speak plain HTTP, zot accepts anonymous pushes, Dex keeps sessions in memory and the operator can read the recorder's key. The registry host in the profile names the namespace pacto-operator-system; to install elsewhere, edit it in the file first.

The browser and the dashboard reach Dex at the same issuer URL, http://pacto-dex:5556/dex. To sign in, point that name at your machine, forward both Services and read the password of admin@example.com:

echo "127.0.0.1 pacto-dex" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system port-forward svc/pacto-dex 5556:5556 &
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system port-forward svc/pacto-dashboard 3000:3000 &
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system get secret pacto-dashboard-oidc \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d

Per-person Kubernetes RBAC needs the API server to trust the Dex issuer through structured authentication with the profile's claim mapping (email and groups, no prefixes). No chart can set that; kind takes it at cluster creation. The API server also accepts only an https issuer, so the bundled Dex needs TLS first. Until then, a Dex sign-in completes and every request is refused, so use token sign-in, which the profile turns on. A token session decides on no held change, so approve with pacto delivery approve (approve or unblock a change).

docs.title: Health and metrics checks
docs.text: The profile keeps the chart's runtime defaults. The metrics dimension of a contract that declares metrics reads Unsupported, and health is read passively, so Pacto can confirm it but never contradict it. To check both actively, add to helm install --set controller.enableProbing=true --set controller.enableMetricsObservation=true; see Opt-in features.

docs.title: Runtime conformance on Kubernetes
docs.text: Runtime conformance checks what a service does on the network against its contract, and reports only what it can prove. On Kubernetes the operator runs it for you: it deploys pacto agent on every node as an optional DaemonSet, the node agent, and merges what it sees with what the Kubernetes API says. It is off by default.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
Take a Deployment whose readiness probe passes but whose process never opened its port. Without the node agent, Kubernetes says the interface is up. With it, the Pacto status says:

contractStatus: NonCompliant
findings:
  - code: INTERFACE_ABSENT
    severity: error
    subject: interface/api
    evidenceRefs:
      - source: k8s
        collector: k8s-observer+ebpf    # the kernel decided this result
        observedAt: "2026-10-18T09:12:44Z"
        detectedAt: "2026-10-18T09:12:44Z"

The node agent adds three findings the Kubernetes API alone cannot produce:

Finding What happened INTERFACE_ABSENT endpoints are ready but no backing pod listens on the interface port DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE the pod only fails to connect to a declared dependency DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED the pod talks to another Pacto service that no dependency declares (a warning)

When the kernel view is incomplete, Pacto says so with Insufficient, Stale or Failed. Silence is never a violation.

Three more checks need no node agent: the interface protocol, how far an interface is exposed and which version a dependency runs. They are listed under complementary checks.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
You need, on every node that runs target pods:

  • Linux 5.11 or later with BTF. The agent pod has no SYS_RESOURCE capability, so on 5.8 to 5.10 the program loads only when the container runtime's RLIMIT_MEMLOCK already covers its maps. Otherwise the node reads Failed. BTF is type information the kernel publishes at /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux; current distribution kernels ship it. The agent runs on kubernetes.io/os: linux nodes only.
  • The agent needs hostPID, the node's /sys/fs/cgroup read-only, root and the BPF, PERFMON and SYS_PTRACE capabilities; everything else is dropped. Only the privileged Pod Security level admits that, so it runs in its own namespace (nodeAgent.namespace, default pacto-node-agent), which the chart creates privileged. The release namespace keeps its own level.
nodeAgent:
  enabled: true          # also turns on controller kernel evidence
controller:
  enableProbing: true    # the protocol fact; also active health probing

nodeAgent.publishInterval sets how often the agent reports. controller.kernelEvidence.namespace and staleness cover an agent you run yourself. Turning the agent off removes its namespace and everything in it. The Helm reference lists every value.

docs.title: What the node agent observes
docs.text:
The agent is a DaemonSet (one pod per node) that the operator creates in the agent namespace. Each pod runs pacto agent --sink kubernetes from the Pacto runtime image (ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard, the image the Evidence Server runs; --node-agent-image overrides it). It uses eBPF: a small program the kernel runs safely when an event happens. The program hooks the kernel tracepoint inet_sock_set_state, which fires when a TCP socket changes state, and keeps four events:

  • a socket starts listening;
  • a listening socket closes;
  • an outbound connection is established;
  • an outbound connection fails before it is established.

Each event is matched to a pod through the cgroup that created the socket, which names the pod, or else through its network namespace, the private network stack every pod gets. The agent maps network namespaces to pod UIDs by reading /proc: a process's cgroup path names its pod, and its ns/net link names its network namespace. It also reads the listening sockets from /proc at start and again every resync (60 seconds by default), so an event lost in between heals at the next resync.

The agent keeps its node's view in a NodeRuntimeObservation object named after the node. The view holds, per pod, its listeners and, per peer address and port, the count of successful and failed connections and when each last happened. Peers expire ten minutes after their last attempt.

Every publish interval (30 seconds by default) it renews a Lease named after its node, the heartbeat the operator reads, and rewrites the object only when the view changed (details).

docs.title: What it collects
docs.text:
The node agent collects what every pacto agent collects (see what Pacto watches). It opens no port, and its Role lets it write only NodeRuntimeObservation objects and Leases in the agent namespace, so its evidence never leaves the cluster API.

An admission policy keeps each agent to the objects named after its own node (details).

docs.title: How the evidence flows
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    K["Kernel: TCP socket events"] --> A["Node agent<br/>one pod per node"]
    P["/proc baseline and resync"] --> A
    A --> N["NodeRuntimeObservation<br/>one per node"]
    API["Kubernetes API"] --> O["Operator observer"]
    N --> O
    O --> E["EvidenceSet"]
    E --> V["validation.Evaluate"]
    V --> S["Pacto status"]

Each time the operator checks a Pacto, it lists the target workload's running pods, finds each pod's node object and merges what it says into the interface and dependency observations. The result is one EvidenceSet (the list of observations about the service), judged by the same engine as without the agent. Only node objects named after their node and carrying the agent's labels count. Node objects trigger no check of their own; the periodic requeue reads them.

The collector field of a finding names where its evidence came from: k8s-observer is the Kubernetes API alone, k8s-observer+ebpf means kernel evidence decided or qualified the result and ebpf means only the kernel saw it. The runtime observations reference lists them.

docs.title: Merge rules
docs.text:
The kernel can confirm and, with complete coverage, contradict. Silence alone is never a contradiction.

Dimension Kernel says Result Interface a ready backing pod listens on the target container port present Interface endpoints are ready, every ready backing pod has complete coverage and none listens absent, through the stabilization window, then INTERFACE_ABSENT Interface a ready pod has partial coverage, a failed node or a stale node Insufficient, Failed or Stale: never present, never absent Interface a ready endpoint names no pod, or names one that is not running Insufficient unless another backing pod listens: never absent Interface no ready endpoints, or a UDP or SCTP Service port the kernel is not consulted Dependency a recent success to the provider's cluster IP or an endpoint IP, not older than the last failure reachable Dependency a recent failure newer than the last success, and no address with a recent success unreachable, through the stabilization window, then DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE Dependency a recent success while the provider has no ready endpoint Insufficient: the kernel never overrides a Kubernetes negative Dependency no recent connection the Kubernetes result stands, unless it is inconclusive and a node is stale or failed Other Pacto services a recent success, by the same rule, to a Service of another Pacto target that no declared dependency resolves to DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED, a warning

The backing pods are the pods the ready EndpointSlice endpoints for the port name, so a canary the Service selects outside the workload counts. When no endpoint names a pod, the workload's pods stand in, and they can confirm the interface but never contradict it.

Pacto judges connections per peer address from their timestamps and ignores the lifetime counts. Recent means within the staleness bound below. A timestamp from before the pod started is ignored, because a reused network namespace can carry another pod's history. With several pods the worst coverage wins: stale, then failed, then partial. DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED is a warning, because a contract's dependency list may be incomplete, so it never makes a contract NonCompliant. Pacto skips it entirely while a declared dependency resolves to no Pacto target, by ref or by name (a local or other non-OCI ref, or an OCI ref no Pacto carries): that dependency could be the service the pod reached, so reporting it would be a false positive.

docs.title: Freshness and coverage
docs.text:
A pod's kernel view is usable at one of four levels:

  • Complete: the node object is fresh, collection is Running, the pod has its own network namespace, a /proc baseline was taken after the pod started, no event was dropped since and no bound was hit.
  • Partial: readable but incomplete: collection is Degraded, the pod shares the host network namespace, it is not mapped yet or it was truncated.
  • Failed: the node's collection state is Failed, which reads as COLLECTION_FAILED.
  • Stale: no node object, or no heartbeat (Lease renewal, else lastPublished) within the staleness bound, which reads as EVIDENCE_STALE. The bound is three publish intervals unless controller.kernelEvidence.staleness sets one.

Degraded carries the reason PodLimitExceeded, ResyncFailed or EventsDropped. Failed carries LoadFailed, AttachFailed or RingBufferFailed; a kernel without BTF fails to load, and one older than 5.11 can fail to load.

docs.title: Complementary checks
docs.text:
These checks refine an interface or dependency the operator has already observed. Each is judged only when that parent observation is Observed (and, for interfaces, present). A check with no usable fact is listed in status.evaluationCoverage.unverified and never changes the contract status, so a cluster without probing keeps its status.

Contract field Fact and source Contradiction interfaces[].type protocol probe: the operator sends an HTTP/2 preface to the Service port and classifies the answer as http1, http2, tls or other; needs controller.enableProbing openapi answering other, or grpc answering http1 or other: INTERFACE_PROTOCOL_MISMATCH interfaces[].visibility exposure, see how exposure is decided an internal interface (the default) that is external: INTERFACE_VISIBILITY_MISMATCH dependencies[].compatibility the provider's status.contract.version from its Pacto resource; when several targets match the ref, the one version inside the range picks the target a version outside the range: DEPENDENCY_VERSION_MISMATCH, an error for a required dependency and a warning for an optional one state.persistence.scope a writable PersistentVolumeClaim volume in the pod template is shared when more than one pod runs at once (Deployment, ReplicaSet or StatefulSet replicas, Job parallelism); StatefulSet volume claim templates give each replica its own claim; a claim opened or mounted read-only everywhere is ignored local scope with a shared claim: PERSISTENCE_MISMATCH

docs.title: How exposure is decided
docs.text:
Exposure is external only on positive evidence of an address outside private networks: a public spec.externalIPs entry, a LoadBalancer Service with no internal load balancer annotation whose status carries a public IP or a hostname not starting with internal-, or an Ingress in the Service's namespace that routes to the port and whose status carries such an address. Private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT and unique local addresses are not public. Exposure is internal only for a ClusterIP Service that no Ingress or HTTPRoute routes to. Everything else is unknown: a NodePort Service (the node network may be private), an internal or address-less LoadBalancer, an address-less Ingress, any HTTPRoute (the gateway's address is not read) and a failed read. The internal annotations recognized are GKE (networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type and cloud.google.com/load-balancer-type: Internal), AWS (service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-internal and aws-load-balancer-scheme: internal), Azure, IBM, Oracle, OpenStack and Alibaba Cloud.

tls, no answer and asyncapi leave the type unverified. Unknown exposure leaves visibility unverified. A public interface seen only in-cluster stays unverified too, because a gateway the operator cannot see may expose it. shared scope with per-replica claims stays unverified, because the shared store may live outside the cluster. The field coverage reference has the rule for every contract field.

docs.title: Resource bounds
docs.text:
Bound Value CPU request and limit 50m and 200m (nodeAgent.resources) Memory request and limit 64Mi and 256Mi, which also pays for the ring buffer Ring buffer 256 KiB; a full buffer drops events and counts them Pods per node 256 Listeners per pod 64 Connection peers per pod and per node 128 and 4096 Peer retention ten minutes after the last attempt

A pod past a bound is marked truncated, which makes its coverage partial.

docs.title: Try it on kind
docs.text:
make test-acceptance-kind-runtime-conformance builds the operator, starts a kind cluster with the node agent and runs every scenario on this page against a real kernel, including the "ready but nothing listening" case above. make e2e-runtime-conformance-kind-up does the same and keeps the cluster, so you can run kubectl get pactos -A yourself. The other tests:

  • make -C integrations/kubernetes test-ebpf loads and attaches the real program in a privileged container (needs Docker).
  • go test ./pkg/validation/ -run TestFieldCoverage checks the field coverage inventory against the schema and the tests it names.

The limitations page lists what this evidence cannot see.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
When a Pacto shows a status you did not expect, this page tells you why and what to change. Start with the status the operator wrote on the Pacto object: it holds the verdict, the stage that produced it and one finding per problem.

kubectl describe pacto <name>
kubectl get pacto <name> -o yaml                   # the whole object
kubectl get pacto <name> -o yaml | yq '.status'    # only the status, if you have yq

Runtime observations lists every finding code referenced below.

docs.title: Reading the conditions
docs.text:
status.contractStatus says what the verdict is. The conditions say which stage produced it, which is usually what you need to fix. There are three, and each one's reason is a fixed identifier you can match on:

Condition Status Reason What happened ContractValid True Parsed The contract loaded and passed validation. ContractValid True ReferenceOnly Same, and the contract declares no spec.target, so nothing further is observed. ContractValid False Invalid The contract loaded and is structurally wrong. status.validation names the errors. ContractValid Unknown Unavailable The contract could not be obtained -- registry unreachable, auth rejected, tag not found. Validity is undetermined, so status.validation is deliberately left empty. RuntimeObserved True Found Runtime evidence was collected. RuntimeObserved False ObservationFailed A cluster query errored. The message carries the API error. ReadinessSatisfied True Satisfied score >= minScore. ReadinessSatisfied False BelowMinScore The gate is not met. The message breaks the score down by claim status. ReadinessSatisfied False Expired The assessment is past its expires: date, which scores it 0.

Two absences are meaningful:

  • RuntimeObserved is missing entirely when the reconciliation stopped before observing: a reference-only contract, or one that failed at ContractValid. No observation ran, so none failed.
  • ReadinessSatisfied is missing entirely when the contract declares no readiness: block.

Conditions are sticky: each keeps its lastTransitionTime while its status is unchanged, and carries the observedGeneration it was set from. A condition whose observedGeneration is behind metadata.generation was not re-evaluated on the latest spec.

docs.title: Reading the events
docs.text:
